title: IL-29 · ThreatLocker Zero-Trust CBT with AI — Cybersecurity Mastery Bootcamp
tagline: Zero-trust endpoint defense at operator depth — ThreatLocker mastery, MIT-grade security reasoning, AI-augmented triage, and interview-day readiness.
blurb: IL-29 is a cybersecurity mastery bootcamp built around zero-trust endpoint defense: you will operate allowlisting, ringfencing, elevation control, storage control, network control, and Detect triage the way a Cyber Hero support operator does — under pressure, with evidence, and with every decision documented. MIT 6.858 computer-security concepts, machine-learning anomaly detection, and the prereq math spine give your decisions first-principles depth, while independent-preparation tracks for Security+, CySA+, CISSP, GSEC, MIT xPRO, and the Google/IBM certificates convert that depth into credentials. The course culminates in a ThreatLocker panel interview simulation and two portfolio capstones, so you walk into the October 13 interview already operating at the job's bar.
honestyNote: This is an independent preparation and practice course aligned to publicly published exam objectives and a real interview experience. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by ThreatLocker, MIT xPRO, MIT OpenCourseWare, CompTIA, ISC2, GIAC, SANS, Google, or IBM; it confers no certificate and grants no credentials. Exam facts (domains, weights, question counts, durations, passing scores, program lengths and prices) reflect publicly published objectives and program descriptions as of October 2026 — always verify against the vendor's current published objectives before booking. ThreatLocker product descriptions reflect publicly documented platform capabilities; portal workflows are taught generically and no affiliation with ThreatLocker is claimed. Hours are honest estimates from the module workload formula.
objectives: Operate a zero-trust endpoint defense platform at operator depth: allowlisting, ringfencing, elevation control, storage control, network control, Detect triage, and centralized Defender configuration.
Triage blocked actions like a Cyber Hero: read the denied event, classify severity, investigate the process tree, disposition every alert, and escalate with evidence.
Run break-fix under default-deny: diagnose hash-mismatch and policy breaks, scope the impact, fix through the exception workflow, and close the loop with process changes.
Execute the incident response lifecycle (NIST 800-61): scope, contain, verify, preserve evidence, escalate, and write post-incident reports with hardening actions.

Apply MIT 6.858 computer-security concepts — threat models, control hijacking, privilege separation, sandboxing, web security, TLS, side channels, authentication, privacy, security economics — to endpoint defense decisions.
Build and evaluate ML anomaly detectors and use AI triage copilots safely: AI proposes, the human disposes, and every AI claim is verified against primary evidence.
Use the prereq math spine (logic, boolean/bitwise, number theory, probability, linear algebra) to reason about policies, crypto, and detection statistics including Bayes' theorem for alert triage.

Prepare independently for CompTIA Security+ SY0-701, CySA+ CS0-003, ISC2 CISSP, GIAC GSEC, the MIT xPRO Professional Certificate in Cybersecurity, and the Google/IBM cybersecurity certificates — aligned to their publicly published objectives.
Map adversary behavior to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and explain 'why we blocked this' to technical and non-technical stakeholders.
Walk into the ThreatLocker IT Infrastructure Specialist panel interview with operator-grade technical depth, STAR behavioral stories from real history, and a same-day execution plan.
arc: IL-29 takes you from zero-trust theory to operator reality: first you master each ThreatLocker module as a working tool, then you learn to run it under pressure through break-fix triage, Detect alert queues, and live incident scenarios. MIT 6.858 concepts, AI-assisted SOC workflows, and the prereq math spine give you the reasoning depth behind every policy decision, while the certification tracks and the ThreatLocker panel simulation convert that depth into credentials and a job offer. You finish with two portfolio capstones and an operator gate you can clear twice in a row — the bar for interview-day confidence.

drills.title: Scenario: trace the attack, name the gate

handsOnLab.brief: You will inventory a real Windows machine's running processes with PowerShell, classify each binary as known-good or unknown using signature and publisher data, and write the minute-by-minute decision trace showing which NIST-model gate would fire against a simulated attack chain. This turns the architecture from a diagram into an operator artifact.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every binary in the CSV has a classification; every attack step in trace.md names a specific gate and verdict; no blanket path exceptions remain in policy-decisions.md.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A folder containing process-inventory.csv, policy-decisions.md, and trace.md — your machine's allowlist baseline plus the attack trace.
steps: On a Windows test machine, open PowerShell as Administrator and run Get-Process | Select-Object Name, Path | Sort-Object Name | Format-Table -AutoSize to list running processes.
For each unique executable path, run Get-AuthenticodeSignature <path> and record the SignerCertificate subject (publisher) and Status (Valid/NotSigned).
Export the inventory to CSV: build a small loop writing Name, Path, Publisher, SignatureStatus to process-inventory.csv.
Classify each row: KNOWN-GOOD (valid signature from a recognized publisher AND business-needed), REVIEW (valid signature but unknown publisher or unneeded), UNKNOWN (unsigned or hash-only).
Write policy-decisions.md: for each REVIEW/UNKNOWN binary, write the allow or deny decision with a one-line justification, as if you were the Policy Engine.

Draft the attack trace: on paper or in trace.md, write the 9:02 AM macro attack from the notes against YOUR inventory — name which of your actual running apps would be the initial vector and which gate fires at each step.
Identify your three riskiest REVIEW items and write the ringfence rule each would need (e.g., 'deny child process creation for <app>').
Write the offline-posture decision: if the agent cannot reach the policy server, do new executions fail closed or open on your design? Justify in two sentences.
Review policy-decisions.md and flag any rule shaped like 'allow everything in <folder>' — rewrite it as a scoped rule.
Read the finished trace.md end to end and confirm every attack step meets a named gate with a verdict.
handsOnLab.title: Build the deny-by-default decision trace

choices: On the protected machine the attack dies at the first gate it meets — ringfence blocks the macro's child-process spawn or allowlisting blocks the unknown binary before it runs, Detect alerts at the attempt stage, and network/storage gates contain lateral movement and exfiltration; on the default-allow machine nothing evaluates the payload until a signature fires after encryption has started.
Both machines behave the same until the antivirus signature updates, since allowlisting is just another signature list.
The protected machine encrypts faster because the agent consumes CPU; the default-allow machine is safer due to lower overhead.
The protected machine requires the user to approve each block in real time, so the outcome depends on the user clicking correctly.

notes.title: What 'zero trust' actually means
NIST SP 800-207: the logical model (PE, PA, PEP)
Default-allow vs default-deny: the economics of the two models

notes.body: Assume breach is the psychological core of zero trust: design as though the attacker is already inside. This is not pessimism; it is engineering discipline. If you assume the perimeter will fail — because it will, via phishing, a vendor compromise, or a zero-day — then every internal system must defend itself, every lateral path must be gated, and every credential must be treated as stealable. The practical consequences for an endpoint operator are concrete. First, blast radius: assume any single machine can be compromised, so design so that one compromised machine cannot become ten. That means workstation-to-workstation traffic is denied by default (you will build this in M06), local admin is removed (M04), and data cannot walk out on a USB stick (M05). Second, no implicit trust between services: the accounting app server does not trust requests just because they arrive from the office subnet; each request is authenticated and authorized. Third, continuous diagnostics and mitigation: you do not audit quarterly and hope; you monitor the enforcement points continuously and treat every blocked action as a signal (that signal pipeline is M07). Worked example: two designs for a 200-seat company. Design A trusts the LAN: flat network, local admins everywhere, file shares open to 'Authenticated Users.' One phished credential gives the attacker the workstation, the admin hash gives them the domain, the open shares give them the data. Mean time from one click to domain-wide ransomware: hours. Design B assumes breach: workstations cannot talk to each other, no local admins, applications allowlisted and ringfenced, USB blocked, egress filtered. The same phished credential yields one isolated workstation whose malicious child processes are blocked at launch, whose lateral movement hits closed ports, and whose exfiltration hits closed egress. The attacker still got in — assume breach concedes that — but the breach stays a single-machine event instead of a company event. The operator gotcha is treating assume breach as a slogan on a slide. It is a test you run against every design: 'if this machine is already owned, what can the attacker reach from here?' If the answer is 'everything,' you do not have zero trust yet; you have a perimeter with extra steps. Make that question a habit and you will naturally produce the policies this course teaches you to build.  One more operational habit: test your assume-breach posture with tabletop exercises, not just architecture diagrams. Pick a scenario — 'the CFO's laptop is compromised right now' — and walk the team through what the attacker can reach from that machine in the first hour. If the honest answer includes the file server, the backup system, or the domain controller, the design has gaps regardless of what the slide deck claims. Run this exercise quarterly; the gaps it finds become the next quarter's policy projects, which is how assume breach turns from a mindset into a roadmap.
notes.title: Assume breach: the mindset that makes the architecture work

notes.body: In the NIST model the PEP is abstract — it can be a gateway, a proxy, an agent. On the endpoint, the application-control agent is the PEP for the most fundamental question a machine can be asked: may this code execute? Everything else the platform does hangs off that gate. Allowlisting (Application Control) is deny-by-default execution: when a process launch is requested, the agent checks identity — hash, certificate, path — against policy and permits only what is explicitly allowed. Ringfencing then constrains what the allowed application may do once running: which child processes it may spawn, whether it may touch the registry, which files it may read or write, which network connections it may open. Elevation Control decides whether the application may run with administrative rights, removing standing local admin and granting just-in-time elevation per policy. Storage Control and Network Control extend the same deny-by-default logic to data paths and network paths. Detect turns every block into an alert, and Configuration Manager keeps the underlying Defender baseline from drifting. See the pattern: each module takes one abuse path and flips it from default-allow to default-deny. The operator insight is that these modules are not seven separate products; they are one policy engine applied to seven questions: may it run, what may it do, with what privilege, where may data go, where may packets go, what was blocked, and is the baseline intact? Worked example: map a single attack chain to the gates. Phishing email delivers a malicious document. Gate 1 (allowlisting): the document's embedded payload tries to drop an unknown executable — blocked, not on the allowlist. Suppose instead the payload is a malicious macro inside an allowed Office app — it passes gate 1 because Word itself is allowed. Gate 2 (ringfencing): the macro tries to spawn PowerShell — Word's ringfence denies child process creation. Suppose the macro instead tries to write to a startup folder — gate 2 denies the file write. Suppose the attacker pivots to credential theft — gate 3 (elevation): no local admin, no privileged foothold. Exfiltration over USB — gate 4 (storage): device blocked. Callback to attacker infrastructure — gate 5 (network): egress denied for the unapproved process. Every step of the kill chain meets a default-deny gate, and each block emits a Detect alert. Common gotcha: presenting the modules as overlapping or redundant. They are layered: each assumes the previous layer can be bypassed and catches what falls through. That is defense in depth expressed as policy, and it is the answer when the panel asks 'isn't allowlisting enough?'
notes.title: The endpoint as enforcement point: how allowlisting fits the model

notes.body: Let us trace the same attack against two endpoints, minute by minute, and watch where each model breaks. The scenario: at 9:02 AM, an accountant opens what looks like a vendor invoice. The document contains a malicious macro. This is a generic pattern — no exotic zero-day, just the commodity attack chain that encrypts companies every week. Against the default-allow endpoint: 9:02:14, the macro executes because Office macros are permitted and nothing evaluates the payload. 9:02:31, the macro drops invoice_helper.exe into the user's temp folder and launches it — no gate checks whether this binary is known-good. 9:03:05, the binary disables shadow copies and begins enumerating network shares; the endpoint firewall allows outbound SMB to neighbors because workstation-to-workstation traffic was never restricted. 9:04:40, it contacts its command server over HTTPS — egress is default-allow, so the callback succeeds. 9:06:12, encryption begins on local files and mapped shares. 9:07:00, the antivirus finally flags the binary by signature — forty-five seconds after the damage started, and the signature only exists because someone else was hit first. Total defender actions before detonation: zero. The model required the threat to be known, and it was not known in time. Against the default-deny endpoint: 9:02:14, the macro attempts to spawn a child process — the Office application's ringfence policy denies child process creation for winword.exe, and the attempt is logged. 9:02:15, the macro's fallback tries to write an executable to the temp folder — the ringfence denies the file write outside approved paths. 9:02:16, suppose the attacker anticipated this and the payload instead arrives as a standalone executable the user is tricked into running: the allowlisting PEP checks the binary's hash and certificate against policy — unknown, so execution is denied before a single instruction runs. 9:02:17, Detect fires an alert: blocked child-process spawn from winword.exe on ACCOUNTING-07. The SOC now has a lead at the attempt stage, not the encryption stage. 9:03:00, even if every application-layer gate somehow failed, the endpoint firewall's default-deny inbound rules block the SMB enumeration of neighbors, and egress filtering blocks the unknown binary's callback. The attack dies at the first gate it meets, and there are five gates. The teaching point is not that default-deny is magic — a sufficiently privileged, signed, allowed application abused in a permitted way can still cause harm, which is why the layers overlap. The point is the shift in who needs to be perfect: default-allow needs the defender to recognize every novel threat before it acts; default-deny needs the attacker to be running explicitly approved code behaving within its fence. Study this trace until you can whiteboard it. The panel will very likely ask some version of 'walk me through what happens when ransomware hits a protected endpoint,' and this minute-by-minute telling — attempt, block, alert, containment — is the answer that shows operator thinking instead of marketing recall.

choices: The Policy Engine, using the trust algorithm over identity, posture, and policy inputs
The Policy Enforcement Point, based on local firewall rules
The Policy Administrator, based on network location
The resource server, based on its own ACLs
quiz.explain: The PE is the brain: it evaluates policy against dynamic inputs (identity, device posture, behavior) and decides. The PEP only enforces what the PE decided via the PA — it never freelances the decision.
quiz.q: Per NIST SP 800-207, which component makes the ultimate grant/deny decision?

choices: It blocks unknown code for not being known-good, so no signature for the new sample is needed
It encrypts all unknown files automatically
It runs every program in a sandbox first
quiz.explain: This is the economics argument: default-allow must enumerate infinite badness and recognize the threat; default-deny enumerates finite goodness, so a never-before-seen binary fails closed at the gate with zero threat intel.
quiz.q: Why is default-deny structurally stronger than default-allow against novel malware?

choices: Prevent the phishing email from arriving at all
Contain the compromise to one machine: no lateral movement, no privilege escalation, no exfiltration
Disconnect the company from the internet
quiz.explain: Assume breach concedes initial compromise will happen; the architecture's job is blast-radius control — gated lateral paths, no standing admin, filtered egress — so one click stays a one-machine event.
quiz.q: An attacker phishes one user in an 'assume breach' design. What is the design's goal?

choices: The ringfence policy denying the Office macro's child-process spawn
The firewall blocking the C2 callback
quiz.explain: The attack dies at the first gate it meets: Word's ringfence denies spawning PowerShell (or writing the payload) at 9:02:14 — before any malicious code executes. The firewall and AV are later layers, not the first.
quiz.q: In the module's ransomware trace, what is the FIRST control to fire on the default-deny endpoint?

choices: Nothing — it balances security and usability
It converts the policy back to default-allow for the exact folder attackers use, defeating the model
It only affects one folder so risk is minimal
Downloads folders are already protected by the OS
quiz.explain: A blanket path exception in the highest-risk directory is default-allow wearing a costume. Attackers deliver payloads precisely to Downloads/temp. The fix is a fast approval workflow, not a hole in the policy.
quiz.q: A junior admin proposes 'allow everything in C:\Downloads so users stop filing tickets.' What is wrong with this?

choices: Encrypting traffic between PEP and resource
Weighing inputs (identity assurance, device posture, behavior, threat intel) to produce the PE's grant/deny decision
quiz.explain: The trust algorithm is the PE's decision function: it combines static policy with dynamic signals into a per-session verdict. It is about authorization logic, not encryption or malware scanning.
quiz.q: What is the trust algorithm's role in the NIST model?

choices: An allowed application can still be abused (e.g., Word spawning PowerShell), so its behavior must also be constrained
Ringfencing replaces the need for an allowlist
quiz.explain: Allowing Word to run says nothing about what Word may do. Trusted-app abuse (living-off-the-land) is the standard bypass of pure allowlisting — ringfencing closes it by denying the malicious behaviors of allowed apps.
quiz.q: Why must allowlisting be paired with ringfencing rather than used alone?

choices: Users route around security (shadow IT, personal devices), creating worse unmanaged risk
The policy database grows too large
Auditors will be impressed by thoroughness
quiz.explain: Slow approvals don't increase security — they export risk outside your visibility. The operational target is minutes-to-hours for standard requests; the queue's age is a security metric, not just a service metric.
quiz.q: Your allowlist approval queue averages 6 days. What is the real risk?

choices: It is a product you purchase to replace firewalls
It is a design discipline: remove implicit trust, enforce per-session policy-driven decisions at every enforcement point
It means trusting nothing, including your own identity provider
It applies only to cloud workloads
quiz.explain: Zero trust is architecture, not a SKU: explicitly grant, narrowly scope, continuously re-verify. You still trust the IdP and policy engine — you stop trusting network location and one-time login.
quiz.q: Which statement about zero trust is correct?

choices: The whole model collapses — no decision is ever requested, so no enforcement occurs
The PA logs the bypass and blocks it retroactively
quiz.explain: The PEP is the gate in the data path. Bypass it and the PE's perfect decisions never execute — this is why agent tamper-resistance and mandatory enforcement (fail closed offline) are non-negotiable.
quiz.q: If the PEP is bypassed (code runs without consulting policy), what is the consequence?

modules.summary: Zero trust is not a product you buy; it is a design discipline that removes implicit trust from the network and from the endpoint. This module maps NIST SP 800-207's logical model (policy engine, policy administrator, policy enforcement point) to what actually runs on a workstation, and shows why deny-by-default is the only sane enforcement posture once you assume breach.

notes.body: Every block of legitimate software is a ticket, and the workflow that handles those tickets determines whether allowlisting survives contact with the business. A good approval workflow has five parts. Intake: a single channel (service desk ticket, portal request) that captures who, what, why, and the file itself or its hash — 'please allow the thing' is not an intake. Verification: the operator confirms what the software actually is — publisher certificate checked, vendor hash compared against the vendor's published value, reputation checked — through channels independent of the requester. Never verify software using the download link the user provides; fetch the vendor's published hash yourself. Decision: approve, approve-with-conditions (scoped, time-bound), or deny, made by someone with the authority and the knowledge — standard business apps by the IT lead, unsigned or unknown-publisher software by the security lead. Implementation: the rule is written with full shape — identity, scope (users/groups/machines), justification, review date — not a bare filename. Communication: the requester is told what was decided and why, because a denied user who understands the reason files better requests next time. Worked example: a designer requests a new video converter. Intake captures the vendor name and the installer hash. Verification: the operator downloads the vendor's published checksum, confirms the hash matches, checks the code signature, and finds the vendor is legitimate but the product bundles an optional adware component. Decision: approve with conditions — allow the application, ringfence it against network access it does not need, scope to the design group, 90-day review. Implementation and communication follow. The SLA is the load-bearing wall: standard requests in four business hours, emergency lane in one hour with post-hoc review. Miss the SLA repeatedly and users learn that security is the department of no — then comes shadow IT. Common gotcha: approvals without expiry on exceptions. 'Temporary' approvals that never expire are permanent rules that skipped the review. Every exception gets an owner and an expiry; the calendar, not someone's memory, enforces the review. Second gotcha: approver shopping — users re-submitting denied requests to a friendlier approver. One intake, one decision record, denials documented with reasons.  Measure the workflow or it will decay. Track three numbers weekly: median time from block to decision, the age of the oldest open request, and the approval rate by category. A median that creeps upward means the approvers are overloaded or the intake is capturing junk — either way, the business is learning that requests go nowhere. Publish the numbers to the approvers themselves; nothing fixes a slow queue like its owner seeing it in a chart. And keep an emergency lane genuinely fast: if the emergency path takes as long as the standard path, users will stop distinguishing them and every request will arrive marked urgent.
notes.title: Application approval workflows that the business can live with

notes.body: The unknown file is the moment of truth for default-deny: a binary with no rule, no library entry, and no reputation. The workflow must be fast, evidence-driven, and default to no. Step one is containment without drama: the file is blocked from executing, and a copy is preserved for analysis — you do not delete evidence you have not examined. Step two is identification: hash it, check the signature status, extract the publisher if signed, note the parent process and the delivery vector (email attachment, USB, download). Step three is independent verification: look up the hash in reputation sources, check the vendor's published hashes, and confirm the publisher through the vendor's own site — not through any link bundled with the file. Step four is the verdict, and there are only three: approve (verified legitimate, business-needed — write the full rule), approve-with-conditions (legitimate but risky — scoped, ringfenced, time-bound), or deny (unverifiable, unnecessary, or malicious — document the reason and, if malicious, escalate to incident response). Worked example: helpdesk receives 'invoice_scan.exe,' unsigned, delivered via email, hash unknown to reputation sources, and the 'vendor' has no website. Verdict: deny. The requester is told why in plain language, the file is retained per the incident process, and the ticket records the decision. Contrast: 'labelprint_driver.exe,' unsigned, needed for the warehouse printers, vendor is a real industrial company with a support line — the operator calls the vendor, confirms the published hash matches, and approves with a hash-pinned rule scoped to the warehouse machines, 90-day review, plus a note to revisit when the vendor starts signing. Common gotcha: treating 'my manager said it's fine' as verification. Authority is not evidence; the manager's approval authorizes the business need, but the file still gets the technical verification. Second gotcha: detonating unknown files on production machines 'just to see.' Unknown binaries are examined in isolated conditions or not at all — curiosity on a production endpoint is how incidents start. The discipline to internalize: every unknown file gets the same four steps, every time, because the one you skip is the one that matters.  For high-risk files, the examination happens under isolated conditions: a disposable virtual machine with no network access to production, snapshots so you can revert, and no credentials or sensitive data present. What you are looking for is behavior, not just identity — what the file tries to do when executed — and you record the observations in the ticket before deleting the VM. Never reuse the analysis VM for anything else, and never move the file to production 'because it looked fine in the sandbox.' The sandbox informs the verdict; the verdict still goes through the approval workflow with its evidence attached.

notes.body: Browsers are the hardest applications to fence because their legitimate function is the attack surface: they download untrusted content, execute scripts, and open network connections by design. The fence cannot be 'deny everything' — it must be 'allow exactly the dangerous things the function requires, and nothing else.' Start with child processes. A modern browser legitimately spawns renderer processes, GPU processes, and its own updater — these are expected children, ideally constrained to the vendor's signed binaries. What it must never spawn is a command shell, a script interpreter, or an arbitrary downloaded executable. So the child-process fence is an allowlist within the fence: the renderer/updater family is permitted, everything else is denied. Next, file writes. The browser legitimately writes downloads to the user's download folder and cache to its profile. It must not write executables to startup folders, system directories, or temp paths that double as launch points — so the file-write fence permits user-content paths and denies execution-path writes. The download folder deserves special attention: it is the highest-risk directory on the machine, and the fence should ensure downloads there cannot be executed directly (that is the allowlist's job at launch, but the fence adds the write-side constraint). Network: the browser needs web access — that is its job — but the fence can still constrain it: deny connections to non-standard ports, deny raw socket behavior, and log aggressively. The updater is the delicate part: the browser must update itself, so the updater binary gets its own narrowly scoped permission to replace the browser's files — and only the browser's files. Worked example: an exploit compromises the renderer and attempts to spawn cmd.exe. The child-process fence denies the spawn — cmd.exe is not in the expected family — and logs the attempt with the renderer as parent. The exploit's fallback tries to write a payload to the startup folder — the file-write fence denies it. The fallback's fallback tries to open a raw connection to a non-standard port — the network fence denies it. Three behaviors, three denials, one alert bundle for triage. Common gotcha: fencing the browser so tightly that updates break. A browser that cannot update becomes the vulnerability — the updater carve-out is not a weakness in the fence, it is load-bearing. Second gotcha: forgetting extensions and plugins as child-equivalents. The fence should account for what the browser is permitted to load, not just what it may spawn.
notes.title: Ringfence design: browsers

notes.body: Office applications are the most attacked and the most fenceable: their legitimate function (editing documents, crunching spreadsheets, managing mail) requires almost none of the dangerous behaviors. The baseline Office fence is strict: deny child-process creation entirely — Word, Excel, and PowerPoint have no legitimate need to launch other programs. Deny registry writes except the vendor's own settings keys — Office does not need to register system services or set Run keys. Constrain file writes to user document locations — deny writes to startup folders, system directories, and temp-execution paths. Deny network sessions except explicitly approved collaboration endpoints and the updater — Word does not need arbitrary outbound connections. Outlook is the exception that proves the rule: it legitimately needs network access to mail servers, so its network fence is scoped to the mail protocols and servers the business uses, not the open internet. Now the honest complication: macros and add-ins. Businesses run on Excel macros — the finance team's month-end workbook is a program, and fencing it naively breaks the business. The operator-grade answer is not 'allow macros' (default-allow for code) but signed-macro policy: only macros signed by approved publishers execute, and even signed macros run inside the fence — they still cannot spawn children or write outside document paths. Worked example: the accounting team's month-end macro workbook. The workbook's macros are signed with the company's code-signing certificate. Policy: allow signed macros from the corporate publisher, and the Excel fence still denies child-process creation and non-document file writes. The macro calculates, formats, and saves — all permitted. An attacker who steals the workbook and adds a shell-spawning macro faces two gates: the signature check (their modification breaks the corporate signature) and the fence (the spawn is denied regardless). Common gotcha: the 'enable all macros for the finance team' exception. That is default-allow for the most macro-attacked applications in the company, scoped to the users with the most sensitive data. If the business truly needs unsigned macros, the compensating controls are a signed-macro migration plan with a date, plus tighter fences (no child processes, no network) on the machines that run them. Second gotcha: Outlook attachments. The fence constrains what Outlook may do, but the attachment the user saves and double-clicks is a new execution — that is the allowlist's gate (M02), and the two layers must be designed together.  Do not forget the browser's loadable code: extensions, plugins, and helper objects execute inside the browser's context with its privileges. A malicious or compromised extension bypasses the child-process fence entirely because it never spawns anything — it simply acts. Your browser policy should therefore govern the extension inventory too: an approved extension list, ideally centrally managed, with the same approval workflow as applications. An unmanaged extension ecosystem on a fenced browser is a fenced front door with the windows open.

notes.body: User Account Control is the prompt everyone loves to hate, and you need to understand exactly what it does and does not do before you layer policy over it. UAC has two prompt types. The consent prompt appears for administrators: 'Do you want to allow this app to make changes?' — a yes/no question to someone who already holds the rights. The credential prompt appears for standard users: 'Enter an administrator username and password' — a demand for credentials the user should not have. UAC's security value is real but narrow: it makes privilege use visible and gives malware one more click to socially engineer. Its weakness is structural: the decision is made by the user, at the moment, under time pressure — which is precisely when users click 'Yes' on whatever the urgent-looking installer demands. Malware has exploited this for years with fake installers that simply ask. Elevation Control moves the decision from the user to the policy. Under policy-driven elevation, the user does not get a yes/no prompt to adjudicate — the agent consults policy: is this application approved for elevation, for this user, under these conditions? If yes, it elevates with full logging. If no, it denies with full logging. The user experience actually improves: legitimate workflows elevate silently per policy instead of interrupting with prompts, while illegitimate ones are denied consistently rather than depending on the user's judgment at 4:55 PM on a Friday. Worked example: the standard-user accountant runs the approved payroll update. Old world: credential prompt, accountant calls helpdesk, helpdesk types the admin password (which the accountant shoulder-surfs), update runs. New world: the payroll updater matches the elevation policy (signed, IT-approved, ticket window), elevates without a prompt, logs the grant. Same outcome, no password shared, full audit trail. Now the attack case: malware drops a fake updater and triggers a UAC consent prompt on an admin's machine — the admin, busy, clicks Yes. Under elevation policy on a standard-user machine, there is no Yes to click: the binary is not in the elevation policy, so it is denied and logged. Common gotcha: thinking UAC 'is' the elevation control. UAC is a speed bump; policy-driven elevation is a gate. Keep UAC enabled (it still catches the unpolicied cases) but never rely on user judgment as the control. Second gotcha: 'quiet mode' UAC settings that auto-elevate. Any setting that removes the prompt without adding policy just removes the speed bump — verify UAC is at a sane level as part of the M08 Defender-plus-baseline work.
notes.title: UAC interplay: prompts are not policy

notes.body: Walk the stolen-credential scenario end to end, because this is the story the panel wants to hear and the threat the control defeats. The setup: a helpdesk technician with local admin on 200 workstations reuses a password. An attacker phishes the technician, harvests the credential, and now holds administrative rights on every machine the technician touched. Under standing admin, the attacker's next moves are textbook: authenticate to workstations with the stolen credential, read credential material from each newly owned machine, escalate toward domain admin, deploy ransomware enterprise-wide. The technician's single credential was a skeleton key because the privilege was standing, broad, and reusable. Now replay with Elevation Control deployed. The technician is a standard user. Their daily elevated tasks — running the approved installer, the driver update — were performed through just-in-time elevation: the task elevated, the account did not. The phished credential is a standard-user credential: it authenticates, but it grants no administrative rights anywhere. The attacker's lateral movement attempts hit closed doors: no admin shares to plunder, no credential store readable, no remote admin tools permitted by Network Control policy. To escalate, the attacker must now defeat the elevation policy itself — requesting elevation for an unapproved binary, which is denied and logged, generating the Detect alert that starts the incident response at the attempt stage. The blast radius collapses from 'the enterprise' to 'one standard-user session.' Worked example with the workflow: the attacker, holding the phished standard credential, submits an elevation request for their payload through the helpdesk channel (the only path). Identity verification fails — the requester cannot prove they are the technician under duress procedures — and even a social-engineered approval would only elevate the named application for a time-bound window, not the attacker's session. Every step is logged. Common gotcha: believing elevation control replaces credential hygiene. It does not — the phished credential still grants the user's data and email. What it does is cap the damage: credential theft without standing privilege is a contained incident, not an enterprise one. Pair it with phishing-resistant authentication and the attacker's path narrows to nearly nothing. Second gotcha: the break-glass account. You will keep one sealed emergency admin credential — and its use must fire an immediate alert, because in a no-standing-admin world, any use of it is an exceptional event worth waking someone for.  Assume the attacker also steals session tokens, not just passwords — tokens can be replayed without the password ever being known. This is why the control pairs with session hygiene: short token lifetimes, and elevation decisions that re-verify rather than trusting an existing session blindly. The principle is the same as everywhere in this course: standing artifacts — passwords, tokens, privileges — are what attackers reuse. Shrink what stands, time-bound what is granted, and log every grant so the reuse window is visible.

notes.body: Legitimate business needs removable media, and the policy must serve them without becoming a hole. The carve-out pattern has four elements: company ownership, encryption, registration, and named roles. The field technician who images machines on customer sites genuinely needs a bootable USB drive — so the company issues it: a company-owned, hardware-encrypted drive, registered by serial number to the named technician, with read-write allowed by policy. If the drive is lost, the revocation procedure runs: the serial is blocked, the exposure is assessed (what data was on it — the answer should be 'nothing sensitive, by policy'), and a replacement is issued. Contrast with the hole version: 'field techs may use USB drives' — personal sticks, unencrypted, unregistered, unrevocable. The other common carve-outs follow the same pattern. The sales rep presenting at a client site: read-only access for presentations from a registered drive, time-bound to the trip, no write permission — the function needs read, so read is what is granted. The executive with the board presentation: same pattern, scoped to the event. The IT backup role: registered external drives, IT machines only, with the backup software's identity in the allowlist so only the backup process may write. Each carve-out states the role, the registered devices, the permitted direction (read, write, or both), the scope, and the review date — and each is reviewed on schedule, because roles change and drives get lost. Worked example: the lost-drive drill. A field tech reports their encrypted drive missing. Step one: block the serial in policy — the drive is now unusable on any company machine even if found. Step two: exposure assessment — pull the issuance record: what was provisioned on it? (Imaging tools and drivers; no customer data, per the provisioning standard.) Step three: document the incident, reissue, and review whether the provisioning standard held. The drill is the proof that the carve-out was engineered, not just permitted. Common gotcha: carve-out creep. 'The field techs have USB, why can't sales?' — because the exception was scoped to a role with a demonstrated need, and convenience is not a need. Every expansion request goes through the same four-element test. Second gotcha: encrypted-but-unregistered. Encryption without registration means you cannot revoke the specific device — the policy cannot name what it does not know. Registration is what makes the carve-out manageable.  Standardize what goes on the issued drives. The provisioning checklist should state exactly what is installed (imaging tools, drivers, the approved transfer utility), what is forbidden (customer data at rest — the drive is a transport, not storage), and how the drive is labeled and tracked (asset tag tied to the serial in the register). When a drive is lost, this standard is what makes the exposure assessment fast: 'per the provisioning standard, no customer data was on it' is an answer you can give confidently only if the standard exists and is followed. Audit the issued drives annually against the checklist.
notes.title: Legitimate carve-outs: encrypted, registered, named

notes.body: Every blocked storage attempt is a signal, and the incident walkthrough turns the signal into a verdict. The scenario: at 3:12 PM, the SOC receives a Detect alert — blocked USB mass-storage write on WORKSTATION-23, user j.chen, attempted files: \fileserver\finance\client_master.xlsx and two more. Step one is triage, and triage starts with context, not conclusions. Pull the alert's full context: device ID and whether the device is registered, the user's role and group, the exact file paths, the timestamp, and the user's recent alert history. Step two is pattern assessment: is this a first-time single attempt (possibly curiosity or a mistake) or part of a pattern (repeated attempts, multiple machines, off-hours)? Check the user's history for prior blocked storage, network, or execution alerts — a cluster across modules is far more significant than an isolated event. Step three is the user contact, handled as an interview, not an accusation: 'We saw a blocked write to a USB device on your machine this afternoon — can you walk me through what you were trying to do?' Innocent explanations are common: the new hire who did not know the policy, the manager trying to work from home, the misconfigured backup script. Step four is the verdict and it has three branches. Benign: document the explanation, provide the approved workflow (the secure file-transfer process), close the ticket. Policy violation without malice: document, retrain, and consider whether the workflow gap that drove the attempt needs fixing — repeated 'violations' often signal a broken legitimate process. Malicious or suspicious: escalate to incident response — isolate the machine, preserve the logs, image if warranted, and begin the insider-threat procedure per company policy. Step five is the feedback loop: whatever the verdict, the policy learns — a confusing block message gets rewritten, a missing legitimate workflow gets built, a new device class gets a rule. Worked example of the pattern that matters: j.chen's single blocked attempt turns out to be the third this week, each on a different workstation, each targeting finance files, each after 6 PM. No single alert is conclusive; the pattern across time, machines, and targets is the finding. That is why the walkthrough insists on history: the SOC triages patterns, not just events. Common gotcha: treating every block as an incident. Alert fatigue kills SOCs — the triage workflow exists to spend investigation effort proportional to the pattern's seriousness. Second gotcha: skipping the user interview. Logs tell you what happened; only the human tells you why — and 'why' is what separates the training opportunity from the insider case.

steps: On a Windows test machine, run Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalPort, OwningProcess | Sort-Object LocalPort -Unique to list listening TCP ports.
For each listening port, resolve the owning process: Get-Process -Id <PID> | Select-Object Name, Path — record process name and path.
Classify each listener: EXPECTED (system services, approved apps), REVIEW (unknown process listening — investigate), REMOVE (unneeded service — disable it).
Check UDP listeners too: Get-NetUDPEndpoint | Select-Object LocalPort, OwningProcess — classify the same way.
For each EXPECTED listener, write the firewall rule it needs: port, protocol, allowed remote scope (e.g., 'loopback only,' 'management subnet only,' 'local subnet'), and justification.
Write the default rules first: deny all inbound, deny workstation-to-workstation (SMB 445, RDP 3389, WinRM 5985/5986 between peers), then add your scoped exceptions above them.
Write the egress baseline: allow web (80/443) for approved browsers/apps, allow DNS to the company resolvers, deny-by-default egress for unknown processes.
Test one rule live: use New-NetFirewallRule to block outbound for a test process, verify with Test-NetConnection that the connection fails, then remove the rule.
Document the dynamic-ACL concept for two of your rules: under what condition does the port open (e.g., 'while the approved backup agent runs') and when does it close.
Write the troubleshooting runbook: app breaks after firewall change — identify the blocked flow (log), check the owning process, verify the destination, write the scoped exception.
Read the finished rule set as an attacker on the LAN: name which of your allowed rules you would abuse for lateral movement — then tighten the scope of the riskiest one.

notes.body: If lateral movement is the attacker's expansion, the command-and-control callback is their lifeline: the compromised machine must talk to the attacker's infrastructure to receive instructions, exfiltrate data, or download stage two. Network Control cuts the lifeline with egress filtering — outbound connections gated by process identity. The rule is simple: approved processes may reach approved destinations; unknown processes reach nothing. When the M01 ransomware tried to contact its server over HTTPS at 9:04:40, the egress policy evaluated the owning process: unknown binary, no rule — denied. The callback failed before the first byte, and the attempt became a Detect alert naming the process. Note what this does to the attacker's economics. Without egress filtering, any code that runs gets a free phone line home. With it, the attacker must hijack an approved process's legitimate connection — possible (browser injection, for example) but far harder and noisier than a direct callback. The destination side matters too: even approved processes should not reach arbitrary destinations. The browser may reach the web — that is its job — but the backup agent should reach only the backup infrastructure, the updater only the vendor's endpoints. This is the network equivalent of ringfencing: the allowed app gets the network scope its function needs, nothing more. Worked example: the updater compromise scenario. An attacker compromises a software vendor and trojans the update (the supply-chain nightmare). The trojaned updater is signed by the vendor, so it passes the allowlist. It tries to phone home to the attacker's server — but the updater's network fence permits only the vendor's update endpoints. Denied, logged, alerted. The supply-chain attack dies at the egress gate because the destination was never in the approved set. This is defense in depth paying off: the layer that failed (identity) is caught by the layer that constrains behavior (network scope). Common gotcha: 'allow all outbound HTTPS' as the egress policy. HTTPS to anywhere is a callback channel with encryption — the attacker's favorite. Egress policy must be per-process and per-destination-class, or it is not a policy. Second gotcha: DNS. Egress filtering on connections without DNS filtering leaves the DNS-tunneling path open — the complete design filters both, and the M07 triage workflow treats anomalous DNS as the signal it is.  Treat DNS as part of the egress policy, not as someone else's problem. Malware that cannot open a direct connection will try DNS tunneling — encoding data in DNS queries — which sails through a firewall that filters connections but not name resolution. The complete design points endpoints at company resolvers, logs and inspects DNS queries, and treats anomalous DNS (high entropy, unusual query rates, tunneling patterns) as the detection signal it is. The M07 triage workflow should include a DNS-history check for any host under investigation.
notes.title: Blocking C2: cutting the lifeline with egress filtering

notes.body: Servers and workstations need opposite firewall postures, and applying the wrong template is a classic junior mistake. Workstations consume: they browse, they run office apps, they talk to servers. They almost never need to accept inbound connections — so workstation policy is default-deny inbound, period, with rare scoped exceptions (the approved remote-support tool, the management agent's window). Servers serve: the web server must accept inbound 80/443, the file server must accept SMB from its clients, the domain controller must accept authentication traffic. Server policy is therefore scoped-allow inbound per service: each listening service gets a rule naming the ports, the permitted sources, and nothing else. The discipline is identical — least privilege — but the shape inverts: workstations deny nearly everything inbound, servers allow precisely what they serve. Worked example: the mis-templated web server. A new web server accidentally receives the workstation firewall template: inbound 80/443 denied, and the site is down. The fix is not 'open everything' — it is the server template: allow TCP 80/443 inbound from the load balancer and the monitoring hosts, allow admin ports (RDP/SSH/WinRM) from the jump host only, deny everything else, and deny server-to-workstation initiation except the management paths. Conversely, the workstation that someone 'fixed' by applying the server template now accepts inbound SMB from the subnet — a lateral-movement gift. The rule: the template follows the role, and role changes trigger policy review. The management-plane design deserves its own attention: servers need administration, and administration needs paths. The correct pattern is the jump host (or privileged access workstation): admin protocols are permitted only from the hardened jump host to the servers, never from workstations to servers directly, and never between servers except the specific service traffic. This turns the admin path into a chokepoint you can monitor, log, and protect — instead of a mesh of standing admin access. Common gotcha: 'the server needs internet access' as a blanket statement. Servers need specific destinations (update servers, vendor endpoints, monitoring) — each named, each scoped. A server with unrestricted outbound is a C2 launchpad waiting for a compromise. Second gotcha: forgetting the server's own workstation-like behaviors. Servers browse the web for 'quick downloads' — they should not; software comes through the deployment pipeline. The server egress policy should be as tight as its inbound.  Harden the jump host like the crown jewel it is: no internet browsing, no email, allowlisted applications only, every session logged, and access requiring phishing-resistant authentication. A compromised jump host inherits its administrative reach — the chokepoint becomes the prize. Review who holds jump-host access quarterly, because the list grows silently and every name on it is a path to every server. The jump host is the one machine where 'inconvenient security' is the entire point.

steps: Define your three alert types: (1) blocked application execution (allowlist deny), (2) blocked child-process spawn (ringfence deny), (3) blocked storage/network attempt (storage or network deny).

For each type, write the runbook section: trigger description, default severity, context to gather (process, parent, user, machine, time, history), triage steps in order, verdict branches (benign / policy violation / incident), and escalation criteria.
Set the SLAs: triage start time per severity (e.g., critical 15 min, high 1 hr, medium 4 hr) and document them in the runbook.
Write the MDR handoff template: fields for who/what/when/where, blocked action with context, checks completed, evidence links, and the specific ask.
Now triage sample alert 1: 'Blocked execution of invoice_helper.exe (unsigned, temp folder) on ACCOUNTING-07, user m.reyes, 9:02 AM.' Write the verdict with reasoning.
Triage sample alert 2: 'Blocked child-process spawn: winword.exe attempted powershell.exe on ACCOUNTING-07, user m.reyes, 9:02 AM, encoded arguments.' Write the verdict with reasoning.
Triage sample alert 3: 'Blocked USB mass-storage write on WORKSTATION-23, user j.chen, files: client_master.xlsx, 6:47 PM, third occurrence this week.' Write the verdict with reasoning.
Triage sample alert 4: 'Blocked outbound HTTPS from unknown process update_svc.exe on IT-04, 2:14 AM, destination unlisted.' Write the verdict with reasoning.

Review all five triages: confirm each cites evidence (not gut feeling), each follows the runbook's steps, and each ends with a concrete next action.

notes.body: When an alert exceeds your authority, evidence, or expertise, it goes to the managed detection and response provider — and the quality of your handoff determines the quality of their response. The MDR handoff is a package, not a forward: it contains everything the MDR analyst needs to act without re-doing your triage. The package has six fields. Who/what/when/where: user, machine, timestamp, alert ID — the identifiers that let them pull their own telemetry. The blocked action with full context: which policy fired, which process and parent, what was attempted, the arguments or targets — the factual core. What you already checked: the triage steps completed and their results — 'verified the binary hash against the vendor's published value: no match' saves them an hour. Your verdict and reasoning: incident-suspected, with the two or three facts that drove it — they will form their own judgment, but they deserve your read. The evidence links: alert IDs, log locations, ticket numbers — no 'the logs are somewhere in the console.' The specific ask: what you need — 'please confirm whether this hash appears in your wider telemetry' or 'requesting containment approval for these three machines.' Worked example: the 2 AM unknown-process alert. Handoff: 'ACCOUNTING-07, user m.reyes, 02:14 — blocked outbound HTTPS from update_svc.exe (unsigned, temp path) to unlisted destination. Checked: binary not in allowlist, hash unknown to reputation, parent is a scheduled task created yesterday, user states they were asleep. Verdict: suspected intrusion — the process identity, timing, and persistence mechanism all indicate malice. Evidence: alert DET-8841, process tree in ticket IR-2203. Ask: please check your telemetry for this hash across our estate and advise on containment scope.' That handoff gets action in minutes; a bare alert forward gets questions for an hour. The escalation criteria in your runbook define when the handoff happens: suspected incidents go immediately, pattern-level suspicions go with the pattern summary, and anything involving crown-jewel assets goes faster. Common gotcha: handoff as abdication. The MDR extends your team; it does not replace your triage. A handoff that says 'please investigate this alert' with no context is a confession that you skipped the workflow. Second gotcha: no feedback loop. When the MDR closes the case, their verdict comes back into your runbook — the tuning, the new detection, the lessons learned. Handoffs without feedback are a treadmill.  Set handoff SLAs with the MDR provider in the contract, not in the crisis. Define the severity-to-response-time mapping, the escalation path when the SLA is missed, and the format of the verdict that comes back — because the feedback is what tunes your runbook. Review the handoff quality quarterly with real tickets: were the packages complete, were the asks specific, did the verdicts come back in time to act? The MDR relationship is operated like any vendor relationship: measured, reviewed, and improved.
notes.title: MDR handoff: packaging the alert for action

notes.body: The runbook is the module's deliverable because it makes triage a property of the organization, not of whoever happens to be on shift. A Detect alert runbook has six parts, and you will write one in the lab. Part one: the trigger — which alert, from which policy, in plain language ('blocked child-process spawn from an Office application'). Part two: default severity and SLA — how fast triage starts. Part three: context to gather — the exact fields and where to find them (process, parent chain, user, machine, time, the user's alert history). Part four: triage steps in order — the five-input workflow from this module, written as checkable steps. Part five: verdict branches — what benign, violation, and incident each look like for this alert type, with two or three concrete examples per branch. Part six: escalation criteria — exactly when this goes to the MDR, to IR, or to management, with the handoff package template attached. Worked example: the runbook section for 'blocked USB mass-storage write.' Trigger: storage policy deny on removable-media write. Severity: medium default; high if finance/engineering asset or repeat pattern. Context: device ID and registration status, user and role, file paths and byte counts, the user's 30-day alert history. Triage: check registration (registered drive blocked = possible stale exception), check the files (sensitive paths raise severity), check history (pattern = intent). Verdicts: benign — new hire unaware of policy, first occurrence, non-sensitive files (action: educate, close). Violation — repeat attempts, no malice indicators (action: retrain, check workflow gap). Incident — sensitive targets, multiple machines, off-hours, or combined with other module alerts (action: isolate, preserve, escalate to IR). Escalation: any incident-verdict goes to IR immediately; any pattern of three-plus attempts goes to the security lead same-day. The runbook also carries the tuning section: after 30 days, which alerts proved benign-by-pattern get documented suppressions — each suppression naming the pattern, the owner, and the review date. Common gotcha: the runbook as shelfware. A runbook nobody opens during triage is documentation theater — it must be short enough to use mid-incident, linked from the alert itself, and updated every time a triage teaches something new. Second gotcha: verdict branches without examples. 'Use your judgment' is not a branch — the examples are what let a junior analyst triage like a senior at 3 AM.  Version the runbook and review it on a schedule — monthly for the active sections, quarterly cover to cover. Every triage that teaches something new produces a runbook update: a new example in a verdict branch, a tightened escalation criterion, a new tuning rule. Keep a changelog so analysts can see what changed and why; a runbook that silently mutates loses trust. The review meeting is short when the changelog does the talking: what did we learn, what did we change, what needs re-tuning.

notes.body: Configuration drift is entropy applied to security settings: the slow divergence between what the baseline says and what the machines actually run. It has a dozen causes — the tech who 'temporarily' changed a setting, the GPO that stopped applying after an OU move, the laptop that missed three policy cycles, the admin who added an exclusion directly on the machine and never told anyone. Drift detection is the continuous comparison of intended vs actual, machine by machine, setting by setting, and it is what separates managed from unmanaged. The mechanics are straightforward: the manager collects each machine's effective Defender configuration on a schedule, compares it to the baseline, and reports every divergence with the machine name, the setting, the expected value, and the actual value. The operator's workflow on a drift report is fixed: verify the divergence is real (not a reporting artifact), determine the cause (authorized change? rogue change? policy failure?), remediate (re-push the baseline or process the authorized change through change control), and document. Worked example: the Tuesday drift report. 197 machines clean. WORKSTATION-14: real-time protection disabled (expected: enabled). WORKSTATION-31: exclusion path C:\tools\ added (not in baseline). SERVER-02: cloud protection set to basic (expected: advanced). Three divergences, three investigations. WORKSTATION-14: the 'slow machine' tech from this module's first note — remediation: re-push baseline, address the actual performance cause, counsel the tech on the change process. WORKSTATION-31: an admin added it directly during an incident last week and forgot — remediation: process it as a proper exclusion request or remove it. SERVER-02: the OU move broke GPO inheritance — remediation: fix the OU linking, re-push, verify. The report turned three silent holes into three closed tickets in one morning. That is the entire value proposition. Common gotcha: drift reports nobody reads. The report must have an owner, a review cadence (daily for critical settings, weekly for the full baseline), and an SLA for remediation — an unread drift report is the same as no drift detection. Second gotcha: treating drift as purely technical. Repeated drift from the same team is a process signal: either the baseline is wrong for their workflow (fix the baseline or grant a proper exception) or the change discipline is broken (fix the discipline). The drift pattern tells you which.  Automate the drift check — a scheduled task or pipeline job that runs the comparison, files the report, and opens tickets for divergences above the threshold. Manual drift review works for twenty machines and collapses at two hundred; the automation is what makes the control scale. Keep the automation's own health monitored: a drift job that silently stopped running is worse than no job, because the dashboard still shows the last green report. Monitor the monitor.
notes.title: Drift detection: intended vs actual, continuously

notes.body: Defender and allowlisting are complementary, not competing — and the operator must be fluent in which question each answers. Defender asks 'is this file malicious?' It scans content against signatures, heuristics, and cloud verdicts, and it acts on malice found. Allowlisting asks 'may this code execute?' It checks identity against policy and acts on the absence of approval. A signed-but-malicious file can pass the allowlist and be caught by Defender's behavior monitoring; an unknown-but-benign tool can be blocked by the allowlist while Defender finds nothing wrong with it. Neither is sufficient alone; together they cover the matrix of known/unknown crossed with malicious/benign. The operational consequence is that both need management, and the management must agree. The exclusion list and the allowlist are the two documents most likely to contradict each other: an application excluded from Defender scanning but blocked by the allowlist (confused users, mysterious failures), or an application allowlisted but hammered by Defender heuristics (performance complaints, pressure for bad exclusions). The centralized console's value is making both visible in one place so the contradictions surface before the tickets do. Worked example: the backup agent. It is allowlisted (signed, approved, needed on all servers). Defender's behavior monitoring flags its volume-shadow-copy activity as ransomware-like. Without central visibility, the server team demands a broad exclusion and the security team refuses — stalemate. With both policies visible, the operator writes the precise fix: a process exclusion for the backup agent's binary (narrowest scope), documented with the vendor's confirmation that the behavior is expected, 90-day review — and notes the compensating control (the agent is allowlisted and ringfenced, so the blind spot is fenced). The rollout discipline for baseline changes mirrors every rollout in this course: pilot ring (IT and a friendly department), one-week monitoring of blocks, detections, and performance complaints, staged expansion, and a rollback trigger defined before the push ('if legitimate blocks exceed N per day, we revert and review'). Common gotcha: changing the baseline and the allowlist in the same window. When the backup breaks on Monday, you need to know which change did it — sequence the rollouts, never stack them. Second gotcha: the 'Defender found nothing, so we're fine' fallacy in reverse. Defender finding nothing means no known malice detected; the allowlist blocking an unknown means no approval exists. Both signals matter, and the M07 triage workflow treats them as the complementary evidence they are.  Keep one exceptions register, not three. The allowlist exceptions, the Defender exclusions, and the firewall exceptions all describe deliberate blind spots or openings — review them together quarterly, because a machine with an exclusion in all three is a machine with no controls left. The joint review is where the dangerous combinations surface: the unsigned tool that is allowlisted, excluded from scanning, and granted firewall exceptions is a policy decision that deserves executive visibility, not three separate tickets nobody connected.
notes.title: Defense in depth: Defender plus allowlisting, managed together
Rollout rings and the boring audit

objectives: Explain why centralized Defender management matters and what decays without it.
Write a complete Defender baseline: protection settings with values, rationales, and change control.
Apply the exclusion discipline: five required fields, narrowest scope, review dates, compensating controls.
Detect and remediate configuration drift, and prove consistent configuration to an auditor.

choices: It installs Defender on new machines
It centrally manages Defender configuration — one baseline pushed everywhere, with continuous drift detection
quiz.explain: The value is consistency plus proof: one baseline, pushed centrally, with intended-vs-actual comparison per machine. Installation and signatures are adjacent but separate concerns.
quiz.q: What does Configuration Manager do for Microsoft Defender?

choices: Inconsistent settings, forgotten exclusions, silently disabled protection — each machine becomes its own policy
quiz.explain: Unmanaged configuration decays into folklore: the 'standard' exists on paper while machines diverge. Central management plus drift detection is what keeps the standard real.
quiz.q: What happens to Defender configuration without centralized management?

choices: It scans on a fixed schedule only
It scans files as they are accessed — the always-on guard
quiz.explain: Real-time protection is the moment-of-contact layer: malware is caught when touched, not at the next scheduled scan. Everything else in the stack assumes it is on.
quiz.q: What is real-time protection?

choices: It backs up files to the cloud
It gets rapid verdicts on unknown files from cloud telemetry — covering what local signatures have never seen
quiz.explain: Local signatures cannot know brand-new files; the cloud checks global telemetry in seconds. This is the collective-intelligence layer of the stack.
quiz.q: What is cloud-delivered protection's role?

choices: It locks Defender settings against unauthorized changes — malware cannot silently blind the guard
quiz.explain: Tamper protection guards the guards: the settings that everything else depends on cannot be quietly disabled by malware or a compromised admin.
quiz.q: What does tamper protection protect?

choices: Exclude the whole drive for simplicity
Process exclusions (narrowest) are preferred; path exclusions must avoid user-writable locations; never exclude executables or temp/download folders
quiz.explain: The narrowness ladder: process beats path beats extension. Temp, downloads, and executable types are where malware lives — excluding them blinds the guard exactly where it matters most.
quiz.q: A vendor requests an exclusion for their application. What is the correct scoping?

choices: The total number of files scanned
The gap between the intended baseline and machines' actual settings — found by continuous comparison
quiz.explain: Drift is entropy: settings diverge through rogue changes, broken policy application, and forgotten temporaries. The drift report names each divergence for remediation.
quiz.q: What is configuration drift?

choices: Defender asks 'is this malicious?' (content); allowlisting asks 'may it run?' (identity) — layered, complementary
quiz.explain: Different questions, different layers: a signed-but-malicious file can pass identity and fail scanning; an unknown-but-benign tool can fail identity while scanning finds nothing. Together they cover the matrix.
quiz.q: How do Defender and allowlisting relate?

choices: Push to all machines Friday at 5 PM
Pilot ring first, monitor blocks and performance, expand in stages with a defined rollback trigger
Change the baseline and the allowlist simultaneously
quiz.explain: Baseline changes are rollouts: staged, monitored, reversible. Stacking simultaneous changes makes failures unattributable; Friday big-bangs make weekends miserable.
quiz.q: What is the correct way to roll out a Defender baseline change?

choices: The versioned baseline document plus the per-machine drift report — intended vs actual, with remediation tickets for divergences
quiz.explain: The document claims, the drift report proves. An auditor samples machines against the baseline; the remediation tickets show the control is operated, not just documented.
quiz.q: An auditor asks for proof of consistent AV configuration. What do you present?
