modules.title: Policy Troubleshooting & Break-Fix
modules.summary: When allowlisting breaks a legitimate application, the operator's job begins: a diagnosis workflow that finds the exact denied action, reads block events like evidence, handles the classic breakage patterns — updaters, installers, macros — and applies exceptions with change-control discipline. You will build a break-fix runbook you could actually use on shift.
objectives: Run the four-step diagnosis workflow: identify the blocked action, check the policy, test the exception, document.
Read a block event's fields — process, parent, action, target — and reconstruct what the application tried to do.
Diagnose and fix the three classic breakage patterns: updaters/installers, macros/scripts, and removable media.
Write exceptions that are narrow, time-bounded, owned, and reviewed — never broad permanent holes.
Test exceptions safely in a canary ring before fleet-wide rollout.
Prove whether a breakage is the policy or something else by isolating variables.

notes.title: The diagnosis workflow: blocked action, policy, exception, document
Reading block events like a detective
Breakage pattern: updaters and installers
Breakage pattern: macros and scripts
notes.body:
Macros and scripts live in the exact territory Ringfencing was built to control: legitimate automation that is also the favorite weapon of attackers. A macro is code inside a document; a script is code run by an interpreter like PowerShell or a Windows script host. The platform's stance is deny-by-default: Word does not get to launch PowerShell, Excel macros do not get to write executables, scripts do not run unless explicitly permitted. When a legitimate business process depends on a macro, the breakage feels personal — 'you broke my spreadsheet' — but the rule exists because malicious documents use the identical mechanism.

Worked example: the finance team has a monthly close spreadsheet with macros that pull data and generate reports. After the Ringfencing tightening, the macros are blocked — Excel cannot launch the data tool the macro calls. Diagnosis: block events show excel.exe as parent, the data tool as the blocked child process, action execute. The macro itself is legitimate — you verify with the finance lead, check the spreadsheet's origin, and confirm it has been in use for a year. The fix: a narrowed exception permitting Excel to launch that specific data tool, for the finance group only, with the spreadsheet's location restricted to the finance share. You do not permit Excel to launch arbitrary processes, and you do not permit macros fleet-wide. Verification: run the month-close workflow end to end on a canary machine. Documentation notes the business owner and sets a review date — because the day that spreadsheet gets a malicious copycat, you want the scope to be as small as possible.

Operator gotchas: the dangerous shortcut is 'allow macros for the finance team' as a blanket permission — that is not an exception, it is surrendering the control. Exceptions must name the specific parent, the specific child, and the specific scope. Another is the unsigned-macro problem: if the business macro is unsigned, anyone can modify it and the exception still applies — push the business toward signing macros or storing them in a controlled location. And never forget the alternative: sometimes the right fix is not an exception but a better workflow — a small script run by the IT team on a schedule can replace a fragile user macro entirely.

The sustainable answer for macro-heavy businesses is trusted locations plus signing, not per-macro exceptions forever. Designate controlled shares where macro-enabled files live; the policy permits macro execution only for files in those locations, and only those locations are writable by the document owners — not by email attachments or downloads. Push the business toward signing macros: a signed macro from a known publisher is verifiable in a way an unsigned one never is. The migration path: inventory current macros, move them to trusted locations, sign what matters, and set a date after which unsigned macros outside trusted locations stop working. It is a project, not a ticket — but it ends the endless exception treadmill for macros.

notes.title: The exception discipline: narrow, temporary, owned, reviewed
notes.body:
Every exception is a deliberate hole in a deny-by-default wall, so exceptions need the discipline of a bank vault log. A proper exception has five attributes. Narrow: the smallest scope that solves the problem — specific process, specific action, specific group, never 'allow everything for everyone.' Temporary: an expiry or review date, because today's legitimate need is tomorrow's forgotten hole. Owned: a named business owner who can answer 'do you still need this?' Owned by a person, not a department. Justified: the business reason written down, so the next admin does not have to guess. Reviewed: a calendar date when the exception gets re-examined, and a default action if the owner does not respond — usually removal or re-approval.

Worked example — an exception request done right: 'Request: permit the imaging application's updater process to write to the program install path and reach the vendor update server. Scope: Imaging group, 6 machines, updater process identity only. Business justification: the imaging software updates monthly; without this, each update breaks the app and blocks X-ray appointments. Owner: Dr. Patel, practice owner. Expiry: 12 months, with quarterly verification that the updater identity has not changed unexpectedly. Approved by: [you], after verifying the updater's signature against the vendor. Rollback: remove the exception; the app continues running on its current version.' Compare the bad version: 'Allowed imaging updater.' One of these survives an audit; the other is a mystery hole.

Common mistakes: permanent exceptions with no review date — they accumulate until the policy is decorative. Overly broad scope — 'allow for the whole organization' when six machines needed it. Missing owners — 'the finance team' cannot answer an email; a named human can. And the meta-mistake: no exception inventory. If you cannot produce a list of every active exception with owner and review date in five minutes, you do not have exception discipline — you have exception folklore. Build the inventory from day one; module 9's compliance report depends on it.

Run the exception review as a real meeting, quarterly, with the owners in the room. The agenda is mechanical: for each active exception, the owner answers 'do you still need this?' in thirty seconds. Still needed: confirm the scope is still minimal and reset the review date. Not needed: remove it now, verify nothing breaks, document the removal. Owner absent: default to removal after one grace cycle — exceptions without advocates are the ones that rot. The meeting takes an hour for a healthy inventory and pays for itself the first time it kills a years-old exception nobody remembered. Publish the minutes: the inventory, the removals, the renewals. Visibility keeps exceptions deliberate instead of folkloric.

notes.title: Testing exceptions in a canary ring
notes.body:
An exception is a policy change, and policy changes get the lifecycle: test before fleet-wide rollout. The canary ring is a small set of representative machines — your own workstation, one or two volunteers per affected group, covering the machine types and software combinations in scope. The test plan has three parts: the positive test (the legitimate workflow now works — launch the app, run the real task, confirm the output), the negative test (the things that should still be blocked are still blocked — try the adjacent bad action and confirm the deny), and the soak (leave it for at least one full business cycle, watching block events for surprises).

Worked example: the finance macro exception from the last note. Canary ring: your test VM, plus two finance workstations whose owners agreed to test. Positive test: open the month-close spreadsheet, run the macros, verify the report generates and the data tool launches. Negative test: from Excel, try to launch an unapproved process — confirm it is still denied. Try modifying the macro to call something new — confirm denied. Soak: three business days, watching the block feed for the finance group. Day two: you see a deny for a different helper the macro occasionally calls during quarter-close — not in your exception. You add it narrowly, re-test, and extend the soak. Only then do you roll out to the full finance group. The soak caught what the lab test missed, which is exactly why the soak exists.

Operator gotchas: canary machines that are not representative — testing only on your pristine admin workstation misses the weird software combinations of real user machines. Include at least one 'messy' machine. Another is the too-short soak: testing for an hour catches syntax errors, not behavioral surprises; a full business cycle is the minimum. And the negative test is the one everyone skips and the one that matters most — an exception that accidentally permits more than intended is worse than no exception, because it is invisible. Prove the deny still works, every time.

Choose canaries for representativeness, not convenience. Cover the axes of variation: machine types (laptop versus desktop versus kiosk), OS and driver versions (the driver-variant miss from the deployment module is the cautionary tale), software combinations (the machine with the weird legacy app), and user behaviors (the power user who exercises edge features). Five machines spanning the variation beat twenty identical ones. Recruit volunteers explicitly — they get fixes first and a direct line to support — and rotate them so nobody burns out. Document the canary set per application class, because the right canaries for the billing app differ from those for the warehouse scanners. Representativeness is the whole game.

notes.title: When it is not the policy: isolating variables
notes.body:
The hardest break-fix skill is proving a negative: demonstrating that the policy is NOT the cause, so you stop changing security controls and start fixing the real problem. Users blame the security platform for everything — it is the newest, most visible change, and 'the security thing did it' is cognitively easy. Your job is bisection: change one variable at a time until the cause is isolated. The method: reproduce the problem, check the block events for that exact timeframe — if there is no deny event for the failing action, the policy is probably not the cause. Then test on a machine outside the policy scope, or temporarily move a test machine to a permissive test policy, and see if the problem persists. If it persists without the policy, the policy is innocent.

Worked example: 'The invoice app is broken since your update.' You check block events for the affected machines across the failure window: zero deny events for the invoice app or its helpers. The policy did not fire. Next, you test on a machine in the IT group that never received the billing policy: same failure. The policy is innocent — twice proven. Now you look elsewhere: the vendor pushed an app update the same night, and the app's own log shows a database connection failure. The real cause is a database credential rotation that the app update mishandled. You hand the evidence to the app vendor instead of carving exceptions into a policy that was never the problem. Imagine the alternative: you had 'fixed' it with a broad exception, the app still failed, and now you have both a broken app and a hole in your policy.

Common mistakes: the correlation trap — 'it broke after the policy push, therefore the policy broke it.' Post hoc reasoning is the number-one cause of unnecessary exceptions. Another is testing without a control: changing two things at once and not knowing which one mattered. And the political mistake: telling the user 'it is not our policy' without evidence. Bring the evidence — the empty block log, the failing test outside policy scope — and the conversation stays professional. 'Here is the proof it is not the policy, and here is what I found instead' makes you the hero, not the obstacle.

Build the 'not the policy' evidence package as a habit, because you will present it weekly. The package: the block-event query for the failure window showing zero denies for the failing action, the reproduction on a machine outside the policy scope failing identically, and your alternate hypothesis with its own evidence — the vendor's update notes, the application's error log. Present it as help, not defense: 'I have ruled out the policy with these two tests — here is what I found instead, and here is my recommended next step.' Users who see this package twice stop blaming the platform reflexively; they start bringing you better symptoms. The evidence package does not just win the argument — it trains the organization to troubleshoot with you instead of against you.

notes.title: Change control for people who hate paperwork
notes.body: Change control has a reputation problem: it sounds like bureaucracy, so operators skip it, and then nobody knows why the policy looks the way it does. The fix is making the control lighter than the chaos it prevents. For routine exceptions, the control is four lines: what changed, why, who approved, how to undo it — written before the change, not after. For standard changes (the tenth identical updater exception), a pre-approved template: fill in the blanks, no meeting required. For emergency changes (the 2 AM SEV-1), the control is 'act now, document within the hour, review tomorrow' — the paperwork follows the fix, but it still happens. What never happens: an undocumented change. The day you cannot explain a policy line is the day you have lost control of the fleet. Worked example — the emergency change log entry: 'EMERGENCY 2026-10-07 02:14 — What: rolled back last night's Ringfencing tightening on the billing group to the previous version. Why: SEV-1, billing app blocked on 6 machines, root cause not yet isolated, business impact immediate. Approved by: on-call lead (verbal, 02:10). Undo of the undo: re-apply the tightening after root-cause diagnosis in the test ring. Follow-up: post-mortem scheduled today 10 AM; the tightening stays in the test ring until then.' Forty seconds to write, and it answers every question the morning shift, the manager, and the auditor will ask. Compare: no entry, and Monday's admin finds a policy that does not match Friday's documentation, with no idea why. Operator gotchas: change control theater — a three-page form for a one-line change just teaches people to bypass the process. Match the weight of the control to the risk of the change. Another is the approval bottleneck: if every exception needs a manager's signature, exceptions pile up and users suffer — pre-approve the routine patterns and reserve human approval for the novel and the broad. And review the change log itself monthly: if you find entries you cannot understand, the process is failing even if everyone is filling in the form. The goal is a fleet whose every policy line has a reason, an owner, and an undo path. Audit the change log monthly, because the process rots silently. Read every entry and ask: do I understand what changed and why? Is the approver named? Is there an undo path? Flag the entries that fail — not to punish, but to find where the process is too heavy (people bypass heavy processes) or too vague (the template needs better prompts). Track two numbers: what fraction of policy changes have complete log entries, and how many emergency changes got their within-the-hour documentation. A process with total bypass is not a process; lighten it until compliance is the path of least resistance. Change control that people actually follow beats perfect change control that everyone routes around.

cards.front: What are the four steps of the break-fix diagnosis workflow, in order?
cards.back: Identify the blocked action precisely, check the policy, test the exception, document.

cards.front: Which fields of a block event matter most?
cards.back: Process, parent process, action, target, the denying policy and level, timestamp, machine, user.

cards.front: Why is the parent process often more important than the blocked process?
cards.back: It reveals the real story — e.g., winword.exe launching powershell.exe at 2 AM means a malicious document, not an admin script.

cards.front: Name four ways an updater breaks allowlisting.
cards.back: New file hashes, new install paths, new helper process names, new behaviors (file writes, network) the policy never saw.

cards.front: For frequently-updating apps, what is more sustainable than chasing hashes?
cards.back: Approving the vendor's signed updater process and its defined install behavior — not each new binary hash.

cards.front: What are the five attributes of a proper exception?
cards.back: Narrow, temporary (expiry/review date), owned by a named person, justified in writing, reviewed on a calendar date.

cards.front: What three parts make a canary test plan?
cards.back: Positive test (legitimate workflow works), negative test (adjacent bad actions still denied), soak (a full business cycle of monitoring).

cards.front: Why is the negative test the most important part of exception testing?
cards.back: An exception that accidentally permits more than intended is worse than none — it is an invisible hole. Prove the deny still works.

cards.front: How do you prove the policy is NOT the cause of a breakage?
cards.back: Bisection: check block events for the failure window (no deny = probably innocent), then reproduce outside policy scope — if it still fails, the policy is innocent.

cards.front: What is the correlation trap in troubleshooting?
cards.back: 'It broke after the policy push, therefore the policy broke it' — post hoc reasoning that causes unnecessary exceptions.

cards.front: What is the emergency change-control rule?
cards.back: Act now, document within the hour, review tomorrow — the paperwork follows the fix but still happens.

cards.front: What is the difference between a block event needing an exception vs. incident response?
cards.back: A legitimate business action wrongly denied needs an exception; a malicious-pattern block (Word spawning PowerShell at 2 AM) needs investigation, not an exception.

quiz.q: Ticket: 'Nobody in billing can open the invoice app since this morning.' What is your FIRST step?
choices: Push an exception allowing the invoice app everywhere.
Pull the block events for the billing machines this morning and identify the exact blocked process, parent, action, and target.
Roll back last night's policy push immediately.
Reinstall the invoice app on all billing machines.
quiz.explain: Step one of the workflow is identifying the blocked action precisely — process, parent, action, target. Everything else (policy check, exception, rollback) depends on knowing exactly what was denied. Acting before identifying produces sloppy, over-broad fixes.

quiz.q: Block event: powershell.exe blocked, parent winword.exe, 2:14 AM, network connection to an external IP, user not at work. What is the correct response?
choices: Create an exception so Word can launch PowerShell; the user probably needs it.
Treat as a potential incident: isolate the machine, find the document, investigate — do not create an exception.
Ignore it; the platform blocked it so there is no problem.
quiz.explain: The parent chain (Word launching PowerShell at 2 AM to reach an external IP) is the classic malicious-document pattern. The platform did its job; your job is incident response. An exception here would legalize the attack path.

quiz.q: After a browser auto-update, the browser will not launch: new binary hash denied, temp installer denied, new helper process denied by Ringfencing. What is the disciplined fix?
choices: Approve the temp installer's hash globally and disable Ringfencing for the browser until things settle.

Verify the update is legitimate, update approvals to the new identities, narrowly permit the updater's defined behavior, update the Ringfencing rule for the renamed helper, test on canaries, then roll out.
Tell users to stop updating the browser.
quiz.explain: Each breakage mode gets a narrow, verified fix: new identities approved after legitimacy verification, updater behavior permitted narrowly, Ringfencing updated for the renamed helper, canary-tested. Global approvals and disabling controls trade a morning's inconvenience for permanent holes.

quiz.q: Finance has a legitimate macro that needs Excel to launch one specific data tool. What is the correct exception scope?
choices: Allow macros for the entire finance team.
Permit excel.exe to launch that specific data tool, for the finance group only, with the spreadsheet restricted to the finance share — and push toward signed macros.
Allow Excel to launch any process for finance.
Disable Ringfencing for the finance group.
quiz.explain: Exceptions name the specific parent, the specific child, and the narrowest scope. Blanket macro permission is surrendering the control; the narrowed exception preserves both the business workflow and the security boundary.

quiz.q: You test an exception: the legitimate workflow works. What critical test remains before rollout?
choices: Nothing — the positive test is sufficient.
The negative test: confirm adjacent bad actions are still denied, then soak for a full business cycle watching block events.
Ask the user if they are happy.
Immediately roll out to the whole fleet to save time.
quiz.explain: The negative test proves your exception did not accidentally open more than intended — an invisible over-permission is worse than no exception. The soak catches behavioral surprises that lab tests miss, like the quarter-close helper in the worked example.

quiz.q: 'The app broke after your policy push' — but there are zero deny events for the app in the failure window, and it also fails on a machine outside the policy scope. What do you conclude?
choices: The policy is guilty; the logging must be broken.
The policy is innocent — twice proven. Stop changing security controls and investigate the real cause (e.g., the vendor's own update).
Add an exception anyway, just in case.
Re-push the policy to fix the logging.
quiz.explain: Bisection proved it twice: no deny in the window, and failure without the policy. Changing controls now would create holes without fixing anything. Bring this evidence to the user and the vendor — it keeps the conversation professional and factual.

quiz.q: Which exception request is audit-proof?
choices: 'Permit the imaging updater process to write to the install path and reach the vendor update server; scope: Imaging group, 6 machines; owner: Dr. Patel; expiry 12 months with quarterly verification; approved after signature check; rollback: remove the exception.'
quiz.explain: The audit-proof exception has all five attributes: narrow scope, expiry/review, named owner, written justification, and a rollback path. 'Will review later' without a date means never.

quiz.q: It is 2 AM, a SEV-1 policy breakage is blocking a business function, and the cause is unclear. What is the change-control-correct move?
choices: Wait until morning when the change board meets.
Roll back to the last known-good policy now to restore service, document within the hour, and hold a post-mortem review before re-applying.
Make no changes; document the outage instead.
Disable the agent on affected machines.
quiz.explain: Emergency change control is 'act now, document within the hour, review tomorrow.' Rolling back to known-good restores service fastest; the documentation and post-mortem preserve governance. Waiting for a morning meeting trades hours of outage for process theater.

quiz.q: Your canary test uses only your pristine admin workstation. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing — the admin workstation is the most important machine.
Canaries must be representative: include volunteer machines from the affected group, including at least one 'messy' real-world machine, or you will miss real-world software combinations.
Canary testing is unnecessary for small changes.
You should test on the CEO's machine instead.
quiz.explain: A pristine admin workstation does not represent the fleet's software combinations. The canary ring exists to catch what the lab misses — it must include real user machines from the affected groups.

quiz.q: A user demands you 'just turn off the blocking' for their department because exceptions take too long. How do you respond?
choices: Explain what the control protects them from, commit to a fast verification timeline for their legitimate need, and offer the narrowed exception path — while documenting the request.
Turn it off quietly and turn it back on later.
quiz.explain: Disabling a control for a department is surrendering the security boundary for convenience. The operator move is empathy plus discipline: acknowledge the friction, speed up the legitimate path, keep the control intact — and document the request in case the pattern repeats.

items.prompt: Recite the four break-fix steps in order.
items.answer: Identify the blocked action, check the policy, test the exception, document.
items.explain: No skipping — acting before identifying produces sloppy exceptions.

items.prompt: Name the six key fields of a block event.
items.answer: Process, parent process, action, target, denying policy/level, timestamp + machine + user.
items.explain: Read them in relationship — the parent chain is often the real story.

items.prompt: Name four ways updaters break allowlisting.
items.answer: New hashes, new paths, new helper processes, new behaviors.
items.explain: A major version update can produce all four at once.

items.prompt: What are the five attributes of a proper exception?
items.answer: Narrow, temporary, owned, justified, reviewed.
items.explain: Every exception is a deliberate hole — log it like a vault entry.

items.prompt: What are the three parts of a canary test?
items.answer: Positive test, negative test, soak for a full business cycle.
items.explain: The negative test proves the deny still works; the soak catches behavioral surprises.

items.prompt: How do you prove the policy is NOT the cause?
items.answer: Check block events for the failure window, then reproduce outside policy scope — if it still fails, the policy is innocent.
items.explain: Bisection beats the correlation trap.

items.prompt: What is the emergency change-control rule?
items.answer: Act now, document within the hour, review tomorrow.
items.explain: The paperwork follows the fix but still happens.

items.prompt: Block events show the billing helper denied at 8:47 AM on six machines; the helper's hash changed overnight. Walk the workflow.
items.answer: Step 1: identified — helper process, parent the billing app, action execute, hash changed by vendor update. Step 2: policy correct per intent but business-wrong. Step 3: narrow exception to the new helper identity for the billing group, canary-test with a real invoice. Step 4: document cause, change, approver, verification, 90-day review.
items.explain: The full loop: identify precisely, judge policy intent, narrow exception, verify on a real workflow, document.

items.prompt: A macro exception request says 'allow macros for finance.' What do you do?
items.answer: Refuse the blanket scope; rewrite it narrowed — specific parent (excel.exe), specific child (the data tool), finance group only, share-restricted, with owner and review date.
items.explain: Blanket macro permission surrenders the control the platform exists to provide.

items.prompt: During the soak you spot a deny for a different helper the macro calls only at quarter-close. What happened and what do you do?
items.answer: The lab test missed a behavioral path — exactly what the soak is for. Add the helper narrowly, re-test, extend the soak before fleet rollout.
items.explain: This is the soak earning its keep; do not skip it or shorten it after a surprise.

items.prompt: The user insists 'your update broke it' but there are no deny events and it fails off-policy too. Script your reply.
items.answer: 'I checked the block logs for the failure window and tested outside the policy — the policy did not fire and the failure happens without it, so the cause is elsewhere. Here is what I found instead [vendor update / credential issue], and here is my next step.'
items.explain: Evidence, not argument: the empty block log plus the off-policy reproduction keeps it professional.

items.prompt: You need an exception for a one-time vendor remote session tonight. Write the exception attributes.
items.answer: Narrow: vendor's remote tool process, this machine only, tonight's window. Temporary: expires tomorrow morning. Owned: named requester. Justified: vendor support case number. Reviewed: auto-expiry plus verification the session ended.
items.explain: One-time needs get the tightest scope of all — time-boxed to the session window.

items.prompt: A department head asks for a permanent exception 'so we never have this problem again.' How do you respond?
items.answer: Explain that permanent exceptions accumulate into decorative policies; offer a 12-month exception with quarterly reviews and a named owner instead — and suggest fixing the underlying workflow if the need is truly permanent.
items.explain: Permanent means forgotten. Time-boxed with reviews keeps the hole deliberate and visible.

handsOnLab.title: Build a break-fix runbook with five realistic scenarios
handsOnLab.brief: Write the runbook you would want open on your second monitor during a shift: five realistic breakage scenarios, each with symptoms, diagnosis steps, the policy check, an exception draft, a test plan, and a rollback — plus the blank templates you would reuse for scenario six.
steps: Set up your runbook document with five scenario sections plus a templates appendix. Each scenario gets the same headings: symptoms, diagnosis, policy check, exception draft, test plan, rollback, documentation.

Scenario 1 — the blocked payroll run: write the symptoms (payroll app fails Friday morning), the block-event fields you would pull, and the exact narrowed exception you would draft for the payroll group.

Scenario 2 — the updater breakage: a design app auto-updates overnight and will not launch. Write the four updater breakage modes to check, the legitimacy verification steps, and the canary test plan including the negative test.

Scenario 3 — the macro block: finance's month-close spreadsheet macros are denied. Write the diagnosis (parent/child chain), the narrowed exception with all five attributes, and the argument for pushing the business toward signed macros.

Scenario 4 — the USB block: a warehouse scanner's storage is denied after a Storage Control tightening. Write the inheritance check (which level broke the scanner exception), the fix, and the user communication.
Scenario 5 — the false alarm: 'the app broke after your policy push' with zero deny events. Write the bisection procedure, the evidence you would gather, and the professional reply script.
For each scenario, write the rollback: the exact undo action if your fix makes things worse.
Build the blank templates appendix: the four-line change log, the exception request form (five attributes), the canary test plan (positive/negative/soak), and the escalation package.

Add a 'triage cheat sheet' page: the four workflow steps, the six block-event fields, and the three questions to ask every caller ('what changed just before?', 'show me the exact error', 'who else is affected?').
Review all five scenarios for scope creep: flag any exception you wrote that is broader than necessary and narrow it.
Have a peer (or your future self) read scenario 3 cold and attempt the diagnosis from your written steps alone. Fix anything they stumble on.
Save the runbook as break-fix-runbook.md and note the date of your next self-review.
handsOnLab.deliverable: break-fix-runbook.md with five complete scenarios (symptoms, diagnosis, policy check, exception draft, test plan, rollback, documentation), the templates appendix, and the triage cheat sheet.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Each scenario traces symptom to root cause to verified fix; every exception draft has all five attributes; the cheat sheet fits on one page; a cold reader can execute scenario 3.

mockTask.q: Panel question: 'You pushed a policy change Friday at 4:55 PM. Monday morning the helpdesk queue is on fire. Walk me through what happened and what you do now.'
choices: Immediately roll back the change, then investigate calmly: pull block events from the weekend, identify the exact denied actions, and explain the Friday-afternoon timing mistake and the change-window discipline you will follow.
Blame the users for not reporting issues over the weekend.
Push a broad exception allowing everything the helpdesk mentions to quiet the queue fast.
Deny that the policy change could be related since it worked on your machine.
mockTask.explain: The panel is testing ownership and method. The strong answer owns the timing mistake (Friday changes are an operator error), restores service first via rollback, then diagnoses with evidence — and names the systemic fix: evening change windows, canary rings, no Friday pushes. Deflection or broad exceptions fail the judgment test.

modules.title: ThreatLocker Deployment Projects
modules.summary: Rolling out deny-by-default across a real organization: pilot rings, Learning Mode baselining, stakeholder communication, go/no-go gates, rollback plans, and the success metrics that prove the project worked. You will write a complete 90-day deployment plan for a 200-endpoint fictional company.
objectives: Design pilot rings for a staged rollout and explain what each ring proves.
Run a Learning Mode baselining window and turn its output into initial policies.
Write stakeholder communications — the exec one-pager and the user announcement — that prevent rollout panic.
Define go/no-go gates with measurable criteria for each rollout wave.
Build a rollback plan that fits deny-by-default semantics: revert policy, not panic.
Track the success metrics that prove the deployment worked: coverage, blocks, exceptions, ticket trends.

notes.title: Rollout phases and pilot rings
Learning Mode baselining: listening before enforcing
notes.body: Deny-by-default has a cold-start problem: on day one, the platform does not know what 'normal' looks like for this specific organization. Learning Mode solves it by observing first and enforcing later. During the baselining window, the agent watches which applications execute, which processes they spawn, what files and network resources they touch — and records it all without blocking. At the end of the window, you review the learned baseline and convert it into initial policies: the applications people actually use become the allowlist, and everything else remains denied. The baselining window must cover a full business cycle — at least two weeks, ideally including a month-end or equivalent peak — because the payroll app that runs monthly will not appear in a three-day sample. Worked example: Meridian's Ring 1 baselining runs for three weeks. The learned data shows 214 distinct applications across the 20 volunteers. Reviewing, you categorize: 160 are standard business apps and OS components — approved. 22 are department-specific tools (dictation, label software, scanner utilities) — approved with group scoping. 18 are updaters and installers — handled via updater rules, not individual approvals. 9 are personal or redundant (three different PDF readers, two music apps, a game) — not approved; users get the standard alternatives. 5 are unknown — investigated, two turn out to be a forgotten remote-access tool that gets removed, three are vendor utilities that get approved narrowly. The baseline review is where you discover what the organization actually runs versus what IT thought it ran — the gap is always embarrassing and always valuable. Operator gotchas: the too-short window — baselining for a long weekend and missing the monthly processes, which then break on day one of enforcement. The unreviewed baseline — approving everything learned without categorization just allowlists the organization's bad habits, including that forgotten remote-access tool. And baselining during abnormal periods: if you baseline over the holidays or during a migration, 'normal' is wrong. Time the window for a representative business period, review every category with a human, and remember that the baseline is a starting point — policies keep evolving after enforcement begins. Run the baseline review as a working meeting, not a solo task. Attendees: you, one person from IT who knows the software inventory, and a representative from each major department. Walk the categorized list — approve, scope, updater-rule, reject, investigate — making decisions out loud and recording each with its rationale. The department reps catch what IT misses ('we still use that old label tool twice a year'), and their presence builds the buy-in you will need at enforcement. Time-box the investigate items: each gets an owner and a 48-hour deadline, not an indefinite parking lot. End with the approved baseline signed off — that signature turns 'IT's project' into 'our policy.'

notes.title: Stakeholder communication: the exec one-pager and the user announcement
Go/no-go gates between waves
notes.body:
Each ring ends at a gate, and gates have criteria — otherwise 'the pilot went fine' is a feeling, not a fact. A go/no-go gate checks four things. Breakage rate: how many blocking tickets per machine in the ring, and is the trend falling? If Ring 1 generated 40 tickets on 20 machines, something is wrong with the policies, not the users. Resolution time: are break-fix tickets closing within the committed window? A growing backlog means the support team is underwater and the next ring will drown them. Exception quality: are the exceptions created narrow, owned, and reviewed — or is the team punching holes to keep up? User sentiment: a quick pulse survey — do users understand what to do when blocked? If they are working around the platform instead of requesting approvals, the communication failed. Go means all four are healthy; no-go means pause, fix, and re-gate — never 'go and hope.'

Worked example — Meridian's Ring 1 gate review. Breakage: 14 tickets on 20 machines over two weeks — high, but 11 were the scanner and dictation issues now fixed with exceptions; the trend is falling. Resolution: average 3 hours, within the 4-hour commitment. Exceptions: 6 created, all narrow with owners and review dates — quality good. Sentiment: pulse survey, 16 of 20 say they understand the block message and the request process; 4 are confused about USB drives — communication gap to fix before Ring 2. Decision: conditional GO — proceed to Ring 2 after sending the USB clarification to all staff and adding the scanner exception to the baseline. The gate did its job: it caught the USB confusion before it became 90 confused users instead of 4.

Operator gotchas: gates without teeth — if the answer is always 'go,' you do not have gates, you have ceremonies. Define the criteria before the ring starts, when you can still be objective. Another is the sunk-cost push: 'we have spent six weeks, we cannot pause now' — pausing for one week to fix policies is always cheaper than a failed Ring 3. And document every gate decision with its data; when the post-mortem asks why Ring 2 went ahead, 'the numbers supported it, here they are' is the answer that ends the discussion.

Document every gate decision with its data, and write the no-go recovery plan before you need it. The gate record: the four metrics, the decision (go, conditional go, no-go), any conditions, and the signatures. The no-go plan, written in advance: what gets fixed, who owns each fix, the re-gate date, and what the held rings do meanwhile. A no-go without a recovery plan becomes an indefinite stall — the project loses momentum and dies quietly. A no-go with a dated recovery plan is just a delay with a purpose. Teams that handle their first no-go well earn the credibility that makes every subsequent gate honest; teams that never say no-go eventually ship a failure.

notes.title: Rollback plans under deny-by-default
notes.body:
Rollback in a deny-by-default world does not mean uninstalling the platform in a panic — it means reverting policy to the last known-good state, which is fast, controlled, and does not surrender the security boundary. Your rollback plan has three tiers. Tier 1, policy revert: the previous policy version is one action away — you restore it for the affected group and the breakage stops. This handles 90 percent of bad pushes. Tier 2, ring halt: stop the rollout wave, keep completed rings on the new policy if they are healthy, hold the rest. This contains a wave-specific problem. Tier 3, enforcement pause: for a truly catastrophic misconfiguration, temporarily relax enforcement to monitor-only for the affected scope while you diagnose — the platform still sees everything, it just stops blocking. Note what is NOT on the list: mass uninstallation, which destroys your visibility exactly when you need it most.

Worked example: during Meridian's Ring 2, a Ringfencing tightening for the label software goes out Tuesday evening. Wednesday morning, 12 warehouse machines cannot print shipping labels — the tightening blocked the driver's new helper process, which the canary ring missed because the canary machines had a different driver version. Tier 1 response: revert the label policy to the previous version for the warehouse group — 10 minutes, labels printing again. Then diagnose calmly: the driver version difference explains the miss. Fix: update the policy for both driver versions, test on both, re-push Wednesday evening. The rollback was boring and fast, which is the entire point — because the plan existed before the incident, nobody had to invent it under pressure.

Common mistakes: no rollback plan at all — the team discovers during the incident that nobody knows how to revert. The untested rollback — reverting has its own steps and they should be rehearsed, not read for the first time at 2 AM. And the pride trap: refusing to roll back because 'the policy is correct, the users need to adapt' — if the business cannot ship labels, the policy is wrong for now regardless of its theoretical merit. Roll back, fix, re-deploy. Speed of recovery is the metric, not stubbornness.

Rehearse the rollback before Ring 1 — a game day, not a document review. Pick a test group, push a deliberately breaking policy change, and execute the Tier 1 revert under time pressure: who authorizes, what gets clicked, how you verify service restored, how you communicate. Time it. The rehearsal always reveals something: the revert needs a permission nobody has, the verification step is vague, the communication template is missing. Fix all of it now, while the stakes are zero, and write the lessons into the runbook. The team that has rolled back on purpose rolls back calmly in the incident; the team meeting the revert button for the first time at 2 AM does not.

notes.title: Success metrics: proving the deployment worked
notes.body:
A deployment project ends with evidence, not a feeling. Track five metrics from day one so the final report writes itself. Coverage: percentage of the fleet with healthy agents and current policy — the goal is effectively 100 percent, and every gap gets a named reason. Block volume: denied executions per week by category — this should spike at enforcement start (the platform discovering the organization's shadow IT) then settle to a low baseline. Exception inventory: count of active exceptions with owners and review dates — growing slowly and deliberately, never exploding. Ticket trends: break-fix tickets per week — high in early rings, falling steadily; a rising trend means policies or communication are failing. Time-to-approve: how fast legitimate requests get approved — this measures whether security is enabling or obstructing the business.

Worked example — Meridian's 90-day numbers. Coverage: 198 of 200 agents healthy (two machines in storage, documented). Block volume: week 1 of enforcement saw 412 denied executions — mostly unapproved installers and personal software users tried to run; by week 8 the baseline is ~15 per week, mostly updater edge cases. Exceptions: 23 active, all narrow, all owned, earliest review date in 60 days. Tickets: Ring 1 averaged 7 per week, Ring 3 averaged 2 per week — the trend the gates demanded. Time-to-approve: median 45 minutes against a 2-hour commitment. The executive summary: 'In 90 days we moved 200 endpoints to deny-by-default. The platform denied 1,900+ unauthorized executions with zero reported malware incidents. Twenty-three deliberate exceptions are tracked and reviewed. Approval median is 45 minutes. Two machines await reimaging.' That is a project that gets funded again.

Operator gotchas: vanity metrics — 'we blocked 10,000 things' without categories or outcomes impresses nobody who matters. The missing baseline — if you did not measure ticket volume before the project, you cannot prove the trend improved; start measuring in week one. And the metric nobody tracks: user workaround attempts. If Storage Control blocks are falling but USB-related helpdesk calls are rising, users may be finding ways around the control — investigate the behavior, not just the numbers.

Build the dashboard in a spreadsheet before you automate anything — the manual version teaches you which numbers actually matter. One tab per metric, one row per week: coverage with gap explanations, block volume by category, exception inventory with review dates, tickets per week with the ring annotated, time-to-approve median. Add a notes column for context ('Ring 2 wave 1 started,' 'holiday week'). Review it at every gate and monthly in steady state. Only automate after three months of manual tracking, when you know exactly which numbers you read and which you ignore. The spreadsheet-first discipline prevents the classic failure: an expensive automated dashboard of metrics nobody reads, while the number that matters lives in someone's head.

notes.title: The 90-day plan: putting it all together

cards.front: What does each pilot ring prove? (Rings 0-3)
cards.back: Ring 0 (IT): platform behavior with zero business risk. Ring 1 (volunteers): real workflows with cooperative users. Ring 2 (half fleet): scale effects and weird combinations. Ring 3 (all): proven policies, experienced support.

cards.front: What is Learning Mode's purpose in a deployment?
cards.back: Observe-before-enforce baselining: the agent records normal application behavior without blocking, so the baseline can be reviewed and converted into initial policies.

cards.front: How long should a baselining window run, and why?
cards.back: At least two to three weeks covering a full business cycle including month-end — so periodic processes like payroll are observed, not missed.

cards.front: What three questions does the exec one-pager answer?
cards.back: What are we doing and why (business terms), what disruption to expect, and what is needed from leadership (visible sponsorship).

cards.front: What three questions does the user announcement answer?
cards.back: What is changing on my computer, what to do when something legitimate is blocked, how fast support will respond.

cards.front: What four things does a go/no-go gate check?
cards.back: Breakage rate and trend, resolution time vs commitment, exception quality (narrow/owned/reviewed), user sentiment (do users understand the process?).

cards.front: What are the three rollback tiers under deny-by-default?
cards.back: Tier 1: revert policy to last known-good. Tier 2: halt the rollout wave. Tier 3: pause enforcement to monitor-only for the affected scope.

cards.front: Why is mass uninstallation NOT a rollback tier?
cards.back: It destroys visibility exactly when you need it most; policy revert restores service without surrendering the security boundary.

cards.front: Name the five deployment success metrics.
cards.back: Coverage, block volume by category, exception inventory health, ticket trends, time-to-approve.

cards.front: What should block volume do over a healthy rollout?
cards.back: Spike at enforcement start (discovering shadow IT), then settle to a low baseline — a rising trend means policies or communication are failing.

cards.front: What are the five phases of the 90-day plan?
cards.back: Foundation (days 1-14), pilot (15-35), scale (36-60), complete (61-80), harden and handover (81-90).

cards.front: Why does the plan need a risk register?
cards.back: A plan without named risks and mitigations is a wish — the register (exec escalation, legacy apps, support overload, missed periodic processes) is what makes it executable.

quiz.q: You have 200 endpoints and an executive demanding full deployment this month. What is the operator-correct response?
choices: Deploy to all 200 at once to meet the deadline.
Hold the ring structure: explain that compressing rings moves breakage from pilot into production where it costs ten times more, and propose the fastest safe schedule with dates.
Deploy to the executive's machine first to win support, then everyone else.
quiz.explain: The rings are the schedule — skipping them does not save time, it relocates the cost. The professional move is a clear explanation of the tradeoff plus a committed fast schedule, not silent compliance or refusal.

quiz.q: Your Learning Mode window ran over a holiday week. What is the risk?
choices: No risk; the platform learns the same way regardless.
The baseline captures abnormal behavior as 'normal' and misses periodic processes — re-run the window over a representative business period.
The baseline will be more secure.
quiz.explain: Baselining during abnormal periods bakes wrong 'normal' into policy and misses the monthly processes that then break on enforcement day. The window must cover a representative business cycle.

quiz.q: Ring 1 gate review: 14 tickets on 20 machines, average resolution 3 hours (commitment 4), 6 narrow exceptions with owners, but 4 of 20 users confused about USB blocks. Decision?
choices: NO-GO — any confusion fails the gate.
Conditional GO — fix the USB communication gap first, then proceed; the gate caught a small problem before it scaled.
GO — confusion is the users' problem.
Skip Ring 2 and go straight to Ring 3 to save time.
quiz.explain: Gates exist to catch exactly this: a small, fixable issue before it becomes 90 confused users. Conditional go with the comms fix is the gate working as designed — neither blind approval nor pointless delay.

quiz.q: Wednesday morning, 12 warehouse machines cannot print after Tuesday's policy tightening. What is the Tier 1 rollback?
choices: Uninstall the agent from all warehouse machines.
Revert the label policy to the previous version for the warehouse group — minutes, printing restored — then diagnose calmly.
Wait to see if it resolves itself.
Push a fleet-wide exception for all printing.
quiz.explain: Tier 1 is policy revert to last known-good: fast, controlled, preserves the security boundary and visibility. Uninstallation destroys visibility; waiting wastes business hours; fleet-wide exceptions are scope creep under pressure.

quiz.q: Which metric trend signals a failing rollout?
choices: Block volume spiking at enforcement start.
Break-fix tickets rising week over week after Ring 2.
quiz.explain: Early spikes are expected discovery; rising tickets after scale means policies or communication are failing. The trend is the signal — falling ticket volume is what the gates demand.

quiz.q: A VP's unapproved screen-capture tool gets blocked and they escalate over your head. What should have prevented this?
choices: Nothing — VPs are exempt from policy.
The exec one-pager signed in week one plus a VIP approval SLA, so leadership backs the process instead of overriding it.
quiz.explain: This is the risk-register scenario: visible leadership sponsorship plus a fast VIP path handles it. Without the signed one-pager, every executive exception becomes a political incident that punches holes in the rollout.

quiz.q: The baseline review finds a forgotten remote-access tool on several machines. What do you do?
choices: Approve it — it was in the baseline, so it must be normal.
Investigate: unreviewed baselines allowlist bad habits. Remove the tool if unauthorized; approve narrowly only if legitimate.
quiz.explain: The baseline is observed behavior, not approved behavior — approving everything learned without categorization allowlists the organization's bad habits. The review is where you discover what IT thought the fleet ran versus what it actually runs.

quiz.q: Your canary ring missed a driver-version difference that broke 12 machines in Ring 2. What is the systemic fix?
choices: Ensure canaries cover the real variant space (driver versions, machine types) and record the lesson: the post-mortem updates the canary selection criteria.
quiz.explain: Canaries must be representative of the variant space, not just numerous. The miss becomes a process improvement: update selection criteria so the next rollout's canaries cover known variants.

quiz.q: The 90-day plan ends at day 80 with 'deployment complete.' What is missing?
choices: The harden-and-handover phase (days 81-90): exception audit, automated reports, finished documentation, retrospective, transition to steady-state ownership.
quiz.explain: Days 81-90 convert a deployed platform into sustainable operations with an owner. Skipping handover leaves a working deployment that slowly rots — the most common way good projects die.

quiz.q: Users are working around blocks with portable apps instead of requesting approvals. Which gate check failed?
choices: User sentiment — they do not understand or trust the request process, so the communication failed.
quiz.explain: Workarounds signal that users find the approved path harder than evasion — a communication and process failure, not a technical one. The pulse survey exists to catch this before it becomes culture.

items.prompt: What does each ring (0-3) prove?
items.answer: Ring 0: platform behavior, no business risk. Ring 1: real workflows, cooperative users. Ring 2: scale effects. Ring 3: proven policies, experienced support.
items.explain: Each ring buys knowledge the previous one could not.

items.prompt: How long should Learning Mode baselining run?
items.answer: 2-3 weeks minimum, covering a full business cycle including month-end.
items.explain: Periodic processes must be observed, not discovered on enforcement day.

items.prompt: What does the exec one-pager cover?
items.answer: What and why in business terms, expected disruption with the support plan, what leadership must provide (visible sponsorship).
items.explain: Signed before the rollout, it is your shield when executives escalate.

items.prompt: Name the four gate checks.
items.answer: Breakage rate/trend, resolution time, exception quality, user sentiment.
items.explain: Define criteria before the ring starts, when you can still be objective.

items.prompt: What are the three rollback tiers?
items.answer: Policy revert, wave halt, enforcement pause to monitor-only.
items.explain: Revert policy, not panic — never mass-uninstall.

items.prompt: Name the five success metrics.
items.answer: Coverage, block volume by category, exception inventory, ticket trends, time-to-approve.
items.explain: Track from day one so the final report writes itself.

items.prompt: Ring 2 tickets are rising week over week and resolution time just breached the commitment. What do you do?
items.answer: Invoke the gate: pause the next wave, diagnose whether it is policy quality, support capacity, or communication — fix the cause, then re-gate. Do not push into Ring 3 hoping it improves.
items.explain: Rising tickets after scale is the failing-rollout signal; gates without teeth are ceremonies.

items.prompt: The baseline categorized 214 apps; 9 are unknown. Walk through handling them.
items.answer: Investigate each: identify the software and its business purpose, remove what is unauthorized (like the forgotten remote-access tool), approve narrowly what is legitimate, document every decision.
items.explain: Unknown is not a category — it is a to-do list. The review is where shadow IT gets found.

items.prompt: A department was never interviewed and their legacy app breaks in Ring 3. What failed in the plan?
items.answer: The application inventory step — every department gets interviewed before Ring 2. Now: Tier 1 rollback for that group, diagnose, narrow exception, and add the interview to the pre-rollout checklist.
items.explain: This is the risk-register scenario; the mitigation was the inventory interviews.

items.prompt: Two machines sit in storage with no agent. Coverage reads 198/200. How do you report this?
items.answer: Report 99% with the two machines named, explained (in storage, documented), and tracked for reimaging — never round up to 100% silently.
items.explain: Every coverage gap gets a named reason; silent rounding is how gaps become permanent.

items.prompt: Time-to-approve median is 6 hours against a 2-hour commitment. What is the business risk?
items.answer: Users experience security as obstruction and start working around it — approve faster (staffing, pre-approved patterns) or watch workaround culture grow.
items.explain: Approval speed measures whether security enables or obstructs the business.

items.prompt: Write the one-paragraph executive summary of Meridian's 90-day results.
items.answer: 'In 90 days we moved 200 endpoints to deny-by-default: 1,900+ unauthorized executions denied, zero reported malware incidents, 23 tracked exceptions all owned and reviewed, approval median 45 minutes against a 2-hour commitment, 198/200 agents healthy.'
items.explain: Evidence, not adjectives: coverage, blocks with outcomes, exceptions governed, speed, gaps named.

handsOnLab.title: Write a 90-day deployment plan for a fictional 200-endpoint company
handsOnLab.brief: Produce the complete deployment plan package for Meridian Logistics (fictional, 200 endpoints): timeline with gates, ring design, baselining plan, both communications, rollback plan, metrics dashboard, and risk register. This is the document you would defend in front of a panel.
steps: Write the company profile: Meridian Logistics, 200 endpoints — 150 office, 40 warehouse across two buildings, 10 servers. Note the business rhythms that matter: month-end close, warehouse shipping peaks, the legacy label printer.
Design the four rings with machine counts, selection criteria for Ring 1 volunteers, and what each ring must prove. Put calendar dates on every ring assuming a week-1 start.
Write the Learning Mode baselining plan: duration, which machines, the review categories (approve, scope, updater-rule, reject, investigate), and who attends the review.
Draft the exec one-pager: the business why, honest disruption expectations, the support plan, and the specific ask of leadership. Keep it to one page.
Draft the user announcement for Ring 2: what changes, what to do when blocked, the response commitment, the workaround warning, the one-sentence why.
Define the gate criteria numerically: max tickets per machine per ring, resolution-time commitment, exception quality bar, sentiment survey threshold. Write the gate review template.
Write the three-tier rollback plan with the exact steps for Tier 1 (policy revert), who can authorize each tier, and the rehearsal you will run before Ring 1.
Build the metrics dashboard template: the five metrics, where each number comes from, the healthy trend for each, and the threshold that triggers concern.
Write the risk register: at least six risks (executive escalation, legacy app, support overload, missed periodic process, driver variants, user workarounds) with a mitigation for each.
Lay out the 90-day timeline: foundation, pilot, scale, complete, harden-and-handover — with every gate and communication marked on the calendar.
Write the day-90 executive summary as if the project succeeded: fill it with the realistic numbers from this module's worked example.
Save the package as deployment-plan.md and read it end to end as the skeptical executive. Fix anything that would not survive their questions.
handsOnLab.deliverable: deployment-plan.md containing the company profile, ring design with dates, baselining plan, exec one-pager, user announcement, gate criteria and template, rollback plan, metrics dashboard, risk register, 90-day timeline, and the day-90 executive summary.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every ring has dates and gate criteria; both communications answer their three questions; the rollback plan names who authorizes each tier; the risk register has six risks with mitigations; the plan survives a 30-minute skeptical read.

videos.title: ThreatLocker official YouTube channel
videos.blurb: Official deployment walkthroughs and best-practice content — use it to see how the vendor frames rollout phases and baselining, then compare against the operator discipline in this module. Channel; duration varies.

mockTask.q: Panel question: the CEO asks, 'Why should we pay for a project to block things that already work?' Give your two-minute answer.
choices: 'Because ransomware is scary and the news says so.'

'Because what 'works' today includes every unapproved installer, personal app, and malicious attachment your users run — last year one attachment cost three days of downtime. Deny-by-default blocks what is not approved before it executes: our pilot data shows hundreds of unauthorized executions stopped per week with legitimate work approved in under an hour. You pay to convert unknown risk into a governed list.'
mockTask.explain: The winning answer translates to business terms: names the actual cost (downtime), explains the mechanism in one line (blocks unapproved before execution), cites pilot evidence, and frames the outcome (unknown risk becomes a governed list). Fear, compliance, and peer pressure are weak closes; quantified risk reduction is the strong one.
