modules.title: MIT 6.858: Privilege Separation & Capabilities
modules.summary: Least privilege as a software design discipline: splitting programs into privileged and unprivileged parts, capabilities as unforgeable tokens of authority, and the confused-deputy problem. You will map these ideas directly onto Elevation Control and Ringfencing. Independent study in our own words; no affiliation claimed.
objectives: Apply least privilege to software design: give each component only the authority its job requires.
Design a privilege-separated program: split privileged operations from unprivileged parsing and input handling.
Explain capabilities as unforgeable, delegable tokens of authority and contrast them with ambient authority.
Diagnose the confused-deputy problem in a realistic scenario.
Map privilege-separation concepts onto Elevation Control's just-in-time elevation model.
Map capability thinking onto Ringfencing policies that bound what each application may do.

notes.title: Least privilege in software design
Privilege separation: splitting programs
Capabilities as unforgeable tokens
Ambient authority and the confused deputy
notes.body:
The confused deputy is the classic failure of ambient authority, and it is worth learning by heart because you will see it in the wild. A deputy is a privileged program that acts on behalf of less-privileged requesters — a compiler service, a backup daemon, a web app writing files. The confusion: the deputy cannot tell which authority it is exercising — its own, or the requester's — so an attacker tricks it into using its superior authority for the attacker's purpose. The deputy is not malicious and not buggy in the ordinary sense; it is doing exactly what it was asked. It was just asked by the wrong party, and it had no way to know.

Worked example: a shared 'document converter' service runs with write access to the company's report archive. Any employee can submit a document and name an output path — the service converts and writes the result. An attacker submits a conversion with the output path set to the archive's billing summary, and the input crafted so the 'converted' output overwrites it with garbage. The service, holding archive-write authority ambiently, happily destroys the billing summary on the attacker's behalf. The service was confused about whose authority it wielded: it used its own (write the archive) when it should have used the requester's (write only the requester's own files). The capability fix: the service receives from each requester a capability for the destination — a token the requester legitimately holds. The attacker holds no capability for the billing summary, so the write is refused. The deputy is no longer confused because it never wields its own authority on a requester's behalf — it only exercises the authority the requester delegated.

Operator relevance: you will meet confused deputies in endpoint policy. A backup agent with write-everywhere authority that takes instructions from user-writable config files is a deputy waiting to be confused. When you scope Ringfencing and Storage Control policies, ask of every privileged application: 'who can instruct this program, and can a lesser party aim its authority at something they should not reach?' If yes, narrow the authority or the instruction channel. The confused deputy is not a coding curiosity — it is a design-review question.

Spot the web's confused deputy: cross-site request forgery. Your browser holds your ambient authority as a logged-in session, and a malicious site tricks your browser into wielding it — submitting a transfer, changing your settings — while you merely visited a page. The browser was the confused deputy, unable to distinguish your intent from the attacker's. The fixes are capability-shaped: per-session anti-forgery tokens bind the authority to the legitimate page, and cookie policies stop the ambient authority from traveling cross-site. Every time you implement or review these defenses, you are applying this module's lesson — the deputy problem is not a historical curiosity but a daily web reality.

notes.title: How this shows up in Elevation Control
notes.body:
Now map the theory onto the platform. The standing-local-admin problem is ambient authority at the endpoint: every program the user runs inherits administrative power, so every bug in every program is a privilege-escalation bug waiting to happen. Elevation Control applies privilege separation to the whole endpoint: the user — and everything they run — operates unprivileged by default. When a specific application legitimately needs elevation, the platform grants just-in-time elevation delegated to that application via policy — a capability-like grant: this application, this operation, now, for this long. The authority is no longer ambient ('the user is an admin, so everything is admin'); it is a scoped token issued per need.

Worked example: an accounting application needs to update itself, which requires writing to a protected directory. Old world: the user is a local admin, so the updater — and everything else on the machine, including the user's browser with its twenty tabs of untrusted content — runs with full privilege. New world: the user is standard. The updater launches; the platform recognizes the approved updater identity and elevates just that process for the update operation per policy. The browser, the document viewer, the chat app — all still unprivileged. A phishing document exploiting the viewer now yields an unprivileged process, and there is no ambient admin authority to steal. The elevation was a capability: bound to the specific application, issued just in time, gone when the operation completes. If the updater itself is later compromised, the damage is bounded by what the elevation grant permitted — which is why the grant must be narrow, not 'elevate everything this vendor ships.'

Operator gotchas: the broad elevation grant — 'elevate anything signed by Vendor X' recreates ambient authority with extra steps; scope elevation to the specific application and operation. Another is elevation without expiry discipline: just-in-time must actually end; review what stays elevated. And user experience: if legitimate elevation takes ten minutes of approval latency, users will demand admin rights back — the approval path must be fast (module 10's support discipline) or the architecture loses politically what it gained technically.

Design the approval workflow with two paths: the fast path for known-good patterns (pre-approved application identities elevate in seconds, logged for audit) and the deliberate path for the novel (unknown requests get human review with the business justification). The fast path keeps the business moving — this is what prevents the 'give me admin back' revolt. The deliberate path is where judgment lives — and where you collect the data to promote patterns into the fast path over time. Measure both paths' latency like the deployment module's time-to-approve metric, because the workflow's speed is the architecture's political survival. A just-in-time system with multi-hour latency is just-in-time in name only.

notes.title: How this shows up in Ringfencing
notes.body:
Ringfencing is capability thinking applied per application: instead of each program wielding the user's full ambient authority, each allowed application gets exactly the authority its job requires — and the platform enforces the boundary. The document viewer may read documents and write to the documents folder; it may not launch script interpreters, edit the registry, or open network connections. Those denials are not punishments; they are the application operating under least privilege. When the viewer's parser is exploited (module 14's scenario), the hijacked process finds its capability set is precisely the viewer's job description — and a shell, a network exfiltration, or a registry persistence mechanism is not in it.

Worked example — writing a Ringfencing policy as capabilities. Application: the firm's PDF reader. Job analysis: it needs to read PDF files from user directories and the document share, write nothing except print spooling, launch no child processes, touch no registry keys beyond its own settings, and reach no network addresses. The policy expresses exactly that: read allowed on the document paths, write denied except the spool path, child-process execution denied, registry writes denied outside its key, network denied. Each rule is a capability grant or refusal. Test it against the confused deputy: can a malicious PDF instruct the reader to write an executable somewhere? The write rules say no — the reader holds no write capability beyond the spool path, so there is nothing for the attacker to aim. Can it be tricked into launching a helper that does the damage? Child execution is denied — no deputy to confuse.

Common mistakes: the 'allow everything the app asks for' policy — learning what an app touches and permitting all of it just re-creates ambient authority with paperwork; the job analysis must be normative (what SHOULD it need), not merely descriptive. Another is forgetting the updater: the reader's updater legitimately needs network and install-path writes — that is a separate, narrower policy for the updater identity, not a hole in the reader's policy. And policy drift: applications gain features, features need new capabilities, and nobody reviews whether the old grants are still minimal — the review-date discipline from module 11 applies to Ringfencing policies too.

Think of per-application Ringfencing as a firewall where the 'network' is the operating system: just as a network firewall defines which hosts may talk to which, the application policy defines which resources each application may touch. The mental model transfers directly — default deny, explicit allows, rules scoped to identity (the application, not the address), and denied attempts logged as intelligence. When you explain Ringfencing to network engineers, use their vocabulary: it is a host firewall for application behavior. The analogy is honest because the principles are identical; only the enforcement point moved. And like firewall rules, application rules need the same hygiene: reviewed, minimal, documented, with expiry on the temporary.

notes.title: Design exercise: privilege-separating a fictional updater
notes.body: Let us do the full design exercise, because this is the skill the interview panel will probe. Target: 'QuickPatch,' a fictional third-party updater that downloads and installs application updates. Current design: runs as a privileged service, fetches manifests over HTTPS, parses them, downloads binaries, executes installers — all as one privileged process parsing untrusted network input. Threat model: the update server could be compromised, a network attacker could tamper with manifests, and the manifest parser is complex code facing untrusted data. A single bug anywhere yields full system privilege. Separated design, step by step. Identify the truly privileged operations: writing to the install directories and executing the installer. Everything else — fetching, parsing, verifying — needs no privilege. Split: an unprivileged fetcher/parser downloads the manifest and binaries, parses them, and verifies signatures against pinned vendor keys. It then asks the privileged installer a single narrow question: 'install this verified package,' passing a capability — a handle to the downloaded, signature-verified file, not a path it could swap. The installer validates: is the signature valid, is this package in the approved set, is the target directory the application directory? Only then does it write and execute. The channel between them carries exactly one operation with exactly one validated payload. Now attack your own design (the iterate step from module 13). Attack one: compromise the update server and serve a malicious manifest — defeated, the parser verifies signatures against pinned keys and the installer re-validates. Attack two: exploit the parser with a malformed manifest — yields an unprivileged process that can only ask the installer to install signature-valid packages; the installer refuses. Attack three: swap the file between verification and install (time-of-check to time-of-use) — defeated by passing a handle, not a path; the installer validates the handle's contents. Residual risks, stated honestly: a bug in the small installer itself, a compromised vendor signing key, a malicious but properly signed update from the vendor. Each residual is explicit and owned — which is the honest endpoint of the exercise. Practice delivering this design aloud in five minutes: it is exactly the shape of a strong panel answer. Practice the whiteboard narrative until it is smooth, because the panel will ask for exactly this shape: 'Design something secure.' Open with the threat model (thirty seconds), sketch the split (one minute), define the narrow channel and its validation (one minute), attack your own design out loud (one minute), and close with honest residuals (thirty seconds). The self-attack is the differentiator — most candidates present a design; few volunteer its weaknesses before being asked. Bring a marker-friendly diagram: two boxes, one arrow, the validation checks labeled on the arrow. Five minutes, one whiteboard, zero bluffing — that is the performance this module has been building toward.

cards.front: State the principle of least privilege.
cards.back: Every component holds only the authority its job requires — excess authority is pre-authorized damage when the component is compromised.

cards.front: What is privilege separation, structurally?
cards.back: Splitting a program into a small privileged monitor (few validated operations, distrusts input) and a large unprivileged worker (handles dangerous parsing/input with no privilege).

cards.front: What must the privileged part do with every request from the unprivileged part?
cards.back: Validate it against policy — blind obedience recreates the monolith's risk; the monitor must distrust the worker.

cards.front: What is a capability?
cards.back: An unforgeable token naming a specific object and permitted operations — authority comes from holding the token, not from identity.

cards.front: Contrast ambient authority with capabilities.
cards.back: Ambient: authority from who you are (user/groups), inherited by everything you run. Capabilities: authority from which tokens you hold, each scoped to an object and delegable precisely.

cards.front: Give a classic real capability example.
cards.back: A file descriptor: names one open file, permits specific operations, cannot be forged or guessed, and can be handed to another process to delegate exactly that authority.

cards.front: What is the confused deputy problem?
cards.back: A privileged program acting for requesters cannot distinguish its own authority from the requester's, so an attacker tricks it into wielding superior authority for malicious ends.

cards.front: What is the capability fix for the confused deputy?
cards.back: The deputy exercises only authority the requester delegated via capabilities — it never wields its own ambient authority on a requester's behalf.

cards.front: How is Elevation Control capability-like?
cards.back: It replaces ambient local-admin with just-in-time elevation granted per application via policy — a scoped, temporary authority token instead of standing privilege.

cards.front: How is Ringfencing capability thinking?
cards.back: Each allowed application gets exactly the authority its job requires (read/write/execute/network scoped per app) instead of the user's full ambient authority.

cards.front: What is the defining property of a capability, and what breaks it?
cards.back: Unforgeability — if the token is guessable (a filename, an incrementable integer), it is not a capability.

cards.front: In the QuickPatch design, why pass a file handle and not a path to the installer?
cards.back: To defeat time-of-check-to-time-of-use swaps: the installer validates the handle's actual contents rather than trusting a path the parser could change after verification.

quiz.q: A program runs as full administrator 24/7 because it writes one config file at startup. What is the least-privilege redesign?
choices: Keep it as is; rewriting is expensive.
Run unprivileged; use a tiny audited helper holding only the config-write authority, exposing one validated operation.
Run as administrator but add a firewall.
quiz.explain: Redistribute authority so the big, buggy, input-facing code holds none of it. The helper is small enough to audit; the 'sometimes needs privilege' becomes a scoped grant, not a lifetime one.

quiz.q: In a separated design, the privileged monitor opens whatever path the unprivileged worker names. What is wrong?
choices: The separation is theater: the monitor blindly obeys, so compromising the worker still yields arbitrary file access. The monitor must validate every request.
quiz.explain: Splitting without distrust changes nothing — the attacker aims the monitor's authority through the worker. Validation of every request against policy is what makes separation real.

quiz.q: Why is a file descriptor a capability but a filename is not?
choices: A descriptor is an unforgeable reference to a specific open object with fixed operations; a filename is guessable, re-targetable ambient naming — anyone can name any file.
quiz.explain: Unforgeability is the defining property. A filename can be guessed or swapped (symlink attacks); a descriptor cannot be minted by the holder and names exactly one object.

quiz.q: The document-converter service overwrites the billing summary because the attacker named it as the output path. What failed?
choices: The converter has a buffer overflow.
Confused deputy: the service wielded its own archive-write authority for a requester who held no such authority. Fix with per-request destination capabilities.
quiz.explain: The service was not buggy in the ordinary sense — it could not distinguish its authority from the requester's. Capabilities fix it by ensuring the deputy only exercises delegated authority.

quiz.q: A user is a local admin, so their browser runs with full privilege. What does Elevation Control change, architecturally?
choices: It removes ambient admin: everything runs unprivileged by default; only specific applications get just-in-time scoped elevation via policy — a phishing exploit now yields an unprivileged process.
quiz.explain: The architectural move is ambient-to-scoped: standing privilege becomes per-application, just-in-time grants. Exploitation still happens, but the inherited authority — the real prize — is gone.

quiz.q: Your Ringfencing policy for the PDF reader permits everything the reader was observed doing, including launching a helper updater with network access. What is the flaw?
choices: There is no flaw; observation is policy.
Descriptive-only policy re-creates ambient authority with paperwork — the updater needs a separate narrow policy; the reader's job analysis should be normative (what it SHOULD need).
PDF readers do not need policies.
quiz.explain: Permitting all observed behavior confuses description with authorization. Separate identities get separate policies, each scoped to the job — that is capability thinking, not behavior recording.

quiz.q: An elevation grant reads 'elevate anything signed by Vendor X.' Why is this dangerous?
choices: It recreates ambient authority with extra steps — any current or future Vendor X binary, including a compromised updater, inherits elevation. Scope to the specific application and operation.
quiz.explain: Broad grants defeat the purpose of just-in-time scoping. The grant must name the application and operation — otherwise one compromised vendor binary escalates everything.

quiz.q: In the QuickPatch design, the parser verifies signatures and the installer re-validates. Why validate twice?
choices: Defense in depth across the trust boundary: the unprivileged parser's verification can be bypassed if the parser is compromised, so the privileged installer must independently validate before acting.
quiz.explain: The installer distrusts the worker — that is the separation contract. Each side of a trust boundary validates independently, because the other side may already be compromised.

quiz.q: A capability system has no revocation story. What is the risk?
choices: Delegated authority cannot be taken back — a compromised holder keeps its power indefinitely. Design expiry or indirection upfront.
quiz.explain: Easy grant and delegation without revocation is a one-way ratchet. 'We will figure out revocation later' means never — build expiry or revocable indirection into the design.

quiz.q: Which statement best captures the module's through-line?
choices: Privilege is necessary, so accept the risk.
Assume components will be compromised; architect so each holds minimal authority — separation, capabilities, and per-app policies bound what any single compromise can achieve.
Remove all privileges from all software.
quiz.explain: The through-line from least privilege through separation and capabilities to Elevation Control and Ringfencing: design for compromise, bound the blast radius architecturally, never rely on any single component's correctness.

items.prompt: State least privilege in one sentence.
items.answer: Each component holds only the authority its job requires.
items.explain: Excess authority is pre-authorized damage.

items.prompt: What are the two parts of a separated program, and what does each do?
items.answer: Small privileged monitor (few validated operations) + large unprivileged worker (dangerous parsing, no privilege).
items.explain: The monitor distrusts and validates everything the worker sends.

items.prompt: Define a capability.
items.answer: Unforgeable token naming a specific object and permitted operations.
items.explain: Authority from holding the token, not from identity.

items.prompt: What is the confused deputy?
items.answer: A privileged program tricked into wielding its own authority for an attacker's purpose, unable to distinguish its authority from the requester's.
items.explain: Fixed by exercising only delegated capabilities.

items.prompt: How is Elevation Control capability-like?
items.answer: Just-in-time per-application elevation via policy replaces ambient local admin — scoped, temporary authority tokens.
items.explain: Standing privilege becomes per-need grants.

items.prompt: How is Ringfencing capability thinking?
items.answer: Each app gets exactly its job's authority (read/write/execute/network scoped) instead of the user's ambient authority.
items.explain: A hijacked app finds only its job description in its capability set.

items.prompt: Why must the monitor validate every worker request?
items.answer: Blind obedience lets a compromised worker aim the monitor's authority arbitrarily — separation without distrust is theater.
items.explain: Validation is the separation contract.

items.prompt: A backup agent takes its include-list from a user-writable config file and runs with read-all-files authority. Diagnose.
items.answer: Confused deputy: a lesser party (any user editing the config) can aim the agent's superior authority at files they should not reach. Fix: privileged launcher validates the config against policy, or the agent reads only via capabilities it is granted per job.
items.explain: Ask of every privileged app: who can instruct it, and can a lesser party aim its authority?

items.prompt: Your team proposes running the new chat app as admin 'because it needs to update itself.' Counter with the separated design.
items.answer: App runs standard; a tiny audited updater holds install-path write authority, invoked only for signature-verified packages via a narrow channel — the chat parser never holds privilege.
items.explain: 'Needs admin sometimes' is the design opportunity, not the verdict.

items.prompt: An API uses incrementing integer IDs as 'capabilities' for customer records. What is wrong?
items.answer: They are forgeable — incrementing the integer accesses another customer's record. Real capabilities must be unforgeable (unguessable tokens bound to the object).
items.explain: Guessable IDs are ambient naming with extra steps; the confused-deputy and IDOR families live here.

items.prompt: Elevation approvals take 20 minutes and users demand admin rights back. What is the real problem?
items.answer: The approval path is too slow — architecture loses politically what it gained technically. Fix the support latency (fast verification, pre-approved patterns), not the architecture.
items.explain: Security that obstructs the business gets routed around; speed the legitimate path.

items.prompt: A Ringfencing policy has not been reviewed in two years and the app gained three features. What do you do?
items.answer: Re-run the job analysis: map each new feature to required capabilities, prune grants the job no longer needs, set the review date — policy drift silently re-creates ambient authority.
items.explain: Authority creeps with features; the review-date discipline exists for exactly this.

items.prompt: Deliver the 5-minute QuickPatch design to a panel. What is the structure?
items.answer: Threat model (compromised server, parser bugs) → split (unprivileged fetch/parse/verify, tiny privileged installer) → narrow channel (one validated operation, handle not path) → self-attack (malicious manifest, parser exploit, TOCTOU swap) → honest residual risks.
items.explain: Model, split, validate, self-attack, residuals — the shape of a strong design answer.

handsOnLab.title: Least-privilege review of three everyday programs
handsOnLab.brief: Pick three programs you actually use, inventory the authority each holds versus what its job requires, and sketch a privilege-separated redesign for one of them. You produce the kind of review a security architect would commission.
steps: Choose three everyday programs: e.g., a document viewer, a chat application, and a backup or sync tool. Prefer ones you genuinely run.

For each, build the holds-vs-needs table: columns for authority (files it can read/write, processes it can launch, network it can reach, privilege level it runs at), what it holds today, what its job actually requires, and the gap.
Be honest about the gaps: mark every 'holds but does not need' cell — these are the pre-authorized damage if the program is compromised.
Pick the program with the worst gap. Write its threat model in four lines: asset, adversary, surface, boundary (module 13's loop).

Sketch the separated redesign: name the privileged operations (the tiny set), describe the unprivileged worker and what it handles, and define the narrow channel between them (operations, validation rules).
Run the confused-deputy check on your design: who can instruct the privileged part, and can a lesser party aim its authority somewhere wrong? Fix what you find.
Define the capability inventory for the redesign: what tokens the worker holds at startup, what it can delegate, and the revocation/expiry story.
Write the residual risks honestly: what your redesign does not fix (e.g., a bug in the tiny privileged part, a compromised signing key).
Map your redesign onto platform controls: which parts would Elevation Control and Ringfencing enforce on a real endpoint, and what the policies would roughly scope.
Condense the redesign to a 5-minute spoken walkthrough and practice it aloud.
Save as least-privilege-review.md with the three tables, the redesign, the deputy check, capabilities, residuals, and the platform mapping.
handsOnLab.deliverable: least-privilege-review.md with holds-vs-needs tables for three programs, a full privilege-separated redesign of the worst offender, the confused-deputy check, capability inventory with revocation, honest residuals, and the Elevation Control/Ringfencing mapping.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every program has a holds/needs/gap table; the redesign's privileged interface is tiny and validated; the deputy check found and fixed at least one aiming path; residuals are explicit and owned.

mockTask.q: Panel question: 'Our admin tool runs as SYSTEM all the time because it occasionally needs it. Convince me to change that.'
choices: 'Running as SYSTEM is fine if the code is good.'

'Every bug in that tool is a full-system-compromise bug today, because ambient SYSTEM authority is inherited by all its code including the network parser. Split it: a tiny audited helper holds the SYSTEM-only operations behind validated requests, the big input-handling code runs unprivileged — so the next parser bug yields a low-privilege process, not the kingdom. On our endpoints we enforce the same idea with just-in-time elevation per application.'
'We should rewrite the tool in a safe language.'
mockTask.explain: The winning answer quantifies the current risk (every bug = SYSTEM), proposes the concrete separated design, names the outcome (parser bug yields low-privilege), and connects to the platform's Elevation Control — theory, design, and operational mapping in one answer. That is what a panel means by 'depth.'

modules.title: MIT 6.858: Sandboxing & Isolation
modules.summary: Confinement as a security primitive: sandboxing native code, seccomp syscall filtering, the isolation spectrum from processes to containers to VMs, and the performance-security tradeoff. You will map every concept onto Ringfencing policies you can actually write. Independent study in our own words; no affiliation claimed.
objectives: Explain what a sandbox guarantees: bounded authority for untrusted or compromised code.
Describe why sandboxing native code is hard: system calls as the escape hatch.
Sketch a seccomp-style syscall filter policy for a realistic application.
Compare processes, containers, and VMs on the isolation spectrum and choose correctly.
Reason about the performance-security tradeoff with concrete overhead thinking.
Write a Ringfencing-style sandbox policy that blocks defined attack scenarios while preserving the workflow.

notes.title: What sandboxing is: bounded authority for dangerous code
Sandboxing native code: the hard parts
seccomp and syscall filtering: policy at the kernel door
The isolation spectrum: processes, containers, VMs
notes.body:
Isolation mechanisms sit on a spectrum of strength versus cost, and choosing correctly is an operator skill. Processes: the OS separates memory and gives each process its own file-descriptor table and user identity — cheap (microseconds to create), but a compromised process still shares the kernel, the filesystem view, and the network stack with everyone else. Containers: OS-level virtualization that adds namespaces (separate views of processes, network, filesystem mounts) and resource limits around groups of processes — still sharing one kernel, but with a much smaller visible world per container; cheap enough to run dozens per host. Virtual machines: a hypervisor emulates hardware, and each VM runs its own full kernel — the strongest isolation on the list, because a compromised VM must escape the hypervisor rather than just the OS; but heavy (gigabytes of memory, seconds to boot) and operationally complex.

Worked example — three ways to isolate a risky document converter, and the reasoning for each. As a sandboxed process with a syscall filter: cheapest, fastest, sufficient if the threat is parser bugs and the policy is tight — the converter never legitimately needs the network, so the filter denies it outright. As a container: better when the converter needs a whole toolchain (fonts, libraries, temp space) — the container gives it a private filesystem and no network namespace, containing both the exploit and the mess. As a VM: justified when the documents come from active adversaries and the converter handles the CEO's inbox — the hypervisor boundary means even a kernel exploit in the guest stays in the guest. The choice follows the threat model (module 13): match the isolation strength to the adversary tier and the blast radius, and do not pay VM costs for process-level threats.

Common mistakes: container-as-security-boundary thinking — containers share the kernel, so a kernel vulnerability breaks all containers on the host; containers are a packaging and weak-isolation tool, not a VM. Another is VM sprawl: isolating everything in VMs 'to be safe' creates an unmanageable, unpatched fleet of mini-servers — each VM is a machine you must maintain. And the performance cop-out: 'VMs are too slow so we will not isolate' — measure; the spectrum exists precisely so you can pick the cheapest mechanism that meets the threat.

Know the middle ground: microVMs — virtual machines stripped to the minimum, booting in milliseconds with tiny memory footprints — built for the 'VM isolation at container speed' use case. They do not replace the spectrum's reasoning; they add a point on it, letting you buy near-VM isolation for workloads that could never afford full VMs. The operator lesson is not the technology but the habit: revisit your isolation choices as the mechanisms evolve, because a choice that was correct three years ago may be wrong today. The spectrum moves; your architecture should move with it, guided always by the threat model rather than by novelty.

notes.title: The performance-security tradeoff, honestly
notes.body:
Every isolation mechanism costs something — CPU cycles, memory, latency, operational complexity — and pretending otherwise produces security designs nobody deploys. The honest approach is quantifying the cost against the threat. Context switches between a sandboxed process and its monitor cost microseconds; for a network service handling thousands of requests per second, that can be measurable but is usually dwarfed by network latency. Syscall filtering adds per-call overhead in the nanoseconds — negligible for most workloads, noticeable only in syscall-heavy hot loops. Containers add near-zero runtime overhead (no emulation, just kernel bookkeeping) — their cost is operational: image management, orchestration, patching the fleet of images. VMs add real overhead: emulated or virtualized hardware, duplicated kernels in memory, I/O indirection — single-digit to double-digit percentage performance costs plus minutes of provisioning time.

Worked example — reasoning it through for the endpoint fleet. Should every workstation application run in its own VM? The security gain is real (hypervisor isolation per app), but the cost is absurd: hundreds of VMs per user, unmanageable patching, destroyed battery life and user experience — the design fails the deployability test. Should the PDF reader get a Ringfencing policy (application-layer sandbox)? Cost: near zero at runtime, some policy-maintenance effort. Gain: the reader's parser bugs are contained to the reader's job description. The tradeoff is overwhelmingly favorable — this is why application-layer sandboxing won on endpoints. Should the browser's renderer get OS-level sandboxing with a tight syscall filter? Cost: engineering effort by the browser vendor, modest runtime overhead. Gain: the most-attacked code on the machine (web content parsing) is contained. Also favorable — which is why modern browsers do exactly this. The method: name the cost, name the threat it addresses, and check that the ratio makes sense — security economics, not security vibes.

Common mistakes: the 'performance is paramount' veto that kills all isolation — usually asserted without measurement; measure first, then decide. The reverse: gold-plating low-risk components with VM-grade isolation while the actual crown jewels run unconfined — the threat model should allocate the isolation budget, not habit. And ignoring operational cost: a sandbox nobody can maintain becomes a sandbox with a stale, hole-ridden policy — the cheapest mechanism you will actually maintain beats the perfect one you will abandon.

Use the latency-budget method for services: start from the user-visible budget — say two hundred milliseconds per request — allocate it across components, and give security mechanisms their explicit slice. If the sandbox costs two milliseconds of a two-hundred-millisecond budget, the discussion is over — it fits. If it costs fifty, you negotiate: can the check be cached, moved off the hot path, or applied selectively to untrusted inputs? The budget turns 'too slow' from a veto into an engineering problem with numbers. And it exposes the real tradeoffs: teams routinely spend large slices on analytics tracking while vetoing slivers of sandboxing — the budget makes the priorities visible, which is often the actual problem.

notes.title: Mapping sandboxing onto Ringfencing policies
notes.body:
Here the course converges: Ringfencing is sandboxing at the application-policy layer, and everything in this module maps onto writing better Ringfencing policies. The sandbox guarantee becomes the policy's promise: this application may do exactly its job, nothing more. The syscall-filter mindset becomes the rule-writing discipline: enumerate what the application legitimately needs — which files, which registry areas, which network destinations, which child processes — and deny everything else by default. The job analysis from module 15 becomes the policy's source document: normative (what it should need), not merely descriptive (what it was observed doing). And the escape mindset from the next note becomes the review question: 'if this application were fully hijacked, what could it still do under this policy?'

Worked example — a Ringfencing-style policy for the firm's PDF reader, written as a sandbox spec. Identity: the reader's executable. File rules: read allowed on user document directories and the shared drive; write denied everywhere except the print spool path; execute denied for any file the reader writes (no drop-and-run). Process rules: child process creation denied entirely — the reader has no legitimate children; the updater is a separate identity with its own narrow policy. Registry rules: writes allowed only under the reader's own key. Network rules: denied — the reader never legitimately needs the network; updates come through the separate updater. Now the attack scenarios. Malicious PDF exploits the parser: the hijacked reader tries to write a payload — denied except spool path, and spool writes are not executable. Tries to launch PowerShell — child creation denied. Tries to exfiltrate via the network — denied. Tries to persist via registry run keys — denied outside its own key. The policy holds because each rule was derived from the job, and the job never included those actions.

Operator gotchas: the policy written from observation alone — 'the reader touched these 200 files, allow them all' — is a sandbox in name only; normative analysis must prune it. The forgotten updater path: updates need network and install writes, so give the updater its own tight policy rather than punching holes in the reader's. And the 'temporary' loosening — 'allow network for now, we will tighten later' — later never comes; write the tight policy first and loosen only with the exception discipline from module 11.

Review policies with a checklist, quarterly per application: is the identity still correct (no renames, no updater drift)? Is every allow still in the job description (prune the cruft)? Are the denies still holding (spot-check the block logs for the actions that should be denied)? Has the application gained features needing new analysis? Is there a temporary loosening past its expiry? The checklist takes twenty minutes per app and prevents the two slow killers: policy drift (accumulating cruft) and bit rot (rules that stopped matching reality). Assign each application's review to a named owner — policies without owners are policies without maintenance, and unmaintained sandboxes are decorative.

notes.title: When sandboxes fail: the escape mindset
notes.body: Close the module where serious operators live: assuming the sandbox will be tested and thinking like the escape artist. Sandboxes fail in a taxonomy worth memorizing. Policy gaps: the filter allows a syscall the designer forgot is dangerous — the classic is allowing an obscure syscall with powerful side effects, or argument constraints with a loophole. Trusted-component compromise: the sandbox's own enforcement code has a bug — the monitor, the filter loader, the policy parser. Side channels: the sandbox bounds syscalls but the attacker exfiltrates data via timing, shared caches, or other channels the policy never considered. Composition failures: two sandboxes, each sound alone, interact badly — the classic is a sandboxed process that can ask an unsandboxed helper to do its dirty work (the confused deputy again, wearing a sandbox costume). And the oldest: the sandbox was never actually enabled in production — deployed in monitor mode, or disabled for 'compatibility' and never re-enabled. Worked example — auditing a sandbox with the escape mindset. Target: the PDF reader policy from the last note. Policy gaps: does 'write allowed to the spool path' let the attacker write a malicious file the print spooler then executes? Check what consumes the spool path — the boundary moved, not disappeared. Trusted components: who parses the policy, and does the parser face untrusted input? Composition: the reader is denied network, but can it write a file to a synced cloud folder that exfiltrates on sync? The cloud sync app is a separate identity with network rights — the reader just found a deputy. Side channels: can the hijacked reader encode stolen data in the printed output? Possibly — printing is allowed, and the information flow was never bounded, only the syscall set. Each finding does not necessarily kill the design, but each must be answered: tighten, monitor, or explicitly accept and document. The escape mindset is not paranoia — it is the iterate step of module 13 applied to your own sandbox. Final synthesis of the 6.858 arc: threat modeling taught you to reason from goals and adversaries; control hijacking showed what memory bugs give attackers; privilege separation and capabilities showed how to bound authority by design; sandboxing showed how to bound it at runtime. The through-line never changed: perfect code is impossible, so architecture assumes compromise and contains it. On the endpoint, that architecture has a name — deny-by-default application control with per-application boundaries — and you now understand it from the silicon up to the policy. That is operator-grade depth, and it is exactly what the October 13 panel is hoping to hear. Think like the escape researcher for a day: their workflow is recon (map the sandbox's boundary — which syscalls, which IPC channels, which helpers), differential analysis (what does the sandboxed app do differently — the differences are the policy), and chaining (the parser bug gets code execution, the helper's permissive channel gets the escape — two medium bugs become one critical). Borrow the workflow defensively: recon your own sandbox's boundary, enumerate its helpers and their authority, and ask which two-bug chain breaks it. Researchers publish their escapes; read them as free audits of the patterns you deploy. Every public sandbox escape is a lesson someone else paid for — collect them.

cards.front: What guarantee does a sandbox provide?
cards.back: Bounded authority: even compromised or malicious code cannot act outside the box the policy defines — though escapes exist, so it is one layer, not a verdict.

cards.front: Why is sandboxing native code harder than sandboxing scripts?
cards.back: Native code runs directly on the processor and can issue system calls — the OS front door — so the sandbox must interpose on every syscall path without missing one.

cards.front: What is seccomp, in one sentence?
cards.back: A Linux mechanism letting a process irreversibly restrict its own (and children's) permitted system calls, with argument constraints, enforced by the kernel.

cards.front: Why is seccomp's irreversibility important?
cards.back: The policy is a cage, not a suggestion — once installed, the sandboxed code cannot remove its own restrictions even when fully hijacked.

cards.front: What makes a syscall filter strong vs weak?
cards.back: Argument constraints ('open, read-only only') and job-derived minimalism make it strong; broad syscall classes ('file access') make it weak.

cards.front: Order processes, containers, VMs by isolation strength and state the cost of each.
cards.back: Processes (cheapest, share kernel/filesystem/network view) < containers (namespaces + limits, still one kernel) < VMs (own kernel via hypervisor; strongest, heaviest: memory, boot time, patching burden).

cards.front: Why are containers not a VM-grade security boundary?
cards.back: They share the host kernel — one kernel vulnerability breaks every container on the host.

cards.front: How do you honestly evaluate the performance-security tradeoff?
cards.back: Name the cost (cycles, latency, operational burden), name the threat it addresses, check the ratio — measure rather than assert, and let the threat model allocate the isolation budget.

cards.front: How does Ringfencing map to sandboxing?
cards.back: It is sandboxing at the application-policy layer: each allowed app gets exactly its job's authority (files, registry, network, child processes) with deny-by-default — the policy is the sandbox.

cards.front: What is the normative vs descriptive question in policy writing?
cards.back: Normative: what SHOULD the app need (prunes the policy). Descriptive: what was it observed doing (re-creates ambient authority with paperwork). Policies must be normative.

cards.front: Name four sandbox failure modes.
cards.back: Policy gaps (forgotten dangerous syscalls), trusted-component bugs, side channels (timing, caches), composition failures (sandboxed code aiming an unsandboxed deputy) — plus the classic: never actually enabled.

cards.front: What is the through-line of the four 6.858 modules?
cards.back: Perfect code is impossible, so architecture assumes compromise and contains it — from threat models through hijacking, privilege separation, to sandboxing.

quiz.q: A sandboxed font parser is hijacked via a parser bug. It tries to open the user's documents, create a network socket, and map executable memory. The filter allows only: read the input file, write the output pipe, allocate non-executable memory, exit. What happens?
choices: All three attacker actions succeed; the sandbox failed.
All three are denied by the filter — the hijack succeeded but achieved nothing, because the policy was derived from the job.
The parser crashes before the hijack.
quiz.explain: This is the sandbox guarantee working: control flow was hijacked, but every path to useful action crossed the filter and died. Job-derived minimalism is what makes the box hold.

quiz.q: Why must native-code sandboxes interpose on system calls?
choices: Syscalls are the OS front door to files, network, processes, and memory — any unmediated path to the kernel is a sandbox hole.
quiz.explain: Native code's power is direct kernel access. The sandbox boundary IS the syscall boundary — miss one path (an obscure syscall, a shared-memory channel) and the box leaks.

quiz.q: Your seccomp filter allows 'openat' without argument constraints. What is the weakness?
choices: The filter allows file opens generally instead of read-only opens of specific targets — argument constraints are what make the filter strong; without them it is a weak, broad permission.
quiz.explain: Broad syscall classes re-create the risk inside the box. 'Allow openat but read-only' versus 'allow openat' is the difference between a sandbox and a suggestion.

quiz.q: You need to isolate a document converter handling attachments from active adversaries, aimed at the CEO's inbox. Which isolation and why?
choices: A VM — the adversary tier (targeted, high value target) justifies hypervisor isolation; a kernel exploit in the guest stays in the guest.
No isolation — the converter is trusted.
quiz.explain: The threat model allocates the isolation budget: active adversaries plus a high-value target justify the VM's cost. Containers share the kernel — insufficient against an adversary who may bring kernel exploits.

quiz.q: A team rejects all sandboxing as 'too slow' without measurements. What is the operator response?
choices: Accept the veto; performance is paramount.
Measure first: syscall filtering costs nanoseconds per call, containers near-zero runtime overhead — the veto is usually asserted without data, and the spectrum offers cheap options.
quiz.explain: Security economics, not vibes: quantify the cost against the threat. The isolation spectrum exists so you can pick the cheapest mechanism that meets the threat — most objections evaporate on measurement.

quiz.q: Your Ringfencing policy for the PDF reader was built purely from observed behavior — 200 files allowed. What is wrong?
choices: It is descriptive, not normative — it re-creates ambient authority with paperwork. Prune to what the job SHOULD need.
quiz.explain: Permitting everything observed confuses description with authorization. The job analysis must be normative — otherwise the 'sandbox' permits whatever the app happened to touch, including the attacker's paths.

quiz.q: The PDF reader is denied network, but it can write to a cloud-synced folder, and the sync app has network rights. What failure mode is this?
choices: Composition failure — the sandboxed reader aims an unsandboxed deputy (the sync app) to exfiltrate; the boundary moved, not disappeared.
quiz.explain: The confused deputy in sandbox costume: each component's policy is sound alone, but together they compose an exfiltration path. Audit the deputies your sandboxed apps can reach.

quiz.q: The sandbox policy was deployed in monitor-only mode 'temporarily' six months ago. What is this, and the fix?
choices: The classic never-enabled failure — a monitor-mode sandbox enforces nothing. Fix: enforce now, handle the breakage with the exception discipline, and never deploy security in permanent 'temporary' mode.
It is still protecting via logging.
quiz.explain: Monitor-only is visibility, not containment. 'Temporary' without an expiry is permanent — enforce, manage the breakage properly, and put expiry discipline on every temporary relaxation.

quiz.q: A hijacked reader encodes stolen data in its allowed printed output. Which sandbox property does this defeat?
choices: None directly — the sandbox bounded authority (syscalls), not information flow; exfiltration via allowed outputs is a side/covert channel the policy never considered.
quiz.explain: Sandboxes bound authority, not information flow, unless explicitly designed for it. Allowed outputs are legitimate channels that can carry stolen data — the escape mindset asks about flows, not just calls.

quiz.q: What connects this module back to module 13's first-principles loop?
choices: The escape mindset IS the iterate step: define the sandbox's goal and adversary, design the policy mechanism, then attack your own design (policy gaps, deputies, side channels) and refine.
Threat models are only for networks.
quiz.explain: The loop never left: goal (bound the app's authority), adversary (hijacked app), mechanism (the policy), iterate (escape-mindset audit). First-principles reasoning applies to sandboxes exactly as to networks.

items.prompt: What does a sandbox guarantee, and what does it not?
items.answer: Bounded authority for code inside; not absolute safety — escapes exist, so it is one layer.
items.explain: Converts 'any bug is total compromise' into 'bug plus escape is compromise.'

items.prompt: Why must native sandboxes interpose on syscalls?
items.answer: Syscalls are the kernel's front door; any unmediated path is a hole.
items.explain: The sandbox boundary is the syscall boundary.

items.prompt: What is seccomp and why does irreversibility matter?
items.answer: Irreversible, kernel-enforced syscall restriction; the cage cannot be opened by the code inside.
items.explain: Policy as cage, not suggestion.

items.prompt: Order processes, containers, VMs by isolation strength.
items.answer: Processes < containers (share kernel) < VMs (own kernel via hypervisor).
items.explain: Match strength to adversary tier; do not pay VM costs for process threats.

items.prompt: Why are containers not VM-grade boundaries?
items.answer: Shared kernel — one kernel bug breaks all containers on the host.
items.explain: Packaging and weak isolation, not a security boundary.

items.prompt: How is Ringfencing sandboxing?
items.answer: Application-policy-layer sandbox: each app gets exactly its job's authority, deny-by-default.
items.explain: The policy is the sandbox.

items.prompt: Name four sandbox failure modes.
items.answer: Policy gaps, trusted-component bugs, side channels, composition failures (+ never enabled).
items.explain: The escape-mindset audit checklist.

items.prompt: Write the syscall-allow list for a log-uploader that reads one log file and POSTs it to a fixed HTTPS endpoint. Justify each entry.
items.answer: read (the log), write (sockets + logs), openat read-only (the log path), socket/connect (TCP to the fixed endpoint only — ideally constrained), TLS needs (getrandom), mmap non-exec, exit. Denied: execve, open-write elsewhere, ptrace. Each entry traces to the job: read log, send log, nothing else.
items.explain: Job-derived minimalism with argument constraints; every allow must be justified.

items.prompt: The uploader's library update starts needing a new syscall and breaks under the filter. What is the maintenance discipline?
items.answer: Treat filter updates like policy changes: verify the new syscall is legitimate (not the library phoning home unexpectedly), constrain its arguments, canary-test, document — filters evolve with software.
items.explain: Filters need maintenance alongside updates; a breakage is a review prompt, not just an annoyance.

items.prompt: A vendor's 'sandboxed' app runs with full network, all files readable, and no syscall filter — but in a container. Assess.
items.answer: Sandbox theater: the container adds namespaces but the policy inside is ambient authority. Demand the actual confinement policy (syscall filter, file/network scoping) or treat it as unsandboxed.
items.explain: Containers are not magic; without a deny-by-default policy inside, the box is decorative.

items.prompt: Your Ringfencing policy blocks the PDF reader's new 'cloud save' feature users love. Walk through the decision.
items.answer: Job analysis: is cloud save in the reader's legitimate job? If yes, scope it — specific domains, specific account, via the reader identity only, with Storage Control awareness. If it is feature creep, say no with the business reason. Either way, exception discipline: narrow, owned, reviewed.
items.explain: Features change the job; re-run the normative analysis rather than reflex-allowing or reflex-denying.

items.prompt: Audit finds the spool-path write rule lets the reader drop files the spooler service executes. What do you do?
items.answer: Boundary moved, not disappeared: constrain writes to non-executable formats, verify the spooler's consumption, or route through a sanitizing intermediary — then re-run the attack scenarios against the tightened rule.
items.explain: Follow the data past your boundary: who consumes what you allow, and with what authority?

items.prompt: Explain the whole 6.858 arc in 60 seconds to the panel.
items.answer: 'We assume code has bugs, so we architect containment: threat models tell us what matters and who attacks; understanding hijacking tells us what bugs give away; privilege separation and capabilities bound authority by design; sandboxing bounds it at runtime. On the endpoint that architecture is deny-by-default with per-app boundaries — so even a successful exploit hits a wall.'
items.explain: The arc in one breath: assume compromise, bound the blast radius, at every layer from silicon to policy.

handsOnLab.title: Write a Ringfencing-style sandbox policy for a document viewer
handsOnLab.brief: Pick a real document viewer, derive its job normatively, and write a complete sandbox policy spec — file, process, registry, and network rules — then attack your own policy with three scenarios and verify the legitimate workflow survives. A policy document a real admin could implement.
steps: Choose a real document viewer you use (a PDF reader, an office viewer). Install nothing new — use what you have.
Write the normative job analysis: in one paragraph, what SHOULD this viewer need? List every legitimate capability: which files it reads, what it writes, whether it needs children, network, registry.

Inventory the descriptive reality: check what the viewer actually touches (recent files, its install directory, temp paths, any network calls you can observe). Note every gap between descriptive and normative.
Write the file rules: read-allowed paths (enumerated), write-allowed paths (minimal — spool/temp only), execute denied on anything the viewer writes.
Write the process rules: child process creation allowed or denied, with the justification. If the viewer has an updater, specify it as a separate identity with its own narrow rules.
Write the registry/configuration rules: which keys the viewer may write (its own settings), everything else denied.
Write the network rules: allowed destinations enumerated or fully denied, with the justification tied to the job analysis.

Attack scenario 1: a malicious document exploits the viewer. Walk through what the hijacked process attempts (payload write, process launch, exfiltration, persistence) and verify each is denied by your rules.

Attack scenario 2: the confused deputy — can the viewer be aimed at something through an allowed path (cloud-synced folders, spool consumers, helper apps)? Document what you find and tighten the rules.
Attack scenario 3: the updater — verify the updater's narrow policy cannot be abused to grant the viewer new capabilities (scope, signature checks, separate identity).
Positive test: walk through the legitimate workflow (open, read, print, save-as) under your policy and confirm nothing breaks. Adjust with exception discipline if needed.
Save as sandbox-policy.md: job analysis, the four rule sections, the three attack walkthroughs with verdicts, the positive test, and review-date discipline.
handsOnLab.deliverable: sandbox-policy.md with the normative job analysis, file/process/registry/network rule sections, three attack-scenario walkthroughs with deny verdicts, the positive workflow test, and the review schedule.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All three attack scenarios are denied by specific rules you can name; the legitimate open/read/print/save workflow survives; the updater is a separate identity; every rule traces to the job analysis.

mockTask.q: Panel question: 'We ringfenced the PDF reader — no child processes, no network — and now users complain it cannot print. Walk me through it.'
choices: Loosen the policy to allow child processes so printing works.

Diagnose first: check the block events to confirm printing is what is actually denied (vs. a coincidental issue), identify the exact mechanism the reader uses to print (spool path writes vs. a helper process), then permit narrowly — e.g., write to the spool path only — verify printing on a canary, and keep the child-process and network denials intact.
Tell users printing is a security risk and remove printers.
Disable Ringfencing for the reader until the vendor fixes it.
mockTask.explain: The panel tests whether you reflex-loosen or diagnose-then-narrow. The strong answer verifies the actual denied action, finds the minimal legitimate mechanism (spool writes, not child processes), and preserves the rest of the sandbox — sandbox judgment under user pressure, which is the daily reality of the role.
