modules.title: MIT 6.858: Authentication — Passwords to Passkeys
modules.summary: Authentication done right: password hashing with salts and work factors (bcrypt/Argon2 concepts), why MFA matters and which factors resist phishing, TOTP internals, and FIDO2/passkeys — the phishing-resistant endgame. Includes a password-hasher and TOTP lab in pure Python.
objectives: Explain why passwords must be salted, slow hashes and compare bcrypt and Argon2 conceptually.
Design a registration/login flow with proper hashing, verification, and constant-time comparison.
Describe TOTP (time-based one-time passwords) internals: shared secret, time step, HMAC truncation.
Explain FIDO2/passkeys: public-key challenge-response, origin binding, and why it resists phishing.
Prioritize authentication controls as an operator: password policy, MFA rollout order, auth-log monitoring.

notes.title: Storing passwords: salts, work factors, and slow hashes
Attack patterns: stuffing, spraying, and the reuse catastrophe
MFA: what the factors are and which ones actually help
notes.body:
Multi-factor authentication combines independent categories: something you know (password), something you have (phone, hardware key), something you are (biometrics). The security comes from independence — compromising one factor shouldn't compromise the others.

TOTP (time-based one-time passwords, the 6-digit codes in authenticator apps): the server and your app share a secret established at enrollment (usually via QR code). Both compute code = truncate(HMAC(secret, floor(now / 30s))). The 30-second time step means codes rotate; the server accepts the current and adjacent windows to tolerate clock skew. Worked implication: anyone holding the shared secret can generate valid codes — so the enrollment QR/code is itself a credential (screenshot it = clone the factor), and server-side the secret must be stored encrypted. TOTP resists replay (codes expire) and remote guessing, but it does NOT resist phishing: a fake login page can relay your password and your current code to the real site in real time.

SMS codes are the weakest common factor: SIM-swap attacks (social-engineering the carrier to port your number) hand the attacker your codes, and SMS is plaintext over SS7-era infrastructure. Use TOTP or better over SMS everywhere you have a choice; keep SMS only as a last-resort recovery path, and protect recovery paths as carefully as login paths — attackers target the weakest link, which is usually 'forgot my authenticator.'

Push-based MFA (approve/deny prompts) improved usability but introduced push fatigue: attackers spam prompts until the tired user taps Approve. Number matching (the login screen shows 'enter 47' and the push asks for the number) defeats blind approval. The ranking for new deployments: phishing-resistant factors (FIDO2) first, TOTP second, push with number matching third, SMS last. Rollout order as an operator: administrators and privileged accounts first (they're the highest-value targets), then everyone.

The enrollment ceremony deserves as much care as the login, because whoever enrolls the factor owns the account. For TOTP, the QR code or setup key is a credential — display it once, require immediate verification (enter two consecutive codes), and warn the user that screenshots clone the factor. For FIDO2, registration binds the new credential to the verified session: require the existing strong factor (or in-person proofing for first enrollment), show the user what they're approving ('add security key to your account?'), and register the credential's metadata so support can identify it later. Backup codes — the recovery factor — should be generated at enrollment, shown once, and stored hashed server-side like passwords (they're bearer credentials). A deployment detail that saves incidents: let users name their factors ('YubiKey — laptop bag') and show last-used times; when the 3 AM login comes from an unnamed factor, both the user and your analysts have context. Enrollment is authentication's front door — guard it like one.

notes.title: FIDO2 and passkeys: phishing-resistant authentication
notes.body:
FIDO2 (WebAuthn + CTAP) replaces shared secrets with public-key cryptography, and passkeys are its consumer-friendly form: the private key lives on the user's device (phone, laptop, hardware key), and the server stores only the public key. There is nothing to phish, nothing to stuff, and nothing valuable in a server breach.

The ceremony, step by step. Registration: the server sends a challenge (random nonce) plus its identity (the origin, e.g., login.example.com). The device generates a fresh keypair scoped to that origin, stores the private key, and returns the public key plus a signature over the challenge. Login: the server sends a new challenge; the device signs it with the origin-scoped private key (after a local gesture — biometrics or PIN — proving user presence); the server verifies the signature with the stored public key.

Why this resists phishing — the worked attack: the attacker builds a pixel-perfect fake at login-examp1e.com and you 'log in' with your passkey. Your device checks the origin: the credential was registered for login.example.com, and the challenge comes from login-examp1e.com. The origins don't match, so the device refuses to sign. There is no code for you to be tricked into relaying, unlike TOTP. The phishing page gets nothing — not a password, not a one-time code, not a signature valid anywhere else. Origin binding is the whole game, and it's enforced by the device, not by user vigilance.

Passkeys add syncability: platform vendors sync the private keys across a user's devices via their cloud account (protected by the account's own authentication), which solves the 'lost my hardware key' problem that stalled earlier FIDO deployments at the cost of making the platform account the new crown jewel. Discoverable credentials (usernameless login) let the device offer accounts directly. Operator considerations: plan account recovery before rollout (what happens when someone loses all devices?), keep a fallback factor for edge cases, and know that passkeys don't fix authorization — they prove who, not what they're allowed to do.

Two passkey deployment realities to plan for. First, synced vs device-bound: platform passkeys sync across the user's devices via their cloud account (convenient; the cloud account becomes the crown jewel — protect it with its own phishing-resistant MFA), while security keys and some platform configurations keep keys on one device (stronger; loss means recovery flow). Enterprises often want the latter for privileged accounts and accept the former for general users — a tiered policy, documented. Second, attestation: during registration, the authenticator can provide an attestation statement about its make and model, letting the server enforce 'only certified hardware keys for admins.' Use attestation as an allowlist ('these models permitted'), not a denylist, and have a process for new models. Recovery remains the hard part: with no passwords to reset, losing all devices means a rigorous identity-proofing flow (document verification, manager approval, cooldown with alerts to backup contacts). Design and test this flow before rollout — the first real recovery shouldn't be improvised during an incident.

notes.title: Failure patterns: how authentication breaks in practice
The operator's authentication checklist
notes.body: Turn the module into an actionable checklist you can run against any system you inherit: Password policy that actually works: require length (12+ characters; passphrases welcome), check against breach lists and trivial variants at set time, and stop demanding arbitrary complexity rules and 90-day rotations — the evidence has long shown those produce Password1! → Password2! patterns. Complexity theater is worse than useless because it consumes goodwill. Storage audit: confirm salted slow hashes (bcrypt/Argon2) with a current work factor; confirm no plaintext, no unsalted fast hashes, no reversible encryption of passwords; confirm constant-time comparison on verification. MFA posture: enumerate every privileged account and confirm phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys/FIDO2) or at minimum TOTP; eliminate SMS where possible; document and harden recovery paths; enable number matching on push. Session hygiene: fresh random ids at login, Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite flags, absolute plus idle timeouts, invalidation on logout and password change (M17's design). Monitoring: alert on spraying patterns (many accounts, few passwords, one source), stuffing indicators (logins from breached-credential intelligence), impossible-travel and new-device logins, MFA fatigue (many pushes, one approval), and recovery-flow abuse. Feed these into your detection thinking from M23: authentication telemetry is your richest behavioral feature source. Interview bridge: ThreatLocker's Elevation Control removes standing local admin and grants just-in-time elevation per application via policy — that's authentication-adjacent least privilege on the endpoint. When the panel asks how you'd secure admin access, you now have the full stack: strong auth to prove who, MFA to prove it's really them, and just-in-time elevation so the privilege exists only when needed. Turn the checklist into a rollout plan with metrics. Phase one — privileged accounts: enumerate every admin, service, and break-glass account; require phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys/security keys); eliminate SMS; document and test recovery. Metric: percentage of privileged accounts with phishing-resistant MFA — target 100%, reported weekly until it holds. Phase two — general users: TOTP minimum, passkeys offered and encouraged, SMS deprecated with a sunset date. Metric: MFA coverage and factor-strength distribution. Phase three — continuous: monitor the detection queries from the attack-patterns note, run a tabletop exercise ('the CFO's phone with the authenticator is stolen at 9 PM — walk through recovery'), and audit enrollment and reset logs quarterly. Report to leadership in risk terms: 'account-takeover expected loss reduced by X, remaining gap is Y.' And keep the human factor in view: the smoothest MFA rollout still fails if the helpdesk reset procedure is one phone call with public details — verify the recovery path with the same rigor as the login path, because attackers will.

cards.front: Why must password hashes use a unique salt per user?
cards.back: Defeats rainbow tables — attackers must attack each user's hash individually instead of precomputing one dictionary for all.

cards.front: What is a work factor / cost parameter?
cards.back: Tunable slowness in the hash function: legitimate logins pay it once, attackers pay it per guess. Raised over time as hardware improves.

cards.front: bcrypt vs Argon2 — one line each?
cards.back: bcrypt: adaptive-cost Blowfish-based hash, long scrutiny history. Argon2: memory-hard PHC winner — resists GPU/ASIC cracking.

cards.front: Why is SHA-256(password) wrong even when salted?
cards.back: It's designed for speed — GPUs try billions of guesses/sec. Password hashing must be deliberately slow and memory-hard.

cards.front: Credential stuffing vs password spraying?
cards.back: Stuffing: breached pairs tried everywhere (exploits reuse). Spraying: few common passwords tried against many accounts (dodges per-account lockout).

cards.front: How does TOTP work (three parts)?
cards.back: Shared secret + HMAC over floor(time/30s), truncated to digits. Server and app compute the same code independently.

cards.front: Why is SMS the weakest MFA factor?
cards.back: SIM-swap attacks port the number to the attacker; SMS travels over legacy signaling infrastructure in the clear.

cards.front: What is push fatigue and its fix?
cards.back: Spamming approve/deny prompts until the user taps Approve. Fix: number matching — the push asks for the number shown on the login screen.

cards.front: FIDO2/passkeys in one sentence?
cards.back: Origin-scoped public-key challenge-response: the device signs the server's challenge with a private key that never leaves it.

cards.front: Why are passkeys phishing-resistant?
cards.back: Origin binding: the device only signs challenges from the registered origin, so a fake site gets no usable signature — nothing to relay.

cards.front: What's the usual weakest link in an MFA deployment?
cards.back: Account recovery — SMS fallback, security questions, or helpdesk resets weaker than the login flow itself.

cards.front: Effective password policy in one line?
cards.back: Length over complexity, breach-list checks at set time, no forced rotation theater.

quiz.q: An attacker steals a user table hashed with unsalted SHA-256. What happens next?
choices: One precomputed rainbow table cracks common passwords for all users almost instantly
Each user must be attacked individually
quiz.explain: No salts = one dictionary serves every row; fast hash = billions of guesses/sec. This is exactly the catastrophe salts plus work factors prevent.

quiz.q: Why is Argon2's memory-hardness valuable against attackers?
choices: GPUs/ASICs excel at tiny parallel computations; forcing 64MB+ per guess cripples their advantage
It removes the need for salts
quiz.explain: Cracking economics: attackers win with massively parallel cheap hardware. Memory-hardness changes the cost equation against them while legitimate servers pay it once per login.

quiz.q: Logs show 3 failed logins each across 2,000 accounts from one IP, using 'Welcome2026!'. This pattern is…
choices: Password spraying — throttle by source, alert on the pattern, block common passwords
A brute-force attack on one account
quiz.explain: Few passwords × many accounts × one source, deliberately under per-account lockout thresholds = spraying. Per-account lockout alone won't catch it.

quiz.q: A phishing page relays the victim's password AND current TOTP code to the real site in real time. Why does this work against TOTP but fail against passkeys?
choices: TOTP codes are bearer values valid during their window; passkeys are origin-bound signatures unusable on the wrong origin
Phishing pages can't display TOTP prompts
quiz.explain: A TOTP code is a string anyone can forward within 30 seconds. A passkey signature is bound to the real origin by the device itself — the fake origin gets nothing usable.

quiz.q: During FIDO2 login, what does the server verify?
choices: A signature over its fresh challenge, made by the private key matching the registered public key, for the correct origin
That the user typed a password
quiz.explain: Challenge-response: fresh challenge defeats replay, origin binding defeats phishing, public-key crypto means the server never holds a phishable secret.

quiz.q: An admin account has a 20-character random password but no MFA. An intern account has MFA. Which is the priority fix?
choices: The admin account — privileged targets are attacked first; password strength doesn't replace a second factor
The intern account — interns click phishing links
quiz.explain: Attackers target privilege, not password length. MFA rollout order is a security decision: admins and high-value targets first.

quiz.q: Your app says 'username not found' vs 'wrong password' distinctly. What's the issue?
choices: Username enumeration — attackers can harvest valid accounts for spraying/stuffing
quiz.explain: Distinct errors are an oracle for account existence. Use one generic 'login failed' message; log specifics server-side.

quiz.q: After a password change, old sessions stay valid. Why is this wrong?
choices: A compromised session survives the remediation — password changes must invalidate all sessions
quiz.explain: Password reset is incident response for the account. Leaving sessions alive leaves the attacker's access alive — 'log me out everywhere' must be real.

quiz.q: Which comparison is correct for verifying a password-reset token in Python?
quiz.explain: M19's lesson applied: secret comparison must be constant-time. == leaks via early exit; compare_digest doesn't.

quiz.q: A deployment uses push MFA without number matching. Users report 3 AM approval prompts. Diagnosis and fix?
choices: Push fatigue attack — enable number matching, alert on prompt bursts, investigate the source
Normal behavior — tell users to approve
quiz.explain: Prompt-bombing at 3 AM is an attacker hoping for a half-asleep tap. Number matching makes blind approval useless; bursts are a detection signal.

items.prompt: Three ingredients of proper password storage?
items.answer: Unique salt per user, slow hash (bcrypt/Argon2), tunable work factor.
items.explain: Salt defeats rainbow tables; slowness defeats guessing; tuning keeps pace with hardware.

items.prompt: Why not SHA-256 for passwords?
items.answer: Built for speed — billions of guesses/sec on GPUs.
items.explain: Password hashing must be deliberately slow and memory-hard.

items.prompt: Stuffing vs spraying in one line each?
items.answer: Stuffing: breached pairs reused everywhere. Spraying: common passwords vs many accounts.
items.explain: Different patterns, different detections.

items.prompt: TOTP's three ingredients?
items.answer: Shared secret, HMAC, 30-second time step.
items.explain: Both sides compute the same rotating code independently.

items.prompt: Why does TOTP fall to real-time phishing?
items.answer: The code is a bearer value — anyone can relay it within its window.
items.explain: No origin binding, unlike FIDO2.

items.prompt: The phishing-resistance mechanism in passkeys?
items.answer: Origin binding — the device signs only for the registered origin.
items.explain: A fake origin receives no usable signature.

items.prompt: First accounts to get phishing-resistant MFA?
items.answer: Administrators and privileged accounts.
items.explain: Attackers target privilege first.

items.prompt: Scenario: breach of a competitor's forum; next day your login success rate spikes from unusual IPs. Diagnosis and response?
items.answer: Credential stuffing with the breached pairs; force MFA challenges on risky logins, check passwords against breach lists, alert users to rotate reused passwords.
items.explain: Successes that look legitimate are the stuffing signature — failure counting won't see them.

items.prompt: Scenario: helpdesk resets passwords over the phone with only 'name and employee ID' as verification. Finding?
items.answer: Recovery weaker than login — public/guessable verifier; require verified out-of-band identity proof and alert the user.
items.explain: Attackers take the weakest path to the account.

items.prompt: Scenario: choosing between SMS codes and TOTP for a new internal app. Recommendation?
items.answer: TOTP minimum; prefer passkeys. SMS only as last-resort recovery, never primary.
items.explain: SIM-swap defeats SMS; TOTP resists replay; passkeys resist phishing.

items.prompt: Scenario: user loses the phone with their authenticator and there's no recovery process. What should have existed?
items.answer: Pre-planned recovery: backup codes issued at enrollment, verified out-of-band reset with cooldown and user alerting.
items.explain: Design recovery with login-grade rigor before rollout, not during the incident.

items.prompt: Scenario: code review finds password comparison with ==. Fix and why?
items.answer: hmac.compare_digest — == is an early-exit timing oracle on the hash.
items.explain: M19 applied: secret comparison is always constant-time.

items.prompt: Scenario: the panel asks how you'd secure local admin on endpoints. Tie this module to ThreatLocker.
items.answer: Strong auth + phishing-resistant MFA to prove identity, then Elevation Control for just-in-time per-app elevation — privilege exists only when needed, no standing admin.
items.explain: Authentication proves who; just-in-time elevation limits what that who can do.

handsOnLab.title: Password hashing and TOTP in pure Python
handsOnLab.brief: Build a correct password registration/login flow with hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac (stdlib), then implement TOTP from RFC 6238 primitives and validate it against the RFC's published test vectors.
steps: Create auth_lab.py. Implement register(password): generate 16 random bytes via secrets.token_bytes, derive with hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', pw, salt, 600_000), store salt+iterations+derived.
Implement verify(password, record): recompute and compare with hmac.compare_digest. Confirm correct password passes, wrong fails.
Demonstrate the salt's job: register the same password twice; show the stored hashes differ.
Demonstrate the work factor: time 600k vs 60k iterations; compute attacker cost for a million guesses at each setting.
Write the 'never do' list as code comments: plaintext, unsalted SHA-256, global salt, == comparison.

Implement totp(secret, time_step=30, digits=8): counter = int(time.time())//30; msg = struct.pack('>Q', counter); hs = hmac.new(secret, msg, hashlib.sha1).digest(); dynamic-truncate per RFC 4226; mod 10^digits.
Validate against RFC 6238 Appendix B test vectors (secret '12345678901234567890'): fetch the expected values from the RFC text and assert your implementation matches at least two timestamps.
Simulate clock skew: verify your verifier accepts counters within ±1 step and rejects ±10 steps.
Write a phishing-relay thought experiment in comments: why a stolen TOTP code works within its window but a passkey signature for the wrong origin is useless.
Write auth-report.md: your measured hash timings, the TOTP validation results, and the operator checklist applied to one real account you own (MFA status, recovery path).
handsOnLab.deliverable: auth_lab.py (hasher + TOTP + RFC validation) and auth-report.md with timings, validation results, and a personal MFA/recovery audit.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Same password yields different stored hashes; TOTP output matches the RFC 6238 test vectors; your report names the recovery path for your own most important account.

mockTask.q: Panel question: we're rolling out MFA to 500 endpoints. The team proposes SMS codes because 'everyone has a phone.' What's your recommendation?
choices: Push for phishing-resistant factors (passkeys/FIDO2) for admins first, TOTP as the baseline, SMS only as last-resort recovery — SMS falls to SIM-swap and TOTP falls to real-time phishing relay
SMS is fine — it's still a second factor
Skip MFA and require longer passwords instead
Deploy SMS now and never revisit the decision
mockTask.explain: Not all factors are equal: SMS is defeated by SIM-swap, TOTP by real-time relay, while FIDO2's origin binding resists phishing entirely. Prioritize admins (highest-value targets), choose factors by strength, and harden recovery paths — the usual weakest link.

modules.title: MIT 6.858: Privacy — Tracking, Anonymity & Private Browsing
modules.summary: How web tracking actually works (cookies, fingerprinting, and the tricks beyond them), onion routing and what Tor does and doesn't hide, the limits of private browsing, the data-broker economy in general terms, and concrete endpoint privacy defenses.
objectives: Explain first-party vs third-party cookies and how third-party cookies enable cross-site tracking.
Describe browser fingerprinting techniques and why blocking cookies alone doesn't stop tracking.
Walk through onion routing: three-hop circuits, layered encryption, and what each relay knows.
State precisely what Tor hides, what it doesn't, and the limits of private browsing mode.
Apply endpoint privacy defenses: tracker blocking, cookie policy, DNS privacy, and Tor vs VPN trade-offs.

notes.title: How tracking works: cookies first
Fingerprinting: you are your configuration
notes.body: Browser fingerprinting identifies you without storing anything: it measures your browser's configuration, which turns out to be surprisingly unique. The EFF's research found the overwhelming majority of browsers carry a unique fingerprint. What gets measured: User-Agent string (browser, version, OS), screen resolution and color depth, installed fonts (enumerated via CSS/JS tricks — font lists are highly distinguishing), canvas fingerprinting (render hidden text/graphics to a and hash the pixels — GPU, drivers, and font rendering make the output subtly unique per machine), WebGL renderer strings (your exact GPU model), timezone and language, plugins, and even audio-context fingerprints (how your hardware processes a test signal). Worked example: a tracker runs 20ms of JavaScript collecting these signals, hashes them into an ID, and keys your profile to it. You clear cookies — the fingerprint is unchanged. You use private browsing — same fingerprint. You switch browsers on the same machine — often still linkable via hardware signals. This is why 'I block third-party cookies' is necessary but insufficient. Defenses are imperfect by nature: Tor Browser standardizes fingerprints (every Tor Browser user looks identical — the anonymity-set approach), Brave and Firefox randomize or block the most entropy-rich APIs (canvas randomization, font enumeration limits), and reducing uniqueness means accepting some site breakage. The fundamental tension: the web platform exposes rich capability APIs for legitimate features, and each one is a fingerprinting signal. As an operator, the actionable version is: know that fingerprints defeat cookie hygiene, recommend browsers with fingerprint resistance for sensitive work, and test your own exposure with EFF's Cover Your Tracks (used in this module's lab). Interpreting Cover Your Tracks results correctly matters. 'Your browser has a unique fingerprint' doesn't mean you're doomed — it means your configuration is distinguishable among tested browsers, and the defense is joining a large anonymity set (Tor Browser's uniformity) rather than chasing uniqueness-zero, which is nearly impossible on a mainstream browser. 'Blocking tracking ads: yes / invisible trackers: partial' tells you where your blocker wins and where fingerprinting or CNAME cloaking slips past. A useful hardening progression to demonstrate in the lab: stock browser (unique, unblocked) → + tracker blocker (trackers blocked, still unique) → hardened Firefox/Brave (randomized canvas, limited fonts — less unique) → Tor Browser (uniform). Each step trades some convenience for unlinkability, and seeing the test flip from 'unique' to 'nearly identical to others' makes the anonymity-set concept concrete. Note for operators: recommend this progression to users by threat level instead of one-size-fits-all — the journalist and the casual shopper need different stacks.

notes.title: Tor and onion routing: how anonymity is built
Private browsing: what it does and its hard limits
notes.body:
Private/incognito mode is one of the most misunderstood features in computing. Here's exactly what it does: it runs a browser session that keeps no local persistent state — no history, no cookies, no cache, no form data written to disk — and discards the session's temporary state when the window closes.

What that protects against: someone with physical access to your device later (a family member, a coworker, a thief) finding where you browsed. That's it. That's the entire threat model.

What it does NOT do — and users consistently believe otherwise: it does not hide your browsing from your ISP, your employer, or the websites you visit (your IP is unchanged, fingerprinting works identically, and trackers fingerprint private windows just fine). It does not make you anonymous. It does not encrypt anything. Your employer's monitoring, the coffee shop's packet capture, and the site's analytics all see the same traffic as a normal window.

Worked misconception to kill in user training: 'I used incognito, so IT can't see it.' IT sees DNS queries, destination IPs, and — on a managed device — possibly full TLS inspection. Incognito changed nothing on the network. The correct mental model: private browsing protects against local forensics, roughly equivalent to 'browse, then carefully delete history and cookies' done automatically.

Operator guidance: when users ask for privacy, match the tool to the threat. Local snooping → private browsing (or better, separate OS profiles). ISP/employer visibility → VPN or Tor (with the trade-offs in the next notes). Cross-site tracking → tracker blocking + fingerprint-resistant browser. State surveillance → Tor with operational discipline. Recommending 'just use incognito' for any network-level threat is malpractice — know the limits and say them plainly.

Two browser features people confuse with privacy modes are worth distinguishing. Container tabs (Firefox Multi-Account Containers and similar): they isolate cookies and storage per container, so your 'shopping' container's trackers can't read your 'banking' container's state — this is first-party isolation done right, and unlike private windows, it persists usefully. Use containers for role separation (work, personal, shopping) as daily hygiene. Second, DNS leakage: even with HTTPS everywhere, classic DNS queries broadcast every domain you visit in plaintext to the local network — private browsing changes nothing here. DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) to a trustworthy resolver closes that specific leak (the resolver still sees queries, so choose it deliberately). And the employer question from the notes, answered precisely: on a managed device, assume the company can see everything — installed certificates, endpoint agents, and proxy logs see past incognito, past DoH, past VPN. The honest guidance: use work devices for work, personal devices for personal, and don't confuse the two threat models.

notes.title: The data-broker economy, in general terms
notes.body:
Behind the tracking mechanisms sits an industry: data brokers that collect, aggregate, and sell personal information. Understand its shape in general terms, because it determines what 'privacy' can realistically mean.

The pipeline: collection (trackers, apps, loyalty programs, public records, purchase histories), aggregation (matching disparate records to one identity via email hashes, device IDs, names/addresses), enrichment (appending inferred attributes — interests, demographics, propensities), and sale or licensing to advertisers, insurers, employers, and sometimes government buyers. The product being sold is attention sorted by predicted value — and increasingly, risk scores about you that you'll never see.

Why this matters beyond advertising: aggregated data enables price discrimination, discriminatory targeting, and social engineering fuel (attackers buy the same enrichment data). Breaches of brokers expose dossiers people never consented to assemble. And the 'free service' bargain — you pay with behavioral data — means the economic incentive to collect is structural, not a bug in any one company.

Regulatory context stays general here: various jurisdictions have enacted privacy laws giving residents rights like access, deletion, and opt-out of sale, and the landscape keeps shifting. As an operator, your durable takeaways don't depend on any specific statute: minimize collection (don't log what you don't need), minimize retention (delete on schedule), and treat third-party trackers on your own sites as data sharing you're responsible for — audit what your pages embed, because their collection becomes your liability story.

The broker economy has a consumer-facing side you should know: most jurisdictions with privacy laws now give residents rights to opt out of sale/sharing and to request deletion, and broker registries exist where you can find who's holding your data. The practical reality is whack-a-mole — opting out of one broker while hundreds remain — which is why the durable advice is minimization at the source: don't give the data in the first place (skip loyalty programs that exist to track, use masked emails and virtual cards where offered, deny app permissions that don't serve the app's function). For operators, the breach-correlation angle matters: attackers enrich phishing with broker data (your role, your address, your recent purchases), so user training should assume the attacker knows public-plus-broker facts about the target. And when your company suffers a breach, remember the notification math from M22: the cost isn't just forensics — it's every customer's newly rational distrust, which is why 'collect less, keep it briefly' is the cheapest breach-cost control ever invented.

notes.title: Endpoint privacy defenses: a practical stack

cards.front: First-party vs third-party cookie?
cards.back: First-party: set by the site in the address bar. Third-party: set by an embedded other-domain resource — the cross-site tracking backbone.

cards.front: How does a third-party cookie track you across sites?
cards.back: The same tracker script embedded on many sites reads its one cookie everywhere, keying a unified browsing profile to you.

cards.front: Two non-cookie tracking tricks?
cards.back: ETag/cache identifiers and CNAME cloaking (tracker hiding behind a first-party subdomain). Any persistent per-user state is identifier-shaped.

cards.front: What is browser fingerprinting?
cards.back: Identifying you by your configuration (fonts, canvas, WebGL, screen, UA) — no storage needed, survives cookie clearing and private mode.

cards.front: Tor's three relays and what each knows?
cards.back: Guard: your IP, not destination. Middle: only neighbors. Exit: destination, not your identity. No single relay knows both ends.

cards.front: What does the Tor exit relay see?
cards.back: Destination and plaintext of unencrypted traffic — HTTPS is still required for content confidentiality.

cards.front: What does Tor NOT protect against? (three)
cards.back: Browser fingerprinting, de-anonymizing logins, and global timing/correlation observers.

cards.front: What exactly does private browsing protect against?
cards.back: Local forensics — no history/cookies/cache persisted on the device. Nothing on the network; not anonymity.

cards.front: Why doesn't private browsing stop fingerprinting?
cards.back: Fingerprinting measures live configuration, not stored state — private windows fingerprint identically.

cards.front: VPN vs Tor — the honest difference?
cards.back: VPN moves ISP-level visibility to the provider (not anonymity). Tor hides who-talks-to-whom via three-hop onion routing (slower, stronger).

cards.front: The data-broker pipeline in four stages?
cards.back: Collection, aggregation (identity matching), enrichment (inferred attributes), sale/licensing.

cards.front: Endpoint privacy stack (four layers)?
cards.back: Block third-party cookies + tracker blocker, fingerprint-resistant browser, private DNS (DoH), and context separation (containers/profiles).

quiz.q: news.example and shop.example both embed tracker.example's script. How does the tracker link your visits?
choices: Its third-party cookie is readable on both sites, keying one profile to you
It reads the sites' first-party cookies
It needs your login on tracker.example
It can't — the SOP prevents this
quiz.explain: The SOP blocks cross-origin reads between the sites, but the tracker's own script reading its own cookie on each site is same-origin every time — that's the mechanism.

quiz.q: You block all third-party cookies. A tracker still recognizes you. Most likely how?
choices: Browser fingerprinting — configuration signals need no stored state
quiz.explain: Fingerprinting (canvas, fonts, WebGL, screen) identifies the machine without storage, surviving cookie clearing and private windows.

quiz.q: In Tor, which relay knows both your IP and your destination?
choices: None — that's the point of the three-hop design
quiz.explain: Knowledge is split: guard knows client IP, exit knows destination, middle knows neither. No single relay has the full picture.

quiz.q: You use Tor to log into your personal email, then post anonymously. What went wrong?
choices: The login de-anonymized the session — identity revealed at the application layer
The guard relay stole the password
quiz.explain: Tor hides network identity, not application identity. Logging in tells the service exactly who you are; anonymity requires not identifying yourself.

quiz.q: An employee believes incognito mode hides browsing from corporate monitoring. Correct them:
choices: Incognito only prevents local persistence; the network, DNS, and managed-device monitoring see everything as usual
quiz.explain: Private browsing's threat model is local forensics only. Network observers see identical traffic — IPs, DNS, and on managed devices potentially full inspection.

quiz.q: A site loads analytics from metrics.shop.example, which is a CNAME to tracker infrastructure. Why do this?
choices: CNAME cloaking — it looks first-party to cookie blockers while serving the tracker
quiz.explain: By aliasing a first-party subdomain to the tracker, the requests dodge third-party classifications — a deliberate evasion of cookie policy.

quiz.q: Why does Tor Browser try to make all users look identical rather than unique?
choices: Anonymity-set approach — blending into a crowd defeats fingerprinting
quiz.explain: You can't prevent measurement, so you standardize what's measured: if every user fingerprints identically, the fingerprint identifies no one.

quiz.q: A 'free' mobile app's privacy policy describes sharing 'de-identified' location history with 'partners.' The realistic concern?
choices: Aggregation and enrichment re-identify and broker the data — de-identification of rich behavioral data rarely holds
There is no concern with de-identified data
Only the app developer sees it
quiz.explain: The broker pipeline (collect → aggregate → enrich → sell) routinely defeats naive de-identification — location histories are famously re-identifiable.

quiz.q: Your company website embeds five third-party marketing scripts. From a privacy standpoint, you should…
choices: Audit what each collects — their collection becomes your liability story; minimize to what's needed
Block them only in the EU
quiz.explain: Third-party scripts run with your origin's privileges and exfiltrate your visitors' data. Minimizing collection and retention is the durable posture regardless of jurisdiction.

items.prompt: First-party vs third-party cookie?
items.answer: First-party: the site you're on. Third-party: an embedded other domain.
items.explain: Third-party cookies are the cross-site tracking backbone.

items.prompt: How does the third-party cookie link visits across sites?
items.answer: Same tracker script on many sites reads its one cookie everywhere.
items.explain: Same-origin to the tracker each time — the SOP doesn't block it.

items.prompt: What is fingerprinting, in one line?
items.answer: Identifying you by configuration (canvas, fonts, WebGL) with no stored state.
items.explain: Survives cookie clearing and private mode.

items.prompt: Tor's three hops and their knowledge?
items.answer: Guard: client IP. Middle: neighbors only. Exit: destination.
items.explain: No single relay knows both ends.

items.prompt: What does the exit see?
items.answer: Destination plus plaintext of unencrypted traffic.
items.explain: HTTPS still required for content confidentiality.

items.prompt: Private browsing's actual threat model?
items.answer: Local forensics only — no disk persistence.
items.explain: Network observers see everything as usual.

items.prompt: VPN vs Tor in one line?
items.answer: VPN: new ISP you trust. Tor: hides who-talks-to-whom via onion routing.
items.explain: A VPN is not anonymity.

items.prompt: Scenario: marketing wants a new analytics script on the customer portal. Your review steps?
items.answer: Ask what it collects, where data goes, retention, and whether it's needed; prefer self-hosted/first-party; document the decision.
items.explain: Embedded third parties exfiltrate visitor data with your origin's privileges.

items.prompt: Scenario: a user needs to research a sensitive topic without their ISP profiling it. Recommendation?
items.answer: Tor Browser (not Chrome-over-Tor), no logins, fingerprint-standardized — matched to the network-observer threat.
items.explain: VPN only moves trust; Tor addresses the actual observer.

items.prompt: Scenario: devtools shows 40 third-party requests on your homepage. Action?
items.answer: Inventory them, justify or remove each, consider self-hosting critical ones.
items.explain: Every embed is a data-sharing relationship.

items.prompt: Scenario: employee asks if incognito hides activity from the company's filter. Answer?
items.answer: No — the filter, DNS, and device management see it all; incognito only skips local history.
items.explain: Match the tool to the threat; don't let the myth persist.

items.prompt: Scenario: logs show logins from Tor exit nodes. Automatic block?
items.answer: Not automatically — Tor is dual-use; investigate context (account, behavior) before judging.
items.explain: The tool isn't the verdict; behavior is.

items.prompt: Scenario: how do Storage Control and Network Control relate to privacy?
items.answer: They constrain exfiltration paths — data that can't leave the endpoint can't be brokered; allowlisting shrinks tracker/malware surface.
items.explain: Managed-endpoint privacy is partly a data-loss-prevention problem.

handsOnLab.title: Track the trackers: personal privacy audit
handsOnLab.brief: Inventory third-party tracking on three real sites with browser devtools, test your own browser's fingerprint resistance with EFF's Cover Your Tracks, and produce a workstation privacy-hardening checklist.
steps: Open a fresh browser profile (no extensions yet). Open devtools → Network tab.
Visit three sites: a news site, an online store, and a blog. For each, record: total requests, count of third-party domains, and any tracker-looking names.
In devtools → Application → Cookies, note first-party vs third-party cookies set by each site.
Install uBlock Origin, reload each site, and record how the third-party counts change.
Visit https://coveryourtracks.eff.org/ and run the test. Record: does your browser block tracking ads/invisible trackers? Is your fingerprint unique?
Repeat the Cover Your Tracks test in a private window and note what changes (expect: nearly nothing — that's the lesson).
If you're willing: run it once more in Tor Browser (free download) and compare the fingerprint result.
Write privacy-audit.md: per-site third-party inventory, your Cover Your Tracks results across configurations, and what each result means.
Draft workstation-privacy-checklist.md: cookie policy, tracker blocker, browser choice, DNS (DoH) setting, container/profile separation — each with the threat it addresses.
Apply the checklist to your own primary workstation and note what changed.
Write one paragraph: which of your daily tools (VPN? private mode?) you previously over-trusted, and what actually covers that threat.
handsOnLab.deliverable: privacy-audit.md (site inventories + Cover Your Tracks results) and workstation-privacy-checklist.md (hardening steps mapped to threats).
handsOnLab.checkpoint: You can state your browser's fingerprint uniqueness result, the third-party request counts before/after blocking, and which threat each checklist item addresses.

mockTask.q: Panel question: a customer asks whether our portal's 'private browsing support' keeps their activity private from their employer. How do you answer honestly?
choices: Private browsing only prevents local persistence on the device — their employer's network monitoring, DNS, and any device management still see the activity; I'd explain the actual threat model and suggest appropriate tools
Yes, private browsing makes them fully anonymous
Yes, as long as they also clear cookies afterward
No, private browsing does nothing at all

modules.title: MIT 6.858: Security Economics
modules.summary: Why rational actors produce insecure systems: misaligned incentives, externalities, the economics of patching, cyber-insurance's moral hazard, breach disclosure, and how to reason about security spending like a business — including ALE math and the Gordon-Loeb investment bound.
objectives: Explain misaligned incentives and externalities: why the party that can fix insecurity often doesn't pay for it.
Describe the market-for-lemons dynamic in security products and its consequences.
Analyze the economics of patching: costs, delays, and attacker reuse of disclosed vulnerabilities.
Compute annualized loss expectancy (ALE = SLE × ARO) and compare controls by cost-effectiveness.
Explain cyber-insurance's adverse selection and moral hazard, and how disclosure rules shift incentives.

notes.title: Misaligned incentives: who pays vs who can fix
The market for lemons: why buyers can't reward security
The economics of patching: why the window stays open
Investing wisely: ALE math and the Gordon-Loeb bound
notes.body:
Security spending needs a decision rule, or it becomes vibes. The standard quantitative frame: Annualized Loss Expectancy.

ALE = SLE × ARO, where SLE (single loss expectancy) is the cost of one incident and ARO (annualized rate of occurrence) is how often you expect it per year. Worked example: a ransomware incident would cost $500,000 (SLE: recovery, downtime, legal) and you estimate a 20% chance per year (ARO = 0.2). ALE = $500,000 × 0.2 = $100,000/year of expected loss. A backup-and-recovery control costing $30,000/year that cuts the probability to 5% (new ALE $25,000) saves $75,000 in expected loss for $30,000 — a good buy. A $150,000 control achieving the same reduction is a bad buy on these numbers. The math forces the two questions that matter: how much does it cost, and how much risk does it remove?

Honest caveats: SLE and ARO are estimates, often rough — garbage in, garbage out. Use ranges, not false precision ($300k–$800k, 10–30%), and decide whether the conclusion survives the range. Tail risks (low probability, catastrophic loss) break naive ALE thinking — that's what insurance and resilience engineering are for.

The Gordon-Loeb model (a published result from 2002, widely taught) adds a striking bound: the optimal security investment for a given vulnerability never exceeds about 37% (1/e) of the expected loss. The intuition: security has diminishing returns — the first dollars buy the most risk reduction, and beyond a point you're spending more than the risk is worth. You don't need the proof memorized; you need the discipline it represents: every control purchase should clear the bar of 'does this reduce expected loss by more than it costs,' and 'more security spending' is not always the answer — sometimes the rational move is accepting the risk or transferring it.

Ranges beat point estimates, and Monte Carlo makes ranges rigorous without much effort: instead of ALE = single SLE × single ARO, sample SLE and ARO from your estimated distributions (uniform between your low/high bounds is a fine start) a few thousand times and look at the resulting ALE distribution — the median, the 90th percentile, and how often each control wins. The lab's sensitivity step does this by hand; the scripted version is ten lines with the random module. Two more decision tools for the kit: risk appetite statements ('we accept expected losses under $X/year per scenario without further controls') turn endless debate into policy, and the qualitative risk matrix (likelihood × impact on a 1–5 scale) handles the scenarios you can't quantify — use it to prioritize, then quantify the top items properly. The discipline that ties them together: every estimate gets a source and a date ('ARO 0.2/year — based on industry incident data for our sector, reviewed annually'), so next year's you can update instead of guess. False precision is the enemy; documented ranges are the practice.

notes.title: Cyber-insurance: risk transfer and its perverse incentives
notes.body:
Cyber-insurance transfers financial risk to an insurer for a premium. In theory it smooths catastrophic losses; in practice it creates two classic insurance problems:

Adverse selection: the organizations most eager to buy insurance are the least secure (they know their risk; the insurer doesn't). If insurers can't distinguish, premiums reflect the average risk pool — overcharging the secure, undercharging the insecure, and driving the secure to self-insure. Insurers fight this with security assessments before underwriting — which is why applications now demand MFA, backups, and EDR: the questionnaire is the screening mechanism.

Moral hazard: once insured, the incentive to maintain security weakens — 'the insurer pays if we get breached.' Insurers counter with policy conditions (maintain the controls you attested to, or the claim is denied), sublimits, and rising premiums after incidents. The equilibrium emerging in the market: insurance as a complement to security, not a substitute — coverage requires verifiable controls, which perversely makes insurers some of the most effective enforcers of security baselines in the industry.

Ransomware and insurance interact toxically: if policies reliably pay ransoms, attackers price that in and target insured organizations. This is the externality again — one organization's insured ransom payment funds attacks on everyone else. Expect policy and insurer behavior to keep shifting here; the economics point toward less ransom coverage over time.

Operator relevance: you'll fill out these questionnaires. Answer them honestly and treat them as a free gap assessment — every control the insurer demands is one your risk management should already want. And when leadership asks 'can't we just insure it,' your answer is the economics: insurance transfers money, not downtime, reputation, or operational chaos — and it increasingly requires the security program anyway.

The ransomware-payment question is where insurance economics meets ethics and policy. Insured ransom payments create a perverse loop: reliable payment funds the next campaign's R&D, raising everyone's premiums and attack volume — the externality from the notes, with victims' money as the fuel. This is why insurers increasingly sublimit or exclude ransom payments and why several jurisdictions have debated or enacted restrictions: the socially optimal move (don't pay) conflicts with the individual victim's optimal move (pay to recover faster). As an operator, your pre-incident position should be: backups that make payment unnecessary (tested restores, offline copies — the insurer's questionnaire demands them because they break the payment loop), an incident-response retainer so the 2 AM decision isn't improvised, and a written policy on ransom decisions made with leadership before the crisis. Insurance then covers what it's good at — the financial tail — while your controls handle what it's bad at: downtime, trust, and operational continuity.

notes.title: Disclosure, breach notification, and thinking like a business
notes.body: Breach disclosure rules change the economics by making insecurity visible: when organizations must notify victims and regulators, the reputational and legal costs of a breach become certain and attributable, which finally prices some of the externality back onto the negligent party. Disclosure doesn't prevent breaches; it changes the investment calculus that precedes them — which is exactly the point. Notification itself has economics: direct costs (forensics, legal, call centers, credit monitoring), plus the harder-to-measure trust cost. Organizations sometimes learn about breaches from third parties precisely because internal detection was underfunded — another incentive story: detection spending competes with feature spending until disclosure rules make undetected breaches expensive. Pulling it together — thinking like a business about security: (1) Frame every control in expected-loss terms (M22's ALE math), not fear. (2) Attack the incentive problem, not just the technical one: automatic updates beat awareness campaigns because they remove the decision. (3) Prefer verifiable claims over trusted claims when buying (the lemons lesson). (4) Remember the externality: your unpatched system is someone else's attack infrastructure, and increasingly, regulation and insurance are pricing that back onto you. Interview application: when the ThreatLocker panel asks why zero trust / allowlisting matters, the economic answer complements the technical one — breaches are expensive and certain-visibility rules make them attributable, while deny-by-default is a verifiable architectural control that reduces the expected loss across the whole fleet. Speak dollars and incentives alongside packets and policies; that's what separates an operator from a technician. Disclosure obligations keep expanding, so learn the shape: public companies in major markets now face timed breach-notification duties to regulators and investors (measured in days, not quarters), and sector rules add their own clocks. The effect on incentives is the point — when the CFO must sign a filing describing the incident, security budgets stop being abstract. Your job in that world is the board-ready narrative: translate the technical program into the three questions directors actually ask — what are our top risks in dollars (ALE ranges), what are we spending to reduce them and is it working (control effectiveness, MTTD/MTTR trends), and what's our residual exposure (the risks we've explicitly accepted). Practice the five-minute version: one slide of expected-loss math, one slide of control ROI, one slide of accepted risks with owners. Operators who speak this language get funded; operators who speak only in CVEs get tolerated. The economics module's final lesson is a career one: the security program that can't justify itself in business terms doesn't survive contact with the budget cycle.

cards.front: Security economics' core observation in one line?
cards.back: The party that can fix insecurity rarely pays for it — costs and control sit in different hands (externalities).

cards.front: What is an externality, with a security example?
cards.back: A cost imposed on third parties — e.g., your unpatched device joining a botnet that attacks others.

cards.front: The market for lemons, applied to security?
cards.back: Buyers can't verify security before purchase, so they won't pay extra for it — vendors underinvest and the market converges on minimum viable security.

cards.front: Two market fixes for the lemons problem?
cards.back: Independent audits/certifications and bug bounties — costly signals that lemons can't easily fake.

cards.front: Why does patching rationally lag? (two reasons)
cards.back: Patch costs are certain and immediate; breach benefits are probabilistic and invisible. Plus patch-day breakage risk.

cards.front: Why does disclosure help attackers in the short term?
cards.back: Attackers reverse-engineer patches to build exploits, then scan for the unpatched — the patch advertises the vulnerability.

cards.front: ALE formula and what each term means?
cards.back: ALE = SLE × ARO. SLE: cost of one incident. ARO: expected incidents per year.

cards.front: The Gordon-Loeb bound, in plain words?
cards.back: Optimal security investment for a vulnerability stays below ~37% of expected loss — diminishing returns make overspending irrational.

cards.front: Adverse selection in cyber-insurance?
cards.back: The least secure most want insurance; insurers screen with security questionnaires to price risk.

cards.front: Moral hazard in cyber-insurance?
cards.back: Being insured weakens the incentive to stay secure — countered by policy conditions and claim denial for lapsed controls.

cards.front: Why do insurers now demand MFA/backups/EDR?
cards.back: The underwriting questionnaire screens adverse selection — coverage requires verifiable controls.

cards.front: How do breach disclosure rules change incentives?
cards.back: They make breach costs certain and attributable, pricing the externality back onto the negligent party — shifting pre-breach investment.

quiz.q: A vendor ships fast with known bug classes; customers pay breach costs. The economic term and the fix direction?
choices: Externality — align incentives via liability, so the vendor internalizes the cost
Market for lemons — buy more features
quiz.explain: The vendor's decision ignores costs borne by others. Liability rules are the lever that forces the decision-maker to face the true cost.

quiz.q: Why can't buyers reliably reward secure products with higher prices?
choices: Information asymmetry — security is invisible before purchase, so claims can't be verified (lemons market)
quiz.explain: You can demo features, not absence of vulnerabilities. Unverifiable claims get no premium, so investment in real security isn't rewarded.

quiz.q: A bug bounty is economically significant because…
choices: It's a costly signal — only vendors reasonably confident in their code invite adversarial probing
quiz.explain: Costly signals separate the market: a lemon vendor won't invite scrutiny. That's why bounties carry information beyond the bugs found.

quiz.q: SLE $200,000, ARO 0.5. A $40,000/year control cuts ARO to 0.1. Good buy?
choices: Yes — ALE drops from $100,000 to $20,000, saving $80,000 for $40,000
Yes — any control is worth it
No — the control costs more than the SLE
quiz.explain: ALE before: 200,000 × 0.5 = 100,000. After: 200,000 × 0.1 = 20,000. Expected savings $80k > $40k cost — it clears the bar.

quiz.q: Same scenario, but the control costs $120,000/year. Now?
choices: No — $80,000 expected savings doesn't cover $120,000 cost; accept, reduce scope, or find cheaper mitigation
quiz.explain: The Gordon-Loeb discipline: spending more than the risk reduction is worth destroys value. Find a cheaper control or explicitly accept the residual risk.

quiz.q: An insurer's application demands MFA, offline backups, and EDR before quoting. This primarily combats…
choices: Adverse selection — screening out the riskiest applicants the insurer can't otherwise distinguish
quiz.explain: The questionnaire is a screening mechanism: high-risk orgs either can't qualify or pay more, keeping the risk pool sustainable.

quiz.q: After buying ransomware coverage, a company deprioritizes backup testing. This is…
choices: Moral hazard — insurance weakened the incentive to maintain the control; expect claim conditions to punish it
quiz.explain: Insured parties underinvest in prevention. Insurers respond with conditions — lapse the attested controls and the claim is denied.

quiz.q: Why did automatic updates beat decades of 'please patch' awareness campaigns?
choices: They remove the human decision — patching economics favored delay, so automation changed the incentive, not the awareness
quiz.explain: The barrier was never knowledge; it was certain immediate cost vs uncertain benefit. Automation deletes the decision where the bad economics lived.

quiz.q: Patch released Tuesday; exploits observed Thursday; your fleet patches monthly. The structural problem?
choices: Attacker marginal cost is near zero after disclosure while your patch cycle is slow — prioritize by exploitability and shrink the window
quiz.explain: Disclosure arms attackers quickly; defenders must patch everywhere. Triage by active exploitation and compress the cycle for exposed systems.

items.prompt: Core observation of security economics?
items.answer: Who can fix insecurity ≠ who pays for it.
items.explain: Misaligned incentives produce insecure equilibria.

items.prompt: Define externality with an example.
items.answer: Cost imposed on third parties — unpatched device in a botnet attacking others.
items.explain: Unpriced harms don't enter the decision-maker's math.

items.prompt: Lemons market in one line?
items.answer: Unverifiable security claims get no price premium, so vendors underinvest.
items.explain: Information asymmetry punishes the secure.

items.prompt: ALE = ?
items.answer: SLE × ARO.
items.explain: Expected yearly loss = cost per incident × incidents per year.

items.prompt: Gordon-Loeb bound?
items.answer: Optimal investment ≤ ~37% of expected loss.
items.explain: Diminishing returns; overspending destroys value.

items.prompt: Adverse selection vs moral hazard?
items.answer: Adverse selection: riskiest buy most (screening problem). Moral hazard: insured try less (incentive problem).
items.explain: Insurers fight with questionnaires and claim conditions.

items.prompt: Why did auto-updates win?
items.answer: Removed the human decision where delay was rational.
items.explain: Fix incentives, not just awareness.

items.prompt: Scenario: leadership asks 'can't we just buy insurance instead of the EDR rollout?' Your answer?
items.answer: Insurance transfers money, not downtime/reputation — and underwriting now requires the EDR anyway; it's a complement, not a substitute.
items.explain: The questionnaire is the market telling you the controls are required regardless.

items.prompt: Scenario: a vendor claims 'AI-powered unhackable endpoint.' Your evaluation?
items.answer: Unverifiable claim (lemons market) — demand verifiable architecture, test results, incident history; prefer testable properties like deny-by-default.
items.explain: Buy claims you can verify, not claims you must trust.

items.prompt: Scenario: two controls both cut ARO from 0.4 to 0.1 on a $500k SLE; one costs $60k/yr, the other $200k/yr. Pick and justify.
items.answer: The $60k one: expected savings $150k/yr; the $200k one costs more than it saves.
items.explain: ALE math: 500k×0.3 = $150k saved. Spending beyond savings is irrational.

items.prompt: Scenario: critical vuln disclosed; your patch window is 30 days. Economic argument to compress it?
items.answer: Disclosure arms attackers in days while exposure compounds daily expected loss — the delay's risk cost now exceeds the rollout-haste cost; patch exploited vulns first.
items.explain: Prioritize by exploitability; quantify the window as carried risk.

items.prompt: Scenario: the panel asks why allowlisting matters — give the economic half of the answer.
items.answer: Breaches carry certain, attributable costs under disclosure rules; deny-by-default is a verifiable control that cuts expected loss fleet-wide, unlike unverifiable 'detection' claims.
items.explain: Speak dollars and incentives alongside packets — that's the operator level.

handsOnLab.title: ALE worksheet and security business case
handsOnLab.brief: Build a quantitative control-comparison worksheet in Python: estimate SLE/ARO ranges for three realistic scenarios, compute ALE, evaluate candidate controls by expected savings vs cost, and write a one-page business-case memo recommending a spend.
steps: Create econ_lab.py with a scenario dict: name, SLE range (low/high), ARO range (low/high).
Define three scenarios: (1) ransomware via unpatched VPN, (2) credential-stuffing account takeover wave, (3) laptop theft with unencrypted drive.
Compute ALE ranges: ALE_low = SLE_low × ARO_low, ALE_high = SLE_high × ARO_high. Print a table.
For scenario 1, model two controls: automated patching ($25k/yr, ARO→0.05) vs cyber-insurance rider ($60k/yr, transfers 70% of SLE). Compute residual ALE for each.
For scenario 2, model MFA rollout ($40k/yr, ARO→0.05) vs doing nothing. Compute expected savings.
Apply the Gordon-Loeb sanity check: flag any control whose cost exceeds ~37% of the scenario's expected loss.
Run sensitivity: double the ARO estimate and note which recommendations flip — write down why ranges beat point estimates.

Write business-case.md: one page, addressed to a CFO — the three scenarios, recommended controls with expected-savings math, the sensitivity caveat, and what you'd monitor to validate the ARO estimates.
Include one paragraph on incentives: which recommendation fixes an externality or a lemons problem, not just a technical gap.
Re-read the memo as the CFO: is every number either estimated with a range or flagged as an assumption? Fix any false precision.
handsOnLab.deliverable: econ_lab.py (ALE worksheet with ranges and control comparisons) and business-case.md (one-page CFO memo with math).
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every recommendation shows expected savings vs cost with ranges, the Gordon-Loeb check flags any overspend, and the memo reads credibly to a non-technical executive.

mockTask.q: Panel question: our CFO asks why we should fund an allowlisting rollout instead of just buying more cyber-insurance. Give the economic answer.
choices: Insurance transfers money, not downtime or reputation — and underwriting increasingly requires the controls anyway; allowlisting is a verifiable deny-by-default control that cuts expected loss (ALE) across the fleet, which beats paying premiums on unreduced risk
Insurance is always cheaper, so agree with the CFO
Allowlisting is free so there's no decision to make
mockTask.explain: The economic frame: compare expected-loss reduction per dollar. Insurance doesn't reduce breach probability or operational pain, and its questionnaires now demand the controls — so the 'instead' is false. Verifiable prevention beats financed risk.
