notes.body:
Precision, recall, and F1 are the working vocabulary for evaluating any detector — learn them as ratios on the confusion matrix, not as slogans. The matrix: rows are ground truth (actually malicious / actually benign), columns are the detector's verdict (flagged / not flagged). Four cells: TP (true positives — caught badness), FP (false positives — false alarms), FN (false negatives — missed badness), TN (true negatives — correctly ignored). Precision = TP/(TP+FP): of everything flagged, how much was real — the analyst's 'is this alert worth my time' number. Recall = TP/(TP+FN): of all real badness, how much was caught — also called true-positive rate or sensitivity. FPR = FP/(FP+TN): of benign events, how many false-alarmed. Worked on a concrete matrix — TP=90, FP=30, FN=10, TN=870 (1,000 events, 100 actually malicious). Precision = 90/(90+30) = 90/120 = 0.75. Recall = 90/(90+10) = 90/100 = 0.9. F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R) = 2(0.75)(0.9)/(0.75+0.9) = 1.35/1.65 ≈ 0.818. F1 is the harmonic mean — it punishes lopsided tradeoffs: precision 1.0 with recall 0.01 gives F1 ≈ 0.02, exposing the 'flag nothing, be precisely right' cheat that accuracy would hide. (Accuracy here would be (90+870)/1000 = 96% — sounds great, misses 10% of attacks.) The tradeoff is fundamental: lowering the threshold catches more (recall up) but alarms more (precision down, FPR up). There is no threshold with both perfect — the detector's quality is the whole tradeoff curve, which is the ROC of the next note. Choose the operating point economically: estimate the cost of a false positive (analyst minutes) and a false negative (breach risk), and pick the threshold minimizing expected cost — not the threshold maximizing F1, unless your costs happen to be symmetric. Common mistake: reporting accuracy on imbalanced data. The M25 vendor demolition ('99.9% accurate, 0% recall') is the canonical example — accuracy is the metric you quote when you want to hide the tradeoff.

Choose the metric by the decision it informs. Tuning a threshold? Watch precision and recall move against each other and pick the economic optimum. Comparing two detectors for purchase? Compare full ROC curves, not single points — a detector that wins at your operating region is what matters. Reporting to leadership? Precision ('what fraction of analyst hours were well spent') and alert volume, because that is the budget they feel. Hunting false negatives? Recall on a labeled set, because precision is silent about misses. Debugging a bad week? The confusion matrix itself — which cell grew tells you what changed (FP spike means benign traffic shifted or the threshold drifted; FN spike means the attacker adapted or there is a coverage gap). And never let anyone optimize accuracy on your imbalanced data — the vendor demolition stands. One more: when classes are imbalanced, also report the raw counts alongside ratios. 'Precision 0.75' could be 3/4 or 750/1000 — the ratio is the same, the evidence behind it isn't. Ratios summarize; counts justify. Give both, always.
notes.title: Precision, recall, F1: reading the confusion matrix

notes.body:
A ROC curve shows the detector's entire tradeoff surface: true-positive rate (recall) on the vertical axis versus false-positive rate on the horizontal, traced as the threshold sweeps from 'flag everything' (top-right: TPR=1, FPR=1) to 'flag nothing' (bottom-left: 0,0). A perfect detector hugs the top-left corner (TPR=1 at FPR=0); a random detector is the diagonal (flagging at random catches badness exactly as often as it false-alarms). Real detectors bow toward the top-left, and the area under the curve (AUC) summarizes the bow in one number: 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is coin-flip. Worked intuition with the synthetic example from your lab: benign scores cluster around 0, malicious around 2 (both with spread 1). At threshold 1.0 you catch most malicious (high TPR) with moderate false alarms; at threshold 3.0 you almost never false-alarm (low FPR) but miss much malicious (low TPR). The ROC is the curve connecting these operating points — and moving the threshold slides you along it, never off it. Two honest uses. First, comparing detectors: if detector A's ROC is everywhere above B's, A is better at every tradeoff — no threshold games can rescue B. If the curves cross, the 'better' detector depends on your operating region (low-FPR region for SOC triage, high-TPR region for pre-breach hunting). Second, choosing the operating point: mark your cost ratio on the curve — the optimal threshold is where the marginal true positive is worth the marginal false positives. AUC's honest limit: it averages over all thresholds including absurd ones (FPR=0.9 is not an operating point anyone uses), so for SOC work, partial AUC over the low-FPR region is the serious metric. Common mistake: 'our model has 0.99 AUC' as a deployment argument. AUC measures ranking quality across thresholds; your deployment lives at one threshold, on your base rate, with your costs. Report the confusion matrix at the operating threshold — AUC is the trailer, not the movie.

For imbalanced detection problems, the precision-recall (PR) curve is often more honest than ROC. ROC's FPR uses true negatives in the denominator — and when benign events number in the millions, the FPR stays tiny even with thousands of false alarms, making the ROC look deceptively good. The PR curve plots precision vs recall directly: it shows what the analyst experiences (how much of my queue is real?) at each recall level. Worked intuition: our SOC sensor at 99% TP and 1% FP has a fine-looking ROC point (TPR 0.99, FPR 0.01 — near the top-left!) but a PR point of (recall 0.99, precision 0.001) — the PR curve exposes the operational reality the ROC hides. Rule of thumb: balanced classes, use ROC; imbalanced (the security norm), use the PR curve, with area under the PR curve as the summary. Report both when comparing detectors, but make decisions on the PR curve at your operating region. And the same threshold economics apply: pick the PR point where marginal costs balance. The curve changes; the decision method doesn't. Metrics are lenses — choose the lens that shows the thing you are deciding about.
notes.title: ROC curves: the full tradeoff picture

notes.body:
Detection also needs counting statistics: how many events to expect, and whether today's count is weird. Two distributions cover most operational questions. The binomial counts successes in n independent yes/no trials: P(exactly k) = C(n,k)·p^k·(1−p)^(n−k). Worked: 100 logins, each independently 1% likely malicious. P(at least one malicious) = 1 − P(none) = 1 − 0.99^100 ≈ 1 − 0.366 = 0.634. A 1% per-login risk becomes a 63% certainty of at least one bad login in a hundred — scale converts rarity to routine again, the quantitative backbone of 'assume breach.' Expected count: n·p = 1. The Poisson counts events in continuous time or space when they occur at a constant average rate λ, independently: P(k events) = e^(−λ)·λ^k/k!. Worked: port-scan probes arrive at λ=2 per hour. P(0 in an hour) = e^(−2)·2^0/0! = e^(−2) ≈ 0.135 — a quiet hour happens 13.5% of the time, don't celebrate. P(5 in an hour) = e^(−2)·32/120 ≈ 0.036 — five probes in an hour happens 3.6% of the time by pure chance; investigate, but know the base rate of 'weird-looking' hours. The Poisson's signature property: mean = variance = λ. If your observed counts vary much more than λ (variance ≫ mean), the process isn't simple-Poisson — it's bursty or clustered, which itself is signal (botnets beacon in bursts; humans don't). Operational uses: set alert thresholds from the distribution ('alert when hourly count exceeds the 99.9th percentile of Poisson(λ)') instead of from gut feeling; size log pipelines from expected rates plus headroom; and sanity-check vendor 'anomaly' claims — an 'anomalous' burst with 5% Poisson probability is Tuesday, not an incident. The two distributions connect: binomial with large n and small p approaches Poisson with λ=np — the 100-logins example (λ=1) gives P(0)=e^(−1)≈0.368, matching the binomial 0.366. Common mistake: alerting on counts without a rate model. 'Unusually many' is not a finding until you've computed what 'usual' looks like.

The variance check deserves a worked example because it is a detector you can deploy tomorrow. You monitor DNS queries per minute to a rarely-used internal resolver: historical mean lambda = 4 per minute. Under Poisson, variance should also be about 4 (std about 2). This week you observe minute-counts: mean 4.2, variance 38. Variance far above mean — not Poisson. Something is bursty: maybe a misconfigured retry loop, maybe DNS tunneling exfiltrating in bursts. The check caught what the mean missed (the mean barely moved). Formalize it: track the index of dispersion (variance divided by mean); alert when it exceeds, say, 3 for sustained windows. This is a real, deployed technique — simple, explainable, and sensitive to exactly the shaped traffic attackers generate (beacons, bursts, retries). Caveats: legitimate burstiness exists (batch jobs, cron storms) — baseline per-asset and per-hour, and confirm with a second signal before escalating. But as a cheap first-pass anomaly screen over count data, variance-versus-mean is one of the highest-value statistics in the module. It also generalizes: whenever a model assumes a distribution, check the moments. Models fail at the assumptions, and the assumptions are checkable.
notes.title: Binomial and Poisson: counting events like an operator

notes.body: Close the loop: turn the statistics into a detection-quality program you can run. Four practices. One — characterize every detector with a confusion matrix measured on your data, at your operating threshold, refreshed regularly. Not the vendor's matrix, not last year's matrix: yours, now. Track precision, recall, and F1 over time; a drifting F1 is the earliest warning that the threat landscape or your traffic mix moved. Two — hunt your false negatives deliberately. False positives announce themselves (analysts complain); false negatives are silent. Sample closed-as-benign alerts and re-investigate a random subset deeply; sample raw event streams the detectors never flagged and hunt manually. Estimate the miss rate with a confidence interval and report it alongside precision — a detector with 90% precision and unknown recall is half-characterized. Three — price your thresholds. For each detection tier, write down the cost of a false positive (analyst triage minutes × volume) and the cost model of a false negative (expected breach cost × probability the miss matters). Set thresholds where marginal costs balance, and re-price when volumes change — a threshold that was optimal at 1,000 alerts/day is wrong at 10,000. Four — evaluate like a scientist (M26's experiment discipline applies to detectors too): any new detection logic ships with a baseline comparison, pre-registered metrics, and a rollback criterion. 'We deployed the new rule and alerts went up' is not an evaluation; 'precision held at 0.8 while recall rose from 0.7 to 0.85 on the labeled set' is. Worked program sketch for your IDS: monthly, pull 5,000 labeled events (1,000 malicious from confirmed incidents and red-team activity, 4,000 benign sampled from production); run the current ruleset; publish precision/recall/F1 and the ROC operating point; quarterly, run the false-negative hunt on 200 sampled benign-closed alerts. That is a detection engineering practice, not a tool purchase — and it is what separates teams that detect from teams that alert. Common mistake: treating detection as a product rather than a process. Products decay (M27's arms race); processes adapt. The statistics in this module are the process's instrumentation. The labeled set is the hard part — labels are expensive, so be systematic about manufacturing them. Three sources. One: confirmed incidents — every resolved incident's indicators become malicious labels, with timestamps bounding the malicious window. Two: red-team and purple-team activity — schedule it partly to generate labels; every red-team action is a known-malicious event with ground truth, the cheapest high-quality labels you will ever get. Three: benign sampling with verification — randomly sample production events and have analysts verify a subset as benign (this is also your false-negative hunt). Maintain the set like code: versioned, with provenance per label (who labeled, from what evidence, when), and refreshed — last year's labels decay as traffic and threats shift. Size guidance: enough malicious samples that a 5-point recall change is statistically meaningful (hundreds, not dozens). And keep a held-out portion the detection engineers never see — evaluate on it, or you are measuring memorization. A detection program without a maintained labeled set is flying blind with extra steps; with one, every tuning decision becomes a measurement.

notes.body:
Norms measure size; distances measure separation — together they turn 'unusual' into a number. The L2 (Euclidean) norm is the straight-line length: |v| = √(Σvᵢ²). The L1 (Manhattan) norm sums absolute values: |v|₁ = Σ|vᵢ|. Worked: v=[3,4]. L2 = √(9+16) = √25 = 5. L1 = 3+4 = 7. L2 is the geometry you picture; L1 is the 'city blocks' distance and is more robust to outliers (one huge component dominates L2's square, less so L1's sum). Euclidean distance between points is the L2 norm of their difference: d(a,b) = |a−b|. Worked: a=[1,2], b=[4,6]. a−b = [−3,−4]; |[−3,−4]| = √(9+16) = 5. These are the primitives of anomaly detection: k-nearest-neighbors flags points far from their neighbors; clustering groups nearby points; thresholds on distance-to-centroid catch outliers. Worked security example: baseline a server's hourly feature vectors (connections, bytes, failed logins) for a month; compute the centroid (mean vector) and the typical distance from it. Tonight's vector sits at 6× the typical distance — investigate. That is statistical anomaly detection in one paragraph, and every refinement (Mahalanobis distance, which corrects for feature correlations; z-scores per feature) is a sophistication of this idea. Normalization connects back to the vector note: if bytes range over millions and failed logins over tens, Euclidean distance is 99.99% 'bytes distance' — standardize each feature (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation) so distances reflect shape, not scale. The unit sphere matters too: cosine similarity (previous note) is the dot product of L2-normalized vectors — normalizing to length 1 isolates direction from magnitude. Common mistake: computing distances on unnormalized mixed-scale features and wondering why the detector only sees the biggest feature. Normalize first, distance second — always.

Norms also regularize training — penalizing large weights to keep models simple. L2 regularization adds the squared weight norm to the loss: the optimizer prefers small weights spread across features, which smooths the decision boundary (and, not coincidentally, larger margins — the robustness connection again: L2-regularized models tend to be harder to evade because their boundaries sit farther from the data). L1 regularization adds the absolute norm: it drives unneeded weights exactly to zero, performing feature selection — the model tells you which features it actually uses. Worked intuition: with L1, a 100-feature model might keep 12 nonzero weights — you have learned that 88 features were noise, which is a finding about your data, not just your model. The security angle: inspect the surviving features. If your malware detector's L1 survivors are 'file size' and 'compile timestamp' rather than behavioral features, it is keying on spurious correlations — brittle against trivial attacker changes (recompile, pad the file). Regularization is thus also an audit tool: the weights the model keeps reveal what it learned, and what it learned had better be robust.
notes.title: Norms and distances: measuring 'unusual'

notes.body:
Embeddings are the idea that made modern ML work on language, and the intuition is pure geometry: represent items as dense vectors such that closeness in space means similarity in meaning. 'Dense' matters — unlike one-hot vectors (a million-dimensional vector with a single 1, where every word is equally far from every other), embeddings pack meaning into a few hundred dimensions where geometry works. The similarity measure is usually cosine similarity: similar items point the same way. Worked toy example in 2D — word vectors: malware=[0.9,0.1], ransomware=[0.85,0.15], kitten=[0.1,0.9]. cos(malware, ransomware): dot = 0.9×0.85 + 0.1×0.15 = 0.765+0.015 = 0.78. |malware| = √(0.81+0.01) = √0.82 ≈ 0.9055. |ransomware| = √(0.7225+0.0225) = √0.745 ≈ 0.8631. cos = 0.78/(0.9055×0.8631) = 0.78/0.7816 ≈ 0.998 — nearly identical direction: the model learned they mean nearly the same thing. cos(malware, kitten): dot = 0.9×0.1+0.1×0.9 = 0.18. |kitten| = √0.82 ≈ 0.9055. cos = 0.18/(0.9055×0.9055) = 0.18/0.82 ≈ 0.22 — nearly unrelated. Real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions and subtler geometry (king−man+woman≈queen is the famous party trick — vector arithmetic capturing analogies), but the principle is this toy: direction encodes meaning. Security applications: embed process behaviors, log templates, or binaries, then nearest-neighbor search finds 'things like this known-bad thing' — malware family clustering, phishing template matching, and UEBA all use this shape. Two cautions from earlier modules: embeddings are learned from data, so poisoned training data poisons the geometry (M25/M27); and similarity is not identity — 0.998 similar is not 'the same,' so embedding matches are triage leads, not verdicts. Common mistake: treating embedding distance as a probability or a proof. It is a similarity score — useful for ranking and clustering, never a verdict on its own.

Embeddings have their own adversarial angle, and it connects the module's threads. Because embeddings are learned, they are poisonable: slip crafted samples into training and the geometry shifts — the attacker's malware lands near 'benign' clusters. Because similarity is computed by dot product, they are evadable: small input perturbations move the embedding vector across a nearest-neighbor boundary, so 'nearest known-malware' becomes 'nearest benign utility.' And because embedding spaces are dense and high-dimensional, the attacker has room: the curse of dimensionality means tiny pushes find crossings. Defenses mirror the general toolkit: train embeddings on trusted data, monitor the geometry (has the benign cluster drifted?), and never let a nearest-neighbor match be the verdict — it is a triage lead corroborated by independent signals. There is also a privacy angle: embeddings can leak training data (inversion attacks reconstruct inputs from vectors), so treat stored embeddings of sensitive data with the same care as the data. Geometry is powerful, learned, and attackable — the module's refrain, one last time.
notes.title: Embeddings: similarity as geometry

notes.body:
Now the payoff: the linear classifier from M27's evasion lab, understood geometrically. A linear classifier scores s(x) = w·x + b and predicts positive when s > 0. The decision boundary is where the score is zero: w·x + b = 0. In 2D with w=[1,1], b=−3: x₁+x₂−3=0, i.e., the line x₁+x₂=3 — everything above-right scores positive, below-left negative. The weight vector w is perpendicular to the boundary (it points in the direction of steepest score increase — the gradient direction the M27 attacker followed). The margin — a point's perpendicular distance to the boundary — is |w·x+b|/|w|. Worked: x=[2,2]. Score: 1×2+1×2−3 = 1 > 0, positive class. Margin: |1|/√(1²+1²) = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. That 0.707 is the robustness budget: any perturbation with a component larger than 0.707 along −w flips the verdict — and M27's δ=[−0.6,−0.6] (norm ≈0.85) spent exactly that budget. Geometry explains the attack completely: the point sat 0.707 from the line, the attacker pushed 0.85 toward it, the point crossed. Support vector machines make the margin the explicit objective: choose the boundary maximizing the minimum margin over training points — the fattest possible street between the classes. Larger margins mean costlier evasion; that is the geometric reason adversarial training (which effectively pushes points away from the boundary) helps. In higher dimensions the boundary is a hyperplane — same equation, w·x+b=0, with w having one component per feature — and the margin formula is unchanged. The 'curse' from M27 also geometric: in high dimensions, most of a point's neighborhood lies near some boundary direction, so small perturbations find crossings easily. Worked 3D extension: w=[1,−1,0.5], b=0, x=[2,1,2]. Score: 2−1+1 = 2 > 0. Margin: 2/√(1+1+0.25) = 2/1.5 ≈ 1.333. Same mechanics, one more dimension. Common mistake: thinking the boundary is where the data is. The boundary is where the model is maximally uncertain — the most attackable real estate in the feature space, which is why attackers live there.

Do not overlook b, the bias term — geometrically it is the boundary's offset from the origin, and operationally it is the prior baked into the model. With b = 0, the boundary passes through the origin: the classifier is 'fair' between classes at the origin. Our b = -3 shifted the line outward: at the origin (x = [0,0]), the score is -3, confidently negative — the model defaults to negative unless the features push hard positive. That default is a choice with consequences: in detection terms, b encodes the tradeoff between false positives and false negatives before any feature is even considered. Raising b (less negative) moves the boundary toward the negative class — more positives, higher recall, more false alarms: it is the threshold knob from statistics, inside the equation. When you inherit a model, inspect b (and the score distribution): a model with an extreme bias is really a mostly-constant classifier wearing a linear costume. And when you train, remember the bias learns the class balance of the training data — train on 99%-benign data and the bias absorbs that prior, which is correct for that population and wrong everywhere else. The bias is the base rate, smuggled into geometry.
notes.title: How a linear classifier draws its line

notes.body: One more geometric idea, because it powers real anomaly detection: dimensionality reduction and the intuition behind eigenvectors. Real security data has hundreds of features, but the interesting variation often lives in far fewer directions. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) finds those directions: the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix, ordered by eigenvalue (variance captured). Intuition without the full derivation: imagine points scattered mostly along a diagonal line with small perpendicular jitter. The first principal component points along the diagonal (the direction of greatest spread); the second points perpendicular (the jitter direction). Projecting onto just the first component compresses 2D to 1D while keeping the shape that matters. The anomaly-detection trick: learn the principal components of normal traffic, then for each new point measure reconstruction error — project it onto the top components and back, and see how much was lost. Normal points reconstruct well (they fit the learned shape); anomalies reconstruct poorly (they stick out in directions normal data doesn't use). Worked sketch: normal SSH sessions cluster with (bytes, duration) along a line — big transfers take longer. A session with huge bytes and tiny duration reconstructs badly → flag: possible exfiltration-shaped anomaly. That is PCA anomaly detection in a paragraph; your lab implements the core (find the max-variance direction by search). Eigenvectors generally: Av = λv — directions a matrix stretches without rotating, scaled by λ. They appear wherever linear transformations repeat: covariance matrices (PCA), graph adjacency (network centrality — nodes important because important nodes link to them), and Markov chains. You don't need to compute eigendecompositions by hand; you need the intuition — 'the natural axes of the data' — so that when a paper says 'we projected onto the top-k principal components,' you picture the diagonal line, not a black box. And the security caveat, on brand for this course: PCA learns 'normal' from training data — poison that data (M27) and the learned normal includes the attacker's shape. Geometry is powerful, and like every model, it trusts its training data. Common mistake: keeping too few components and discarding the signal, or too many and keeping the noise. The eigenvalue spectrum (how fast variance drops off) tells you where to cut. Eigenvectors have a second security life beyond PCA: graphs. A network's adjacency matrix has a principal eigenvector — and its entries are eigenvector centrality: nodes score highly when connected to other high-scoring nodes. Worked intuition: in a corporate network graph, the domain controller has high centrality (everything talks to it); a workstation that suddenly jumps in centrality is worth investigating — what is it suddenly connected to? Attack-path analysis uses the same math: the attacker's lateral movement follows high-centrality paths, and defenders harden the nodes whose removal fragments the graph. Even PageRank is an eigenvector computation. The unifying idea: when a matrix describes relationships (covariance between features, adjacency between hosts), its eigenvectors reveal the structure's natural axes — the directions along which the system actually varies or connects. Learn to ask 'what are this matrix's eigenvectors?' about any matrix you meet in security tooling, and you will extract insights the raw numbers hide. It is the same question as PCA, asked of a different matrix — which is why the intuition transfers.
notes.title: Eigen-intuition and PCA for anomaly detection

handsOnLab.brief: You will assemble a 90-question mixed practice bank drawn from this module and IL-29's domain coverage, build a simple timer-and-scorecard tracker, and run a full 90-minute simulated gate with domain-level scoring.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Your scorecard shows two consecutive runs at >= 80% overall with no domain below 65%, each on a fresh 90-question set under a strict 90-minute timer.
handsOnLab.deliverable: sy0-701-gate/ folder with bank.md, timer-log.md, and scorecard.md showing two consecutive gate passes with per-domain scores.
steps: Create a folder sy0-701-gate/ with three files: bank.md, timer-log.md, scorecard.md.
In bank.md, write 90 questions: 11 from Domain 1.0, 20 from Domain 2.0, 16 from Domain 3.0, 25 from Domain 4.0, 18 from Domain 5.0 (mirrors the 12/22/18/28/20 weights).
Mark 6 of the 90 as PBQ-style: write them as tasks (order steps, match items, triage a log snippet) rather than multiple-choice.
Number each question and record the answer key on a separate page you cannot see during the run.
In timer-log.md, pre-write your pacing checkpoints: 30 min (target: 30+ answered), 60 min (target: 60+ answered or first pass done), 85 min (final review).
Set a real 90-minute timer. Begin. Enforce the flag-and-return rule: any question taking over 90 seconds gets flagged and skipped on pass one.
When the timer ends, stop writing immediately — unanswered questions stay blank, exactly like exam day.
Score each question, then compute per-domain percentages in scorecard.md.
Apply the gate rule: overall >= 80% AND every domain >= 65%. Record PASS or FAIL with the failing domains listed.
For every missed question, write a one-line root cause: knowledge gap, misread stem, pacing casualty, or distractor trap.
Schedule remediation: each failing domain gets a dated study block before the next gate run.
Repeat the gate with a FRESH question set (never reuse the same 90) until you pass twice in a row.

notes.title: The SY0-701 exam blueprint: format, pacing, and question mix
Domain 1.0 — General Security Concepts (12%): the language of the whole exam
Domain 2.0 — Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations (22%)

notes.body: Domain 3.0 asks how secure systems are built: cloud models and the shared responsibility model, virtualization and containerization security, network architecture (segmentation, DMZ, VLANs, VPNs, SD-WAN), resilience and recovery (redundancy, backups, high availability, disaster recovery vs. business continuity), and secure protocols. The shared responsibility model is the single most-tested idea here. In IaaS the provider secures the physical infrastructure, virtualization layer, and network fabric; you secure the OS, applications, data, and access. In PaaS the provider additionally owns the OS and runtime; you own the application code, data, and identity. In SaaS the provider owns nearly everything up to the application; you own your data, user access, and configuration. Worked example. Scenario: 'A company migrates its customer database to a SaaS CRM. A misconfigured sharing setting exposes customer records to the internet.' Who failed? The customer. Under shared responsibility, the SaaS provider secures the platform; the tenant owns its data and its access configuration. The fix is a configuration review and a data-classification policy, not a ticket to the vendor. Second worked example — architecture choice. 'An industrial control network must never route traffic to the corporate LAN, but engineers need occasional remote diagnostics.' The design answer is segmentation with a jump host (a hardened, monitored bastion in a DMZ-like boundary zone), plus VPN with MFA for the remote leg — defense in depth with the smallest possible trust bridge. Common mistakes: recommending a VPN as if it were segmentation — a VPN extends a network, it does not divide one; and confusing disaster recovery (restoring IT systems, measured by RTO/RPO) with business continuity (keeping the business functioning during disruption). Also know your protocols cold: DNS on 53, HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SSH 22, RDP 3389, SMB 445, LDAP 389/636, SMTP 25/587, SNMP 161, FTP 20/21, TFTP 69, DHCP 67/68, NTP 123, IMAP 143/993, POP3 110/995, Telnet 23 (and why you never use it). Protocol-and-port matching is easy points if you drill it and easy losses if you do not. A third worked example - resilience math in plain language. 'The business needs the ordering system back within 4 hours of a failure, and can afford to lose at most 1 hour of transactions.' That is an RTO of 4 hours (recovery time objective: how fast) and an RPO of 1 hour (recovery point objective: how much data loss). The architecture answer: backups at least hourly (to meet the RPO) plus a tested restore procedure that completes inside 4 hours (to meet the RTO). Exam stems give you the business requirement and ask which backup strategy fits - match the frequency to the RPO and the restore speed to the RTO. Common mistake: swapping the two. RTO is about time to recover; RPO is about data loss tolerance. A second gotcha: high availability (keeping the system running through failures - clustering, redundancy) vs. fault tolerance (continuing through a component failure with zero interruption). Both serve availability, but fault tolerance is the stronger guarantee.
notes.title: Domain 3.0 — Security Architecture (18%): designing it right

notes.body: At 28 percent, Security Operations is the largest slice of the exam and the most operational — this is where your IL-29 hands-on depth pays off. It covers SOC operations and SIEM (log aggregation, correlation rules, alert triage, tuning to kill false positives), vulnerability management (scanning, prioritization, remediation workflows), incident response (the lifecycle: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned), digital forensics basics (order of volatility, chain of custody, imaging), and the security tools of the trade: IDS/IPS, EDR, DLP, firewalls, honeypots, vulnerability scanners, penetration testing vs. vulnerability assessment. Worked example — SIEM triage. You are shown three alerts: (1) a single failed SSH login from an internal workstation, (2) 400 failed SSH logins in 10 minutes from one external IP against a public server, (3) a successful login immediately following alert 2 from the same IP. Analysis: alert 1 is noise (single failure, internal source — likely a typo). Alert 2 is a brute-force/password-spray pattern — a detective control firing as designed. Alert 3 is the critical one: successful authentication after a brute-force burst means probable compromise; the correct action is to contain first (isolate the host, disable the account, rotate credentials), then investigate. This is the exam's favorite ladder: noise, then attack pattern, then successful compromise — and the right answer is always the one that matches the incident-response phase you are in. Second worked example — vulnerability prioritization. A scanner reports: a critical RCE on an internet-facing server, a high-severity flaw on an isolated test VM, and a medium flaw on a domain controller. Priority order: internet-facing critical RCE first (exploitability times exposure), then the domain controller medium (asset criticality elevates it), then the isolated test VM last. Common mistakes: confusing IDS (detective, alerts only) with IPS (preventive, blocks inline); confusing a vulnerability scan (finds weaknesses, no exploitation) with a penetration test (authorized simulated attack, exploits within scope); and answering forensics questions without respecting the order of volatility — registers and cache first, then RAM, then disk, then logs — because volatile evidence dies when you power down. A third worked example - the EDR vs. antivirus question the exam loves. 'A fileless attack runs entirely in memory via PowerShell.' Traditional signature antivirus sees no file and stays silent; EDR sees the process behavior - PowerShell spawning from Word, obfuscated commands, C2 beaconing - and kills the chain. The exam discriminator: signature-based tools match known files; behavior-based tools (EDR) match malicious actions. When the stem says 'fileless,' 'living off the land,' or 'zero-day,' the answer is the behavioral tool. Common mistake: treating DLP as a network-only control - DLP spans endpoint, network, and cloud, watching data in use, in motion, and at rest. And a final Domain 4.0 trap: penetration testing requires written authorization defining scope - the exam treats an unauthorized 'helpful' test as an attack, and the correct answer always starts with the rules of engagement.
notes.title: Domain 4.0 — Security Operations (28%): the heaviest domain, where points live

notes.body: Domain 5.0 is the governance domain: risk management, policies and frameworks, compliance, audits, privacy, and third-party risk. The exam tests whether you think like someone running a security program, not just operating its tools. Risk management vocabulary is the core: a threat is what could happen, a vulnerability is the weakness it exploits, risk is the combination (commonly expressed as likelihood times impact), a risk assessment identifies and evaluates risks, and risk responses are avoid, transfer (insurance, outsourcing), mitigate (apply controls), or accept (document the residual risk and move on). Worked example — risk math. A ransomware attack on the file server is estimated at 30 percent annual likelihood with a $200,000 impact. Annualized risk: 0.30 x 200,000 = $60,000. A backup-and-recovery control costs $25,000 per year and cuts likelihood to 5 percent: new risk = 0.05 x 200,000 = $10,000, plus the $25,000 control cost = $35,000 total, which is less than the $60,000 exposure — so the control is cost-justified. That is the entire logic of risk-based decision making in one calculation, and exam questions dress it in scenarios about whether to buy the control, buy insurance (transfer), or accept. Frameworks and compliance: know what the big names govern without memorizing their clause numbers. NIST CSF organizes cybersecurity outcomes; NIST RMF structures federal risk management; ISO 27001/27002 cover information security management; PCI DSS governs cardholder data; HIPAA governs protected health information; GDPR governs EU personal data; SOC 2 reports on service-organization controls. Privacy concepts: data classification (public, internal, confidential, restricted), data retention and disposal, and the principle of collecting the minimum data necessary. Third-party risk: vendor assessments, right-to-audit clauses, and supply-chain risk — you inherit the security posture of everyone you connect to. Common mistake: answering governance questions with a technical control. When the question asks what the CISO should do about a policy gap, the answer is a governance action (update the policy, run a risk assessment, commission an audit), not 'install a firewall.' A second worked example - the policy hierarchy. 'An employee violates the acceptable-use policy by mining crypto on a workstation.' The policy (managerial, directive) defined the rule; the monitoring that caught it was detective; the disciplinary process is the enforcement. Exam questions ask which document governs a situation - policies set direction, standards set the mandatory rules, procedures give step-by-step instructions, guidelines are recommendations. The discriminator: 'must' language lives in standards, 'how to' lives in procedures. A third mini-example: third-party risk. 'The company adopts a SaaS vendor that suffers a breach.' The controls that should have existed: a vendor risk assessment before signing, a right-to-audit clause in the contract, and a review of the vendor's SOC 2 report. On the exam, supply-chain and vendor questions are always answered with assessment-before-trust - never 'the vendor handles it.'

handsOnLab.brief: You will build a personal SIEM-style log triage practice environment using free log datasets, write correlation rules, tune them against false positives, and run timed PBQ-style triage sets.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Your tuned rules produce under 5% false-positive rate on the practice dataset, and your triage log shows three timed sets at 80%+ accuracy with notes on every miss.
handsOnLab.deliverable: cysa-practice/ folder with triage-log.md, rules.md (correlation rules + tuning history), and three scored timed-set reports.
steps: Create a folder cysa-practice/ with triage-log.md, rules.md, and timed-set-1.md.
Generate or download a free practice log dataset (e.g., a public web-server access log or Windows event log sample) and note its source in rules.md.

In rules.md, write three correlation rules in plain language: brute-force detection (many failures then success), beaconing detection (regular outbound intervals), and lateral-movement detection (unusual host-to-host SMB/WinRM).
Run each rule mentally against a sample of the logs and record in triage-log.md: true positives, false positives, false negatives.
Tune: rewrite each rule to cut false positives without creating false negatives, and document every change in the tuning history section of rules.md.
Build timed-set-1.md: 15 triage questions (log snippet -> attack? phase? next action), mixing the four domains at 33/30/20/17 weights.
Set a 30-minute timer, run the set, score it, and record per-domain accuracy.
For every miss, write the root cause: missed pattern, wrong IR phase, or misclassified vulnerability priority.
Build two more fresh sets (timed-set-2.md, timed-set-3.md) — never reuse questions.
Repeat until all three sets score 80%+ with documented tuning history.
Write a final paragraph in triage-log.md: which rule-tuning lesson was most important and why.

notes.title: The CS0-003 blueprint: analyst work under a 165-minute clock
Domain 1.0 — Security Operations (33%): the SOC analyst's domain
Domain 2.0 — Vulnerability Management (30%): find, rank, fix, verify

notes.body: At 20 percent, Incident Response Management tests whether you can run an incident, not just describe one. The lifecycle: preparation (playbooks, tools, roles, tabletop exercises), detection and analysis (triage, scoping, confirming the incident), containment (short-term: isolate; long-term: cut off the attacker's access paths), eradication (remove the foothold, close the exploited vector), recovery (restore systems, monitor for re-infection), and lessons learned (post-incident review, playbook updates). Evidence handling runs alongside: maintain chain of custody, image before you analyze, respect the order of volatility. Worked example — a phishing-to-ransomware chain. Monday: a user clicks a link; EDR quarantines a payload (detection and analysis begins — is this an incident or an event?). Tuesday: the payload detonated before quarantine on one host and is moving laterally (confirmed incident — now containment: isolate the host, block the C2 domains at the firewall, disable the compromised account). Wednesday: the team removes persistence mechanisms and patches the exploited vector (eradication), then restores encrypted shares from immutable backups (recovery), then holds the post-incident review that discovers the phishing filter rule was disabled — and re-enables it with change control (lessons learned). Notice the discipline: you never eradicate before you contain (the attacker re-enters), and you never skip lessons learned (the same incident recurs). Second worked example — scoping. Three hosts show indicators; the analyst images all three before analysis begins, documents who handled each image and when (chain of custody), and only then starts the deep dive. Common mistakes: jumping to eradication ('just reimage it') before containment and scoping — you lose the evidence and the attacker's other footholds; confusing short-term containment (isolate the host now) with long-term containment (block the C2 infrastructure, rotate credentials enterprise-wide); and forgetting that preparation is a phase too — the team that runs tabletop exercises responds in minutes, the team that does not responds in days. A third worked example - the tabletop as preparation. 'The team runs a tabletop exercise: a simulated ransomware outbreak on a Friday afternoon.' The facilitator walks through each phase: who declares the incident, who isolates, who talks to legal, who decides on restoration. The value is not the scenario - it is discovering that nobody knows who can authorize isolating the finance VLAN. That discovery IS the exercise's product, and the playbook gets updated before a real incident tests it. The exam treats tabletops as a preparation-phase control and loves asking what a tabletop produces (findings about the plan, not about the attacker). Common mistake: confusing incident response with disaster recovery. IR handles the security event (stop the attacker, eradicate, recover securely); DR handles the restoration of IT services after any disruption (the RTO/RPO plan). They overlap at recovery but start from different triggers - the exam separates them by asking what initiated the response. A security incident triggers IR; a hurricane triggers DR and business continuity. Know which plan owns which trigger.
notes.title: Domain 3.0 — Incident Response Management (20%): run the incident

notes.body: At 17 percent, Reporting and Communication is the smallest domain but the one that separates analysts who get promoted from analysts who stay in the queue. It covers report types and audiences, metrics that matter, and stakeholder communication during incidents. The master rule: the report serves the audience, not the author. An executive report leads with business impact, risk, cost, and recommended actions in plain language — no packet dumps, no CVE strings without translation. A technical report gives engineers the indicators, timelines, affected systems, and remediation steps with enough detail to act. A compliance or legal report adds the notification timeline and the evidence-preservation record. Worked example. The same ransomware incident produces three documents. Executive summary (one page): 'On Tuesday, ransomware encrypted the finance share; operations were restored from backups within 8 hours; no customer data left the network; we recommend a $40,000 EDR upgrade and mandatory phishing training; residual risk is medium until the email-filter gap is closed.' Technical report: the full timeline, IOCs, the disabled filter rule, the containment actions with timestamps, the eradication steps, and the verification rescan results. Compliance memo: when the incident was declared, who was notified and when, what data was affected, and the chain-of-custody log for the forensic images. Common mistakes: writing the executive report like a technical one (executives do not care about the malware's mutex name; they care about impact and decisions); omitting recommended actions (a report that describes without recommending is a diary, not an analysis); and forgetting metrics — mean time to detect, mean time to respond, and vulnerability-remediation SLAs are the numbers that prove the security program works. In PBQs, the question often asks which document or which section goes to whom — answer with the audience rule and you will rarely miss. A second worked example - metrics that matter. 'The CISO asks whether the SOC is improving.' The analyst answers with three numbers: mean time to detect (MTTD) dropped from 4 hours to 45 minutes after the new correlation rules; mean time to respond (MTTR) dropped from 8 hours to 2 hours after the playbook update; and vulnerability-remediation SLA compliance rose from 60% to 92%. Those three metrics - MTTD, MTTR, SLA compliance - are the exam's favorite proof-of-program numbers, and any answer choice offering vanity metrics ('alerts processed,' 'logs collected') loses to them. A third mini-example: the compliance report. 'Regulators require evidence that access reviews happen quarterly.' The report includes the review dates, the reviewers, the findings, and the remediation - the who, when, what, and so-what. The exam tests whether you know that compliance reporting is evidence of process, not narrative. Common mistake: writing metrics without baselines. 'MTTR is 2 hours' means nothing; 'MTTR fell from 8 hours to 2 hours after the playbook update' proves improvement. Always pair the number with its before.

handsOnLab.brief: You will build a CISSP domain-study system: a weighted study calendar, a scenario-question bank written in the 'think like a manager' style, and a decision log that records why the management answer beat the technical answer.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Your bank holds 80 scenario questions (10 per domain), your decision log explains the management-over-technical reasoning for 20 of them, and two timed 40-question runs score 75%+.
handsOnLab.deliverable: cissp-prep/ folder with study-calendar.md, scenario-bank.md (80 questions, 10/domain), and decision-log.md.
steps: Create cissp-prep/ with study-calendar.md, scenario-bank.md, decision-log.md.
In study-calendar.md, allocate study hours by domain weight: 16% of hours to Domain 1, 10% to Domain 2, 13% to Domains 3, 4, 5, and 7, 12% to Domain 6, 10% to Domain 8.
Write 10 scenario questions per domain in scenario-bank.md (80 total); every question must have one technically-correct-but-wrong answer and one management-correct answer.
For each question, mark the correct answer and write the discriminator: which CISSP mindset rule decided it.
Run a timed 40-question set (5 per domain) in 75 minutes; score it and record per-domain results.
In decision-log.md, write 20 entries: the question, the tempting technical answer, the correct management answer, and the one-sentence rule that decides it.
Identify your two weakest domains from the run and double their calendar hours for the next two weeks.
Build a second fresh 40-question set and run it under the same timing.
Record both runs; the gate is 75%+ overall with no domain below 60%.
Write a final entry in decision-log.md: your personal top-5 CISSP mindset rules, in your own words.

notes.body: Domains 3, 4, and 5 are the technical core — 39 percent combined — but CISSP tests them through a design-and-decision lens, not a configuration lens. Domain 3, Security Architecture and Engineering (13 percent): security models (Bell-LaPadula for confidentiality, Biba for integrity, Clark-Wilson for well-formed transactions), evaluation criteria, cryptography concepts, physical security, and secure design principles (least privilege, defense in depth, fail securely, economy of mechanism, complete mediation). Domain 4, Communication and Network Security (13 percent): secure network architecture and design, transmission media, network attacks and countermeasures, secure communications (VPNs, TLS, secure protocols). Domain 5, Identity and Access Management (13 percent): identification, authentication (single, multi-factor, and the factors themselves), authorization models (role-based, rule-based, mandatory, discretionary), and accountability (auditing, session management). Worked example — access model selection. Scenario: 'A defense contractor needs a system where access is determined by security clearance and data classification, enforced by the system regardless of user discretion.' That is mandatory access control (MAC) — the system enforces the policy (as in Bell-LaPadula's 'no read up, no write down' for confidentiality). Contrast: a company where managers grant access to their teams' folders is discretionary access control (DAC); a hospital where access follows job function is role-based (RBAC). The exam loves these three-way discriminations — memorize the one-sentence discriminator for each. Second worked example — fail securely. 'A firewall's primary power supply fails during an attack.' The secure design answer: the firewall fails closed (deny all) on its redundant supply or fails over to its HA peer — never fails open, because fail-open during an attack is the attacker winning by power outage. Common mistakes: confusing authentication (proving who you are) with authorization (what you are allowed to do) — the exam separates them relentlessly; and confusing Biba (integrity: no read down, no write up) with Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality: no read up, no write down) — learn them as mirror images. A third worked example - crypto concepts at the CISSP level. Scenario: 'Two parties need to exchange sensitive design documents with confidentiality, integrity, and non-repudiation.' The CISSP answer: encrypt with the recipient's public key (confidentiality - only the private-key holder reads it), sign with the sender's private key (non-repudiation and authenticity), and the recipient verifies the signature with the sender's public key and hashes the document (integrity). The exam tests whether you can assemble the primitives into a solution, not whether you can do the math. The classic trap: 'encrypt with your private key for confidentiality' - wrong, because anyone with your public key can decrypt it; private-key operations prove identity (signing), public-key operations protect confidentiality. A second network-security discriminator: the exam separates secure protocols from their insecure ancestors relentlessly - SSH replaces Telnet, HTTPS replaces HTTP, SFTP/FTPS replace FTP. When a scenario shows Telnet or FTP in use, the finding is the protocol, and the fix is its secure replacement.
notes.title: Domains 3, 4, and 5: architecture, networks, and IAM (39% combined)

notes.body: Domains 6, 7, and 8 close the loop: verify, operate, and build securely. Domain 6, Security Assessment and Testing (12 percent): test strategies, security control testing, vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, audits, and log reviews — the exam tests whether you know which assessment fits which question. Domain 7, Security Operations (13 percent): the SOC world — investigations, logging and monitoring, provisioning, incident management, disaster recovery — but at the management level: are the processes defined, measured, and improving? Domain 8, Software Development Security (10 percent): SDLC security, secure coding, maturity models, databases and data warehousing security. Worked example — assessment selection. Scenario: 'Management wants to know whether the company's access controls are operating effectively across all departments.' The answer is an audit (or security assessment) — a broad evaluation against a standard — not a penetration test (which is a narrow, adversarial test of specific systems) and not a vulnerability scan (which finds technical weaknesses without testing control effectiveness). The discriminator: audits answer 'are we doing what we said?'; pen tests answer 'can an attacker break this specific thing?'; vuln scans answer 'what weaknesses exist?' Second worked example — SDLC root cause. 'A web application ships the same injection vulnerability in three consecutive releases.' The Domain 8 answer: the SDLC lacks secure-coding standards, code review, and security testing gates — patching each release treats the symptom; fixing the development process treats the disease. Common mistakes: recommending a penetration test when the scenario asks for control effectiveness (that is an audit); and answering operations questions with heroics ('work all weekend to rebuild') instead of process ('invoke the disaster-recovery plan, which defines RTO/RPO and roles'). On CISSP, the plan is always the answer — preparation beats improvisation, and the exam rewards the candidate who trusts the process. A third worked example - the SDLC gate question. Scenario: 'A company wants to stop injection flaws from reaching production.' The Domain 8 answer is a set of SDLC gates: secure-coding standards, automated static analysis in the pipeline, mandatory peer code review for data-access code, and dynamic testing in staging - with a policy that blocks release when gates fail. Patching production after each incident is the wrong answer (treats symptoms); the gates treat the disease. The exam's discriminator: any answer choice that fixes the process beats any choice that fixes the instance. A second Domain 6 drill: 'The audit committee wants assurance that the new access-control system works as designed.' The answer is a controls assessment against the requirements - not a pen test (which would test whether an attacker can bypass it, a different question). The exam separates 'does it work as designed' (assessment/audit) from 'can it be broken' (pen test) from 'what weaknesses exist' (vuln scan) with near-religious consistency. Memorize the three questions each answers and you will not miss these.

items.answer: Defense in depth — one layer's failure must not equal compromise.
items.explain: The firewall is one layer; EDR, patching, least privilege, and monitoring are the others.

items.answer: Accountability — every action must trace to an identity.
items.explain: Shared accounts destroy accountability; the fix is individual accounts plus logging.

items.answer: Symmetric for bulk data (fast), asymmetric for key exchange and signatures.
items.explain: Hybrid crypto: asymmetric solves key distribution, symmetric does the heavy lifting.

items.answer: Containment — isolate the host and block the C2, then eradicate.
items.explain: The six steps in order; skipping containment lets the attacker re-enter during eradication.

items.answer: Least privilege — standard users, just-in-time elevation.
items.explain: Removing local admin is the textbook least-privilege control; elevation on demand preserves usability.
items.prompt: Scenario: users run as local admins and malware spreads with their privileges. The principle and the fix?

items.answer: Integrity — the data was altered in transit.
items.explain: CIA mapping: eavesdropping hits confidentiality, alteration hits integrity, outage hits availability.

notes.body: GSEC expects working crypto literacy: what each tool does, when to use it, and what breaks when it is misused — not mathematical proofs. Symmetric cryptography uses one shared key for encryption and decryption (fast, ideal for bulk data; the hard problem is key distribution — getting the shared key to both parties securely). Asymmetric cryptography uses a key pair (public and private); it is slower but solves key distribution and enables digital signatures (private key signs, anyone verifies with the public key) and key exchange. Hashing produces a fixed-length digest of data (integrity checking — the same input always gives the same digest, and any change avalanches the output); it is one-way, not encryption. In practice the three combine: asymmetric crypto exchanges a session key, symmetric crypto encrypts the bulk data, hashing (via HMAC or signatures) verifies integrity. Worked example — verifying a download. You download a vendor installer plus its published hash and signature. Step 1: hash the downloaded file yourself and compare to the published hash — a match proves integrity (the file was not corrupted or altered). Step 2: verify the signature with the vendor's public key — a valid signature proves authenticity (it really came from the vendor) and non-repudiation. Skip step 2 and a tampered file with a recomputed hash fools you; skip step 1 and you trust without verifying. Second worked example — TLS in one paragraph. The client and server use asymmetric crypto to authenticate the server and agree on a session key, then switch to symmetric crypto for the bulk transfer, with hashing-based message authentication on every record. That is why TLS is fast despite using 'slow' asymmetric crypto — the slow part only sets up the fast part. Common mistakes: calling hashing 'encryption' (hashing is one-way; there is no decryption); thinking asymmetric crypto encrypts bulk data (it is far too slow — it handles keys and signatures); and forgetting that crypto without key management is theater — GSEC treats key generation, storage, rotation, and destruction as part of every crypto answer. A third worked example - key management as the exam's crypto trap. 'A company encrypts its backups with AES but stores the key in a plaintext file next to the backups.' The finding: the crypto is theater - anyone who steals the backups steals the key. The fix is key management: generate keys securely, store them separately (a key-management system or HSM), rotate on schedule and on personnel changes, and destroy keys when data is retired (cryptographic erasure). The exam's rule: every crypto scenario is really a key-management scenario. The algorithm choice is rarely the finding; the key handling almost always is. A second discriminator: digital signatures vs. HMAC. Signatures use asymmetric keys and provide non-repudiation (the signer cannot deny signing); HMAC uses a shared secret and proves integrity and authenticity between parties who share it, but not non-repudiation. When the stem needs 'prove who sent it to a third party,' the answer is signatures.
notes.title: Cryptography essentials: symmetric, asymmetric, hashing, and signatures

notes.body: GSEC treats incident handling as a hands-on discipline: the six steps are preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned. Preparation means the team, tools, playbooks, and communication plans exist before the incident — the exam treats an untested plan as no plan. Identification is confirming and scoping: is this an incident or an event, and how far did it spread? Containment has two horizons: short-term (isolate the host now) and long-term (block the C2, rotate credentials, cut off the attacker's paths). Eradication removes the foothold and closes the exploited vector. Recovery restores operations and monitors for re-infection. Lessons learned converts the incident into improved defenses. Evidence handling runs through all of it: image before analysis, maintain chain of custody, respect the order of volatility. Worked example — the full run. 09:00: EDR alerts on a suspicious PowerShell chain (identification begins — analyst confirms it is malicious, not a false positive). 09:20: the host is isolated from the network and the user's credentials are disabled (short-term containment). 09:45: firewall blocks the C2 domains and email gateway blocks the phishing sender (long-term containment). 10:30: persistence mechanisms removed, the exploited macro vector disabled via policy (eradication). 11:00: the host is reimaged from a known-good image and returned to service with enhanced monitoring (recovery). Friday: the post-incident review finds the phishing filter exception that let the email through; the exception is removed and the playbook is updated (lessons learned). Notice what never happens: nobody skips containment to 'just reimage it' — reimaging without scoping destroys evidence and leaves the attacker's other footholds. Common mistakes: eradicating before containing (the classic exam trap); confusing identification with detection (detection is the alert; identification is the analyst's confirmation and scoping); and treating lessons learned as optional paperwork — on GSEC it is a scored phase, and the correct answer to 'what comes after recovery' is always the post-incident review. A third worked example - the chain-of-custody drill. 'An analyst copies suspicious files to a USB drive for analysis, then hands the drive to a colleague with no documentation.' Two failures: the copy is not a forensic image (hashes undocumented, original altered by the copy process), and the handoff has no custody record (who had it, when, why). The correct procedure: image the original with a write blocker, hash the image, log every handler and transfer, analyze the copy. The exam treats any break in this chain as evidence contamination - and in legal contexts, contaminated evidence is inadmissible. A second trap: the 'quick peek' - 'the analyst opens the malware sample on their workstation to see what it does.' That is detonation, not analysis: it alerts the attacker (if beaconing), contaminates the workstation, and destroys the forensic state. Analysis happens on isolated forensic copies, never on production systems. When a stem shows analysis on the original or on a live workstation, the finding is procedure, and the fix is the forensic workflow.
notes.title: Incident handling: the six steps, run in order

notes.body: GSEC is explicitly hands-on about Windows and Linux security — it expects you to know the native controls of both, not just the concepts. Windows: NTFS permissions (file and folder access control, with inheritance and explicit denies), Group Policy (centralized configuration enforcement — password policy, audit policy, software restriction), Windows Defender and its centralized configuration, Event Viewer and Windows event logs (the forensic record), User Account Control (elevation prompts as a least-privilege mechanism), and BitLocker (full-disk encryption). Linux: file permissions (owner/group/other with read/write/execute bits, plus setuid/setgid/sticky bits), sudoers (delegated privilege — who may run what as root), syslog/journald (the logging pipeline), SSH hardening (key-only auth, no root login), and host firewalls (iptables/nftables). Worked example — securing a new server, both platforms. Windows: join it to the domain, apply the hardening GPO (disable unneeded services, enforce password and lockout policy, enable Defender with centralized reporting), set NTFS permissions so the app data folder is accessible only to the service account and the admins group, enable BitLocker, and forward the Security log to the SIEM. Linux: create a service account with no login shell, set restrictive permissions on the app directory (no world-read on configs), configure sudoers so the deploy user may restart only the app service, harden SSH (key-only, no root, non-standard port as obscurity plus fail2ban as the real control), and ship journald to the SIEM. The pattern is identical across platforms: minimize, control privilege, log everything, encrypt data. Common mistakes: answering Windows questions with Linux tools and vice versa (the exam keeps the platforms distinct); forgetting that GPO is the Windows answer to 'how do you enforce this on 500 machines' (the scale answer is always centralized management); and neglecting logging — on GSEC, any hardening answer that omits log forwarding is incomplete, because accountability requires the audit trail. A third worked example - the GPO-vs-manual discriminator. 'Five hundred workstations need USB mass storage blocked.' The manual answer (visit each machine) is operationally absurd; the GSEC answer is Group Policy - one policy, enforced centrally, auditable, reversible. The exam's scale rule: any control applied to more than a handful of systems must be centrally managed, or it is not a control but a wish. A second Linux drill: 'The web server's document root is world-writable.' The finding: excessive permissions (any local user can alter served content - a defacement and malware-distribution risk). The fix: owner-writable only, group-readable as needed, and the service account given exactly the rights its function requires. The exam pairs permission scenarios with the least-privilege principle constantly: when a stem shows broad permissions, the finding is the permission, and the fix is the minimum necessary. A final cross-platform trap: 'the company encrypts laptops with BitLocker but leaves desktops unencrypted because they never leave the office.' Theft is not the only threat - disposal, repair, and insider access all expose desktop disks. The finding is inconsistent encryption policy; the fix is encryption by data classification, not by device mobility.

notes.body: The crosswalk table is this module's core artifact and the tool that prevents the most expensive junior mistake: studying everything twice. Build it as a real table with four columns: certificate topic area (from the public course pages), IL-29 module mapping, coverage verdict (deep / partial / gap), and action (validate / study / skip). Worked example — five rows. Row 1: 'Security foundations' → IL-29 prereq and zero-trust modules → deep → validate via certificate assessment. Row 2: 'SIEM and log analysis' → IL-29 SIEM modules → deep → validate; add timed triage reps from the certificate's labs. Row 3: 'Incident response workflow' → IL-29 IR modules → partial (reporting light) → study the reporting gap, validate the rest. Row 4: 'Security tools overview' → IL-29 tooling modules → deep → validate. Row 5: 'Career and interview preparation' → IL29-M39/M40 → deep → use IL-29's panel sims as the primary prep. The verdict column drives the study plan: 'validate' rows get assessment attempts, 'study' rows get sequenced learning blocks, 'gap' rows get new learning with portfolio artifacts. Second worked example — the no-duplication rule in action. Both IL-29 and the certificate cover access control. Without the table, you study it twice (two weeks). With the table, you take the certificate's assessment once (two hours): pass, and the topic is closed with proof; fail one sub-topic, and you study only that sub-topic. The table pays for itself the first time it kills a redundant study block. Common mistake: building the table from memory instead of from the public course pages. Memory lies about coverage — open both Coursera pages, copy the topic areas verbatim into the table, then map. A crosswalk built on imagination is worse than none, because it gives false confidence about gaps. A third worked example - the table as a living document. Month one: 40 rows, 12 marked 'study.' Month two: 8 of the 12 flip to 'validated' as assessments pass; 2 new gaps appear (topics you did not know you did not know - the table's hidden gift). Month three: the table is 90% validated, and the remaining rows are your genuine frontier - the topics worth deep IL-29 lab investment. The table did not just prevent duplication; it mapped your ignorance precisely, which is the most valuable study artifact there is. A maintenance rule: revisit the table monthly. Certificate pages update, IL-29 grows, and your knowledge changes - a stale crosswalk quietly rots into false confidence. Fifteen minutes a month keeps it honest. A second discipline: the 'skip' verdict needs justification. Marking a topic 'skip' because it is boring is how gaps survive; marking it 'skip' with a written reason ('out of scope for the Oct 13 panel; revisit Q1') is a decision. The table records decisions, not moods.
notes.title: Building the crosswalk table: the no-duplication engine

notes.body: Sequence matters: foundations before tooling, tooling before analyst workflow, workflow before interview prep. Both certificates are designed in that order, and your crosswalk study plan should respect it — skipping ahead to incident response before your log-reading is solid produces the classic failure mode of knowing the IR phases but being unable to read the evidence that triggers them. Worked example — an eight-week integrated plan. Weeks 1-2: foundations — certificate foundations content plus IL-29 prereq modules; done-criteria are assessment passes and a personal glossary you can recite. Weeks 3-4: tooling — SIEM, EDR, vulnerability scanners; done-criteria are lab completions with write-ups (triage a log set, tune a rule, run a scan and prioritize findings). Weeks 5-6: analyst workflow — incident scenarios, reporting; done-criteria are three portfolio artifacts (executive summary, technical report, timeline) from practice incidents. Weeks 7-8: integration — IL-29 panel sims (M39/M40) plus full timed practice sets; done-criteria are gate passes. Notice the pattern: every phase ends in proof, not in 'finished watching.' Second worked example — the weekly rhythm. Monday: new topic (certificate module + IL-29 mapping). Tuesday-Thursday: reps (labs, drills, triage sets). Friday: assessment or artifact (validate or produce). Weekend: review and crosswalk-table update. Ninety minutes a day sustains this; four-hour weekend blocks accelerate it. Common mistake: front-loading video watching and back-loading practice. The research on skill acquisition is unambiguous — spaced, active practice beats passive consumption by a wide margin, and interview panels test active skill. If your week contains more watching than doing, invert it. The certificates give you the sequence; IL-29 gives you the depth; your calendar gives you the reps. All three are required. A third worked example - the taper week. Week 8 is not for new topics: it is full timed sets, panel sims from M39/M40, and artifact polish. Monday: timed 40-question set, score by domain. Tuesday: M39 technical bank aloud, rubric-scored. Wednesday: M40 STAR bank aloud, timed. Thursday: weakest-domain drills only. Friday: rest or light review - the athlete's taper. The science is simple: retrieval practice under mild time pressure consolidates skill; cramming new material the night before degrades it. A second rhythm nuance: protect the morning. If your sharpest hours are 6-9 AM, that is when the hard reps go - triage sets, timed banks, new labs. Afternoons get review, index maintenance, and artifact writing. Ninety focused morning minutes beat three distracted evening hours; schedule like it. A final integration point: the weekly review is also when you update the crosswalk table and the portfolio. Learning, mapping, and proving in one weekly loop - that is the integrated plan running as designed, and it is sustainable for exactly as long as the Oct 13 deadline requires.

notes.title: The program: verified facts and the topic map
Phase 1 — foundations: the language everything else assumes
Phase 2 — defensive: arrive already operating

notes.body: The offensive phase — understanding attacks deeply enough to defend against them — is where many learners feel the most friction, because it requires thinking like the adversary. The program's offensive arc covers how attacks work: reconnaissance, exploitation, persistence, lateral movement, exfiltration — the attack lifecycle that mirrors the defender's IR lifecycle in reverse. IL-29's threat-modeling, attack-technique, MITRE ATT&CK, and adversary-emulation modules are the preparation, and the mindset to build is: every defensive control you know has an attacker working to bypass it, and understanding the bypass is what makes the defense real. Worked example — the attacker's view of your defenses. Take the phishing-to-ransomware chain from the defensive drill and replay it as the attacker: which email filter rule did you evade, and how? Which EDR detection did you dodge, and what technique avoided it? Where did you establish persistence, and what would have caught it? Writing the attacker's playbook for your own defensive scenario is the single best preparation for offensive-phase material — it converts abstract attack techniques into concrete stories. Second worked example — ATT&CK as the bridge. Map each step of your attacker replay to ATT&CK tactics (initial access, execution, persistence, privilege escalation, defense evasion, lateral movement, exfiltration). The mapping exercise does double duty: it prepares the program's ATT&CK content and it gives you the vocabulary to discuss attacks precisely — a skill the Oct 13 panel will notice. The CSA Cloud Controls Matrix gets its cloud-focused version of the same treatment: understand it as structured cloud-security control guidance, and map its domains to the cloud-security concepts in IL-29's cloud modules. Common mistake: treating offensive material as 'hacking fun' separate from defense. On the program's terms — and on the panel's — offensive knowledge exists to serve defense. Every attack technique you learn should end with the question: how would I detect this, and how would I stop it? That question is the entire point of the offensive phase. A third offensive exercise - the purple-team table. Take one ATT&CK technique, e.g., scheduled-task persistence. Red side: how would you establish it, and what would it look like in the logs? Blue side: what detection covers it, and what is the false-positive rate? Then the purple question: what did the exercise teach both sides? Running that table for five techniques builds the offensive-defensive integration the program's arc is designed to produce - and it is directly the mindset the ThreatLocker panel rewards: the operator who thinks like the attacker to defend like a professional. A common mistake in offensive prep is collecting technique names without the detection pairing. A technique you cannot detect is trivia; a technique paired with its detection is capability. For every offensive concept you study, finish with the two sentences: 'I would detect this by...' and 'I would stop this by...' Those sentences are the entire return on investment of the offensive phase.
notes.title: Phase 3 — offensive: think like the attacker to defend like a professional

notes.body: The capstone project is the program's culminating work: a project applying the program's material to a real problem. Your preparation advantage is that IL-29 already produces the raw material — labs, write-ups, analyses, configurations — and a strong capstone proposal is really a curation and extension of work you have already done. Start drafting early: the proposal needs a problem statement (what problem, in three sentences), a scope (what you will build or analyze), the program elements it applies (which NIST framework structures it, which ATT&CK tactics it addresses, which CSA CCM domains it touches), and a done-criterion (what 'finished' looks like). Worked example — a capstone draft from IL-29 artifacts. Problem: 'Small IT teams lack a practical, low-cost detection-engineering workflow.' Scope: 'Build and document a three-rule detection set for a small Windows network — one rule each for credential abuse, lateral movement, and C2 beaconing — with tuning history and false-positive analysis.' Program elements: 'Structured using the NIST framework's Detect function; techniques mapped to MITRE ATT&CK; validated in a lab with written triage procedures.' Done-criterion: 'Three tuned rules with documented tuning history, a triage runbook, and a 10-minute walkthrough video.' Every element of that draft comes from IL-29 labs — the capstone becomes assembly, not invention. Second worked example — the topic-selection test. A good capstone topic passes three tests: it applies at least two program elements (framework + ATT&CK, or defensive + offensive), it produces a demonstrable artifact (not just a paper), and it connects to your career direction (for you: detection, endpoint security, SOC-adjacent operations — all ThreatLocker-panel-relevant). Common mistake: choosing a capstone topic from zero at enrollment. The learners who struggle are the ones who spend the first month finding a topic; the ones who arrive with a draft spend the first month building. Draft now, refine during the program. A third capstone criterion: the demo. A capstone that can be demonstrated - the rules firing on test traffic, the triage runbook executed live, the walkthrough video - beats a capstone that can only be described. Design for demoability from the draft stage: what will you SHOW, not just what will you write? The demonstration is also your panel asset: 'here is my capstone walkthrough' is a stronger Oct 13 artifact than any certificate. A second drafting discipline: the one-page test. If your capstone proposal cannot be understood from one page - problem, scope, program elements, done-criterion, demo - it is not ready. Complexity that cannot be summarized is usually confusion, not depth. Rewrite until the page is clear; the clarity will survive into the execution. And a final topic filter: choose the capstone you will still care about in month five. Twenty-four weeks is long enough for enthusiasm to die - pick the problem that genuinely bothers you, because bothered is sustainable and bored is not.

items.answer: Check physical layer first: cable, link lights, then IP config (ipconfig), then gateway ping, then DNS, then the service.

items.prompt: A workstation cannot reach the file server. Your troubleshooting order?

items.answer: DNS: nslookup the name; if DNS fails but IP works, it is name resolution, not connectivity.
items.explain: 'Can ping 8.8.8.8 but not google.com' is always DNS until proven otherwise.
items.prompt: User can ping 8.8.8.8 but cannot browse. Diagnosis?

items.answer: DHCP: check ipconfig for APIPA (169.254.x.x) — no DHCP lease means no network config.
items.explain: APIPA = the DHCP conversation failed. Check the DHCP server, the relay, and the link.
items.prompt: Workstation has a 169.254.x.x address. What failed?

items.explain: Windows troubleshooting: event logs first, application logs second, process tracing third.

items.explain: Post-ThreatLocker-deploy, 'I need admin' is a policy question, not a permissions hack.
