notes.title: Zero-trust concepts: the philosophy the panel expects you to speak
Allowlisting operations: deny-by-default, done right
Ringfencing scenarios: caging the trusted app

notes.body: Elevation Control solves the oldest tension in Windows operations: users and applications periodically need administrative rights, but standing local admin is how malware gains the keys to the kingdom. The module removes local admin from endpoints and replaces it with just-in-time elevation delegated to applications via policy — the application gets the elevation it needs, when it needs it, without the user ever holding administrative privilege. Worked example — the legacy app problem. A line-of-business application requires administrative rights to update itself. The old world: make the user a local admin (and hand every malware process on that box admin rights too). The Elevation Control world: policy grants that specific application just-in-time elevation for its updater — the update runs elevated, the user stays standard, malware in the user's context stays unprivileged. Your panel answer walks that contrast explicitly, because it shows you understand both the operational pain and the security win. Second worked example — the help-desk ticket. 'I need admin to install the approved printer driver.' The operator's workflow: verify the request and the software's legitimacy, apply the elevation policy for that installer (time-bound, application-scoped), the install completes, elevation expires. No standing admin granted, no ticket ping-pong, full audit trail of what elevated and when. Common mistake: describing elevation control as 'blocking admin tasks.' It enables them — safely. The panel wants to hear that you understand the user-experience side: security that breaks workflows gets bypassed, and bypassed security is no security. The winning framing is always 'the user gets their work done, the attacker gets nothing.' A second trap: confusing elevation control with allowlisting. Allowlisting decides the updater may run; elevation control decides it may run elevated. They compose — and explaining how they compose shows operator-grade understanding. TECHNICAL BANK 4 — elevation control: Q16: 'What does Elevation Control remove?' A: 'Standing local admin rights from endpoints.' Q17: 'How does a legitimate app get admin when it needs it?' A: 'Just-in-time elevation delegated to the application via policy.' Q18: 'Why is removing local admin a malware control?' A: 'Malware inherits its host's privileges; standard-user context blocks persistence and system-wide changes.' Q19: 'User needs admin for one installer. The workflow?' A: 'Verify, apply time-bound application-scoped elevation policy, install completes, elevation expires.' Q20: 'Elevation Control vs allowlisting?' A: 'Allowlisting decides what runs; Elevation Control decides with what privilege it runs.' One more panel nuance: when asked about elevation, always mention the audit trail - every just-in-time elevation is logged with the application, the time, and the policy that granted it. Panels love the accountability angle: least privilege plus full visibility is the complete answer. And connect it to the hiring logic: the IT Infrastructure Specialist who can explain WHY the control exists (malware inherits privilege) and HOW it preserves workflow (the app elevates, the user does not) is demonstrating exactly the operator-plus-communicator blend the role demands.
notes.title: Elevation Control: least privilege without breaking workflows

notes.body: Storage Control applies granular policy to the storage layer: storage devices, file paths, and shares. Its job is blocking data theft and exfiltration — the insider with a USB drive, the malware staging files for theft, the misconfigured share exposing regulated data. The granularity is the point: policy can distinguish device classes (block USB mass storage while permitting USB keyboards and mice), paths (protect the customer-data directory regardless of who touches it), and shares (control who can read or write the finance share, and from where). Worked example — the insider scenario. An employee plugs in a personal USB drive and drags the customer database onto it. Storage Control policy blocks writes to removable mass storage for that data classification — the copy fails, Detect logs the attempt with the indicator, and the SOC has the forensic record. Your panel answer: 'The theft was prevented at the storage layer, before the data left the building, with an auditable event.' Second worked example — the ransomware-adjacent scenario. Malware attempts to stage encrypted archives in a temp directory for exfiltration before detonating. Path-based policy denies the staging writes; the exfiltration step fails even if the malware executed. This is defense in depth at the data layer — network control may catch the C2, but storage control catches the data movement itself. Common mistake: describing storage control as 'USB blocking.' Device control is one facet; path and share policy are the deeper story, and the panel will respect the candidate who leads with data-centric policy rather than device anecdotes. Another nuance: storage policy must be designed around data classification — you protect paths by what the data IS, not by which user touched it last. That data-centric framing connects directly to governance concepts and shows maturity beyond tool operation. TECHNICAL BANK 5 — storage control: Q21: 'What three things does Storage Control govern?' A: 'Storage devices, file paths, and shares.' Q22: 'Block USB drives but allow USB keyboards. How?' A: 'Device-class policy: deny USB mass storage, permit HID devices.' Q23: 'An insider copies the customer DB to USB. What happens?' A: 'Path/device policy blocks the write; Detect logs the blocked attempt.' Q24: 'Why path-based policy instead of user-based?' A: 'Protection follows the data's classification, not whoever touched it last.' Q25: 'How does Storage Control complement Network Control against exfiltration?' A: 'Storage Control stops the data movement; Network Control stops the C2 channel — two layers, one attack.'
notes.title: Storage Control: guarding data at rest and in motion

notes.body: Network Control is the endpoint firewall with dynamic ACLs — access control lists that open and close ports as policy dictates, rather than the static port rules of a traditional firewall. Its operational jobs: block lateral movement (an infected host cannot probe its neighbors), block command-and-control (beaconing out to attacker infrastructure dies at the endpoint), and enforce least-privilege networking per application and per endpoint. The 'dynamic' part matters for the panel: ports open when policy permits the legitimate traffic and close otherwise, shrinking the window in which an attacker can use them. Worked example — the lateral-movement scenario. Malware lands on one workstation and begins scanning the subnet for SMB shares to infect. Network Control policy denies workstation-to-workstation SMB — the scan hits a wall at the first neighbor, Detect logs the blocked attempts, and the incident is one host instead of fifty. Your panel answer: 'The blast radius stayed at one because the endpoint firewall enforced segmentation the network firewall could not see.' Second worked example — the C2 scenario. An endpoint begins beaconing to a newly registered domain every 60 seconds. Network Control blocks the outbound sessions per policy; Detect fires alerts on the blocked indicators of compromise, giving the SOC the domain, the cadence, and the affected host. The analyst's next moves — isolate, image, hunt for siblings — start from that alert. Common mistake: describing network control as 'a firewall.' Every endpoint has a firewall; the operator story is dynamic, policy-driven ACLs plus the Detect telemetry loop. The panel wants to hear the loop: block, alert, investigate, tune. A second trap: forgetting that network control is also a usability story — legitimate applications get the ports they need via policy, so the business keeps working while the attacker starves. TECHNICAL BANK 6 — network control: Q26: 'What makes the ACLs dynamic?' A: 'They open and close ports per policy rather than holding static rules.' Q27: 'How does Network Control limit lateral movement?' A: 'Endpoint firewall policy denies host-to-host traffic like workstation SMB scans.' Q28: 'Beaconing to a new domain every 60 seconds. The response?' A: 'Network Control blocks the sessions; Detect alerts on the blocked IOCs; the analyst isolates and hunts.' Q29: 'Network Control vs the perimeter firewall?' A: 'The perimeter guards the boundary; Network Control enforces policy at every endpoint, including inside the LAN.' Q30: 'Does blocking ports break legitimate apps?' A: 'Policy permits what the business needs — the attacker starves while operations continue.'
notes.title: Network Control: dynamic ACLs and the lateral-movement kill chain

notes.body: ThreatLocker Detect is the telemetry and alerting layer: it alerts on indicators of compromise that the modules block. Understand its role precisely — Detect does not prevent (the modules do that); it informs. Every blocked execution, every caged capability, every denied exfiltration attempt, every killed C2 session becomes an alert with context: what was blocked, which module blocked it, which endpoint, which user, when. That context is what makes the SOC workflow possible. The triage discipline for any Detect alert: verify (is this a true positive? check the indicator against intel and the endpoint's baseline), scope (is it one host or many? search for sibling indicators), contain (isolate the host, disable the account, block the IOC at the perimeter too), document (timeline, actions, evidence preserved), then decide (tune the policy, escalate to incident response, or close as benign with rationale). Worked example — the 2 AM alert. Detect fires: Ringfencing blocked winword.exe from launching powershell.exe on WS-114, user jdoe, 02:14. Verify: the document came from an external sender, the macro hash matches a known malicious sample — true positive. Scope: search Detect for the same document hash and parent-child pattern across the fleet — two more hosts, same hour. Contain: isolate all three, disable the accounts, block the sender domain at the gateway. Document: timeline and IOCs to the ticket. Decide: escalate to full incident response — this is a campaign, not an isolated event. Your panel answer walks exactly that chain, because the panel is testing whether you think in workflows or in single alerts. Second worked example — the false positive. Detect alerts on a blocked installer: the software is legitimate, the vendor just changed its signing certificate. Verify: confirm with the vendor and the change ticket. Decide: update the allowlisting policy for the new certificate, document the exception, close. The discipline is identical — only the verdict differs — and saying so shows the panel you do not cry wolf. Common mistake: treating Detect as the protection. The modules protect; Detect narrates. The operator who confuses the two will misanswer 'what stopped the attack' (the module) vs. 'how did you know' (Detect). TECHNICAL BANK 7 — Detect triage: Q31: 'What does Detect do?' A: 'Alerts on indicators of compromise blocked by the ThreatLocker modules.' Q32: 'Walk a Detect alert triage.' A: 'Verify, scope, contain, document, then tune, escalate, or close.' Q33: 'Ringfencing blocks Word launching PowerShell at 2 AM. First move?' A: 'Verify: check the document source and macro hash — confirm true positive before containing.' Q34: 'Same pattern on three hosts. What changed?' A: 'Scope says campaign — escalate to full incident response, not a single-host ticket.' Q35: 'A blocked installer turns out legitimate. The workflow?' A: 'Verify with vendor and change ticket, update policy for the new certificate, document, close.'
notes.title: ThreatLocker Detect triage: from alert to action

items.answer: Situation: the 2 AM alert. Task: triage and contain. Action: verified, scoped, isolated, documented. Result: contained in 20 minutes, playbook updated.
items.explain: Four clean beats, each one sentence. If any beat is missing, the story is incomplete.
items.prompt: Label the STAR beats: 'Detect fired at 2 AM on three hosts. I owned triage. I verified the true positive, scoped the fleet, isolated the hosts, and documented the timeline. We contained it in 20 minutes and I updated the playbook.'

items.answer: The Result has no number — 'quickly' is not a measurement.
items.explain: Results must be quantified: minutes, percentages, counts. Vague results are the most common STAR failure.
items.prompt: What is weak here: '...and we fixed it quickly, and everyone was happy.'

items.answer: Action — 'we' hides who did what. Rewrite every action beat in first person.
items.explain: Panels hire YOU. 'We isolated the hosts' could mean you watched. 'I isolated the hosts' is a claim of action.
items.prompt: A story says 'we' six times and 'I' zero times. The fix?

items.answer: It is three stories. Pick ONE incident and go deep — one situation, one task, one action chain, one result.
items.explain: Sixty to ninety seconds holds one incident, not a career. Depth beats breadth in behavioral answers.
items.prompt: A candidate's Situation covers three years and four jobs. The fix?

items.answer: Task — the story never states what the candidate was responsible for.
items.explain: Without the Task, the Action has no stakes. Every story needs the mission you owned.
items.prompt: 'The server was down. I rebooted it. It came back up.' Which STAR beat is missing?

items.answer: Honest and complete: name it, own it, show the change. Panels trust owned mistakes; they distrust perfection.
items.explain: The mistake question tests accountability, not the mistake. Deflection fails; ownership with a fix passes.
items.prompt: Is 'I have never made a significant mistake' an acceptable panel answer?

items.answer: Scaffold: S-[a real frustrated user you supported]; T-[what you owned]; A-[the exact steps YOU took to de-escalate and resolve]; R-[measured outcome: time, satisfaction, follow-up].
items.explain: Cyber Hero context: the panel wants de-escalation plus resolution, in your real words.
items.prompt: Prompt 1: 'Tell me about a difficult customer.' Build the scaffold (do not invent the story).

items.answer: Scaffold: S-[a real outage or pressure incident]; T-[your role]; A-[your triage steps in order]; R-[restoration time, what you learned].
items.explain: Pressure answers are triage stories: show the order of your thinking under load.
items.prompt: Prompt 2: 'Describe working an outage under pressure.' Build the scaffold.

items.answer: Scaffold: S-[a real mistake you made]; T-[what was at stake]; A-[how you owned and fixed it]; R-[what changed in your process after].
items.explain: The result must include the process change — otherwise it is confession without growth.
items.prompt: Prompt 3: 'Tell me about a mistake you made.' Build the scaffold.

items.answer: Scaffold: S-[a technology you had to learn fast]; T-[the deadline]; A-[your learning method: docs, labs, mentors]; R-[what you delivered with it].
items.explain: Fast-learning stories need the method, not just the claim — method is what the panel evaluates.
items.prompt: Prompt 4: 'How do you learn new technology quickly?' Build the scaffold.

items.answer: Scaffold: S-[a real team effort]; T-[your part]; A-[your collaboration: communication, handoffs, conflicts handled]; R-[team outcome plus your contribution].
items.explain: Teamwork stories still need YOUR actions in first person — 'we' for context, 'I' for action.
items.prompt: Prompt 5: 'Tell me about a time you worked on a team.' Build the scaffold.

items.answer: Two stories per prompt, both real, both rehearsed aloud and timed at 60-90 seconds.
items.explain: One story is a single point of failure; two gives you range. Rehearsed aloud means actually spoken, not read.
items.prompt: How many stories per prompt, and what does 'rehearsed' mean?

items.answer: Cut it to 90 seconds: keep one incident, the action chain, and the quantified result.
items.explain: Rambling signals unprepared thinking. The 60-90 second window forces one clean story.
items.prompt: Your answer runs 3 minutes. The fix?

items.answer: Attach numbers: minutes to contain, percent improvement, tickets closed, downtime avoided.
items.explain: Quantified results are believable results. 'Better' is an opinion; '40% faster' is evidence.
items.prompt: Your Result says 'things got better.' The fix?

items.answer: Say so plainly: 'I don't have a direct example of X, but here is the closest situation and what I learned.'
items.explain: Honesty beats invention every time. Panels detect borrowed stories; they respect bounded honesty.
items.prompt: You have no real story for a prompt. What do you say?

items.answer: Pause, breathe, then start with the Situation — the structure carries you.
items.explain: STAR is a rescue device: when nerves hit, the four beats give you rails.
items.prompt: Nerves spike mid-answer and you lose your place. The recovery?

items.answer: Prepare 2-3 genuine questions about the role, the team, and success metrics.
items.explain: Questions signal serious interest and give you final-panel intelligence. Never ask nothing.
items.prompt: The panel asks 'what questions do you have for us?' Your move?

steps: Create star-bank/ with prompts.md, stories.md, rehearsal-log.md, panel-day-checklist.md.
In prompts.md, write all 15 behavioral prompts from this module's notes, numbered.
In stories.md, create two scaffold slots per prompt — 30 slots total — each with S/T/A/R headings left BLANK.
Fill each slot with YOUR real history only: real situations, real tasks, real actions, real measured results.
Apply the honesty audit: for every story, ask 'did this really happen, in these details?' Delete or correct anything uncertain.
Time each story ALOUD with a stopwatch; record the time in rehearsal-log.md. Target: 60-90 seconds each.
Cut or expand stories to fit the window: one incident, action chain, quantified result.
Rehearse the full bank aloud twice; mark every story pass/fail on timing and completeness.
In panel-day-checklist.md, write your Oct 13 plan: arrival time, documents, 2-3 questions for the panel, and your opening/closing lines.
Do a final full-bank rehearsal the evening of Oct 12 — warm-up, not new material.
Morning of Oct 13: review the checklist only. Trust the rehearsal.

notes.body: Pressure prompts test triage thinking: what you do first, what you defer, and how you communicate while the clock runs. Prompt 4: 'Describe a time you worked an outage or incident under pressure.' The panel wants the order of your thinking — verify, scope, contain, communicate — not just the fix. Prompt 5: 'Tell me about a time you had to make a quick decision with incomplete information.' Show the decision framework: what you knew, what you assumed, the reversible-vs-irreversible test, and what you did when new information arrived. Prompt 6: 'How do you prioritize when everything is urgent?' The answer is a real triage story: impact times urgency, communicated explicitly, with the deferrals named. Scaffold each with the pressure beats: S-[the real incident], T-[your role in the response], A-[your steps IN ORDER, including what you deliberately deferred], R-[restoration time, blast radius contained, lesson captured]. Worked example — scaffolding Prompt 5. S: '[A real decision you made with incomplete information.]' T: '[What was at stake and what you owned.]' A: '[What you knew, your key assumption, why you chose the reversible option first, how you updated when facts arrived.]' R: '[The outcome and what the decision taught you about deciding under uncertainty.]' Notice the A-beat includes the assumption explicitly — panels respect candidates who name their assumptions, because hidden assumptions are how incidents get worse. Common mistake: the hero narrative — 'I saved the day single-handedly.' Pressure stories that erase the team read as either fiction or arrogance. Name your part precisely and credit the team where it contributed: 'I owned triage; a colleague handled comms; we restored service in 40 minutes.' Precision about your role is more impressive than inflation of it. A second trap: skipping the communication beat. Under pressure, telling people what is happening IS part of the job — stakeholders, users, the next shift. If your A-beat has no communication step, add one from your real memory. A fourth pressure prompt - Prompt 6b: 'Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision during an incident.' The panel tests whether you can dissent productively under load: state the disagreement crisply, propose the alternative with its tradeoff, accept the call once made, and execute fully. Scaffold: S-[the real incident and the decision], T-[your role and what you saw differently], A-[how you raised it: the data, the alternative, the acceptance], R-[the outcome and what the team learned about dissent]. The scoring: loyalty to the decision after it is made matters as much as the courage to raise the concern. 'I argued, lost, then slow-walked the plan' fails catastrophically; 'I argued with data, the lead chose otherwise, I executed fully, and we debriefed after' passes cleanly. Panels ask this because incident dissent handled badly destroys teams - show them you strengthen the team instead.
notes.title: Prompts 4-6: outage, decisions, and triage under pressure

notes.body: The mistake prompt is the integrity test — every panel asks it, and it is the easiest prompt to fail by being too polished. Prompt 7: 'Tell me about a mistake you made at work.' The scoring is entirely about accountability: name it plainly, own it fully, show the fix, and show what changed in your process afterward. The mistake itself should be real and proportionate — not catastrophic (which raises judgment questions) and not trivial (which reads as evasion). Prompt 8: 'Describe feedback you received that was hard to hear.' Same muscle: receive, reflect, change. The structure for both: S-[what happened, no spin], T-[what you were responsible for], A-[how you owned it: who you told, what you fixed, what you changed], R-[the process change and evidence it stuck]. Worked example — scaffolding Prompt 7. S: '[A real mistake: what broke or went wrong because of your action.]' T: '[Why it was yours to own.]' A: '[Who you told and when, the immediate fix, the process change you made so it cannot recur.]' R: '[Evidence the change worked: the next similar situation went cleanly.]' The R-beat is what separates a confession from a growth story — without the process change, you are just describing a failure; with it, you are describing a professional. Common mistake: the humblebrag — 'my mistake was caring too much.' Panels have heard it a thousand times; it signals you are hiding. A second classic: blaming the tool, the process, or the coworker before owning your part. You may mention contributing factors AFTER owning your part — 'the runbook was unclear, and I should have verified instead of assuming' — but ownership comes first, always. The meta-rule: the panel is not evaluating your mistake; it is evaluating what kind of colleague you are when things go wrong. Be the colleague who raises their hand first. A third integrity prompt - Prompt 8b: 'Tell me about a time you received critical feedback on your technical work.' Distinct from Prompt 8 (hard to hear, personal): this one is about the work product - a code review, a config, an analysis that was wrong. Scaffold: S-[the real feedback: what was wrong], T-[what you were responsible for], A-[how you received it (no defensiveness), verified the critique, fixed the work, changed your review process], R-[the improved output and the process change that stuck]. The scoring: defensiveness is the failure mode. 'My first reaction was to explain why I was right; then I tested their claim, they were right, and I fixed it' is a perfect answer - it shows the honest internal reaction AND the professional override. Panels know everyone feels defensive; they are checking whether professionalism wins. A rehearsal note: this story must be about the WORK, not the person - keep every sentence on the artifact and the process, never on personalities.
notes.title: Prompts 7-8: the mistake and the hard feedback

notes.body: Growth prompts test trajectory: are you becoming more capable, and can you prove it? Prompt 9: 'How do you learn new technology quickly?' The panel wants your method, not your claim — docs-first or lab-first, how you structure practice, how you validate understanding, and a real example with a deadline. Prompt 10: 'Tell me about a time you had to learn something fast for a project.' The compressed version of Prompt 9 with stakes: the deadline, the method, the delivery. Prompt 11: 'What are you learning right now?' — and for you, the honest answer involves this course and the Oct 13 preparation, which is a strong answer if you frame it as operator depth, not video consumption. Scaffold the method explicitly: S-[the technology and the deadline], T-[what you had to deliver with it], A-[your learning sequence: e.g., docs overview, lab build, break-fix reps, teach-back], R-[what you shipped and how the method has held up since]. Worked example — scaffolding Prompt 9. S: '[A technology you learned under time pressure.]' T: '[What you needed to do with it and by when.]' A: '[Your actual method: the resources, the lab reps, how you tested yourself.]' R: '[What you delivered, and how you still use that method today.]' The A-beat is the whole answer — a candidate with a real method ('I build the smallest working lab, break it three ways, fix each, then teach it to someone') beats a candidate with a real certificate but no method. Common mistake: answering with a list of technologies instead of a method. 'I learned X, Y, and Z' is a resume; the prompt asked HOW. A second trap: claiming you 'just pick things up.' Nobody does — and the panel knows it. Name the reps: the labs, the docs, the failures, the teach-backs. For Prompt 11 specifically, prepare the IL-29 answer now: 'I am rebuilding my endpoint-security depth for this role — allowlisting operations, ringfencing scenarios, Detect triage — with timed drills and a scored mock panel.' That is specific, role-relevant, and verifiable. A fourth growth prompt - Prompt 11b: 'What is the most useful thing you have learned in the last six months?' The panel tests learning velocity and reflection. Your honest answer draws on this course: the specific operator skill (e.g., Detect triage discipline, ringfencing tradeoff reasoning), why it mattered, and how you learned it (the method from Prompt 9). Scaffold: S-[where you started], T-[what you needed], A-[the learning reps], R-[the capability now, with evidence]. The trap: naming something vague ('I learned a lot about security'). The fix: one specific skill, the method, the proof. Specificity signals real learning; vagueness signals real forgetting. Prepare this answer as the capstone of your growth narrative - it is the story of the last six months told as trajectory, and trajectory is what gets offers.

Prompts 12-15: teamwork, conflict, and 'why ThreatLocker'

The Action — your steps in first person
The Result — skip it if time is short
quiz.explain: The Action gets the most time because the panel is hiring your judgment: what YOU did, in what order, and why. Never skip the Result — unmeasured stories are opinions.
quiz.q: Which STAR beat deserves the most answer time?

choices: Name it plainly, own it fully, show the process change it produced
Pick a trivial mistake to look good
Say you cannot recall any mistake
quiz.explain: The mistake prompt scores accountability, not the mistake. Plain ownership plus a real process change is the passing answer; humblebrags and deflection fail.
quiz.q: How do you answer 'tell me about a mistake you made'?

choices: List every technology you have touched
Say you just pick things up naturally
Describe your learning method with a real deadline-driven example
quiz.explain: The prompt asks HOW you learn. Method plus proof ('docs overview, lab build, break-fix reps, teach-back — used to deliver X by Friday') beats any list.
quiz.q: 'How do you learn new technology quickly?' The panel wants:

choices: Give the closest real situation, name what you did and learned, and note the boundary honestly
quiz.explain: Bounded honesty: the closest real story, plainly framed. Fabrication collapses under follow-up questions; honesty earns trust.
quiz.q: You have no direct experience for a behavioral prompt. What do you do?

choices: 'The user was frustrated because their deadline was at risk, so I listened first, then...'
quiz.explain: Lead with empathy for the person's situation, then your de-escalation and resolution steps. Never badmouth the customer — it fails the prompt instantly.
quiz.q: Which opening passes the difficult-customer prompt?

choices: Name your assumption explicitly and choose the reversible option first
Wait until all information is available
Delegate the decision upward without analysis
quiz.explain: Under uncertainty: state what you know, name the key assumption, prefer reversible moves, update when facts arrive. Panels score the framework, not just the outcome.
quiz.q: A quick decision with incomplete information: the winning approach is:

choices: The other person was simply wrong and you corrected them
A victory lap about winning the argument
The disagreement stated fairly, your approach, the resolution, and the relationship afterward
quiz.explain: Conflict answers need no villains: fair framing, your adult approach (listen, data, options), the resolution, and proof the working relationship survived.
quiz.q: How do you structure the disagreement-with-a-coworker answer?

choices: Ask 2-3 genuine questions about the role, the team, and first-90-days success metrics
quiz.explain: Thoughtful questions signal serious interest and gather real intelligence. 'Nothing' signals disengagement; salary-first signals wrong priorities.
quiz.q: The panel asks 'what questions do you have for us?' Your move:

choices: Review the full question bank once more
Review the panel-day checklist only and trust the rehearsal
Skip breakfast to arrive two hours early
quiz.explain: Game day is performance, not study. New material on the morning creates doubt; the checklist plus rehearsal creates confidence.
quiz.q: Morning of October 13: what do you do?

modules.title: Incident Response Lifecycle (NIST 800-61)
modules.summary: The four-phase incident response lifecycle from NIST Special Publication 800-61 — preparation, detection and analysis, containment/eradication/recovery, and post-incident activity — taught as an operator's playbook for an endpoint fleet. You will learn IR roles, how to build a playbook before anything burns, and how to run a tabletop exercise on a fictional 2 AM ransomware scenario.
objectives: Describe the four NIST 800-61 incident response phases and what belongs in each.
Distinguish incident precursors from indicators and triage alerts by impact and recoverability.
Choose containment actions that stop damage without destroying evidence.
Sequence eradication and recovery so the root cause is gone before systems return.
Run a blameless post-incident review and write an after-action report with owned action items.
Design and facilitate a tabletop exercise for a ransomware scenario.

notes.title: The four phases: NIST SP 800-61's incident response lifecycle
Preparation: everything that must exist before the alert
Detection and analysis: is this actually an incident?
Containment: stop the bleeding without destroying evidence
notes.body: Containment means preventing the incident from spreading while preserving evidence for analysis. NIST describes short-term containment (isolate the host from the network right now) versus long-term containment (temporary firewall rules, disabling VPN accounts, blocking malicious domains at DNS — measures that hold for days while you work). The golden rule: contain first, but contain in a way that keeps your options open. Pulling the network cable or using EDR network-isolation keeps the machine running, which preserves memory evidence; powering the machine off destroys RAM contents and can trigger anti-forensic behavior. Decision criteria for how aggressive to be: how fast is it spreading (ransomware encrypting shares = isolate immediately, even if it disrupts users), whether you understand the mechanism yet (if not, isolate broadly), and business impact of the containment itself (taking the file server offline at month-end close needs executive sign-off — which is why preparation defined who can authorize it). Worked example: ransomware confirmed on three workstations at 2 AM. Step 1: network-isolate all three via EDR (or unplug Ethernet / disable Wi-Fi if no EDR) — do NOT shut them down. Step 2: check the file server for encryption activity and snapshot it. Step 3: block the command-and-control domains at the firewall so any undiscovered infected host cannot receive instructions. Step 4: disable the compromised user accounts in Active Directory. Only after scoping is complete do you move to eradication. Operator gotchas: wiping a machine 'to stop it' before imaging destroys your only copy of the malware and the timeline; telling the whole company 'we have ransomware' before containment is complete can tip off an insider threat actor; and documenting every containment action with timestamps matters — the post-incident review and any legal follow-up will need that log. Containment decisions vary by host role, and the playbook should say so in advance. A user workstation: isolate aggressively, minimal business impact. A file server: isolate, but coordinate — taking it offline halts the whole clinic, so the incident commander weighs encryption spread against business halt, and the answer is usually 'isolate now, the encryption will halt the business worse.' A domain controller: do not isolate blindly — authentication for the entire network depends on it; instead block the malicious outbound traffic at the firewall, disable compromised accounts, and monitor closely while planning a controlled rebuild. These are decisions you want pre-made, not invented at 3 AM. Communication during containment follows the same discipline: the communications lead sends timed updates ('containment in progress, next update at 04:00') to a defined distribution list, and nobody else freelances status reports. A second containment gotcha: watch for the attacker's counter-move. Ransomware crews monitor for containment — when hosts go dark, they may accelerate encryption on remaining hosts or trigger pre-planted persistence. That is why containment should be as simultaneous as possible across the scoped host set rather than trickled one machine at a time. Document the containment timestamp per host; the post-incident review will compare 'scope at containment' versus 'final scope' to judge whether containment was fast and complete enough.

notes.title: Eradication and recovery: remove the cause, restore safely
notes.body: Eradication removes the root cause; recovery brings systems back into production. The order is non-negotiable: never recover before eradication is verified, or you will reinfect clean systems. Eradication means identifying every persistence mechanism and removing all of them — the malicious scheduled task AND the rogue local account AND the backdoored service, not just the one you found first. It also means closing the entry point: patch the exploited vulnerability, reset credentials that may have been stolen (assume all credentials on compromised hosts are burned), and remove the phishing email from every inbox it reached. Recovery then proceeds in priority order: the most critical business functions first, each system rebuilt from known-good media or restored from a backup that predates the compromise — and that you have verified is clean. After recovery comes a period of enhanced monitoring: watch the recovered systems closely for days or weeks, because sophisticated attackers leave second-stage persistence. Worked example: after the 2 AM ransomware, eradication finds the initial access was a phishing email with a malicious attachment, and lateral movement used a stolen domain admin credential. Eradication checklist: delete the malware from all 14 hosts (or reimage them — reimaging from known-good media is the safest eradication for workstations), remove the rogue scheduled task fleet-wide via GPO audit, force-reset ALL domain passwords (the admin credential was stolen, so every credential is suspect), patch the exploited print-spooler-style vulnerability, purge the phishing email from all mailboxes. Recovery order: domain controllers first (rebuilt, not restored, if their integrity is doubted), then the file server from the last pre-incident tested backup, then departments by business priority — billing before the break room PC. Enhanced monitoring: EDR set to high sensitivity on recovered hosts for 30 days, plus a daily review of authentication logs. Common mistakes: recovering from a backup without confirming the backup predates the compromise (attackers dwell for weeks — restore from a backup taken during dwell and you restore the attacker); resetting only the obviously compromised accounts; and declaring victory the day systems come back instead of after the monitoring period. Credential resets deserve their own eradication sub-plan, done in tiers. Tier 1 — known-compromised accounts (the phished user, any account seen in lateral movement): reset immediately during containment. Tier 2 — privileged accounts (domain admins, service accounts): reset during eradication even without direct evidence of compromise, because credential theft is quiet and the cost of missing one is another incident. Tier 3 — all remaining user passwords: forced reset during recovery, communicated clearly so the help desk is not drowned. Service accounts need special care: resetting them without updating every dependent service causes outages, so inventory service accounts during preparation, not during the incident. Validating backups before recovery is equally tiered: confirm the backup timestamp predates the earliest known malicious activity (not just the encryption date — dwell matters), verify integrity with a test restore of a non-critical system first, and scan restored data with current detections before returning it to production. Enhanced monitoring after recovery should be specific, not vibes: EDR in heightened sensitivity on recovered hosts for 30 days, daily review of authentication logs for the first two weeks, firewall alerts on any outbound connection to the previously seen malicious infrastructure, and a weekly scope re-check for the first month. Eradication is only verified when the monitoring period ends clean — declare victory then, not on recovery day.

notes.title: Post-incident activity: the blameless review and the after-action report
notes.body: Post-incident activity is where the incident pays for itself in lessons. NIST 800-61 calls for a lessons-learned meeting held soon after the incident — while memories are fresh — with one ground rule: it is blameless. The moment the review becomes about who clicked the phishing link, people stop telling the truth and you learn nothing. The meeting reconstructs a full timeline (when did the phishing email arrive, when did execution start, when was it detected, when was containment complete), then asks: what went well, what went poorly, what surprised us, and what will we change. Every lesson becomes an action item with a named owner and a due date, or it evaporates. The after-action report (AAR) documents all of this: executive summary, timeline, impact assessment, response actions taken, what worked, gaps found, and the action-item list. Also collect metrics: mean time to detect (MTTD — first malicious action to detection), mean time to respond/contain (MTTR — detection to containment), and scope at containment versus final scope (did it keep spreading after you acted?). Worked example: AAR skeleton for the ransomware incident. Executive summary: 'On Oct 3, ransomware encrypted 14 workstations and one file share; contained within 2 hours of detection; no evidence of data exfiltration; full recovery in 5 days.' Timeline: 01:12 phishing email delivered; 06:40 user opened attachment; 06:41 execution and lateral movement began; 02:00 next-day... (reconstructed from logs). What worked: EDR network-isolation contained hosts in minutes; the phone tree reached the full team by 2:30 AM. Gaps: phishing filter missed the email (action: tune filter, owner: email admin, due: Oct 20); no network segmentation between workstations and file server (action: VLAN plan, owner: you, due: Nov 30); backups had never been restore-tested (action: monthly restore tests, owner: backup admin, due: ongoing). Metrics: MTTD 19 hours (dwell before encryption was noticed), MTTR 2 hours. Operator gotcha: the review must include the people who were in the trenches, not just managers — the help-desk tech who took the first user call often has the most important observation. The after-action report has two audiences and should be written for both: a one-page executive summary (what happened, business impact, what we are changing) and the technical appendix (full timeline, artifacts, indicators). Distribute the technical findings beyond the IR team — detection engineering needs the indicators, IT operations needs the hardening tasks, and training needs the user-facing lesson. Track every action item to closure in whatever system the organization actually checks; an action item that lives only in the AAR document is decorative. Review the metrics quarterly across incidents: is MTTD trending down? Are repeat root causes appearing (the third phishing incident this year means the email control, not the users, is the problem)? Feed systemic findings into the risk register so leadership sees incident lessons as risk reduction, not just IT homework. A final post-incident discipline: the 'pre-mortem' for the next incident. Ask the team, 'It is six months from now and we are breached again through the same vector — what did we fail to do after this incident?' The answers become your highest-priority action items, because they represent the lessons you are most likely to let slide. Incident response maturity is not measured by how well you handle the incident — it is measured by how few of your action items are still open at the next tabletop.

notes.title: IR roles and designing the 2 AM ransomware tabletop

cards.front: Name the four NIST 800-61 incident response phases in order.
cards.back: 1. Preparation. 2. Detection and Analysis. 3. Containment, Eradication, and Recovery. 4. Post-Incident Activity.

cards.front: Precursor vs. indicator — what is the difference?
cards.back: A precursor signals an incident MIGHT happen (e.g., a scan against your firewall). An indicator signals one IS happening or HAS happened (e.g., an EDR alert for credential dumping).

cards.front: What three factors does NIST 800-61 suggest for prioritizing an incident?
cards.back: Functional impact (business disruption), information impact (data accessed/stolen), and recoverability (can we rebuild from clean backups).

cards.front: Short-term vs. long-term containment — give an example of each.
cards.back: Short-term: network-isolate the infected host right now. Long-term: firewall rules blocking C2 domains and disabling compromised VPN accounts for days while you work.

cards.front: Why isolate a ransomware host instead of powering it off?
cards.back: Isolation stops spread while keeping the machine running, preserving memory (RAM) evidence. Powering off destroys RAM contents and timeline evidence.

cards.front: Eradication vs. recovery — which comes first and why?
cards.back: Eradication first: remove every persistence mechanism and close the entry point. Recovering first risks reinfecting clean systems from the still-present attacker.

cards.front: What is 'out-of-band communication' and why does IR need it?
cards.back: A communication channel independent of the compromised systems (separate chat, phone tree, printed bridge number) — because the attacker may control or monitor your normal email/chat.

cards.front: What is the incident commander's job during an incident?
cards.back: Own decisions and the clock: prioritization, authorizing disruptive containment, and coordination — not doing the technical keyboard work.

cards.front: What is a tabletop exercise?
cards.back: A discussion-based walkthrough of a scenario where the team talks through their response without touching systems — it exposes playbook gaps before a real incident.

cards.front: What goes into an after-action report (AAR)?
cards.back: Executive summary, full timeline, impact assessment, response actions, what worked, gaps found, and action items each with a named owner and due date.

cards.front: Define MTTD and MTTR in incident response.
cards.back: MTTD = mean time to detect (first malicious action to detection). MTTR = mean time to respond/contain (detection to containment).

cards.front: What is the ground rule of the lessons-learned meeting?
cards.back: It is blameless — no fault-finding about who clicked or who missed it, so people tell the truth and the team actually learns.

quiz.q: According to NIST 800-61, which phase includes building the IR playbook, defining roles, and testing backups?
quiz.explain: Preparation is everything built before an incident: roles, playbooks, call trees, tooling, tested backups, and relationships with legal, HR, and law enforcement.

quiz.q: A threat intel report warns that ransomware crews are targeting healthcare clinics this month. In NIST terms this is a:
quiz.explain: A precursor signals an incident may occur in the future. An indicator would be evidence it is occurring now, such as an EDR alert or encrypted files.

quiz.q: Ransomware is actively encrypting a file share at 2 AM. Your FIRST containment action should be:
choices: Network-isolate the affected hosts while leaving them powered on
Power off all affected machines immediately
Wipe and reimage the affected workstations
Email all staff warning them about the ransomware
quiz.explain: Isolation stops the spread while preserving memory evidence. Powering off destroys RAM; wiping destroys all evidence and skips scoping; mass email before containment risks tipping off an insider and causes panic.

quiz.q: During scoping you find the phishing email reached 50 inboxes but only 3 users opened the attachment. What does good analysis require next?
choices: Check the other 47 mailboxes and hosts for signs of execution before declaring scope
Assume only the 3 are affected and start wiping them
Delete the email from all mailboxes and close the incident
Wait to see if more alerts fire
quiz.explain: Scope must be evidence-driven: verify each recipient's host for execution artifacts. Assuming scope from the alert count alone is how reinfections happen.

quiz.q: Which eradication step is most commonly skipped, leading to reinfection?
choices: Removing ALL persistence mechanisms and closing the entry point (patching, credential resets, purging the phish)
Blocking the C2 domain at the firewall
quiz.explain: Attackers plant multiple persistence mechanisms. Removing one file while leaving the rogue scheduled task, stolen credentials, and unpatched vulnerability intact guarantees a return visit.

quiz.q: When is the correct time to restore systems from backup?
choices: After eradication is verified and the backup is confirmed to predate the compromise
Before containment, to preserve user data
quiz.explain: Recovering before eradication reinfects clean systems, and restoring a backup taken during attacker dwell restores the attacker. Verify both first.

quiz.q: The lessons-learned meeting should be:
choices: Blameless, held soon after the incident, with action items assigned owners and due dates
Focused on identifying who caused the incident
Delayed a few months until emotions cool
Limited to managers to save time
quiz.explain: Blameless and prompt so people tell the truth; action items without owners evaporate; frontline staff who lived it must be in the room.

quiz.q: Your EDR console is unreachable during an incident and your admin credentials fail. What preparation failure does this reveal?
choices: No offline/out-of-band copy of IR tool credentials and no tested alternate access path
quiz.explain: Preparation requires IR tool access that survives compromise of the normal environment — offline credential copies and out-of-band access paths, tested in advance.

quiz.q: In a tabletop exercise, the facilitator announces: 'The file server is now encrypting and your EDR credentials do not work.' This is called:
choices: An inject — a new fact forcing a decision
quiz.explain: Injects are scripted developments delivered during the exercise to test decision-making under changing conditions — the core mechanic of a tabletop.

quiz.q: MTTD is 19 hours and MTTR is 2 hours for a ransomware incident. What does this tell you?
choices: Detection is the weak link — the attacker dwelled 19 hours before anyone noticed; response once detected was fast
quiz.explain: MTTD measures first-malicious-action to detection (19h dwell = detection gap); MTTR measures detection to containment (2h = strong response). Metrics direct improvement effort at detection.

items.prompt: Phase 1 of NIST 800-61?
items.answer: Preparation
items.explain: Roles, playbooks, tooling, tested backups — all built before an incident.

items.prompt: Phase 2 of NIST 800-61?
items.answer: Detection and Analysis
items.explain: Confirm it is real, triage, and scope how bad it is.

items.prompt: Phase 3 of NIST 800-61?
items.answer: Containment, Eradication, and Recovery
items.explain: Stop spread, remove the cause, restore safely — in that order.

items.prompt: Phase 4 of NIST 800-61?
items.answer: Post-Incident Activity
items.explain: Blameless lessons-learned and the after-action report with owned action items.

items.prompt: Scan against your firewall reported by the ISP — precursor or indicator?
items.answer: Precursor
items.explain: It signals an incident may occur, not that one is occurring.

items.prompt: Outbound traffic to a known C2 server — precursor or indicator?
items.answer: Indicator
items.explain: It signals compromise is occurring or has occurred — act on it.

items.prompt: Who owns decisions and the clock during an incident?
items.answer: The incident commander
items.explain: Prioritization and authorization — not the keyboard work.

items.prompt: Who logs every decision and timestamp during an incident?
items.answer: The scribe
items.explain: Their log becomes the backbone of the after-action report.

items.prompt: One blocked 'Word launched PowerShell' alert on a single host, no other signals. First move?
items.answer: Investigate as a moderate-priority lead: find the delivering email, check the host, see if the email reached other inboxes.
items.explain: The block stopped this attempt, but the delivery vector may have wider reach — scope before dismissing.

items.prompt: Ransomware encrypting shares, spreading host to host. Contain now or finish scoping first?
items.answer: Contain now — isolate affected hosts immediately, then continue scoping.
items.explain: Active spreading outranks complete scoping; you can scope from isolated hosts and logs.

items.prompt: You have isolated 6 hosts but have not found the initial access vector. Wipe them now?
items.answer: No — preserve evidence first (memory, disk image or key artifacts), find the entry point, then eradicate.
items.explain: Wiping before understanding the entry point destroys evidence and leaves the door open.

items.prompt: The CEO demands the file server back online during active containment. Who decides?
items.answer: The incident commander, using the pre-agreed authorization matrix from preparation — not the loudest voice.
items.explain: This is exactly why preparation defines who can authorize disruptive or risky actions.

items.prompt: Post-incident review reveals the backup had never been restore-tested. Write the action item.
items.answer: Action: monthly backup restore tests with recorded results. Owner: backup admin. Due: ongoing, first test within 14 days.
items.explain: Every lesson needs a named owner and a due date or it evaporates.

items.prompt: A news reporter calls during the incident asking about 'the cyberattack.' Who responds and how?
items.answer: Only the communications lead, with a prepared holding statement — no one else freelances.
items.explain: One voice prevents contradictory statements and legal exposure; preparation writes the holding statement in advance.

handsOnLab.title: Tabletop: 2 AM ransomware at a fictional clinic
handsOnLab.brief: You will design and run (solo, with a friend, or with an AI as facilitator) a tabletop exercise for a fictional 150-endpoint healthcare clinic hit by ransomware at 2 AM, then write the after-action report. This is the exact muscle the ThreatLocker panel will probe: calm, ordered incident thinking.
steps: Write the one-page scenario: 'Harborview Clinic, 150 endpoints, 2:00 AM Tuesday. Monitoring alerts: ransomware encrypting files on 3 workstations. You are the technical lead; the IT manager is incident commander.'
Draft the IR roster for the clinic: incident commander, technical lead (you), communications lead, scribe — with a backup for each role and an out-of-band contact method.
Write your preparation checklist: what should have existed before 2 AM (EDR access, offline credential copy, clean install media, phone tree, cyber-insurance breach line).
Script 4 injects on a timeline: T+0 initial alert; T+30 file server encrypting + EDR console unreachable; T+90 news reporter calls; T+4h CEO demands systems back for morning appointments.
Run the tabletop: for each inject, write down your decisions in order — first 15 minutes actions, containment calls, who you notify and when.
For inject 2, decide explicitly: isolate vs. power off, and write your evidence-preservation reasoning.
For inject 3, draft the holding statement the communications lead gives the reporter (2-3 sentences, no technical detail, no blame).
For inject 4, write how the incident commander balances patient-care pressure against reinfection risk — what returns first and under what monitoring.
Build the incident timeline from your run: detection, each decision, containment complete, eradication, recovery milestones.
Write the after-action report: executive summary, timeline, what worked, 3-5 gaps found during the exercise.
Convert each gap into an action item with a named owner and due date.
Add metrics: your MTTD (assume dwell from your scenario), your MTTR (detection to containment in the exercise), and scope at containment.
Re-read the AAR as the panel interviewer: does it show calm prioritization, evidence discipline, and blameless learning? Revise weak sections.
handsOnLab.deliverable: aar-ransomware-tabletop.md — scenario, roster, inject log with your decisions, timeline, after-action report with owned action items and metrics.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: The AAR covers all four NIST phases, names all four IR roles with backups, contains at least 3 action items each with an owner and due date, and your inject-2 decision explicitly justifies isolate-over-power-off for evidence preservation.

mockTask.q: Panel question: It is 2 AM and monitoring shows ransomware encrypting files on three workstations at a clinic. As the technical lead, what is your first move?
choices: Network-isolate the three hosts (leave them powered on), verify the alert is real, and start scoping — which other hosts got the same email or show the same behavior
Immediately wipe and reimage the three workstations to stop the encryption
Power off the entire network including servers to freeze everything in place
Send a clinic-wide email warning everyone not to open attachments
mockTask.explain: Isolate-without-power-off stops spread while preserving memory evidence; verifying and scoping before eradication prevents reinfection from an unknown entry point. Wiping destroys evidence, mass power-off kills RAM forensics, and clinic-wide email before containment causes panic and can tip off an insider.
