modules.title: Live Triage Simulation: Cyber Hero Shift
modules.summary: A full simulated support shift built around 8 tickets of escalating difficulty: a blocked legitimate app, suspected malware, an elevation request, a storage-control false positive, a network-control outage, a Detect alert, an angry customer, and an executive escalation. You triage under time pressure, resolve each ticket against a scored rubric, and compare your resolutions to model answers.
objectives: Triage incoming endpoint-security tickets by severity, business impact, and security risk within minutes.
Distinguish legitimate-application blocks from genuine malware using allowlisting investigation steps.
Resolve elevation, storage, and network-control tickets without weakening the zero-trust posture.
Handle Detect alerts, angry customers, and executive escalations with professional, de-escalating communication.
Document every action so a teammate could take over your queue cold.

notes.title: How a zero-trust support shift actually runs
Ticket 1 & 2: blocked legit app vs suspected malware
Ticket 3: elevation requests without local admin
Ticket 4: storage-control false positive vs real exfiltration
notes.body:
Storage Control governs storage devices, file paths, and shares — so its tickets split into two buckets that demand opposite responses: legitimate workflow friction and actual data theft. Worked example: a clinic's billing clerk plugs in an encrypted USB drive to transfer month-end reports and Storage Control blocks all writes. Investigation: is the drive the clinic's issued encrypted device or a personal one? Is the destination a sanctioned path? If the clerk is doing approved month-end work on a personal drive, the fix is a scoped exception — allow this device class for this user group to these paths, time-bound to month-end — not a permanent 'allow all USB.' Contrast the exfiltration pattern: a departing employee copies the client database to a personal drive at 11 PM. Indicators that flip your posture: off-hours timing, bulk copy of sensitive directories, personal hardware, and resignation/HR context. In that case you don't tune policy — you preserve the evidence trail (block logs, file-access records), notify your lead, and follow the incident response path. The gotcha: users will always describe a block as 'I was just doing my job.' Take that seriously but verify independently — check the block details (device ID, paths, volume) against the stated workflow before touching policy. Every exception gets an owner, an expiry, and a review date; exceptions without expiries become permanent holes with extra steps.

Second worked example — reading a bulk-copy pattern: Storage Control logs show 14 GB copied from the patient-records share to an unrecognized USB device at 22:40 by a user whose shift ended at 17:00. Compare with the legitimate pattern: the same user copies 200 MB to the clinic-issued encrypted drive at 16:30 on month-end days. Volume, timing, device identity, and destination all differ — that's your exfiltration signal, and your action is preserve-and-escalate, not policy-tune. Device-class thinking helps: maintain three classes — clinic-issued encrypted (allowed with scoping), approved vendor devices (case-by-case), personal/unknown (default deny). When the clinic buys new encrypted drives, the exception isn't 'allow USB' — it's 'add these device IDs to the clinic-issued class.' The human conversation matters too: when you deny a personal drive, explain the alternative in the same breath ('use the clinic drive from the front desk — here's where to get one'). Users circumvent controls they experience as pure obstruction; they comply with controls that come with a working path. Document every storage exception with the data classification involved — patient-data paths get your sign-off, not just the IT generalist's.

notes.title: Ticket 5: when network control IS the incident
notes.body:
Network Control is an endpoint firewall with dynamic ACLs that open and close ports — powerful against lateral movement and command-and-control, and fully capable of causing the outage you're asked to fix. Worked example: after a policy push, three finance workstations lose access to the shared accounting drive. Your diagnosis order: (1) confirm scope — is it these three machines only, or the server side too; (2) check what changed — pull the recent policy change log and its timestamp against the outage start; (3) test the hypothesis — does the new network policy's allowed-port set include the file-share traffic (SMB) these workstations need; (4) remediate surgically — adjust the ACL for the finance group rather than disabling Network Control; (5) verify — confirm connectivity restored and that the blocked lateral-movement protections still hold elsewhere. The discipline here is change correlation: in a deny-by-default world, 'it worked yesterday' almost always means 'a policy changed.' Keep a personal rule: never disable a control module to restore service. You narrow the policy, you don't turn it off — because the minute you disable Network Control fleet-wide to fix finance, you've removed the lateral-movement barrier everywhere. If the fix isn't obvious in 15 minutes, roll back the specific policy change and investigate offline; uptime for the business beats elegance of the root cause. Document the policy diff that fixed it — that's your change record.

Worked example with ports: the accounting share breaks after a Network Control push. You check the finance tier's ACL: allowed destinations are the file server on TCP 445 (SMB) and the print server on 9100. The new policy version dropped the 445 rule — someone 'cleaned up' the rule set. Fix: restore the explicit 445 allow for file-server-only, scoped to the finance tier, with a change note referencing the ticket. Verification is two-sided: confirm the share works AND confirm workstation-to-workstation traffic is still denied (test from one finance machine to another — it should fail). Rollback runbook, written before you need it: identify the policy version that broke things, revert to the previous known-good version for the affected tier only, verify service restoration, then diagnose the bad change offline. Never roll back the entire fleet for one tier's problem. Change windows matter: push network policy changes in evening windows with a verification checklist (file shares, printing, backup, authentication) — the four workflows that break most often. And keep a one-page network map of tier-to-tier allowed flows; when the 2 AM call comes, you diagnose from the map, not from memory.

notes.title: Ticket 6 & 7: Detect alerts and the angry customer
notes.body:
Detect alerts on indicators of compromise blocked by the modules; your triage decides whether the block was the whole story or the first chapter. Worked example: Detect fires on a workstation — blocked process injection from a browser helper. Your triage: (1) read the alert fully — which module blocked it, what process tree, what IOC; (2) assess — known-bad indicator or heuristic, single machine or several; (3) contain if warranted — isolate the host from the network while you look; (4) decide the story — commodity adware blocked cleanly (close with notes) vs a pattern across machines (escalate as a possible incident). Never assume a blocked alert is a closed case; a blocked initial attempt is often followed by a second one. Now Ticket 7, the angry customer: their words will be about your product ('your software is broken'), but the underlying emotion is fear of looking incompetent in front of their boss. De-escalation script: acknowledge impact first ('I understand this blocked you during the client presentation — let's get you working'), then diagnose aloud so they hear competence ('I can see the block was our allowlisting policy on this installer — let me verify it and get it approved'), then resolve and confirm ('it's approved now — please retry while I'm on the line'). The gotcha: arguing about who's right while the customer is down. Fix first, explain second, educate never — nobody learns policy architecture while angry. After resolution, a one-line plain-language explanation of why the block happened turns the angry customer into the one who defends the control next time.

Second worked example — the pattern that becomes an incident: three Detect alerts in one morning, all blocked process injection from the same browser helper version, on three different machines. Individually each looks like adware blocked cleanly. Together they're a campaign — same initial vector, same hour. Your move: escalate as a suspected incident, pull the browser helper's deployment history (was it pushed yesterday?), and check whether unblocked machines show the same process tree. The model resolution for Ticket 6 isn't 'closed three alerts' — it's 'correlated, escalated, and found the pushed update.' For the angry customer, the follow-up that converts them: a short email after resolution — what was blocked, why the control exists (one sentence, plain language), and what you changed so it won't recur. Template: 'Hi [name], following up on today's block: our allowlisting stopped an unrecognized installer from running, which is exactly what it's for — but it shouldn't have hit your legitimate tool. I've approved it for your team so this won't happen again. If anything else gets blocked, call me directly.' That email takes two minutes and turns today's complaint into tomorrow's reference story.

notes.title: Ticket 8: executive escalation and the scoring rubric
notes.body: Executive escalations are ordinary tickets wearing expensive suits: same technical work, different communication wrapper. Worked example: the CFO's laptop is blocked from running a board-presentation tool 40 minutes before a board meeting. Technical handling is identical to Ticket 1 — verify the binary, approve by hash, scope to the machine. What changes is cadence and framing: update every 10 minutes even if the update is 'still verifying the file,' speak in business impact ('you'll be able to present at 2:00 — the file checks out clean'), and never say 'policy says no' without the next sentence being the path to yes. Afterward, write the incident summary in executive language: what happened, what you did, how long, and what prevents recurrence. Now the scoring rubric for this whole shift simulation — how your resolutions are judged: correctness of the technical decision (did you approve/deny/isolate the right thing — 40%), security posture preserved (did you avoid weakening controls to buy speed — 25%), communication quality (did the user know what was happening — 20%), documentation (could someone audit your shift — 15%). Timeboxing matters: a perfect resolution delivered after the SLA is a partial score. The model resolutions at the end of this module show the 100-point version of each ticket — compare yours honestly, note where you traded posture for speed, and re-run any ticket you scored below 70 on. Worked example of the executive summary write-up for Ticket 8: 'At 13:20, the CFO's board-presentation tool was blocked by our application allowlisting (unrecognized binary). I verified the file hash against the vendor, confirmed it was legitimate, and approved it for the CFO's laptop at 13:31. The presentation proceeded on schedule. Root cause: the tool was updated yesterday and the new version wasn't in our approved set. Prevention: I've added the vendor's publisher certificate to the executive tier policy so future updates won't block.' Four sentences: what, what you did, how long, prevention. Now score yourself on Ticket 3 (elevation) as a rubric example: correctness — did you scope to the binary, not the session? (40 points possible) Posture — is there an expiry and a log entry, no local admin granted? (25) Communication — does the user know when the elevation applies and what to do next time? (20) Documentation — could an auditor reconstruct the grant? (15). A resolution that grants correctly but forgets the log entry scores 85 — good, not perfect, and the missing 15 is exactly the habit to build. Re-run any ticket under 70 with the model resolution open beside you, then close it and re-run once more from memory.

cards.front: First triage rule when multiple tickets land at once?
cards.back: Threats beat outages, outages beat friction, friction beats requests.

cards.front: What three artifacts does every ticket get?
cards.back: What you observed, what you did, and why — written as you go.

cards.front: Approve a blocked app by filename or by hash/publisher?
cards.back: By hash or verified publisher — filenames lie. Scope to the smallest machine set.

cards.front: Elevation granted to the user or the application?
cards.back: The application only — never hand back local admin to the session.

cards.front: Four scoping questions for an elevation grant?
cards.back: What (exact binary), why (justification), how long (one-time vs recurring), where (which machines).

cards.front: Indicators that flip a storage block from friction to exfiltration?
cards.back: Off-hours timing, bulk sensitive copies, personal hardware, departing-employee context.

cards.front: First diagnostic step when Network Control seems to cause an outage?
cards.back: Correlate scope and timing with the recent policy change log — 'worked yesterday' means a policy changed.

cards.front: Rule when a control module is blocking legitimate work?
cards.back: Narrow the policy — never disable the module fleet-wide to restore service.

cards.front: Detect alert triage sequence?
cards.back: Read the alert fully, assess severity/scope, contain if warranted, decide the story (closed vs incident).

cards.front: Why is a blocked Detect alert not automatically a closed case?
cards.back: A blocked first attempt is often followed by a second — look for patterns across machines.

cards.front: De-escalation order for an angry customer?
cards.back: Acknowledge impact, diagnose aloud, resolve and confirm — fix first, explain second.

cards.front: Executive escalation: what changes vs a normal ticket?
cards.back: Cadence (updates every ~10 min) and framing (business impact language); technical work is identical.

quiz.q: Three tickets land: a Detect alert, a blocked charting app, and an admin-rights request. What order?
choices: Detect alert, charting app, admin request
Charting app, Detect alert, admin request
quiz.explain: Threats beat outages, outages beat friction, friction beats requests. The alert could be active malicious activity; the app is business impact; the request is neither.

quiz.q: A user needs setup.exe approved. What is the correct basis for approval?
choices: Approve by filename across the fleet
Approve by hash or verified publisher, scoped narrowly
Disable allowlisting for their department for the day
Tell them to rename it and try again
quiz.explain: Filenames are attacker-controlled; hash or verified publisher proves identity. Narrow scoping limits blast radius if you're wrong.

quiz.q: Payroll-helper.exe is beaconing to an external IP per Detect. First action?
choices: Isolate the host from the network, then investigate
Wait to see if it happens again
quiz.explain: Contain first to stop potential spread or exfiltration, but preserve memory/logs before reimaging — evidence dies with the reimage.

quiz.q: A developer needs to run an installer requiring elevation. Best practice?
choices: Grant their account local admin for the day
Elevate the installer binary only, on their machine, for this install
Have them install it on a server instead
Deny — developers should never install software
quiz.explain: Elevation Control exists to elevate applications, not users. Scoping to the binary and the event preserves least privilege.

quiz.q: Month-end USB block for a billing clerk. The drive is personal, not clinic-issued. Best response?
choices: Scoped, time-bound exception for the workflow — and flag the personal-drive policy issue
Disable Storage Control until month-end passes
Tell the clerk to email the files to themselves
quiz.explain: Solve the immediate workflow with a narrow, expiring exception while noting the policy gap (personal drives with financial data) for review — not a permanent hole.

quiz.q: After a policy push, finance loses file-share access. Most likely cause?
choices: The file server's disk failed at the same time
The new network policy's ACL no longer permits the share traffic
quiz.explain: In deny-by-default environments, 'worked yesterday, broken today' correlates with policy changes. Check the change log against the outage start time.

quiz.q: You can't find the Network Control misconfiguration within 15 minutes. What now?
choices: Disable Network Control fleet-wide until you figure it out
Roll back the specific policy change, restore service, investigate offline
Keep digging — uptime can wait for a root cause
Ask finance to work without the share today
quiz.explain: Roll back the specific change to restore service, then investigate without the outage clock running. Never trade a fleet-wide control for one team's access.

quiz.q: An angry customer says your software broke their presentation. First sentence out of your mouth should:
choices: Acknowledge the impact and commit to getting them working
Blame the policy their admin configured
quiz.explain: Impact first, diagnosis second. People can't hear explanations while they're down; competence is demonstrated by fixing, then explaining.

quiz.q: The CFO is blocked 40 minutes before a board meeting. How often do you update them?
choices: About every 10 minutes, even if the update is 'still verifying'
Have their assistant check back later
quiz.explain: Executives escalate on silence, not slowness. A steady cadence of honest updates keeps the escalation from growing while you do the same technical work.

quiz.q: Under the shift rubric, which factor carries the most weight?
quiz.explain: A fast wrong answer (approving malware) is catastrophic; correctness dominates, with posture preservation second. Speed matters through SLA timeboxing, not as the top score.

items.prompt: Severity ordering: threats, outages, friction, requests.
items.answer: Threats > outages > friction > requests.
items.explain: Risk to the business decides the queue, not volume or loudness.

items.prompt: Timebox for initial ticket classification?
items.answer: About 10 minutes: resolve, escalate, or contain.
items.explain: Classification must be fast; deep investigation follows for the tickets that earn it.

items.prompt: Block-approval basis: filename, hash, or publisher?
items.answer: Hash or verified publisher.
items.explain: Filenames are trivially spoofed by malware.

items.prompt: Elevation granted to user session or application?
items.answer: Application only.
items.explain: Elevating the session recreates the local-admin risk Elevation Control removed.

items.prompt: Every exception needs which three properties?
items.answer: An owner, an expiry, and a review date.
items.explain: Exceptions without expiries become permanent holes with extra steps.

items.prompt: A blocked Detect alert with no other signs — close it?
items.answer: Not automatically — check for follow-up attempts and cross-machine patterns first.
items.explain: Blocked first attempts are often followed by second attempts.

items.prompt: Network outage right after a policy push — first check?
items.answer: The policy change log correlated with outage start time.
items.explain: Deny-by-default makes policy changes the prime suspect for new breakage.

items.prompt: Forbidden shortcut when a control blocks legitimate work?
items.answer: Disabling the control module.
items.explain: Narrow the policy; never turn off the control.

items.prompt: Ticket: HR's onboarding app blocked by allowlisting, 12 new hires waiting. Your first two actions?
items.answer: Verify the binary (hash, source, publisher), then approve narrowly scoped to HR machines.
items.explain: Business impact is real, but verification comes before approval — same workflow as Ticket 1, executed fast.

items.prompt: Ticket: Detect flags a macro-enabled spreadsheet email attachment that was blocked. User insists it's from a client. Action?
items.answer: Do not approve from the user's word. Verify sender independently, inspect the file safely, treat as suspected phishing until proven otherwise.
items.explain: Malicious attachments routinely arrive as 'expected client files.' User assurance is not verification.

items.prompt: Ticket: IT admin requests standing elevation for a patching tool used weekly. One-time grant or policy rule?
items.answer: Propose a standing application-elevation policy rule for that binary — recurring needs are policy-design signals.
items.explain: Weekly tickets for the same binary mean the baseline policy is incomplete; fix the policy, not the symptom.

items.prompt: Ticket: Storage Control blocks a developer copying a repo to an external SSD. Legit workflow. Fix shape?
items.answer: Scoped exception: this device/user/path, time-bound, with owner and review date.
items.explain: Solve the workflow without permanent allow-all; record the exception properly.

items.prompt: Ticket: after a Network Control update, the backup server can't reach its targets. Scope check first?
items.answer: Confirm whether it's the backup server only or all machines under the updated policy, then correlate with the change log.
items.explain: Scope tells you whether the policy change or the server is the variable; check both sides.

items.prompt: Ticket: user is shouting that 'the security thing' deleted their files. They mean a quarantine. Your move?
items.answer: Acknowledge impact, check what was actually quarantined and why, restore if it's a false positive — fix first, explain second.
items.explain: Quarantine is recoverable; the customer's panic is the immediate problem to manage.

items.prompt: Customer: 'Just turn this thing off, it's costing me money.' Best response shape?
items.answer: 'I hear you — let's get you working right now, and I'll make sure this exact block doesn't happen again.' Then fix narrowly.
items.explain: Validate the cost concern, deliver the fix, and promise prevention — never debate the product's existence.

items.prompt: Executive: 'Why did this happen?' after you fixed their block. Answer in what language?
items.answer: Business-impact language: what happened, what you did, how long, what prevents recurrence. No architecture lecture.
items.explain: Executives want confidence and prevention, not a policy-architecture seminar.

items.prompt: User asks you to approve an app 'because my manager said it's fine.' Sufficient authorization?
items.answer: No — manager say-so is not binary verification. Verify the file, then approve on technical grounds.
items.explain: Social pressure is how malware gets approved. The verification workflow doesn't take verbal shortcuts.

items.prompt: After resolving an angry customer's ticket, what one line earns future trust?
items.answer: A plain-language explanation of why the block happened and what you changed so it won't recur.
items.explain: Understanding converts the angry customer into someone who defends the control next time.

items.prompt: You must tell a user their requested app is denied as unsafe. How?
items.answer: State the decision plainly, give the specific reason (unsigned, known-risk indicator), and offer the safe alternative path.
items.explain: A denied request with a reason and an alternative is service; a denied request with silence is obstruction.

handsOnLab.title: Run the 8-ticket timed shift
handsOnLab.brief: Execute the full Cyber Hero shift: 8 tickets, a running clock, the scored rubric. You will write a resolution for each ticket, score yourself against the rubric, and compare with the model resolutions.
steps: Create shift-log.md with sections: clock start, one section per ticket (T1-T8), and a score table.
Set a 90-minute timer for the whole shift. Log your start time.
T1 (blocked legit app): write your investigation steps and approval decision — binary verification, scope, and policy change — in under 12 minutes.
T2 (suspected malware): write your containment and escalation actions — what you isolate, what evidence you preserve, who you notify — in under 12 minutes.
T3 (elevation request): write the grant decision using the what/why/how-long/where framework — in under 10 minutes.
T4 (storage false positive): write the exception with owner, expiry, and review date — in under 10 minutes.
T5 (network-control outage): write the diagnosis order and the surgical fix (no module disable) — in under 12 minutes.
T6 (Detect alert): write the triage sequence and your close-or-escalate decision with reasoning — in under 10 minutes.
T7 (angry customer): write your exact de-escalation script — first three sentences verbatim — in under 8 minutes.
T8 (executive escalation): write the technical resolution plus the executive-language summary — in under 10 minutes.
Stop the clock. Score each ticket on the rubric: correctness 40, posture 25, communication 20, documentation 15.
Compare each resolution against the model resolutions in the notes; for any ticket under 70, rewrite it to the 100-point version.
Write a 5-line shift retrospective: what slowed you down, which ticket type needs more reps.
handsOnLab.deliverable: shift-log.md with 8 timestamped resolutions, rubric scores, and a retrospective.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every ticket has a resolution written inside its timebox, every ticket is scored on all four rubric factors, and any sub-70 ticket has a rewritten model-grade version.

videos.title: ThreatLocker YouTube channel — product walkthroughs and demos
videos.blurb: Official vendor channel with product walkthroughs and demos of the modules you triage against in this shift — watch an allowlisting and policy demo to ground the ticket scenarios.

mockTask.q: Panel-style question: a user calls, furious, because our agent blocked their application ten minutes into a client presentation. Walk us through your response, in order.
choices: Acknowledge the impact, verify the blocked binary, approve it narrowly if legitimate, confirm they're working, then explain the block plainly
Explain the zero-trust policy architecture first so they understand, then start troubleshooting
Disable the agent on their machine immediately to restore service, then investigate later
Tell them their admin configured the policy and transfer them to their IT department
mockTask.explain: Impact first, verification before approval, narrow scope, confirm resolution, then the plain-language explanation. Disabling the agent trades the whole control for one ticket; lecturing an angry user teaches nothing.

Arrive-early logistics, what to bring, dress, the morning-of routine, a question-asking strategy with five smart questions for the panel, a thank-you note template, and a post-interview debrief checklist.

Arrive with a complete interview kit: documents, portfolio evidence, and questions for the panel.
Answer behavioral questions in STAR format and technical questions with operator-grade depth.

notes.title: Logistics: getting to 1950 W Maitland Blvd on time
What to bring: the interview kit
Dress and first impressions for an infrastructure role
Morning-of routine: energy, calm, timing
notes.body:
The morning of October 13 is execution, not preparation — all studying ends the night before. Worked example routine: wake at 6:00 AM (two full hours before departure buffer), shower, eat a real breakfast with protein (not just coffee — your brain burns glucose under stress), review only three things: your five questions for them, your two strongest STAR stories, and the drive route. No new material — cramming new facts at 7:30 AM only surfaces anxiety. Leave by your planned time with the buffer; in the car, listen to something calm or nothing at all, not a frantic podcast. Arrive 8:15-8:20, do the five-minute car review, walk in ~8:30. While waiting: breathe slowly, review your questions once more, and remind yourself of one true thing — you have done the reps (the triage sim, the capstones, the panel prep). If nerves spike in the room, the reset is physical: feet flat, slow exhale, sip water, then answer. Common mistakes: the all-nighter (sleep deprivation destroys recall and emotional regulation — a tired brain interviews 30% worse), skipping breakfast (hunger reads as irritability), and arriving with zero buffer so the whole morning is a sprint. You want to walk in slightly early, slightly bored, and completely ready — boredom is the feeling of a plan working.

The night-before checklist does more for your morning than willpower: kit packed and by the door, clothes laid out including shoes and belt, alarm set (plus a backup), coffee/breakfast ready to go, phone charging, car fueled or charged with the address already in navigation. Each item you handle tonight is one fewer decision under morning adrenaline. The physiology of nerves: a racing heart is adrenaline preparing you to perform — reinterpret it ('my body is getting ready') rather than fighting it, which research on stress reappraisal shows actually improves performance. The 4-count reset in the waiting room: inhale 4 counts, hold 4, exhale 4, twice — it measurably slows heart rate. Avoid the waiting-room traps: scrolling your phone (it fragments focus and the posture reads as disengaged), rehearsing answers frantically (you're prepared — trust the reps), and too much coffee (jittery hands, dry mouth, bathroom urgency mid-interview). One normal cup with breakfast is the dose. Walk in hydrated, fed, and slightly early — the physical basics are the foundation every technique stands on. Set out your water bottle with the kit the night before — dehydration dulls focus, and you will not want to hunt for water while the clock runs.

notes.title: Question-asking strategy: five smart questions for THEM
notes.body:
'Do you have questions for us?' is not a courtesy — it's the final scored section. Your five questions must show you understand the actual work of an IT Infrastructure Specialist at a zero-trust endpoint company. Worked examples: (1) 'What does the first 90 days look like for this role — what would a strong start accomplish?' (shows you think in outcomes); (2) 'How is the infrastructure team structured, and how does it work with the support and security teams day to day?' (shows you think in collaboration); (3) 'What's the biggest infrastructure challenge the team is facing right now?' (shows you want the real problems — listen hard, this is gold); (4) 'How does the team handle on-call or after-hours incidents?' (shows you understand operational reality); (5) 'What does growth look like from this role — what skills do the strongest people here develop?' (shows ambition with humility). Delivery rules: ask them conversationally, not as an interrogation; ask follow-ups on their answers ('You mentioned the team is rebuilding the lab environment — what's driving that?'); never ask about salary, benefits, or remote work in the first interview unless they raise it; and never ask something the website answers in ten seconds. The gotcha: 'No, I think you covered everything' — it reads as disinterest. Even if they answered everything, ask your best remaining question reframed: 'You touched on the team structure — could you say more about how the infrastructure side collaborates with support?'

Worked example follow-ups that show listening: they say the team is rebuilding the lab environment — you ask, 'What's driving the rebuild — new tooling, or scaling for more endpoints?' They mention on-call rotations — 'How are after-hours alerts triaged — is there a primary/secondary split?' Each follow-up proves you processed the answer, and their answers become thank-you-note material. Questions to never ask in round one, with reasons: salary and benefits (signals the job is a transaction — the recruiter handles compensation), 'how fast can I get promoted' (signals you're already looking past the role), anything answered on the website's careers page (signals zero research), and 'do you monitor employees' style adversarial questions (signals distrust). The meta-rule: every question should make them think 'this person understands the work.' A safe closer if time is short: 'What's the most important problem this role will help solve in the next six months?' — it ends the interview with them picturing you solving it. Write their answer down; it's the first line of your thank-you note.

notes.title: STAR delivery under pressure
notes.body:
Behavioral questions ('Tell me about a time when...') are scored on structure as much as content — STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) keeps a nervous brain from rambling. Worked example — 'Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult user': Situation — 'At a previous support role, a department head's presentation laptop was blocked by our endpoint agent minutes before an all-hands.' Task — 'I needed to restore her access without weakening the security policy.' Action — 'I verified the blocked application by hash, confirmed it was legitimate, approved it scoped to her machine, and stayed on the line while she tested.' Result — 'She presented on time, and I documented the exception so the block wouldn't recur.' Then the closer most candidates skip: the lesson — 'It taught me that speed and verification aren't opposites — you do both, in order.' Keep each STAR to 90-120 seconds; longer and you lose the panel. Prepare five stories that cover: a difficult user, a mistake you made, a time you learned something fast, a disagreement with a colleague, and a time you improved a process. The gotcha: fictional polish. Never invent history — draw on real experience (your labs, your projects, your real work), and it's fine to say 'in a lab environment I built...' Honesty about being junior with strong fundamentals beats a fabricated senior war story that collapses under one follow-up question.

Second worked example — the mistake story, fully built: Situation — 'Early in a support role, I approved an application block exception by filename without verifying the hash — I was rushing to clear a queue.' Task — 'The app turned out to be a renamed unwanted program, and I had to own the error.' Action — 'I immediately revoked the exception, quarantined the file, told my lead exactly what I'd done before they found it, and wrote myself a verification checklist.' Result — 'Nothing spread, but I learned the expensive way.' The lesson closer — 'Since then I verify by hash or publisher every time, no matter how loud the queue is — speed never outranks verification.' Notice the structure: no excuses, self-reported, concrete fix, durable lesson. Timing practice: record each story on your phone and check it's 90-120 seconds — most people discover their 'two-minute' story is actually four. Cut ruthlessly: one situation sentence, one task sentence, two action sentences, one result, one lesson. If a story runs long in the room, land the plane: '...and the lesson was X.' A clean landing beats a perfect story that never ends.

notes.title: Thank-you note template and post-interview debrief
notes.body: Send the thank-you within 24 hours — same day is best. Worked example template: Subject: 'Thank you — IT Infrastructure Specialist interview.' Body: 'Hi [Name], Thank you for your time today — I enjoyed our conversation about [specific thing they mentioned, e.g., the team's lab rebuild]. I'm excited about the IT Infrastructure Specialist role because [one genuine reason tied to what you learned]. [One-line reinforcement: e.g., My background in endpoint triage and zero-trust policy work maps directly onto the challenges you described.] Thanks again, and please let me know if I can provide anything else. Best, Enmanuel Mejia, [phone].' Send one per interviewer if you have names/addresses (ask the recruiter, Alex Starr, for the right contacts), each with a different specific detail — never a mass BCC. Then the debrief checklist, done the same evening while memory is fresh: (1) write down every question they asked and your answer's weak spots; (2) note names, titles, and one personal detail per interviewer; (3) record what excited you and what worried you about the role; (4) list any follow-up you promised ('I'll send that lab writeup'); (5) email the recruiter a brief status note. Then stop — no second-guessing spirals, no 'should I have said.' You executed the plan; the outcome is data, not a verdict on your worth. Filled example — the thank-you note with specifics: Subject: 'Thank you — IT Infrastructure Specialist interview.' Body: 'Hi [Name], Thank you for your time today — I particularly enjoyed hearing about the lab rebuild and how the infrastructure team partners with support on escalations. I'm excited about the IT Infrastructure Specialist role because the zero-trust endpoint work is exactly where I've focused my preparation, and the team's challenges are the kind I want to help solve. Please let me know if I can provide anything else — my portfolio documents are ready to share if useful. Best, Enmanuel Mejia, [phone].' Each interviewer gets a different specific callback (lab rebuild for one, on-call structure for another). The recruiter status note, same evening: 'Hi Alex, today's interview went well — I enjoyed meeting [names]. Thank you for setting it up. Please let me know the next steps whenever you hear.' Short, professional, grateful. Then the debrief form: questions asked (verbatim as you remember), your weak spots (be brutally honest — this is for you), names/titles/one detail each, what excited you, what worried you, promised follow-ups. File it. The interview is over; the system you built for the next one just got better.

quiz.q: What is your target arrival time for the 9:00 AM interview, and why?
choices: 8:15–8:20 AM — buffer for traffic without hovering
8:55 AM — exactly on time is most professional
quiz.explain: 40–45 minutes early absorbs traffic and gives you a calm reset; walking in ~8:30 reads professional, while 7:30 arrival creates awkward waiting.

quiz.q: The single highest-value logistics prep before Oct 13 is:
choices: A timed weekday-morning dry run of the drive
quiz.explain: Tuesday-morning traffic is the variable that can actually make you late; only a real dry run measures it.

quiz.q: How many resume copies, and why that number?
choices: Three — panels often have more interviewers than expected
Ten — hand them to everyone in the building
quiz.explain: Three covers the common panel size plus one spare; offering copies ('in case they're useful') is courteous without being pushy.

quiz.q: Phone protocol for interview day?
choices: Vibrate in your pocket is fine
Fully silent, ideally left in the car
On loud in case the recruiter calls
Face-up on the table so you look connected
quiz.explain: Vibrate is audible in a quiet room; a buzzing phone mid-answer is an unforced error. Silent and out of sight.

quiz.q: A STAR answer should run about how long?
choices: As long as the story takes
quiz.explain: 90–120 seconds holds the panel's attention and forces structure; longer answers ramble and lose the Result.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest of the five questions to ask them?
choices: What does the first 90 days look like for this role?
quiz.explain: The 90-day question shows outcome thinking and invites them to picture you succeeding; salary and timeline questions come through the recruiter.

quiz.q: 'Do you have questions for us?' — they seem to have covered everything. You:
choices: Ask your best remaining question reframed around something they mentioned
Repeat a question they already answered
quiz.explain: 'No questions' reads as disinterest; reframing around their own words shows active listening.

quiz.q: In a STAR story about a mistake, what must the story include?
choices: Proof it wasn't really your fault
The lesson and what you changed afterward
A promise it will never happen again
quiz.explain: Interviewers ask about mistakes to test ownership and growth; the lesson is the scored part, not the excuse.

quiz.q: Thank-you notes: which approach is correct?
choices: One BCC'd email to all interviewers
Individual notes within 24 hours, each with a different specific detail
A LinkedIn connection request with no note
Wait a week so you don't seem desperate
quiz.explain: Individual notes with specific callbacks prove you listened; BCC blasts and delays signal low effort.

quiz.q: It's 8:50 AM, you're parked, and nerves spike. Best reset?
choices: Feet flat, slow exhale, sip water, review your five questions once
quiz.explain: The reset is physical and familiar — new material at 8:50 only feeds anxiety; calm physiology produces calm answers.

items.prompt: 'Tell me about yourself' — structure your 60-second answer.
items.answer: Present (who you are now) → past (relevant path) → future (why this role). End with enthusiasm for the role.
items.explain: It's a professional narrative, not a life story — 60 seconds, forward-leaning.

items.prompt: 'What's your biggest weakness?' — safe framing?
items.answer: A real, non-fatal weakness + what you're actively doing about it. Never a disguised strength.
items.explain: 'I'm a perfectionist' is a cliché that signals evasion; honesty with a fix signals maturity.

items.prompt: 'Why ThreatLocker?' — what must the answer contain?

handsOnLab.title: Full interview rehearsal
handsOnLab.brief: Rehearse the entire Oct 13 performance: timed STAR answers recorded aloud, the five questions practiced, the kit packed, the route dry-run, and the thank-you template personalized.
steps: Write your five STAR stories (difficult user, a mistake, fast learning, a disagreement, process improvement) at 90–120 seconds each — speak them aloud with a timer, not just on paper.
Record yourself answering 'Tell me about yourself,' 'Why ThreatLocker?', and 'What's your biggest weakness?' on your phone; listen back for filler words and rambling.
Practice your five questions for them aloud until each sounds conversational, not read.
Do the weekday-morning dry run to 1950 W Maitland Blvd; record the drive time and parking situation.
Pack the full interview kit the night before the dry run (practice pack): 3 resumes, portfolio one-pager, notebook + pens, questions list, ID, water.
Lay out your interview clothes the night before; check shoes, belt, and grooming.
Write your morning-of timeline working backward from 8:15 arrival: wake, breakfast, departure with buffer.
Draft your thank-you template now with blanks for each interviewer's name and specific detail — personalizing later takes minutes.
Do one full mock: have someone (or a timer) ask you 6 mixed questions; answer standing-to-sitting as you would in the room.
Write a one-page debrief form in advance (questions asked, weak spots, names, follow-ups) so Oct 13 evening is fill-in, not recall.
handsOnLab.deliverable: rehearsal-log.md: timed STAR transcripts, recording notes, dry-run drive time, kit checklist (checked), morning timeline, and the pre-written thank-you template.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: You can recite date/time/address/recruiter from memory, deliver any STAR in under 2 minutes, ask all five questions conversationally, and the kit is packed and checked off.

modules.title: Capstone: Zero-Trust Endpoint Defense Plan
modules.summary: Design a complete ThreatLocker zero-trust deployment for a fictional 150-endpoint healthcare clinic: policy architecture for each module, phased rollout, exception governance, success metrics, and an executive summary. The deliverable is a written defense plan document — portfolio evidence you can discuss in the Oct 13 interview.
objectives: Scope a 150-endpoint deployment: inventory endpoint types, group them, and define policy tiers.
Design per-module policy architecture (Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network Control, Detect).
Sequence a phased rollout with pilot gates, rollback criteria, and communication plans.
Define an exception request/approval process with ownership, expiry, and audit.
Write an executive summary and metrics plan a non-technical leader can act on.

notes.title: The fictional client: clinic profile and constraints
Policy architecture I: allowlisting foundation
Policy architecture II: ringfencing and elevation control
Policy architecture III: storage and network control
notes.body:
Storage Control governs storage devices, file paths, and shares — your answer to both data theft and ransomware spreading via mapped drives. Worked example design: clinical workstations — block all removable media except clinic-issued encrypted drives, and only to the encrypted-drives group; block writes to personal cloud-sync folders for the patient-data directories; allow the backup service account (and only it) to write to the backup share. Kiosks — no removable media at all, no exceptions without your sign-off. Network Control is the endpoint firewall with dynamic ACLs — your lateral-movement barrier. Worked example: clinical workstations may talk to the EHR server, the file server, the print server, and the update server — and nothing else on the LAN; workstation-to-workstation traffic is denied by default, which contains a compromised machine to itself. Servers get ingress rules permitting only their client tiers. The backup server may pull from everyone but initiate nothing outbound except to the offsite target. Gotchas: overly broad 'allow file sharing' rules recreate the flat network you're trying to segment — write ACLs as explicit allowlists of (source tier → destination → port); and test the backup and printing flows explicitly after enabling Network Control, because those are the two workflows most often broken by new firewall policy. Every ACL change follows the change process: propose, peer-review, deploy to pilot, verify, then fleet.

Worked example — the ACL table (section 4 of your document). Rows are (source tier, destination, port/service, purpose): Clinical → EHR server, 443, charting. Clinical → File server, TCP 445, records share. Clinical → Print server, 9100, printing. Clinical → Update server, 443, patching. Admin laptops → same as clinical, plus VPN gateway when offsite. Kiosk → Check-in service, 443, check-in only. Backup server → All tiers, TCP 445, pull backups (initiated by backup server). IT workstations → All tiers, RDP/WinRM, administration (logged). Everything else: deny and log. Note what the table does: a compromised clinical workstation can reach exactly four servers on specific ports — it cannot touch another workstation, the backup server, or the internet at large. Lateral movement is architecturally contained. The backup flow test plan after enabling Network Control: run a full backup cycle from two machines per tier, verify completion, then verify a restore of one file — backup that can't restore is theater. Same for printing: print a test page from each tier. These two workflows plus authentication are your post-change verification checklist, every time.

notes.title: Rollout phases: pilot to full fleet with gates
notes.body:
A 150-endpoint rollout done in one push is a 150-endpoint outage. Your plan phases it with explicit gates. Phase 0 — Prepare (weeks 1-2): inventory and tier endpoints, run learning mode on representatives of each tier, draft baseline policies, stand up the ticket queue and the exception form, communicate to staff what changes and when. Phase 1 — Pilot (weeks 3-4): deploy to 15 endpoints — the 5 IT workstations plus 10 volunteer clinical machines. Success gate: fewer than 2 blocking tickets per machine per week and zero clinical-workflow outages; failure means tune policies, not push forward. Phase 2 — Departments (weeks 5-8): roll one department per week (front desk → exam rooms → billing → admin), each with a 48-hour hypercare window where you're on call for blocks. Phase 3 — Kiosks and servers (weeks 9-10): strictest tiers last, in a Sunday maintenance window, with tested rollback. Phase 4 — Harden (weeks 11-12): remove temporary local admin, tighten ringfences based on observed behavior, first metrics review. Rollback criteria are written before each phase: if blocking tickets exceed the gate threshold or any clinical workflow breaks, revert that phase's policy change within the change window — rollback is a planned action, not an admission of failure. Communication per phase: one plain-language email ('what changes, what to do if something's blocked, who to call'), plus a 10-minute huddle with each department lead. The classic failure: skipping the pilot because 'we're confident in the policies.' Confidence is not a deployment strategy.

Worked example — the hypercare schedule for Phase 2's first department (front desk, week 5): Monday 07:30 — you on site before the clinic opens, policies deployed Sunday night. Monday–Tuesday — you carry the escalation phone; every block ticket gets same-hour response. Wednesday — remote monitoring, check-in call with the department lead at noon. Thursday–Friday — normal queue, but block tickets from front desk stay high-priority. The following Monday — retrospective: block count, resolution times, policy adjustments, then the next department starts. That rhythm repeats per department; by the third one you're mostly observing. The communication email, plain language: Subject: 'Small security update Monday — what to expect.' Body: 'On Monday we're activating a security improvement on front-desk computers. What changes for you: if a program won't open, you'll see a message — call [number] and we'll fix it within the hour. What's protected: patient records and our systems from malicious software. Thank you for your patience during the first two days.' No jargon, a clear action, a named contact, and honesty that days 1-2 need patience. Send it Friday, huddle with the department lead Monday morning.

notes.title: Exception process and governance
notes.body:
Deny-by-default only survives contact with reality if exceptions are fast, fair, and finite. Your governance design: a single intake (ticket form: requester, business justification, application/file/device details with hash where applicable, duration needed), a triage SLA (standard requests: 1 business day; urgent clinical: 4 hours), and an approver matrix — the IT generalist approves standard app additions, you (or the security lead) approve anything touching kiosks, servers, or patient-data paths, and anything permanent needs both. Every exception record carries: what, why, scope (machines/users), expiry, owner, and review date. Worked example: a new ultrasound viewer needs approval — IT verifies the vendor binary, creates a 90-day scoped exception for the imaging workstations, owner: clinic IT lead, review at 60 days to decide permanent policy vs renewal. Standing rules: no permanent exceptions in the first 90 days (everything expires and gets reviewed — this forces policy maturation); no exceptions granted by phone or hallway (intake form or it didn't happen — this is also your social-engineering defense); quarterly exception audit where you present the count, the aging list, and the 'exceptions that should be policy now' recommendations. The gotcha that kills governance: the 'temporary' exception from month one that's still there in month nine. Expiry dates are load-bearing — automate the review reminder if you can, calendar it if you can't.

Worked example — a filled exception record: EX-2026-041 | What: approve ultrasound-viewer v3.2 (SHA256: 9f2e...) for imaging workstations | Why: new ultrasound unit requires v3.2; old version can't read new scans | Scope: 8 imaging workstations, clinical tier | Expiry: 90 days (2026-10-10) | Owner: clinic IT lead | Review: 60 days — decide permanent policy vs renewal | Approved by: [you], [date] | Ticket: #4471. That record answers every future question about the rule. The quarterly audit agenda (90 minutes): (1) exception inventory — count, aging, expiries in next quarter (15 min); (2) expired-but-still-needed: promote to policy or renew with justification (30 min); (3) exceptions that should never have been exceptions — baseline gaps to fix (20 min); (4) approvals review — any approver overloaded or rubber-stamping (15 min); (5) report to the director — one page (10 min). The 'no permanent exceptions in 90 days' rule pays off here: the first audit converts the recurring ones into proper policy, and the baseline gets visibly better each quarter. Governance that visibly improves the baseline earns continued executive support; governance that's just paperwork gets bypassed.

notes.title: Metrics, executive summary, and the defense plan document
notes.body: Executives fund what they can measure, so your plan defines metrics before deployment. Leading indicators (weekly): block events by tier and module (tells you where friction lives), exception request volume and SLA attainment (tells you if governance is keeping up), mean time to resolve a block ticket (tells you the user impact). Lagging/security indicators (monthly): percentage of endpoints with zero local-admin accounts (target: 100% by end of Phase 4), Detect alerts by severity and disposition, policy coverage — endpoints on current policy version (target: 100%). Report honestly: a rising block count after rollout is expected (the system is working and being tuned), not a failure — say so in the report or someone else will misread it. The executive summary (one page, front of the document) follows: the risk in plain language ('our endpoints currently trust anything that runs'), the approach ('deny-by-default across six controls, phased over 12 weeks'), the ask (budget, change windows, staff cooperation), and the outcome ('every endpoint verified, every exception expiring and reviewed'). Your deliverable document structure: 1. Executive summary, 2. Assumptions and scope, 3. Endpoint inventory and tiers, 4. Per-module policy architecture, 5. Rollout phases with gates, 6. Exception process, 7. Metrics and reporting cadence, 8. Risks and rollback plan. Write it so a non-technical clinic director can read sections 1 and 8 and approve — and so a future you could execute sections 3-6 cold. Worked example — the weekly ops report (one page): Week 5 (front-desk rollout): block events 34 (28 allowlisting, 6 ringfencing) — all resolved, mean resolution 42 min; exception requests 9, SLA attainment 100% (all within 1 business day); endpoints on current policy 150/150; local-admin count: 12 remaining (target 0 by week 12); Detect alerts: 3, all benign adware blocked. Narrative line: 'Block volume is elevated as expected during rollout; resolution times are within target and falling.' That narrative line is the honest framing — without it, someone reads '34 blocks' as failure. The executive summary draft (one page): 'Our endpoints currently run anything a user clicks — including malicious software. This plan deploys deny-by-default protection across six controls: only approved applications run, approved apps are restricted in what they can do, nobody has standing admin rights, removable media and network access are controlled, and blocked attacks generate alerts. Rollout: 12 weeks, phased by department, with rollback gates at each phase. We need: Sunday evening change windows, 10 minutes with each department lead, and your approval of the exception policy. Outcome: every endpoint verified under policy, every exception expiring and reviewed, measurable in the weekly report.' Risk, approach, ask, outcome — no jargon.

cards.front: Fictional client and endpoint count?
cards.back: Harborview Family Clinic — 150 endpoints across 5 tiers (clinical, admin, kiosk, server, IT).

cards.front: Why tier policies instead of one flat policy?
cards.back: Kiosks need maximum lockdown, IT needs tools with auditing — one policy either breaks workflows or leaves gaps.

cards.front: Allowlisting deployment order?
cards.back: Learning/discovery phase first (capture the real app set), then enforce deny-by-default.

cards.front: Hash vs publisher approval — when each?
cards.back: Publisher certificate where the vendor signs consistently; hash where they don't or for one-off binaries.

cards.front: Ringfencing in one sentence?
cards.back: Restricts what allowed apps can do — blocks them spawning processes, editing registry, or opening network sessions.

cards.front: Ringfence example: PDF reader?
cards.back: May not spawn powershell.exe, cmd.exe, wscript.exe, or mshta.exe.

cards.front: Elevation Control design for the clinic?
cards.back: Remove local admin fleet-wide; just-in-time elevation to specific application binaries via policy; IT admin via separate logged workflow.

cards.front: Network Control lateral-movement design?
cards.back: Deny workstation-to-workstation by default; explicit allowlists of source tier → destination → port.

cards.front: Rollout phases and gates?
cards.back: Prepare → Pilot (15 endpoints, block-ticket gate) → Departments (weekly, 48h hypercare) → Kiosks/servers → Harden. Roll back a phase if gates fail.

cards.front: Every exception record carries?
cards.back: What, why, scope, expiry, owner, review date. No permanent exceptions in the first 90 days.

cards.front: Key metrics: name three.
cards.back: Block events by tier/module, exception SLA attainment, % endpoints with zero local admin, Detect alert dispositions, policy coverage.

cards.front: Executive summary must let a non-technical director do what?
cards.back: Read sections 1 and 8 and approve — risk, approach, ask, outcome in plain language.

quiz.q: Why do the 10 check-in kiosks get the strictest policy tier?
choices: They're unattended and public-facing with a fixed application set
Kiosks are exempt from security policy
They need the most software installed
quiz.explain: Unattended + public-facing + fixed workload = maximum lockdown with minimum workflow risk. Strictness follows exposure, not newness.

quiz.q: During learning mode, which workflow must you explicitly include?
choices: A full print/scan cycle including drivers and peripherals
Nothing — learning mode captures everything automatically
quiz.explain: Printer drivers and specialty peripherals are the classic learning-mode misses; an incomplete baseline means day-one blocks on real workflows.

quiz.q: The EHR reporting module legitimately launches a helper executable. Correct ringfence?
choices: Allow that specific parent→child chain only
Disable ringfencing for the EHR server
quiz.explain: Ringfencing is surgical: permit the exact legitimate chain, keep everything else denied. Broad allowances recreate the attack surface.

quiz.q: The billing manager needs a quarterly tax-software updater run elevated. Best design?
choices: An elevation rule for that exact updater binary on billing machines
Have IT log in and run it each quarter
Disable Elevation Control on billing machines
quiz.explain: Just-in-time elevation to the specific binary preserves least privilege; making her admin or disabling the control hands back the keys.

quiz.q: Pilot success gate: which is correctly specified?
choices: Fewer than 2 blocking tickets per machine per week and zero clinical-workflow outages
All users say they like the new system
Deploy to all 150 and measure later
quiz.explain: Gates must be measurable and realistic — some friction is expected; clinical outages are not. 'Zero tickets' would fail any real pilot.

quiz.q: A phase's gate fails (blocking tickets exceed threshold). Correct action?
choices: Roll back that phase's policy change within the change window, then tune
quiz.explain: Rollback is a planned action with written criteria, not failure. Pushing through a failed gate converts a policy problem into an outage.

quiz.q: A doctor phones in an exception request from the hallway. Policy says:
choices: Intake form or it didn't happen; take the request properly
Grant it now, file the form later
quiz.explain: Hallway grants bypass verification and audit — and they're a social-engineering vector. The form exists to protect the doctor too.

quiz.q: Why no permanent exceptions in the first 90 days?
choices: To force policy maturation — everything gets reviewed and the good ones become policy
The ticketing system can't store them
quiz.explain: Expiring exceptions force a review where recurring needs get promoted into proper policy — that's how the baseline improves instead of rotting.

quiz.q: Block events rise in weeks 3-4 of rollout. How do you report this?
choices: As a failure of the deployment
As expected — the system is working and being tuned; show the trend alongside resolution times
Hide it from the executive report
quiz.explain: Honest metrics framing prevents misreading: rising blocks with falling resolution times means the control is engaging and governance is keeping up.

quiz.q: Which metric best proves least-privilege is actually achieved?
choices: Percentage of endpoints with zero local-admin accounts
quiz.explain: Outcome metrics beat activity metrics — '100% of endpoints have no local admin' states the security property directly.

items.prompt: Five endpoint tiers for the clinic?
items.answer: Clinical workstations, admin laptops, kiosks, servers, IT workstations.
items.explain: Tiering drives every policy decision downstream.

items.prompt: Allowlisting order of operations?
items.answer: Learn/discover the real app set first, then enforce deny-by-default.
items.explain: Enforcing before learning guarantees day-one breakage.

items.prompt: What does ringfencing stop?
items.answer: Weaponization of trusted apps — allowed apps spawning processes, editing registry, exfiltrating.
items.explain: The attacker lives off trusted binaries; ringfencing cages them.

items.prompt: Elevation Control in one rule?
items.answer: Elevate applications, never user sessions; just-in-time, scoped, logged.
items.explain: Session elevation recreates the local-admin problem.

items.prompt: Storage Control default for kiosks?
items.answer: No removable media at all.
items.explain: Unattended public machines get no removable-media attack surface.

items.prompt: Network Control workstation default?
items.answer: Deny workstation-to-workstation; explicit tier→destination→port allowlists.
items.explain: This is the lateral-movement barrier; defaults matter most.

items.prompt: Rollback is what, philosophically?
items.answer: A planned action with written criteria — not an admission of failure.
items.explain: Pre-written rollback criteria make reverting fast and blameless.

items.prompt: The imaging viewer updates monthly with new hashes and the vendor doesn't sign. Approval strategy?
items.answer: Hash-approve each release through the exception intake with a short SLA; track it as a recurring-policy candidate.
items.explain: Unsigned + changing hashes means per-release verification — and a process cost worth documenting for the vendor conversation.

items.prompt: Front-desk staff share one Windows login on two machines. Policy implication?
items.answer: Flag it: shared logins break per-user scoping and audit. Recommend individual accounts as a Phase 0 remediation.
items.explain: Zero-trust policy assumes identity; shared accounts undermine every control. Fix the identity layer first.

items.prompt: The backup service needs to write to the backup share; ransomware also targets backup shares. Design?
items.answer: Only the backup service account may write to the share; Storage Control denies all other writers; backup server pulls, doesn't accept pushes.
items.explain: The backup path is the highest-value target — it gets the narrowest rule.

items.prompt: A department lead demands the pilot skip their team 'because we're too busy.' Response?
items.answer: No skips — offer them the last department slot and the 48-hour hypercare window, and explain the pilot protects them.
items.explain: Skipping the pilot for the busiest team guarantees their outage is the biggest one.

items.prompt: Two weeks in, exception volume is 3x your estimate. What does this signal?
items.answer: The baseline policies are incomplete — promote the recurring exceptions into policy rather than grinding through tickets.
items.explain: Exception volume is a policy-quality metric; sustained volume means fix the baseline.

items.prompt: The clinic director asks 'are we compliant now?' How do you answer?
items.answer: Honestly: the deployment implements strong technical controls that support the clinic's compliance efforts, but compliance is a legal determination — point them to their compliance advisor.
items.explain: Never certify compliance yourself; describe controls accurately and defer the legal judgment.

items.prompt: Design the weekly ops report: which 4 numbers?
items.answer: Block events by tier/module, exception volume + SLA attainment, mean time to resolve blocks, endpoints off current policy version.
items.explain: Friction location, governance health, user impact, coverage — the four dials of the rollout.

items.prompt: An exception expires tomorrow and the owner is on vacation. Process?
items.answer: The exception lapses unless renewed through intake before expiry — no auto-extension; designate backup owners at creation.
items.explain: Auto-extending exceptions silently is how 'temporary' becomes permanent. Backup owners are set at request time.

items.prompt: Quarterly audit finds 12 exceptions older than 180 days. Action?
items.answer: Review each: promote recurring ones to policy, renew with justification, or revoke. Report the disposition.
items.explain: The audit exists to convert exception debt into policy or remove it.

items.prompt: Detect alerts spike on one clinical workstation. First step per your plan?
items.answer: Follow the IR path from the plan: contain (isolate host), preserve evidence, assess scope — the deployment plan references incident response, it doesn't replace it.
items.explain: Defense plans include the escalation path; the alert still gets full triage.

items.prompt: Director wants the rollout done in 4 weeks instead of 12. Your response?
items.answer: Show the phase gates and what each protects; offer to compress Phase 0/1 prep but not skip pilot gates — speed without gates is an outage plan.
items.explain: Negotiate on schedule using the plan's own logic; never silently drop the safety gates.

handsOnLab.title: Write the Zero-Trust Endpoint Defense Plan
handsOnLab.brief: Produce the full defense plan document for Harborview Family Clinic: 8 sections, policy tables per module and tier, phased rollout with gates, exception process, metrics, and a one-page executive summary.
steps: Create defense-plan.md with the 8-section skeleton: executive summary, assumptions/scope, inventory/tiers, per-module architecture, rollout phases, exception process, metrics, risks/rollback.
Write section 2 (assumptions and scope): state every design assumption explicitly, including the one-IT-generalist constraint.
Build the endpoint inventory table: 5 tiers, counts summing to 150, example machine roles per tier.
Write the allowlisting architecture: learning-phase plan, the 3 policy tiers, hash-vs-publisher rules, the new-software request path.
Write the ringfencing + elevation architecture: parent/child rules for Office/PDF reader, the EHR helper exception, per-binary elevation rules, the IT admin privileged-access workflow.
Write the storage + network architecture: removable-media matrix per tier, backup-share rule, tier→destination→port ACL table.
Write the rollout: 5 phases with week ranges, the pilot gate numbers, hypercare windows, and written rollback criteria per phase.
Write the exception process: intake fields, SLA tiers, approver matrix, the exception record schema, the 90-day no-permanent rule, quarterly audit.
Write the metrics section: weekly leading indicators, monthly lagging indicators, targets, and the honest-framing note on rising early blocks.
Write the one-page executive summary LAST: risk, approach, ask, outcome — plain language, no jargon.
Re-read the full document as the clinic director: can you approve from sections 1 and 8? As the IT generalist: can you execute sections 3-6 cold? Fix gaps.
Export or save as defense-plan.pdf alongside the .md for portfolio use.
handsOnLab.deliverable: defense-plan.md (and .pdf) — the complete 8-section Zero-Trust Endpoint Defense Plan for Harborview Family Clinic.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All 8 sections present; tier counts sum to 150; every policy section names the tier it applies to; the executive summary is one page of plain language; rollback criteria are written before the phases that need them.

mockTask.q: Panel-style question: the clinic's lead doctor demands local admin on all clinical workstations, saying 'I need to install things without waiting on IT.' How do you handle it?
choices: Grant it — the lead doctor outranks security policy
Refuse flatly and cite the policy document
Acknowledge the workflow need, show the just-in-time elevation path for their legitimate installs, offer a 4-hour urgent SLA, and explain the ransomware risk of fleet-wide admin in plain terms
Quietly grant it on their machine only and tell no one
mockTask.explain: You solve the underlying need (fast installs) with elevation tooling and SLA, while making the risk concrete in their language. Flat refusal loses the relationship; silent grants lose the security posture.
