modules.title: Capstone: AI-Augmented SOC Playbook
modules.summary: Design an AI-assisted SOC workflow for a small security team: which tasks get AI help and which never do, evaluation gates that prove the AI earns its keep, human-in-the-loop approval points, metrics that honestly demonstrate value, and the failure modes you must guard against. The deliverable is a playbook document — portfolio evidence of AI-operations judgment.
objectives: Inventory SOC tasks and classify each as AI-suitable, AI-assisted, or human-only with reasons.
Design evaluation gates (accuracy, hallucination, adversarial) before any AI output touches operations.
Place human-in-the-loop approval points using confidence thresholds and blast-radius reasoning.
Define metrics that honestly prove or disprove the AI's value (MTTD/MTTR, precision, hours saved).
Document failure modes — hallucinated IOCs, prompt injection, automation bias — with mitigations.

notes.title: What a small-team SOC actually does
Where AI helps: the task inventory
notes.body:
Walk the SOC workflow and assign each task. AI-SUITABLE: alert summarization ('condense these 12 related firewall blocks into one paragraph'), IOC enrichment drafts (pull together what the threat feed, WHOIS, and sandbox say — as a draft the analyst verifies), timeline assembly from logs, ticket documentation drafts, and knowledge-base search ('which runbook covers a blocked-domain-controller scenario'). AI-ASSISTED: triage prioritization suggestions ('these 5 of 40 alerts share an IOC — investigate as one'), investigation hypotheses ('the process tree suggests credential dumping — check these two artifacts'), and false-positive likelihood scoring. HUMAN-ONLY: isolating a host, blocking an IOC fleet-wide, declaring an incident, communicating with executives or customers, and approving any AI-suggested containment. Worked example: overnight, 40 Detect alerts arrive. The AI clusters them into 6 groups by IOC and process tree, drafts a one-paragraph summary per group with suggested severity, and pre-fills enrichment. The analyst reviews 6 summaries instead of 40 raw alerts, verifies the enrichment on the top 2, and investigates. Time saved is real — but only because a human still verified before acting. The gotcha: letting 'draft' quietly become 'decision.' If nobody reads the AI summary before the ticket closes, you've built automation with a human costume. Every AI output needs a named human verifier and a verification record.

Worked example — the overnight flow with time accounting. 02:00: 40 Detect alerts land. AI pipeline: deduplicate and cluster by IOC and process tree → 6 groups; draft one-paragraph summary per group with suggested severity and key artifacts; pre-fill enrichment (feed hits, first-seen, affected hosts). 08:00: analyst opens 6 summaries (30 min review), verifies enrichment on the 2 suggested-critical (20 min), investigates group 1 fully (45 min), confirms groups 2-6 as benign-with-notes (15 min). Total: under 2 hours for what was 10 hours of raw triage. The remaining 8 hours go to the phishes, the executive question, the firewall request, and — critically — one proactive hunt the team never had time for before. That's the honest value story: not 'the AI does triage' but 'the AI buys back the hours for work that matters.' The gotcha to document: the morning analyst must actually read the summaries. If the team starts bulk-approving groups, add the verification check — require one artifact link opened per group before the 'confirmed' button enables. Friction in the right place: verification should be easy but not skippable. Pilot one task class at a time and measure before expanding — a second AI-suitable task joins the workflow only after the first holds its precision for a full month.

notes.title: Evaluation gates: proving the AI earns its keep
Human-in-the-loop: approval points and confidence
Metrics that honestly prove value
notes.body:
Measure the AI like you'd measure any SOC investment — against a baseline, with honesty about what the numbers can't show. Baseline first: before the AI, record 4 weeks of mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to respond (MTTR), alerts per analyst per shift, false-positive rate, and escalations missed (found later). Then measure with the AI in assisted production. Metrics that matter: MTTD/MTTR deltas (did we get faster?), analyst hours per alert (did toil actually drop, or did we just move it to verification?), AI precision/recall on the labeled set (is it right?), override rate (do analysts trust it — and should they?), and coverage (are we investigating alert classes we previously ignored for lack of time?). Worked example of honest reporting: 'MTTR fell 35%, but 10 points of that came from the new runbooks we wrote during the project — the AI's isolated contribution is roughly 25%.' That sentence is what separates an operator from a vendor pitch. Report the costs too: verification time, evaluation maintenance, and the shadow-period labor. The gotcha: measuring only speed. An AI that triages 3x faster at 70% precision is a liability factory — precision gates the speed claims. And never present a single metric without its definition; 'accuracy' without a labeled set and a date range is marketing, not measurement.

Worked example — the baseline table (4 weeks pre-AI): MTTD 38 min, MTTR 4.2 hours, alerts per analyst per shift 22, false-positive rate 61%, escalations missed (found later) 3. With AI, quarter one: MTTD 31 min, MTTR 2.7 hours, alerts per analyst 34 (more coverage, same heads), false-positive rate 58%, missed escalations 1. The honest report paragraph: 'MTTR fell 36%. About a third of that gain came from the runbooks we wrote during the project and the clustering workflow itself; the AI's isolated contribution is roughly 20-25%. Verification costs: ~45 min per analyst per shift reviewing AI output, plus 4 hours monthly maintaining the labeled set and gates. Net: positive, and precision on the labeled set held at 93%.' Note what that paragraph does: it separates confounded causes, names the costs, and anchors the claim in the labeled set. Definitions appendix (one line each): MTTD measured from alert creation to analyst acknowledgment; MTTR from acknowledgment to containment-or-close; precision = true-critical / AI-labeled-critical on the monthly labeled-set re-run. Without definitions, metrics are negotiable; with them, they're engineering. Review the full metric set monthly with the team and quarterly with leadership — the monthly cadence catches drift early, while the quarterly view shows whether the investment thesis still holds.

notes.title: Failure modes and guardrails
notes.body:
Every AI failure mode in a SOC has a guardrail — design both together. Failure 1 — hallucinated IOCs: the AI invents a 'clean' verdict or a fake threat-feed reference. Guardrail: every AI factual claim must cite its source artifact (log line, feed entry); uncited claims are flagged, and Gate 2 tests for this continuously. Failure 2 — prompt injection via alert content: attackers can embed instructions in phishing emails, filenames, or log strings that the AI then reads. Guardrail: treat all ingested content as untrusted data, never instructions; Gate 3 adversarial tests run on every prompt change; the AI has no tool access that ingested content can invoke. Failure 3 — automation bias: analysts rubber-stamp AI output. Guardrail: the 5% weekly spot-audit plus override-rate monitoring from the human-in-the-loop design. Failure 4 — data leakage: pasting sensitive logs into a third-party model. Guardrail: data classification policy — what log classes may go to which models; prefer models with no training-data retention for sensitive content, and document the decision. Failure 5 — silent degradation: the AI gets worse as threats and logs evolve. Guardrail: scheduled gate re-runs and a 'return to shadow mode' trigger with a named owner. Worked example: during a spot-audit you find the AI marked a real credential-dumping alert 'likely benign' — response per playbook: pull the AI back to shadow for that alert class, root-cause (prompt? model? log format change?), fix, re-gate, then restore. Incident response applies to your AI tooling too.

Worked example — the full response to the credential-dumping miss. Detection: Tuesday spot-audit flags it — AI said 'likely benign (0.88)', blind re-review says credential dumping. Response per playbook section 7: (1) immediate: pull the 'credential-access' alert class back to shadow mode — the AI still suggests, but every suggestion in that class now requires full manual review; notify the team in the standup. (2) Root cause (same day): the labeled set had only 2 credential-dumping examples and the recent log-format change renamed the field the prompt keyed on — the AI was pattern-matching on a field that no longer exists. (3) Fix: update the prompt to the new field, add 15 credential-dumping examples (including this miss) to the labeled set. (4) Re-gate: run all four gates on the alert class; require 100% recall on the malicious examples. (5) Restore: return the class to assisted production with a 2-week heightened spot-audit (10%). (6) Document: the miss, the cause, and the fix go in the monthly report — publicly. That last step is the culture: misses are system data, and hiding them is the only real failure.

notes.title: Writing the playbook document
notes.body: The playbook is the deliverable — a document a new analyst could read and operate from. Structure: 1. Purpose and scope (which team, which fleet, what the AI does and doesn't do); 2. Task classification matrix (every SOC task mapped to AI-suitable / AI-assisted / human-only, with reasons); 3. Tooling and data flows (which models, what data goes where, retention and classification rules); 4. Evaluation gates (the four gates, labeled-set maintenance, schedules, pass criteria, and the return-to-shadow trigger); 5. Human-in-the-loop design (approval points by blast radius, confidence routing, the decision log schema, spot-audit procedure); 6. Metrics and reporting (baseline, the five metrics, honest-reporting template, review cadence); 7. Failure modes and guardrails (the five failures, each with detection and response); 8. RACI and review cadence (who owns the AI pipeline, who runs gates, who audits — and the quarterly playbook review date). Write section 8 first in draft — unnamed ownership is how playbooks die. Then write it so that your interview panel could ask 'how would you make sure the AI doesn't cause an incident?' and you answer by walking them through sections 4, 5, and 7. The portfolio test: a hiring manager reading this should conclude you think about AI as an operator — measured, gated, and accountable — not as an enthusiast. Close the document with known limitations: what the playbook doesn't cover yet and what you'd add with a bigger team. Honest scoping is a senior signal. Worked example — the RACI table. AI pipeline ownership: [SOC lead] — accountable for gate results and production status. Labeled-set maintenance: [analyst rotation] — responsible for monthly refresh with new misses. Spot-audits: [second analyst] — responsible weekly, reports to SOC lead. Prompt changes: [SOC lead] approves, [analyst] implements, Gate 3 re-run required. Data classification decisions: [SOC lead] with IT management consulted. Quarterly playbook review: [SOC lead] accountable, whole team consulted. The interview walkthrough — 'how would you make sure the AI doesn't cause an incident?' Answer by walking sections 4, 5, 7: 'Four evaluation gates before production including adversarial tests; approval points scaled by blast radius with a two-person rule on fleet-wide actions; every decision logged with AI suggestion, confidence, and human verdict; 5% weekly spot-audits; and a defined return-to-shadow response when anything fails.' That's a 60-second answer that proves operator judgment. Known limitations to close the document: 'This playbook covers alert triage and investigation support only — not automated response, which remains a future phase pending its own evaluation. With a larger team we'd add a dedicated detection-engineering review of AI-suggested rules.' Honest scoping signals seniority more than exhaustive claims do.

cards.front: Small-SOC task classification (3 buckets)?
cards.back: AI-suitable (drafts/summaries, human reviews), AI-assisted (suggestions, human decides), human-only (containment, comms, incident declaration).

cards.front: Name three AI-suitable SOC tasks.
cards.back: Alert summarization, IOC enrichment drafts, timeline assembly, ticket-doc drafts, runbook search.

cards.front: Name two human-only SOC actions.
cards.back: Isolating hosts / fleet-wide blocks, and declaring incidents or communicating with executives.

cards.front: Four evaluation gates before production?
cards.back: Labeled-set accuracy, hallucination traps, adversarial prompt-injection tests, 2–4 week shadow period.

cards.front: What does the shadow period measure?
cards.back: AI suggestions logged without action, scored against what analysts actually did — disagreements become training data.

cards.front: Approval gates scale with what?
cards.back: Blast radius — fleet-wide blocks need two-person approval; summaries need a skim review.

cards.front: What three things does every AI-influenced decision log?
cards.back: What the AI suggested, its confidence, and what the human decided.

cards.front: Automation bias countermeasure?
cards.back: Random 5% weekly spot-audits of AI-approved items for full re-review.

cards.front: Five metrics for AI value?
cards.back: MTTD/MTTR deltas, analyst hours per alert, AI precision/recall, override rate, coverage of previously-ignored alert classes.

cards.front: Honest reporting example?
cards.back: Attribute gains separately — 'MTTR fell 35%; ~10 points from new runbooks, ~25% from the AI.' Report verification costs too.

cards.front: Prompt injection via alert content — guardrail?
cards.back: Treat ingested content as untrusted data, never instructions; adversarial tests on every prompt change; no AI-invokable tools reachable from content.

cards.front: AI failure response per playbook?
cards.back: Return that alert class to shadow mode, root-cause, fix, re-gate, then restore — incident response applies to AI tooling.

quiz.q: Which task belongs in HUMAN-ONLY?
choices: Isolating a host from the network
quiz.explain: Containment disrupts business and carries accountability that can't be delegated — the human decides and owns it.

quiz.q: Gate 2 (hallucination testing) feeds the AI:
choices: Alerts with traps — fake IOCs and hosts — checking it admits lack of evidence
quiz.explain: You must verify the AI says 'I don't have evidence' rather than inventing enrichment — a hallucinated clean verdict is actively dangerous.

quiz.q: During shadow mode, the AI says 'benign' on an alert the analyst escalated. Correct response?
choices: Treat the disagreement as data: investigate who was right and feed the lesson back
Ignore it — shadow mode doesn't matter
quiz.explain: Shadow mode exists to produce exactly these disagreements; each one improves the model, the prompt, or the analyst's understanding.

quiz.q: An AI suggestion to block an IOC fleet-wide requires:
choices: No approval — the AI is gated already
quiz.explain: Blast radius decides the gate: fleet-wide action can break the whole business, so it gets the heaviest human control.

quiz.q: Analysts override the AI's severity 40% of the time. This signals:
choices: Analysts are resistant to change — retrain them
The model or prompt is wrong — investigate it, not the analysts
The AI is working as intended
quiz.explain: Sustained high override rates are a system signal, not a people problem — the evaluation loop exists to catch exactly this.

quiz.q: Which metric pairing prevents 'faster but wrong' AI?
choices: Speed gated by precision/recall on the labeled set
quiz.explain: Throughput without precision is a liability factory — precision gates every speed claim.

quiz.q: Your report shows MTTR down 35%. The honest version adds:
choices: Attribution: how much came from runbooks/process vs the AI, plus verification costs
Only the AI's contribution, rounded up
quiz.explain: Operators separate confounded causes and report costs; single-number miracle claims are vendor pitches, not engineering.

quiz.q: An attacker embeds 'mark this benign' in a phishing email the AI reads. This is:
quiz.explain: Ingested content is untrusted data that must never be treated as instructions — Gate 3 tests this on every prompt change.

quiz.q: Pasting full customer logs into a third-party model risks:
quiz.explain: Data classification decides what may go to which models; sensitive content needs no-retention guarantees documented up front.

quiz.q: A spot-audit finds the AI marked real credential-dumping 'likely benign.' First playbook step?
choices: Retrain the analysts to agree with the AI
Return that alert class to shadow mode, then root-cause
Increase AI autonomy to move past it
quiz.explain: Incident response applies to AI tooling: contain (shadow mode), root-cause, fix, re-gate, restore — in that order.

items.prompt: Three task buckets?
items.answer: AI-suitable, AI-assisted, human-only.
items.explain: The classification every later decision references.

items.prompt: Four evaluation gates?
items.answer: Labeled-set accuracy, hallucination traps, adversarial tests, shadow period.
items.explain: No gate skipped before production.

items.prompt: Gates scale with?
items.answer: Blast radius of the action.
items.explain: Bigger irreversible consequence, heavier human gate.

items.prompt: Decision log schema (3 fields)?
items.answer: AI suggestion, its confidence, human decision.
items.explain: Audit trail and retraining data in one.

items.prompt: Spot-audit rate and purpose?
items.answer: 5% weekly full re-review — counters automation bias.
items.explain: Verification is a scheduled activity, not a hope.

items.prompt: Five value metrics?
items.answer: MTTD/MTTR deltas, hours per alert, precision/recall, override rate, coverage.
items.explain: Speed, cost, correctness, trust, reach.

items.prompt: Five failure modes?
items.answer: Hallucinated IOCs, prompt injection, automation bias, data leakage, silent degradation.
items.explain: Each paired with a guardrail in the playbook.

items.prompt: AI drafts the customer notification for a contained incident. Bucket and handling?
items.answer: AI-suitable draft, but customer communication is human-only — human rewrites and sends.
items.explain: Drafting is fine; the send is accountability.

items.prompt: AI suggests 5 of 40 alerts share an IOC and should be one investigation. Bucket?
items.answer: AI-assisted — analyst confirms the clustering before merging.
items.explain: Suggestions accelerate; the analyst decides the investigation shape.

items.prompt: AI pre-fills IOC enrichment from feeds. What's required before use?
items.answer: Analyst verifies the enrichment; every factual claim cites its source artifact.
items.explain: Uncited AI claims are flagged — enrichment is a draft, not evidence.

items.prompt: Overnight, AI wants to auto-isolate a server with no analyst on shift. Allowed?
items.answer: No — containment is human-only; the AI queues it as a high-priority suggestion for the morning analyst with full context.
items.explain: No autonomous containment, ever, in this design — the blast radius rule doesn't sleep.

items.prompt: Which SOC task is the best FIRST AI pilot?
items.answer: Alert summarization/clustering — high toil, low blast radius, easily verified.
items.explain: Pilot where failure is cheap and verification is easy; expand after gates pass.

items.prompt: An analyst never overrides the AI anymore. Signal or success?
items.answer: Warning signal — possible automation bias; check spot-audit results and override trends.
items.explain: Zero overrides is as suspicious as 40% — verification must stay real.

items.prompt: AI cites a threat-feed article that doesn't exist. Failure and guardrail?
items.answer: Hallucination — require source-artifact citation; re-run Gate 2 traps.
items.explain: Uncited claims get flagged; the gate suite re-validates.

items.prompt: Logs show the AI's precision dropped 12 points this month. Playbook response?
items.answer: Return to shadow mode, root-cause (drift? log format change?), fix, re-gate before restoring.
items.explain: Silent degradation gets a scheduled detection (gate re-runs) and a defined response.

items.prompt: A junior analyst pasted a full mailbox export into the AI chat. Issue?
items.answer: Data leakage — violates classification policy; review what was sent, confirm retention terms, retrain.
items.explain: The data-flow section exists so this is a policy violation with a response, not a shrug.

items.prompt: Two analysts disagree with the AI's severity on the same alert class repeatedly. Action?
items.answer: Investigate the class: prompt, model, or labeled-set gap — treat as evaluation data, not insubordination.
items.explain: Sustained disagreement is the evaluation loop working; follow it.

items.prompt: Executive asks 'can the AI just handle nights alone?' Your answer?
items.answer: No — containment and incident declaration stay human-only; the AI queues prioritized work for the morning analyst. Show the blast-radius rationale.
items.explain: The playbook's classification is the shield against autonomy creep — cite it.

handsOnLab.title: Write the AI-Augmented SOC Playbook + run a mini evaluation
handsOnLab.brief: Produce the full 8-section SOC playbook document, then run a hands-on mini-evaluation: score 10 sample AI triage summaries against analyst ground truth and compute precision.
steps: Create soc-playbook.md with the 8-section skeleton: purpose/scope, task matrix, tooling/data flows, evaluation gates, human-in-the-loop, metrics, failure modes, RACI/review.
Draft section 8 (RACI) first: name owners for the AI pipeline, gate runs, audits, and the quarterly review.
Build the task classification matrix: list at least 15 real SOC tasks, each mapped to a bucket with a one-line reason.
Write the data-flow section: which log classes go to which models, retention terms, and the classification rule.
Specify the four gates concretely: labeled-set size and pass criteria, trap examples, adversarial test strings, shadow-period length and scoring method.
Design the human-in-the-loop: approval points by blast radius, confidence routing thresholds, the decision-log schema, spot-audit procedure.
Write the metrics section with the baseline-then-measure method and the honest-reporting template.
Write the five failure modes, each with detection method and playbook response.
Mini-evaluation: write 10 short sample alert summaries as 'AI output' and an analyst ground-truth disposition for each; 3 of the 10 should be deliberately wrong or hallucinated.
Score them in eval-scores.csv: columns alert_id, ai_suggestion, ground_truth, match (y/n), notes. Compute precision = matches/10.
Write a 5-line evaluation memo: precision result, which failure types appeared, what gate would have caught each.
Re-read the playbook as a new analyst: can you operate sections 4-7 from the document alone? Fix gaps.
handsOnLab.deliverable: soc-playbook.md (8 sections) + eval-scores.csv with precision calculation and evaluation memo.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All 8 sections present with named owners; ≥15 tasks classified with reasons; eval-scores.csv has 10 scored rows, a computed precision, and each miss mapped to the gate that would catch it.

videos.title: MIT 6.858 Computer Systems Security (OCW) — threat models and defenses
videos.blurb: MIT's systems-security course lectures on threat models, privilege separation, and network security — the conceptual foundation beneath the SOC workflows in this playbook.

mockTask.q: Panel-style question: it's 2 AM and your AI triage assistant recommends isolating a domain controller immediately, with no human review step in the workflow. What do you do?
choices: Let it isolate — the AI passed evaluation gates, so it's trusted
Wake the on-call analyst: containment is human-only; the AI's recommendation becomes a high-priority queued suggestion with full context, and you review the workflow gap in the morning
Disable the AI for making an out-of-scope recommendation
Isolate it yourself without investigating, to be safe
mockTask.explain: Containment never auto-executes in this design — blast-radius rules don't sleep. The recommendation is valuable as prioritized context, and the missing human gate is a playbook defect to fix, not a reason to either trust blindly or kill the tool.

drills.title: Triage order
drills.prompt: Denied: powershell.exe spawned by winword.exe, encoded command line, first-seen today. Disposition?
choices: Escalate as likely malicious: investigate fully, contain the host, do not allow
drills.explain: Encoded PowerShell from Office + first-seen = classic malicious pattern. Contain and investigate; never allow on hope.

drills.title: Hash mismatch
drills.prompt: Legitimate app updates nightly; each update triggers denials. Sustainable fix?
choices: Publisher-certificate rule instead of per-hash, with version verification
drills.explain: Rule-strength discipline: publisher rules survive updates; hashes don't. Verify the signer chain, then trust the publisher.

drills.title: Privilege separation
choices: Splitting a system into least-privilege components so one compromise doesn't yield all
drills.explain: Compartmentalization: the compromised renderer can't touch the browser kernel. Elevation control is the endpoint expression.

drills.title: Base rate
drills.prompt: Your anomaly detector flags 50 events/day; 1 is real. The operational problem is:
choices: Alert fatigue: precision ≈2% means analysts will ignore it — tune threshold to costs or add corroborating signals
drills.explain: Base-rate math: rare threats + sensitive detectors = false-alarm floods. Cost-aware thresholds and compound signals fix it.

drills.title: 'Why blocked?'
drills.prompt: A non-technical manager asks why the CFO's macro tool was blocked. Best answer:
choices: ATT&CK T1059, hash mismatch, ringfence policy 7.2
Plain language: what the tool tried to do, why that pattern is risky, what safe path exists (ringfenced approval)
drills.explain: Stakeholder language: behavior → risk → path forward. Technique IDs go in the ticket, not the conversation.

terminalSims.title: Allowlist break-fix triage: LedgerPro won't launch
terminalSims.prompt: A user reports the accounting app 'LedgerPro' fails to launch after its updater ran last night. The portal shows the launch was blocked by Application Control. Triage it like a Cyber Hero operator.
script: Confirm the symptom: have the user launch LedgerPro again and note the exact block message/time.
Open the portal alert for the block; read the denied action: which process, which parent, what file identity (hash).
Compare the blocked child's hash to the approved hash in the LedgerPro policy.
Check the policy: does the parent rule cover child processes of LedgerPro's updater?
Grant a time-boxed approval for the new updater hash per the exception workflow.
Have the user retry the launch; confirm success and log the exception with an expiry date.
expected: LedgerPro.exe launches, then its updater child process is denied
Denied action: child process launch; hash differs from approved version
Policy approves the parent binary only; updater child has no rule
Temporary approval granted for the new updater hash (expires in 7 days)
LedgerPro launches cleanly after approval
Exception documented: hash, reason (legit updater), expiry, approver
terminalSims.answer: The updater replaced the child binary, so its hash no longer matches the allowlist. The parent-only rule is doing its job. Fix: time-boxed approval for the new updater hash, verify the launch, document the exception with an expiry — never widen the rule to trust the whole folder.

terminalSims.title: Ringfence block investigation: Word calling PowerShell
terminalSims.prompt: ThreatLocker Detect fired: 'winword.exe attempted to launch powershell.exe - blocked by Ringfencing.' You are on shift. Investigate.
script: Open the Detect alert; capture parent process (winword.exe), child (powershell.exe), user, host, timestamp.
Read the Office ringfence policy: is 'execute other applications' blocked for Word? Confirm the block is policy, not malfunction.
Identify the triggering document: which file did Word have open, where did it come from (email attachment? download?).
Check the host for persistence artifacts: Run keys, scheduled tasks, startup folder (document, do not clean yet).
Follow the runbook: isolate the host from the network if the document source is untrusted.
Write the incident note: alert ID, policy that fired, document source, host status, next step (forensics/MDR handoff).
expected: Alert: winword.exe -> powershell.exe, blocked, Ringfencing policy 'Office apps'
Policy blocks Office apps from executing other applications - block is expected behavior
Triggering file: invoice.docx from an external email attachment
No new persistence artifacts found on a quick check
Host isolated from the network pending review
Incident note filed with alert ID, source document, and escalation to the security lead
terminalSims.answer: Ringfencing did exactly what it is for: a trusted app (Word) was weaponized and the child launch was denied. Treat the block as an IOC, trace the malicious document, check persistence, isolate if the source is untrusted, and hand a clean incident note up the chain.

terminalSims.title: Detect alert triage: three alerts, one shift
terminalSims.prompt: Three Detect alerts queue up at once: (a) blocked registry edit by an updater, (b) blocked network session from a browser to an unknown IP, (c) blocked file write by a PDF reader. Classify and prioritize.
script: Read all three alerts fully: process tree, blocked action, host, user, time.
Classify each by module and action type: updater/registry, browser/network, reader/file-write.
Score severity: which blocked action most resembles weaponization vs routine breakage?
Pick the highest-severity alert and investigate first; park the others with a note.
For the top alert, pull the parent process chain and the file/process that triggered it.
Write triage dispositions for all three: severity, verdict (malicious-likely / break-fix / false-positive-candidate), next step.
expected: Alert details captured for all three (process trees, blocked actions, hosts)
Classification: updater break-fix candidate; browser C2-candidate; reader weaponization-candidate
Priority order: browser network block first, then reader file-write, then updater
Browser alert: parent chain shows updater download launched the browser with args
Reader alert: PDF came from an email attachment opened minutes before
Three disposition notes written with severity, verdict, and next step
terminalSims.answer: Triage is classification before action: read the blocked action, map it to weaponization likelihood, work the worst first. The browser-to-unknown-IP block and the reader file-write from an email attachment outrank a routine updater registry block. Document a disposition for every alert — even the ones you park.

terminalSims.title: Elevation request audit: spot the social engineer
terminalSims.prompt: Five elevation requests sit in the queue. One of them is a social-engineering attempt. Audit the queue and find it.
script: List all five requests: requesting user, application, justification, time, host.
Check each application against the approved elevation policy: is this app allowed to elevate?
Flag anomalies: off-hours requests, apps never elevated before, justifications that don't match the app.
For the suspect request, check the user's recent activity: any password reset, new device, odd login?
Deny the suspicious request with a documented reason; approve or escalate the legitimate ones per policy.
Write the audit note: what was suspicious, what you did, what the helpdesk should tell the user.
expected: Five requests listed with user, app, justification, time
Four match approved elevation policies; one does not
Suspect: remote-support tool requested at 2:14 AM by a user who never uses it, justification 'urgent fix'
User's account had a password reset yesterday from an unrecognized device
Suspicious request denied with reason; four legitimate ones processed
Audit note filed; helpdesk scripted to call the user back on a known number
terminalSims.answer: Elevation Control moves the decision from the user's UAC prompt to your policy queue — which makes the queue a social-engineering target. Audit for the anomalies: unusual app, off-hours, weak justification, account changes. Deny with a documented reason and verify the user out-of-band; never approve an elevation you can't explain.

terminalSims.title: Storage Control exfiltration block: the USB at 5 PM
terminalSims.prompt: Storage Control blocked a USB mass-storage write on a finance workstation: 400 MB of files attempted to a personal drive. Respond.
script: Open the Storage Control block event: device ID, file paths attempted, user, host, timestamp.
Check the storage policy for this group: are personal USB drives denied? Confirm the block is policy-correct.
List the attempted file paths — are they sensitive (payroll, PII) or routine?
Check whether the user has a history of approved USB use or prior blocks.
Follow the runbook: preserve the event evidence, notify the supervisor per policy, interview the user with the helpdesk script.
Write the incident note: what was blocked, sensitivity of data, user explanation, escalation decision.
expected: Block event: personal USB device, 400 MB, paths under the payroll share
Policy denies personal mass storage for the finance group - block is correct
Attempted files include payroll exports (sensitive)
No prior approved USB use for this user; first block event
Evidence preserved; supervisor notified per policy; user interview scheduled
Incident note filed with data-sensitivity assessment and escalation recommendation
terminalSims.answer: Storage Control turned a potential exfiltration into a blocked event with full evidence. Your job is not to unblock it — it is to assess: what data, whose device, what history, what policy says. Preserve the evidence, notify per the runbook, interview the user, and escalate based on data sensitivity, not on how loudly the user complains.

terminalSims.title: Network Control lateral-movement block: the chatty workstation
terminalSims.prompt: Network Control blocked a workstation attempting SMB connections to 20 other hosts in two minutes. The user says 'everything is fine.' It is not fine. Work it.
script: Open the Network Control events: source host, destination hosts, ports (445), timeframe, blocked count.
Check the dynamic ACL state: was SMB ever legitimately open for this workstation? Confirm the blocks are policy.
Look at the source host's recent history: any Detect alerts, new processes, user logins in the last 24 hours.
Pattern-check: sequential host scanning vs a few legitimate shares — this smells like worm behavior.
Follow the runbook: isolate the source host from the network immediately; do not reimage before forensics triage.
Write the incident note: scope (20 hosts attempted), pattern, isolation time, handoff to IR/forensics.
expected: Events: 20 distinct hosts on port 445 within 2 minutes, all blocked
No legitimate SMB ACL for this workstation - blocks are policy-correct
Source host shows a Detect alert 40 minutes earlier: blocked script execution
Pattern is sequential scanning, consistent with worm-like lateral movement
Source host isolated; reimage held pending forensics
Incident note filed with scope, timeline, isolation time, and IR handoff
terminalSims.answer: Twenty SMB targets in two minutes is not a user browsing shares — it is lateral movement, and Network Control's dynamic ACLs stopped it at the first hop. Correlate with the earlier Detect alert on the source host, isolate immediately, hold the reimage for forensics, and hand IR a scoped, timed incident note.

terminalSims.title: PowerShell log triage: find the blocked actions
terminalSims.prompt: You have a Windows event log export from a pilot machine. Use PowerShell to find every blocked application-launch event in the last 7 days, grouped by process name.
script: Import the log export (CSV) into PowerShell with Import-Csv.
Filter rows to the last 7 days using Where-Object on the timestamp column.
Filter further to blocked/denied application-launch events.
Group by process name with Group-Object; sort by count descending.
Export the grouped result to a CSV for the pilot report.
Read the top 3 groups and write a one-line disposition for each (legit updater? unknown? needs policy?).
expected: CSV imported; row count matches the export
Date filter keeps only the last 7 days of events
Only blocked/denied launch events remain
Grouped output: process names with counts, sorted high to low
pilot-blocked-launches.csv written
Three disposition lines: e.g. 'updater.exe x42 - legit updater, needs child rule'
terminalSims.answer: PowerShell turns a raw log export into a triage list in six steps: import, date-filter, action-filter, group, export, disposition. The grouped counts tell you where the policy pain is — the top processes are your first policy fixes for the pilot report.

terminalSims.title: Hash verification of a quarantined file
terminalSims.prompt: A suspicious file was quarantined from a workstation. Before anyone declares it malware or safe, verify its identity properly: hash it, check its signature, and record chain of custody.
script: Copy the quarantined file to your analysis folder; record source host, path, quarantine time, and your name (chain of custody).
Compute SHA-256 with Get-FileHash; record the full hash.
Check the file's digital signature with Get-AuthenticodeSignature; note signer and status.
Compare the hash against your known-good baseline list and note match/no-match (do not upload to third parties without authorization).
Record file metadata: size, timestamps, version info if present.
Write the verification note: hash, signature status, baseline comparison, and your verdict (verified-legit / unknown / suspicious) with reasoning.
expected: Chain-of-custody line recorded: host, path, time, handler
SHA-256 hash computed and recorded in full
Signature status noted (e.g. Valid, signed by vendor / NotSigned)
Baseline comparison result recorded
Metadata captured: size, timestamps, version
Verification note with a reasoned verdict, not a guess
terminalSims.answer: Identity before verdict: hash the file, check its signature, compare to your baseline, and write down every step with chain of custody. A valid vendor signature plus a baseline hash match means legit; an unsigned binary with no match means treat-as-suspicious and escalate. Never declare malware from a filename.

terminalSims.title: Phishing header analysis: the 'IT helpdesk' email
terminalSims.prompt: A user forwarded a suspicious email claiming to be from the IT helpdesk asking them to 're-verify' credentials. Analyze the headers and content like a support operator.
script: Open the full message headers; read the Received chain bottom-up to find the true origin.
Check the From address vs the Reply-To address for mismatch.
Check authentication results: SPF, DKIM, DMARC pass or fail.
Hover (don't click) the links: compare display text to the real destination domain.
Note urgency/threat language and credential-request red flags in the body.
Write the verdict note: phishing or legit, with 3+ cited evidence points, plus the user-facing explanation.
expected: Received chain traced to an origin unrelated to the company's mail
From says 'IT Helpdesk' but Reply-To is an external freemail address
SPF/DKIM fail or are absent; DMARC not enforced for the spoofed domain
Link destinations point to a lookalike domain, not the company portal
Body uses urgency ('account locked in 24 hours') and asks for credentials
Verdict: phishing, with cited evidence and a plain-language user explanation
terminalSims.answer: Phishing analysis is evidence collection: the Received chain gives you origin, Reply-To vs From gives you impersonation, SPF/DKIM/DMARC gives you authentication, and the link destinations give you intent. Cite at least three evidence points in your verdict, then translate it into plain language the user will actually remember.

terminalSims.title: Run the Python anomaly detector on login data
terminalSims.prompt: You have a synthetic login CSV (user, hour, location, success). Run the course's baseline anomaly detector, interpret its precision/recall, and tune the threshold once.
script: Inspect the CSV: columns, row count, and a few sample rows.
Run the detector script with the default threshold; capture its flagged logins.
Using the labeled answer column, compute true positives, false positives, precision and recall by hand.
Raise the threshold and re-run; note how precision and recall move.
Lower the threshold and re-run; note how precision and recall move.
Write the tuning note: which threshold you would ship for a SOC queue and why (alert fatigue vs missed attacks).
expected: CSV inspected: columns and sample rows understood
Default-threshold run flags a set of logins
Precision and recall computed from the labels
Higher threshold: fewer flags, higher precision, lower recall
Lower threshold: more flags, lower precision, higher recall
Tuning note with a chosen threshold justified by the precision/recall tradeoff
terminalSims.answer: A detector is a threshold with a tradeoff: raising it buys precision (fewer false alarms) and costs recall (more missed attacks). Compute both from labeled data, move the threshold both directions to feel the tradeoff, then choose the setting your SOC queue can actually live with — and write down why.

blocks.body:
- Never trust, always verify — every request is authenticated and authorized, every time
- Default-deny: that which is not explicitly allowed is denied — allowlisting is the endpoint enforcement of this
- Assume breach: design as if the attacker is already inside; limit blast radius, not just the perimeter
- Least privilege: every app and user gets the minimum access needed — nothing more, never 'just in case'
- Verify explicitly: identity, device health, and context — not network location
- Policy engine decides, policy administrator executes, policy enforcement point blocks — know the three roles

- Learning Mode baselines, Secured/Monitor enforces — never go straight to Enforce on a new policy
- Identity by hash + certificate + path, in that order of strength — filenames prove nothing
- A patched app is a NEW hash — pre-approve vendor updates or Patch Tuesday becomes ticket Tuesday
- Parent rules do not cover children — updaters and helpers need their own explicit rules
- Monitor-mode first: log what WOULD break for 48+ hours before enforcing
- Every exception gets an expiry date, an approver, and a reason — undocumented exceptions are holes
- Break-fix order: read the blocked action, check the policy, test the exception, document

cheatSheets.title: Ringfencing rules of thumb — one-line memory aids

blocks.body:
- Ringfencing answers: 'this app is allowed, but what is it allowed TO DO?'
- Block trusted apps from executing other apps — Word launching PowerShell is the canonical kill
- Browsers, Office, PDF readers get the tightest rings — they face the internet and email
- Restrict four axes: execute, registry, file read/write, network — scope each to what the app truly needs
- A ringfence block is an IOC, not just a ticket — trace the triggering document or download
- Test the ring with a scripted weaponization attempt before you call it done

cheatSheets.title: Incident response lifecycle — one-line memory aids

blocks.body:
- NIST 800-61 order: Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, Post-Incident Activity
- Scope before you act — one host or a fleet changes everything about containment
- Isolate the session/host, not the server — stop the attacker without creating an outage
- Verify, don't assume: check that blocks held, files open, no ransom notes — then declare
- Preserve evidence before reimaging — reimage destroys the forensics IR needs
- Every incident ends with a timeline, lessons learned, and hardening actions — or it will repeat
- Escalate up the chain with facts (what, scope, containment, verification) — never all-staff panic emails

cheatSheets.title: Crypto math formulas — one-line memory aids

blocks.body:
- gcd via Euclid: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b) — the workhorse under RSA key generation
- Modular arithmetic: (a*b) mod m = ((a mod m)*(b mod m)) mod m — keeps numbers small
- Euler's theorem: a^phi(n) = 1 mod n for coprime a,n — why RSA decryption undoes encryption
- RSA: pick primes p,q; n=pq; phi=(p-1)(q-1); choose e coprime to phi; d = e^-1 mod phi; encrypt c=m^e mod n, decrypt m=c^d mod n
- Diffie-Hellman: both sides compute g^(ab) mod p from exchanged g^a, g^b — shared secret, no shared secret sent
- Hashing is one-way (SHA-256 for file identity); encryption is reversible with the key — don't confuse them
- Salts defeat rainbow tables; work factors (bcrypt/Argon2) defeat brute force — passwords need both ideas

cheatSheets.title: MITRE ATT&CK tactic order — one-line memory aids

blocks.body:
- Tactic order: Reconnaissance -> Resource Development -> Initial Access -> Execution -> Persistence -> Privilege Escalation -> Defense Evasion -> Credential Access -> Discovery -> Lateral Movement -> Collection -> Command and Control -> Exfiltration -> Impact
- IOCs are artifacts (hashes, IPs); IOAs are behaviors (Word->PowerShell) — behaviors survive infrastructure changes
- Map every blocked action to a tactic: it turns 'we blocked X' into a story executives understand
- Ringfencing kills Execution and Defense Evasion; Network Control kills Lateral Movement and C2; Storage Control kills Exfiltration
- Initial Access is usually phishing or external remote services — M44 and M06 are your shields there
- When triaging, ask 'which tactic is the attacker ON?' — it tells you what comes next

cheatSheets.title: Cyber Hero triage — the denied-event loop

blocks.body: Process tree, hash, signer, parent chain, command line. The event tells a story — read all of it before deciding.
Known-good / known-bad / unknown-business / unknown-suspicious. Severity = confidence × asset × blast radius.
Reputation, prevalence, first-seen, behavior (network, persistence). Two independent signals minimum.
Allow (policy entry) · deny (documented) · ringfence (needed but risky) · escalate (out of scope). Every event gets one.
App updated → hash changed → denied. Verify publisher + version, update the policy entry, document.
Scope: who/what's affected. Workaround via exception workflow, never via disabling enforcement.
Fix through policy, not around it. Every exception is a policy entry with an owner and a review date.
Define the attacker (capabilities, goals) before the defense. Controls without a threat model are decoration.
Split into least-privilege components; compromise of one ≠ compromise of all. (See: elevation control.)
Buffer overflows, ROP: attacker redirects execution. Defenses: ASLR, DEP/NX, stack canaries, CFI.
Same-origin policy, CSRF tokens, TLS 1.3 handshake (RFC 8446). Know what the padlock actually proves.
Baseline → features → threshold tuned to base rate → evaluated with cost-aware metrics. AI proposes, human disposes.
'Why we blocked this': tactic + technique + evidence, in stakeholder language. Map every detection.
Security+ (baseline) → CySA+ (SOC) → GSEC/CISSP (depth). MIT xPRO for the 6.858 spine. Independent prep — no affiliation claimed.
Operator depth + STAR stories + live triage narration. The course's mock panel is the rehearsal.
