branchingScenarios.title: Ransomware at 2 AM: the Detect alert that wakes you

start.text: 02:14 AM. Your phone buzzes: ThreatLocker Detect fired on FILESERVER-02 — 'mass file rename blocked by Storage Control; ransomware-like behavior.' The on-call runbook says: assess, contain, escalate. What do you do first?

choices.label: Open the Detect alert and read the full event before touching anything
choices.feedback: Correct first move. The alert shows a single user session renaming hundreds of files under the shared drive; Storage Control denied the writes. You now know scope before acting.

choices.label: Immediately shut down FILESERVER-02 from the portal
choices.feedback: Too fast. You just killed the file server for the whole company with no scoping — morning shift will find an outage AND an incident. Go back and assess first.

choices.label: Call the user whose session is renaming files and ask what they're doing
choices.feedback: The user doesn't answer at 2 AM, and you've tipped off a potentially compromised account. Go back and assess first.

assess-scope.text: Scoped: one user session (j.rivera) on FILESERVER-02, ~800 rename attempts blocked in 6 minutes, writes denied. The session is still active. What's the containment call?

choices.label: Isolate the affected workstation/session and disable the user account per the runbook
choices.feedback: Correct. You cut the attacker's foothold without killing the server. The renames were all blocked, so the data is intact.

choices.label: Just watch the session to 'gather more intel'
choices.feedback: While you watch, the session pivots to a second share. Passive observation during active ransomware behavior is how incidents double in size. Go back.

choices.label: Delete the user's files to 'stop the encryption'
choices.feedback: The files were never encrypted — the writes were blocked. Deleting them would destroy intact data. Go back.

verify-data.text: Contained. Now: were any writes NOT blocked? Storage Control denied the renames, but you must verify integrity before declaring victory.

choices.label: Spot-check the share: confirm files open, check for ransom notes, review the block log for any allowed writes
choices.feedback: Correct. No ransom notes, files open cleanly, block log shows 100% denial. You have verified, not assumed.

choices.label: Assume the blocks held and go back to sleep
choices.feedback: Assumption is the enemy. One allowed write you didn't check becomes the foothold next week. Go back and verify.

escalate.text: Verified intact. It's 2:40 AM. Who needs to know, and in what order?

choices.label: Page the security lead now with a structured note (what, scope, containment, verification), then notify the account owner in the morning
choices.feedback: Correct. The lead gets the facts while it's fresh; the user gets a calm, documented conversation at business hours.

choices.label: Email the whole company about the attack right now
choices.feedback: A 2 AM all-staff email about ransomware creates panic and leaks incident details. Escalate up the chain, not out to everyone. Go back.

post-incident.text: Morning. The lead asks for the post-incident writeup. What makes it complete?

choices.label: Timeline, blocked-action evidence, containment steps, verification results, and two hardening actions (e.g. review j.rivera's access, tighten the share's storage policy)
choices.feedback: Correct. A complete writeup ends with actions that make the next 2 AM call less likely.

choices.label: A one-liner: 'Ransomware blocked, all good.'
choices.feedback: That teaches the organization nothing and protects no one. Go back and write the real report.

branchingScenarios.resolution: The winning path: read the alert fully, scope before acting, isolate the session (not the server), verify data integrity instead of assuming it, escalate up the chain with a structured note, and close with a post-incident report that includes hardening actions. Containment without verification is theater; verification without documentation is wasted.

branchingScenarios.title: Patch Tuesday: the legit app that stopped working

start.text: Wednesday morning after Patch Tuesday. Three users report the shipping app 'ShipFast' crashes on launch. The helpdesk swears 'nothing changed.' The portal shows Application Control blocks on ShipFast's updater service. Diagnose it.

choices.label: Check the blocked-action details: which binary, which hash, what changed vs the approved version
choices.feedback: Correct. The updater's hash changed with the patch; the allowlist still holds the old hash. You found the actual cause.

choices.label: Tell the users to reinstall ShipFast from the vendor site
choices.feedback: A fresh install won't fix a hash-mismatch block — the new binary still isn't approved, and now you've added an unvetted installer to the mix. Go back and diagnose.

choices.label: Temporarily disable Application Control on those machines 'until it works'
choices.feedback: You just turned off the endpoint's primary protection on three machines to fix a crash. That is never the answer. Go back.

scope-impact.text: Root cause found: patch changed the updater hash. Before fixing, how wide is this?

choices.label: Check how many machines ran the patch and show the same block — scope the fix to all of them at once
choices.feedback: Correct. It's 14 machines, not 3. One fix for all 14 beats 14 separate tickets.

choices.label: Fix just the three reported machines and move on
choices.feedback: The other 11 will file tickets by lunch. Scope first, fix once. Go back.

fix-properly.text: 14 machines affected. What's the right fix?

choices.label: Approve the new updater hash through the exception workflow with a note tying it to the vendor patch, then verify launches on a test machine
choices.feedback: Correct. Verified vendor patch + approved hash + test = a defensible, documented fix.

choices.label: Add a blanket allow rule for the whole ShipFast folder to 'prevent this next time'
choices.feedback: A folder-wide allow rule means any malware dropped in that folder runs free. You traded a crash for a hole. Go back.

prevent-repeat.text: Fixed and verified. Patch Tuesday happens every month. What changes so this doesn't repeat?

choices.label: Add a pre-patch step to the change process: check vendor release notes for binary changes, stage the patch on a pilot machine, pre-approve new hashes
choices.feedback: Correct. You turned a break-fix into a process improvement — that's operator maturity.

choices.label: Nothing — you'll just fix it faster next month
choices.feedback: Faster firefighting is still firefighting. Go back and build the process.

branchingScenarios.resolution: Break-fix discipline: diagnose the blocked action (hash changed), scope the impact before fixing (14 machines, not 3), fix through the exception workflow with verification (never disable protection, never blanket-allow a folder), and close the loop with a process change so Patch Tuesday stops being a surprise.

branchingScenarios.title: The elevation request that isn't what it seems

start.text: An elevation request arrives: user m.chen requests admin rights for 'TeamViewer_QS.exe', justification: 'vendor needs to fix my printer urgently.' The phone number in the ticket doesn't match the directory. Walk it.

choices.label: Hold the request and verify the user through a known-good channel before deciding
choices.feedback: Correct instinct. The mismatched phone number is a classic pretexting flag — verify identity out-of-band first.

choices.label: Approve it — the user sounds urgent and printers are a common ticket
choices.feedback: Urgency is the social engineer's favorite tool. You just gave admin to a stranger's remote-access tool. Go back.

choices.label: Deny it silently with no note
choices.feedback: If it's legit, the user is stuck; if it's an attack, nobody learns anything. Denials need documentation. Go back.

verify-identity.text: You call m.chen on the directory-listed number. She says she never requested anything and her printer is fine. Now what?

choices.label: Deny the request with a documented reason, flag the account for a password reset and review, notify the security lead
choices.feedback: Correct. The request was fraudulent; the account may be compromised. Deny, document, reset, escalate.

choices.label: Just deny it and close the ticket
choices.feedback: The attacker still has the compromised account and will try again in an hour. Go back and treat the account as compromised.

check-scope.text: Account flagged. Do you check whether this attacker tried anything else?

choices.label: Review the user's recent elevation requests, login history, and any Detect alerts on their machine in the last 48 hours
choices.feedback: Correct. You find two more denied elevation attempts yesterday — a pattern, not a one-off. Now the lead has a real case.

choices.label: No — one denied request is enough paperwork
choices.feedback: Attackers retry. The pattern is the finding. Go back and look.

harden.text: Pattern confirmed and escalated. What process change makes the next attempt harder?

choices.label: Add an out-of-band identity verification step to the elevation runbook for any request with mismatched contact info, odd apps, or urgency pressure
choices.feedback: Correct. You turned one attack into a standing control — the queue is now hardened against the exact pretext used.

choices.label: Nothing — the team handled it fine this time
choices.feedback: Handling it once is luck; hardening the process is defense. Go back and close the loop.

branchingScenarios.resolution: Elevation queues are social-engineering targets because urgency bypasses thinking. The discipline: verify identity out-of-band on any anomaly (mismatched contact, odd app, urgency), treat a fraudulent request as a compromised account (deny + document + reset + escalate), and always check for a pattern — attackers retry.

branchingScenarios.title: USB exfiltration attempt: the contractor's drive

start.text: Storage Control blocked a contractor's laptop writing 2 GB to a personal USB drive. The files are under the engineering share. The contractor says it was 'just a backup.' Your move.

choices.label: Treat it as a potential exfiltration: preserve the event evidence and assess before accepting the explanation
choices.feedback: Correct. 'Just a backup' to a personal drive of engineering files is exactly what exfiltration looks like. Evidence first, explanations second.

choices.label: Accept the explanation and approve a one-time USB exception so they can finish
choices.feedback: You just authorized the exfiltration you were supposed to stop. Go back.

choices.label: Confiscate the laptop immediately and call the police
choices.feedback: Way over the line for a first block event with no policy for escalation defined. Follow the runbook's proportionate steps. Go back.

assess-data.text: Evidence preserved. The 2 GB includes CAD drawings marked internal-only. The contractor's agreement: does it even permit personal-device copies?

choices.label: Check the contractor agreement and the storage policy; escalate to the supervisor and security lead with the data classification
choices.feedback: Correct. The agreement prohibits personal-device copies of internal-only files. This is now a policy violation with evidence, not a debate.

choices.label: Decide yourself that it's fine since they're a contractor
choices.feedback: Contractor status doesn't override data classification. Go back and check the actual policy.

interview.text: Escalated. The lead asks you to sit in on the contractor interview. What's your role?

choices.label: Present the facts (timestamps, file paths, policy) neutrally and let the lead run the conversation
choices.feedback: Correct. You bring evidence, not accusations. The facts speak; your job is accuracy.

choices.label: Open with 'we know you tried to steal our designs'
choices.feedback: Accusations before the interview turn a fact-finding into a confrontation and can taint the process. Go back.

followup.text: Interview done; the contractor claims misunderstanding. Regardless of intent, what changes going forward?

choices.label: Recommend tightening contractor storage policy (registered devices only, no personal media) and a review of what engineering shares contractors can reach
choices.feedback: Correct. The incident exposed over-broad contractor access — fixing the policy is the durable win, whatever the intent was.

choices.label: Close the ticket — the block worked, so the system is fine
choices.feedback: The block worked this time; the over-broad access that made the attempt possible is still there. Go back and fix the root cause.

branchingScenarios.resolution: Storage Control gave you the gift of a blocked event with full evidence — don't waste it. Preserve first, check policy and data classification, escalate proportionately, and in the interview bring facts, not accusations. The block is the beginning of the response, not the end.

branchingScenarios.title: C2 callback blocked: the quiet workstation

start.text: Network Control blocked an outbound connection from a marketing workstation to an IP with no domain, on a high port, at 3 AM. No user was logged in. The machine 'seems fine.' It isn't. Work it.

choices.label: Treat the blocked callback as an IOC: pull the process that initiated it and check the host's recent history
choices.feedback: Correct. A 3 AM callback to a bare IP with no user logged in is a textbook C2 pattern. The initiating process is your thread to pull.

choices.label: Unblock the IP 'to see what it wanted' — maybe it's a legit service
choices.feedback: You just re-opened a command-and-control channel to watch what happens. That is how you lose. Go back.

choices.label: Ignore it — the block worked, so there's no problem
choices.feedback: The block stopped the callback; it didn't remove the malware making it. Go back and hunt.

find-patient-zero.text: The initiating process is a scheduled task running a script from the user's temp folder, created two days ago. What's the blast radius?

choices.label: Check Network Control and Detect history for the same indicators (IP, script name, task name) across the fleet
choices.feedback: Correct. Two more workstations show the same blocked callback pattern. You have a small outbreak, not a single host.

choices.label: Clean just this one host and close out
choices.feedback: The other two hosts are still beaconing. Always check fleet-wide for the same IOCs. Go back.

choices.label: Isolate all three from the network, preserve the scheduled tasks and scripts as evidence, escalate to IR with the IOC package
choices.feedback: Correct. Isolate, preserve, escalate with IOCs (IP, script hash, task name) so IR can hunt further.

choices.label: Reimage all three immediately to 'get users back to work'
choices.feedback: Reimaging destroys the evidence IR needs and you haven't confirmed the infection vector — it'll come back. Go back.

close-vector.text: Contained and escalated. IR asks: how did it get in? The script dropped two days ago — what's the likely initial access?

choices.label: Check the users' email and download history around the drop time for a phishing lure or malicious download, and recommend blocking the delivery vector
choices.feedback: Correct. You find the phishing email with the malicious attachment from two days ago — now IR can block the sender domain and warn the org.

choices.label: Skip it — containment is done, initial access is IR's problem alone
choices.feedback: Containment without closing the entry vector means reinfection. The operator who found it helps kill the vector. Go back.

branchingScenarios.resolution: A blocked C2 callback is detection gold: it tells you the malware is present and phoning home. Pull the thread (initiating process), hunt the IOCs fleet-wide (one host is never the whole story), then isolate, preserve evidence, and escalate with an IOC package. Never unblock to 'see what happens' and never reimage before forensics.

branchingScenarios.title: The AI triage copilot hallucinates

start.text: Your AI triage copilot summarizes a Detect alert: 'Benign — Chrome updater performing routine maintenance.' But the blocked action was chrome.exe launching a script from the temp folder. The AI is confident. You shouldn't be. What now?

choices.label: Distrust the summary and read the raw alert yourself: parent, child, path, hash
choices.feedback: Correct. The raw alert shows the 'updater' is an unsigned binary in temp — nothing like a real Chrome updater. The AI hallucinated a benign story.

choices.label: Accept the AI summary — it's usually right and you're busy
choices.feedback: 'Usually right' is how a hallucinated benign verdict lets malware walk past you. The AI doesn't get a vote on verdicts. Go back.

choices.label: Immediately isolate the host based on your own read
choices.feedback: Your read says suspicious, but one analyst's read isn't a verdict either — run it through the evaluated decision layer first. Go back.

decide-layer.text: Your read contradicts the AI. The workflow says 'AI proposes, human disposes' with an evaluated decision layer. What does that mean here?

choices.label: Score the alert against the decision checklist (signed? known path? expected parent? prior baseline?) and make the human verdict
choices.feedback: Correct. Checklist: unsigned, temp path, abnormal parent chain, no baseline. Human verdict: suspicious — isolate and escalate.

choices.label: Ask the AI to reconsider and go with its second answer
choices.feedback: Asking the hallucinator to double-check itself is not a control. The human is the decision layer. Go back.

feedback-loop.text: Verdict made: suspicious, host isolated, escalated. The AI was wrong. What do you do about the copilot?

choices.label: Log the failure with the alert ID, the AI's claim, and the ground truth — feed the evaluation set so the copilot improves
choices.feedback: Correct. Every AI miss is training data for the evaluation loop. That's how 'AI-assisted' stays honest.

choices.label: Turn the copilot off forever — AI can't be trusted
choices.feedback: One failure doesn't invalidate the tool; it invalidates blind trust. The answer is evaluation and guardrails, not abandonment. Go back.

calibrate.text: Failure logged. Going forward, what's your personal rule for using the copilot on the next shift?

choices.label: Use summaries for triage ordering, but read the raw alert before any verdict — and spot-check one AI summary per shift against primary evidence
choices.feedback: Correct. That's a calibrated workflow: AI for speed, primary evidence for verdicts, spot-checks to keep the AI honest.

choices.label: Trust the copilot again once the vendor ships an update
choices.feedback: Vendor updates don't remove your verification duty. The guardrail is your workflow, not their release notes. Go back.

branchingScenarios.resolution: AI proposes, human disposes: never let a summary override the raw alert. When the AI hallucinates a benign story, read the primary evidence, run your own decision checklist, make the human verdict — then log the miss into the evaluation set. The guardrail isn't 'don't use AI'; it's 'verify every AI claim against primary evidence.'

branchingScenarios.title: Interview curveball: 'Tell me about a time you were wrong'

start.text: October 13, 9:00 AM, Orlando. The panel is going well. Then: 'Tell me about a time you were wrong about a security call — and what it cost.' The room goes quiet. Answer it.

choices.label: Give a real STAR story: the wrong call, what it cost, what you changed — specific and owned
choices.feedback: Correct. 'I approved an elevation I shouldn't have during a busy shift; it led to a policy review and now I verify out-of-band on any anomaly.' Honest, specific, growth-showing.

choices.label: Say 'I've never really made a wrong security call' and smile
choices.feedback: Nobody believes that, and now they doubt your self-awareness more than your skills. Go back and be real.

choices.label: Tell a story where you were secretly right all along
choices.feedback: The humblebrag dodge is transparent to interviewers. They asked for a failure — give them one. Go back.

follow-up.text: They nod. Follow-up: 'Our Cyber Heroes sometimes have to tell an angry customer their app stays blocked. How do you handle that?'

choices.label: Explain the why in plain language, offer the exception path, stay calm and documented — the customer deserves the reasoning, not just the no
choices.feedback: Correct. That's the support-triage mindset: firm on policy, human in delivery, always a documented path forward.

choices.label: Say you'd unblock it to keep the customer happy
choices.feedback: You just told a zero-trust company you'd bypass zero trust for politeness. Go back.

close-strong.text: Last minute. 'Any questions for us?' — your closer.

choices.label: Ask about the team's hardest triage call this month and what good looks like in the first 90 days
choices.feedback: Correct. It shows operator curiosity and a desire to meet their bar, not just get hired.

choices.label: 'No, I think you've covered everything!'
choices.feedback: You just left your strongest minute on the table. Always have questions. Go back.

debrief.text: You're out of the building. The interview is fresh — what do you capture right now?

choices.label: Write the debrief immediately: every question asked, your answers, what landed, what you'd sharpen, and the names and roles of each interviewer
choices.feedback: Correct. A same-day debrief is interview gold — it feeds your thank-you notes and your preparation for round two.

choices.label: Relax — you'll remember the important parts later
choices.feedback: You won't. Details decay in hours. Write it now while it's fresh. Go back.

branchingScenarios.resolution: Curveballs test self-awareness, not perfection: own a real mistake with its cost and your fix (STAR, 60-90 seconds), hold the policy line with angry customers while staying human, and close with questions that prove you think like an operator already on the team.

branchingScenarios.title: After the interview: the thank-you timing decision

start.text: The October 13 panel went well. You're in the car by 10:30 AM. The thank-you note: when, to whom, and saying what?

choices.label: Send individual thank-you emails this afternoon — one per interviewer, each referencing something specific they said
choices.feedback: Correct. Same-day, specific, individual. It shows attention and professionalism while the conversation is fresh.

choices.label: Wait a week so you don't seem desperate
choices.feedback: A week later the note is irrelevant — hiring decisions move in days. Same-day is professional, not desperate. Go back.

choices.label: Send one group email to everyone to save time
choices.feedback: A group blast signals low effort. Individual notes with specific references signal genuine engagement. Go back.

content.text: Writing the notes. What goes in them — and what stays out?

choices.label: Gratitude, one specific discussion point per person, a brief reaffirmation of fit — no salary talk, no begging, no new claims
choices.feedback: Correct. The note closes the loop on the conversation; it doesn't reopen negotiation.

choices.label: Add 'I'm confident I'm the best candidate and hope to hear about the offer soon'
choices.feedback: Presumptuous and it reframes gratitude as expectation. Keep it professional. Go back.

follow-through.text: Notes sent. Now the waiting. What's the disciplined follow-through?

choices.label: Log the debrief (questions asked, your answers, what you'd improve), follow their stated timeline, one polite check-in if it lapses
choices.feedback: Correct. Debrief while it's fresh, respect their timeline, one check-in max. Then keep preparing — momentum beats waiting.

choices.label: Email the recruiter daily for updates
choices.feedback: Daily check-ins read as anxiety, not enthusiasm. One polite follow-up after their timeline lapses. Go back.

round-two.text: A week later: the recruiter calls — they want a second round, deeper technical. How do you use everything you've captured?

choices.label: Re-read your debrief, drill the questions you fumbled, and prepare two new operator stories that show growth since round one
choices.feedback: Correct. Round two rewards the candidate who visibly leveled up between rounds — your debrief is the study guide.

choices.label: Wing it — you already passed round one, so you're fine
choices.feedback: Round two is harder, not a formality. Preparation compounds. Go back.

branchingScenarios.resolution: Post-interview discipline: individual thank-you notes the same afternoon, each with a specific reference to that interviewer's conversation; no salary talk, no presumption; then a written debrief, respect for their timeline, and at most one polite check-in. Professional persistence, not pressure.

clickSims.title: Create an allowlist policy for a line-of-business app

steps.screen: Portal dashboard; the Policies section is visible in the main navigation.
steps.instruction: Open the Policies section and start a new Application Control (allowlisting) policy.
steps.feedback: A blank new-policy form opens with policy type selection.

steps.screen: New-policy form; policy type options listed.
steps.instruction: Choose the Application Control / allowlisting policy type and name the policy after the app and site (e.g. 'LedgerPro - Accounting').
steps.feedback: The policy editor opens with empty rule sections.

steps.screen: Policy editor; application identity section empty.
steps.instruction: Define the application's identity: add the vendor's signed binary by its certificate and record the current file hash.
steps.feedback: The application identity is recorded with certificate + hash.

steps.screen: Policy editor; child-process / execution rules section.
steps.instruction: Set the child-process rule: decide whether the app may launch other processes, and scope it to the updater only — not a blanket permission.
steps.feedback: The child-process rule covers the updater explicitly.

steps.instruction: Target the policy to the Accounting computer group only — not the whole organization.

steps.screen: Policy editor; review pane summarizing the policy.
steps.instruction: Review the full policy: identity, child rules, targeting. Then save it in Monitor/Learning mode first, not Enforce.
steps.feedback: Policy saved in Monitor mode; the portal confirms it is staged.

steps.screen: Policy list; the new policy shows 'Monitor' status.
steps.instruction: Open the policy's activity view and confirm it is logging what it WOULD block without denying anything.
steps.feedback: Monitor-mode hits appear; no user impact.

steps.screen: Activity view after a 48-hour monitor window; clean results.
steps.instruction: After the monitor window with no unexpected blocks, switch the policy to Enforce and document the change with date and approver.
steps.feedback: Policy is enforced; the change is documented.

clickSims.title: Build a ringfence policy for the company browser

steps.instruction: Start a new Ringfencing policy and name it for the browser fleet (e.g. 'Ringfence - Chrome - All Workstations').
Target the browser application by its signed identity so the ringfence follows the real browser, not just a filename.
steps.feedback: The browser is targeted by identity.

steps.screen: Ringfence editor; restriction categories listed (execute, registry, file, network).
steps.instruction: Block the browser from executing other applications/processes — the classic weaponization path.

steps.screen: Restriction categories; registry and file sections.
steps.instruction: Restrict registry edits and limit file write access to the browser's own profile and download folders.
Leave normal web traffic allowed but review the network restriction options for unusual protocols the browser never needs.
steps.feedback: Network posture reviewed; unnecessary protocols denied.

steps.instruction: Target the workstation fleet, save in Monitor mode, and verify in the activity view that legitimate browsing is unaffected.
steps.feedback: Monitor-mode data confirms no legit breakage.

steps.screen: Activity view; one week of clean monitoring.
steps.instruction: Promote to Enforce and log the change. Note the test you ran: a scripted browser-launch of a helper app should now be denied.

clickSims.title: Create a just-in-time elevation policy for IT tools

steps.instruction: Start a new elevation policy for the IT support toolset.
Add the approved support tools by signed identity — remote support and disk utilities the helpdesk actually uses.
steps.feedback: Approved tools listed in the policy.

steps.instruction: Scope elevation to just these applications — not blanket local admin for the user.
Configure the request workflow: who approves, what justification is required, and the time-box for each grant.
steps.feedback: Request workflow configured with time-boxed grants.

steps.instruction: Confirm every elevation grant is logged with user, application, timestamp, and approver — the audit trail is the point of Elevation Control.
steps.feedback: Audit logging confirmed for all grants.

steps.instruction: Target the helpdesk group, save, and run a test: request elevation for an approved tool and confirm it works, then for an unapproved app and confirm it is denied.
steps.feedback: Approved tool elevates; unapproved app is denied. Policy verified.

clickSims.title: Write a USB storage rule for the finance group

steps.instruction: Start a new storage policy scoped to removable media for the Finance group.
Select USB mass-storage devices as the controlled class.
Set the default to deny for personal/unregistered drives; allow only company-registered encrypted drives by device ID.
Add path rules: block writes of the payroll and PII shares to any removable media regardless of device.
Target the Finance computer group and user group; save in Monitor mode first.
Review what would have been blocked, confirm no legitimate workflow breaks, then enforce and notify Finance of the new rule.

clickSims.title: Configure a dynamic ACL for a database server

steps.instruction: Start a new network policy for the database server role.
Target the DB-SERVERS computer group.
Allow the database port inbound only from the application-server group — not from the whole network.
Enable dynamic behavior: ports open only while the authorized application session is active, then close automatically.
steps.feedback: Dynamic ACL enabled on the rule.

steps.instruction: Deny unexpected egress (e.g. the DB server initiating outbound connections it never legitimately makes).
Save in Monitor mode, verify app connectivity is unaffected, then enforce during the maintenance window and document.

clickSims.title: Triage a Detect alert queue end to end

steps.screen: Detect alert queue; several new alerts listed with severity indicators.
steps.instruction: Sort the queue by severity and time; note the count of unacknowledged alerts.
Open the highest-severity alert and read it fully: process tree, blocked action, host, user, timestamp.
Pivot to related events on the same host in the last 24 hours — look for a pattern, not a single event.
steps.feedback: Host timeline shows the alert in context.

steps.instruction: Set the disposition: severity, verdict (malicious-likely / break-fix / benign), and the next step. Acknowledge the alert.
For the malicious-likely verdict, open the escalation: attach the alert ID, process tree summary, and your notes to the security lead.
Work the remaining alerts the same way; confirm the queue is empty and every alert has a disposition note.

clickSims.title: Push a centralized Defender policy and detect drift

steps.screen: Configuration Manager dashboard; Defender policy templates visible.
steps.instruction: Open the Microsoft Defender configuration section and select the standard workstation template.

steps.screen: Template settings: real-time protection, cloud protection, exclusions.
steps.instruction: Verify real-time protection and cloud-delivered protection are enabled; review the exclusion list and remove any stale entries.
Target the workstation fleet group and stage the policy.
Deploy and watch the status view until the fleet reports compliant.
Confirm the deployment is reflected in the compliance dashboard and record the policy version as the new baseline.
steps.feedback: Baseline recorded; dashboard reflects the push.

steps.instruction: Open the drift view: find any machine whose local Defender settings differ from the pushed policy and remediate from the console.

clickSims.title: Onboard a new computer to the portal

steps.screen: Computers section; the fleet list is visible.
steps.instruction: Open the Computers section and start the new-computer onboarding flow.
steps.feedback: The onboarding flow opens with install options.

steps.screen: Onboarding options: installer download and grouping.
steps.instruction: Download the agent installer for the correct OS and assign the machine to its site/group during onboarding.
Run the installer on the target machine with the grouping token/key provided by the portal.

steps.screen: Portal computers list; the new machine appears.
steps.instruction: Confirm the machine appears in the portal with a healthy agent status and correct group.

steps.screen: Policy assignment view for the new machine.
steps.instruction: Verify the correct policies applied to the new machine (allowlist, ringfence, elevation, storage, network baselines) and run a quick health check.

steps.screen: New machine desktop; policies confirmed applied.
steps.instruction: Run a safe verification test: attempt a known-blocked action (e.g. launching an unapproved test binary) and confirm it is denied and logged.
steps.feedback: Test action denied and logged - the machine is truly protected.

studyGuide.title: Study guide: how to work IL-29 in 12 weeks
studyGuide.note: totalHours/totalMinutes are filled by the assembler from module estimatedMinutes; the 0 values here are placeholders.
pacing: INTERVIEW FAST-TRACK (do first if Oct 13 is near): jump straight to IL29-M39 (technical drill), IL29-M40 (STAR bank), and IL29-M46 (interview-day game plan), then return to Week 1. The interview does not wait for the syllabus.

Weeks 1-2 — Platform core, IL29-M01 to M08 (~4 modules/week): zero-trust architecture, allowlisting, ringfencing, elevation, storage, network control, Detect, Configuration Manager. Labs in this phase are the job: do every one hands-on.

Weeks 3-4 — Operations, IL29-M09 to M16: portal administration, Cyber Hero support ops, break-fix runbooks, deployment planning, then MIT 6.858 concepts part 1 (threat models, control hijacking, privilege separation, sandboxing).
Weeks 5-6 — Deep technical, IL29-M17 to M24: MIT 6.858 part 2 (web security, network/TLS, side channels, authentication, privacy, security economics) plus ML for anomaly detection and LLM security.

Weeks 7-8 — AI + math, IL29-M25 to M32: AI supply chain, AI-assisted SOC workflows, adversarial ML, then the prereq math spine (discrete math, boolean/bitwise, number theory, probability, linear algebra). Do the math with pencil and paper, not just reading.

Weeks 9-10 — Certification readiness, IL29-M33 to M40: Security+, CySA+, CISSP, GSEC, Google/IBM crosswalk, MIT xPRO readiness, then the ThreatLocker panel technical drill and STAR bank. Take every cert gate in this window.

Weeks 11-12 — Field readiness, IL29-M41 to M48: IR lifecycle, forensics, ATT&CK mapping, security awareness, the live Cyber Hero triage shift, interview-day execution, and both capstones. Finish with the operator gate (gate-threatlocker-operator) twice in a row.
rules: Interview date beats syllabus order: if the panel is within 2 weeks, run the fast-track (M39, M40, M46) first.
Never skip the hands-on lab — the interview tests what you have done, not what you have read.
Drills to green before the next module; re-take any quiz below 80%.
Every break-fix gets a written disposition: cause, fix, and the process change that prevents recurrence.
Log every AI-assisted triage decision with the evidence you checked — the copilot never gets the final vote.
Score every cert gate twice in a row before booking any real exam.
Build the GSEC open-book index as you study; the index is the exam strategy.
Finish with the operator gate twice consecutively — that is your interview-day confidence bar.

timeFormula: estimatedMinutes per module = instruction + videos + drills + hands-on lab, set per module by the author; course total = sum of module estimates. Declared hours are the honest rounded sum.

glossary.definition: ThreatLocker's analyst role: triaging blocked actions with operator depth.
Nothing runs unless explicitly allowed — the platform's core.
Execution control by hash, publisher, or path.
Just-in-time admin rights with approval and audit.
Egress and network-access policy for endpoints.
The recorded allow/deny/ringfence/escalate decision on an event.
Diagnosing and resolving policy breakage through the exception workflow.
Defined attacker capabilities/goals preceding defense design (6.858).
Least-privilege component split limiting compromise blast radius.
Redirecting program execution (overflows, ROP); countered by ASLR/DEP/CFI.
Adversary tactics/techniques: the mapping language for 'why we blocked this.'
ML assistance proposing dispositions; the human verifies and decides.
Incident handling lifecycle: preparation → detection/analysis → containment/eradication/recovery → lessons.

faq.q: How is IL-29 different from IL-24?
faq.a: IL-24 is the assessment-prep CBT (pass the 120-minute test). IL-29 is the mastery bootcamp: operator depth, MIT 6.858 security reasoning, ML detectors, AI triage, cert mapping (Security+ → CySA+ → CISSP/GSEC), and panel interview prep. IL-24 is the door; IL-29 is the career.

faq.q: Do I need to know ThreatLocker's product before starting?
faq.a: No — the course builds from Zero Trust doctrine (IL-11 concepts) to platform operations. Company facts and product stack are taught as explicit objectives.

MIT's Computer Systems Security: threat models, control hijacking, privilege separation, sandboxing, web security, TLS — the reasoning layer under the operator skills. Independent study, no affiliation.

faq.q: How do I practice triage without the platform?
faq.a: The course's denied-event scenarios + process-tree exercises + the Cyber Hero loop drills. The pattern (read → classify → investigate → disposition) transfers to any default-deny platform.

faq.q: AI proposes, human disposes — what does that mean operationally?
faq.a: Copilots and detectors suggest; every disposition requires human-verified evidence. The course drills the verification habit because automation bias is the real risk.

faq.q: Which cert should I target after this course?
faq.a: Security+ SY0-701 for baseline, CySA+ CS0-003 for SOC depth, then GSEC/CISSP as experience allows. The certGates map each exam to modules with readiness thresholds.

tips: Follow the guided path in order — each module unlocks the next. The sequence is the curriculum; skipping ahead breaks the chain.
This course maps to CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 and CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 (independent preparation — no affiliation). Weight your drill time toward the heaviest exam domains shown in the cert gates.

The math modules (Discrete Math & Logic for Security, Boolean Algebra & Bitwise Operations for Operators, Number Theory & Modular Arithmetic for Crypto) are load-bearing — finish them before the applied modules that assume them.
Quiz-gated modules need 70%+ to unlock the next. When you miss a question, ask Noah to walk you through the miss Socratically before re-attempting.
Do each hands-on lab twice — once following the guide, once from a blank screen. The second pass is where the skill sticks.
This is a 431-hour course: at 10 focused hours a week it takes about 11 months. Short daily sessions beat weekend cramming — pace it like a semester.
